en: The Sub-commentary on the Commentary to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
An Explanation of the Text of the Preface In explaining this preface, the main text is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying the title; second, identifying the author; and third, interpreting the original text.

The title of the *Commentary on the Sub-commentary* (*Jingshu Chao*) at the beginning of the text is fully explained as follows: Regarding the term "Preface" (*xu*), it signifies "cause" (*you*) and "beginning" (*shi*).

It is called a "preface" because it sets forth the causes and conditions for the emergence of the teaching and the gradual origins of its composition. Furthermore, the *Preface* arises because of the *Sub-commentary*;

the *Sub-commentary* arises because of the *Commentary*; and the *Commentary* arises because of the Sūtra. These three layers follow one another in successive dependence. The Master of the Commentary, looking up to [the Sūtra],...
Because this work was composed in accordance with the sacred virtue [of the Great Master], a general preface is provided to precede the *Chao* (Excerpts); thus it is called a "Preface" (*xu*).
[The phrase] "Narrated by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Dahuayan Monastery":
"Qingliangshan Dahuayan Monastery" refers to the physical location upon which [the author] relies. Qing...
It is cool; auspicious clouds gather in the sky, and the lush forests rise majestically. Snow still falls in summer, and in winter, hard ice accumulates.
Since it has never known the heat of summer, it is called Mount Qingliang (the Cool Mountain). As for the mountain’s prominence: the earth rises in tiered ridges and many peaks stand together.
With Min and E reaching the Milky Way and steep ridges leaning against the heavens, it is rightly named a Great Mountain. As for the Great Huayan Monastery, it is a secluded hermitage.

The name of this monastery was also called Kairin-ji (Flower Garden Temple). In front of the temple there was a garden several *kō* in area, which was named Kairin because auspicious grasses would occasionally sprout and spread there in extraordinary ways;
thus it was called Kairin-ji. As for the term "shamon" (śramaṇa), it refers to one who is able to correctly exert and describe [the truth].
In Sanskrit it is fully called *śramaṇa*, which means "one who exerts effort. A sutra states: "It is called 'exertion' (*śrama*) because one exhausts [defilements]."

Because his mind reached the fundamental source, he was titled a *śramaṇa*. However, there are distinctions between the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), as well as between the path of manifestation and the path of purification, as described in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*.

The two characters following this were the title of the Master of the Commentary (*ṭīkā*). Throughout the Tang dynasty’s nine dynastic houses and seven emperors, he served as the gate-teacher (*dvāra-guru*);
the Emperor specifically bestowed upon him the title "Qingliang" (Cool and Pure), as detailed in the inscriptions and biographies that recount his life.
The Master of the Commentary humbly states that he does not compose [anything new], intending to say: "I merely expound the meanings of the ancients to produce this sub-commentary;

it is not a new creation. The Most Holy One bestowed his instructions, reflecting the profound ultimate of the one mind; the Great Being propagated and elucidated them, illuminating the mysteries of the subtle words.

[End of section]. Regarding the three main sections following "The Most Holy One" (Zhìshèng xià): first, the origin and transmission of the initial teaching; second, the beginning and end of the emergence of this commentary (*chāo*).

Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, a general clarification of all teachings; second, a specific indication of the present sutra. Furthermore, within the first of these, there are four sections: first, clarifying the Tathāgata...
First, explaining the sutra: (1) clarifying that the Bodhisattva composed the treatise; (2) granting and refuting to dispel obstacles; and (3) revealing the intent of the sutra.
Now, for the first part—clarifying that the Tathāgata preached the sutra: within these two sections, the Three Jewels, the Most Holy Ones, are fully manifested.

First is the Buddha, who bestows his instructions; second is the Dharma; and third is the Mahāsattvas, the Saṅgha. Because the Three Jewels are the most auspicious, my sutra begins by speaking of them.

"Ultimate" (*zhì*) means the limit; "sage" (*shèng*) means correctness. Because the Tathāgata is able to realize the dharma-realm to its furthest extent through correct wisdom, and there is nothing that surpasses him, he is named the "Supreme Sage" (*zhìshèng*).
Furthermore, "supreme" distinguishes him from those who are sages at the stage of cause, thereby distinguishing him from ordinary beings.
The *Jíxuánjì* states: "Sage" means birth. Observing the birth of things, one knows their beginning and end; his wisdom penetrates the Great Way and responds [to all things]."

Because his transformations are inexhaustible, he is named the Ultimate Sage (*paramārtha-ārya*). However, as the various teachings differ, they are briefly divided into five. First, the Hīnayāna teaching:

it posits the fivefold body (*pañcākāya-kāya*) as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the sixteen-foot body as the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the body that appears according to the species [of beings] as the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*);

thus it is named the Ultimate Sage. Second, within the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, there are two schools. First, within the School of Destroying Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhañjana-nikāya*), by means of...

In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), that which is free from all marks and is not comprised of the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases (*skandha-dhātv-āyatana*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

its manifestation according to the needs of beings is termed the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is the second position among the holy ones. In the school of those who establish characteristics (*lakṣaṇavāda*), the pure dharma-realm (*viśuddhadharmadhātu*) is taken as the Dharma-body, while the mental states associated with the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) and their manifestations are taken as the Enjoyment-body and the Emanation-body. This is the third position among the holy ones, representing the Final Teaching (*paryantayāna*).

Based on the *Awakening of Faith*, taking the "greatness of essence" as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the "greatness of characteristics" as the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the "greatness of function" as the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for others constitutes the fourth stage, the Ultimate Holy One.
Within the four sudden teachings, the undifferentiated three bodies—absolute, beyond words, and the nature of the single reality—constitute the fifth stage, the Ultimate Holy One.
The Perfect Teaching takes the inexhaustible clouds of bodies of the Dharma-realm as the true [Dharma-body].

The characteristics [of the Buddha] should be understood as mutually integrated, where the one and the many are without obstruction, and the ten bodies are perfected; thus, he is called the "Ultimate Sage" (zhìshèng).

If we were to discuss this according to its true nature, only a Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiào) is designated as the Ultimate Sage. As for the phrase "bestowing the edicts" (chuígào): "bestowing" (chuí) means to spread.
It refers to spreading forth the canonical edicts to proclaim the Dharma-transformation and benefit sentient beings; therefore, it is called "bestowing the edicts. Furthermore—

In the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents), there are chapters such as the "Great Announcement" (*Dagao*) and the "Announcement to Kang" (*Kangao*). It is said that what is addressed to superiors is called a "Gao" (Announcement), while what is issued to subordinates is called a "Hao" (Proclamation);

furthermore, it is stated that the words of the King are termed "Hao," yet these are not fixed rules. Now, it is said that the Tathāgata expounds the twelve divisions of the Tripitaka to benefit sentient beings;
therefore, he is said to have "bequeathed his Hao. Regarding the phrase "a mirror for the one mind," "mirror" is a metaphor. Mirror... [text ends]... is a metaphor.

The function of a clear mirror serves as a metaphor for the teachings that can express [the truth]; the image within the mirror serves as a metaphor for the profound ultimate of the one mind, which is the reality expressed by those teachings.
Qingliang said: "Using the sacred teachings as a bright mirror, one illuminates and sees one's own mind;
using one's own mind as a lamp of wisdom, one illuminates the profound purport of the sutras. This is precisely that meaning. Now, I shall provide a brief [explanation] based on the five teachings.

Clarifying "One Mind": First, in the teachings of the Hīnayāna, external objects are substantially real, and "one mind" is provisionally established because the various results experienced are produced by karma created by the mind.
Second, in the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, the *ālayavijñāna* of maturation is taken as "one mind" to negate the existence of external objects.
Third, in the Final Teaching, it is called "one" because the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is inherently endowed with all meritorious qualities.
The Four Sudden Teachings speak of the "One Mind" because they advocate for the cessation of all phenomena and the absence of any fixed locus;

the Five Perfect Teachings speak of the "One Mind" because they encompass all existence in its totality, wherein every phenomenon is mutually unimpeded. This is because the Tathāgata establishes teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings;

thus, while there are a thousand differences, their various paths lead to the same destination, and they are all of one principle. "Ultimate Mystery" (xuánjí) means profound and wondrous; it is even more mysterious than the mysterious.
"Profound" (*you*) means remote; "ultimate" (*ji*) means exhaustive. This refers to the fact that the ultimate principle is subtle, abstruse, deep, and far-reaching, difficult to fathom.
Thus, Laozi said: "Within the vast and dark void, all wonders reside. These are all realms of inconceivable wonder. Furthermore, Master Haihui said:
"The myriad phenomena of the forested world reach their ultimate in emptiness; the hundred rivers and many streams reach their ultimate in the sea."
Because it reaches the ultimate limit of all sages and saints up to the Buddha, and because it reaches the ultimate perfection of all teachings, it is called "Mysterious Ultimate" (xuánjí).

Regarding the term "Great Being" (dàshì): according to the *Pǐxiu Jì* (Record of Pen-shuo), one is called a Great Being because they resolve upon the Great Mind, believe in the Great Dharma, understand the Great Teachings, cultivate the Great Practices, and realize the Great Fruit. Furthermore, as for the "Great Being": [text continues].

"Virtuous" (*bhadra*) is a title of honor; it applies universally to both ordinary beings and sages. If we discuss those who have extensively propagated and elucidated [the teachings], it also includes the masters of other commentaries and sub-commentaries.

Therefore, whether in the Western Regions or the Eastern Land (China), those who composed treatises and exegeses on the sutras—be they Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages (*bhūmi*) or eminent worthies of their own times—all intended to transcend the various ranks and surpass the common intellects. Because they propagated the Way and benefited sentient beings, they were named "Great" (*mahā*).
Regarding the phrase "to propagate and expound" (*hong-chan*): "propagate" (*hong*) means great; "expound" (*chan*) means to open up.

Whether it be establishing sects and founding teachings, manifesting the correct and refuting the heterodox, loftily erecting the banner of the Dharma, or widely propagating the sacred transformation—all these constitute propagation and exposition.

"Candle" refers to a lamp or candle, which carries the sense of illumination and clarity; thus, the subsequent scripture says: "For example, a treasure in the darkness cannot be seen without a candle."
It can be seen that if the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, even those with wisdom cannot clearly comprehend it.
What was said above regarding the "mirror" refers to seeing [the truth] immediately upon illumination, like those of superior faculties who gain understanding directly from the sutras.

What is called the "candle" refers to seeing [the truth] while in darkness, like those of inferior faculties who must first encounter the commentaries and sub-commentaries before they can develop understanding. This is also as described in the *Awakening of Faith* concerning the four types of faculties.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that all three categories [of teachings] share this same intent. "Subtle words" (*weiyán*) refers to the subtle and wondrous Dharma;

thus they are called "subtle words. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states, "Stirring the river of eloquence to extol the subtle words," and as the preface to the *Xiaojing* says, "After the Master passed away, the subtle words ceased"—in both cases, the sacred teachings are designated as "subtle words. Regarding "profound significance" (*yōuzhì*), "profound" (*yōu*) means distant.
"Yězhì" (幽致) means "tendency" or "orientation. Because the principle of the aforementioned profound ultimate is obscure, remote, and deep, it is called "obscure tendency" (yōuzhì).
Although one has forgotten the realm of verbal explanations and essential meanings, one remains vast and expansive within the ocean of literary expressions and doctrines.

Although "forgetting the mind" (忘懷) is mentioned below, there are two parts: first, the concession that the Dharma is beyond words; second, the refutation that it does not obstruct verbal expression. Regarding the first:
although one concedes that it is wordless, a question may be raised: "The previous statement says that the principle is profound and ultimate, and the subtle words are obscure and hidden;
only by forgetting the mind and cutting off deliberation can one accord with it. Why then do you set forth such extensive discourse?"
Does this teaching intend to disturb people? Therefore, it is said "even though one forgets the mind within the realm of the expressed meaning.

To "forget the mind" means to forget emotions and sever discursive thought; this is called "forgetting the mind. "Expressed meaning" refers to the principle that is expressed. "Realm" refers to a domain;
it means that the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) which express [the truth] possess the sense of inclusion. Since one now transcends all of these, it is stated thus.
▲ Furthermore, "vast and expansive" (hàohàn) refers to descending to seize upon the ineffable without obstructing speech.

This means that because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess great wisdom, they accord with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) above; and because they possess great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they descend to bestow verbal teachings below.

"Vast and expansive" describes the appearance of a great body of water. The Preface to the Commentary states: "Profoundly deep, one forgets words, yet the waves and ripples of the ocean of teaching are vast and expansive. This means:
Because the text of this great sūtra is vast and its principles profound, it is likened to the ocean.
This is intended to employ the traces of the "elephant" metaphor to exhaustively explore the inexhaustible meaning.

Regarding the four points below, they demonstrate the intent of the sūtra; first, examples are cited to establish the teaching, and subsequently, one awakens to and enters [the truth] through these words.
Now, first, the examples cited to establish the teaching: "Gai" (蓋) refers to the introductory phrase that follows what precedes and initiates what comes after;
"yu" (欲) means "about to"; "ji" (寄) means "to entrust"; and "xiang-xi" (象繫): "xiang" (象) refers to the hexagram images (*xiang*), while "xi" (繫) refers to the appended explanations (*xi-ci*).

These are the texts of the Ten Wings of the *Zhou Yi*, specifically: (1) the *Shang Tuan* (Upper Judgment), (2) the *Xia Tuan* (Lower Judgment), (3) the *Shang Xiang* (Upper Image), (4) the *Xia Xiang* (Lower Image), and (5) the *Shang Xi* (Upper Appendix).

The five sections on "Lower Ties" (*xiàxì*), the six sections on "Words" (*wén*), the seven sections on "Explaining the Hexagrams" (*shuōguǎ*), the eight sections on "Sequencing the Hexagrams" (*xùguǎ*), and the nine sections on "Miscellaneous Hexagrams" (*záguǎ*)—the disciples of the Zheng school all agree on this view that these were all composed by Confucius to praise and clarify the Way of the *Yī*, and to bring forth its ultimate meaning up to the hexagram *Yí*.
This is like the intent of a Bodhisattva composing treatises to explain the sūtras; as for "traces" (*jì*), it is like seeking a rabbit by first following its tracks.

"Having caught the rabbit, one forgets the tracks; having caught the elephant, one forgets the words. This means that by relying upon the traces of words and images, one accords with the principle that transcends words.

As the subsequent scripture states: "To thoroughly understand that phenomena do not reside in words, one skillfully enters the realm of wordlessness while being able to manifest verbal teachings like echoes throughout the world"—this is precisely its meaning. [The section] "Exhausting the Infinite" concludes the preceding part on "Relying on Words."
"Awakening into the ultimate" means reaching the limit. The *I Ching* says: "Exhausting principle and exhausting nature, one reaches destiny.
This "limitless intent" refers to the principle of the supreme mystery of the aforementioned single mind; it means employing provisional words and images to accord with that which is wordless.
It is not that there is a wordless state to which one can resort as a dwelling. As the subsequent scripture states: "Although one does not rely on the path of language..."
Furthermore, one does not cling even to the absence of speech; thus, we know that the nature of words is detached from them.
Although one speaks all day long, there is no speaking—how could one possibly maintain silence by binding one's tongue?
The principles and patterns of this sutra are such that they cannot be grasped or expressed in words.

This section of the sutra specifically elucidates the present scripture to extend its underlying intent; it is divided into two parts: first, the designation and indication, and second, the praise of its excellence. Regarding the first:
this great sutra is vast and extensive in its wording, beyond the scope of the ordinary mind to fathom. Within the realm of words and symbols, three versions are briefly indicated.
As for the upper version, the sutra contains as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousandfold world systems.

Among the chapters numbering as many as the atoms within the four continents, the original version of this sutra contained four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters; the abbreviated version contained one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters.
The version currently transmitted consists of forty-five thousand verses. How much more so, then, regarding even a single word of this Dharma?
The gates of this scripture are written with the ink of the ocean and cannot be exhausted. "Principle" (li) refers to that which is elucidated by the meaning;
it spans horizontally across the Three Piṭakas and penetrates vertically through the Ten Schools. Through the six aspects and ten mysteries, its wondrous functions unfold in infinite layers.

This ocean-seal body of the teaching is so brilliantly manifested that even Bodhisattvas remain bewildered and Śrāvakas cannot fathom it. Is it not because the literary patterns and principles of this sutra are beyond the reach of thought?
This is the deliberation. That which "cannot be adequately extolled" is a later expression of admiration for his excellence.
Regarding the Jin translation, the Master Youbi (Xianshou) largely attained its essential gateway.

Following the Jin translation, the *Chao* (Excerpts) was compiled; regarding its origins and development, first he composed commentaries based on the sutras, and subsequently requested the collection of the *Chao* text.

The initial section is divided into three parts: first, the Eastern Jin translation which first reveals [the meaning]; second, the Tang translation which later elucidates it; and third, the commentary composed for wide dissemination. Within the first part, there are two sections:
first, the profound and subtle intent; second, how Xianshou attained this intent. Regarding the first, the profound and subtle intent:

the "Eastern Jin Translation" refers to the translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra in the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty. This constitutes the sixth [section].
The "Biographies of the Translators" for the ten-fascicle sutra: "Translating" (yìfān) refers to rendering the Sanskrit (*bānyǎn*) into Chinese;

"profound" (*yōu*) means hidden, and "secret" (*mì*) means esoteric. Because the texts of the Jin dynasty were frequently obscure and abstruse, making it difficult to attain realization, they are described as "profound and secret.
[From] *Xuánshǒu* [below]: Later, Xuánshǒu attained the essential meaning; the *Zuǎnlíngjì* states that the monk Fǎzàng, whose courtesy name was Xuánshǒu, penetrated...
Having awakened to the True Principle and profoundly fathomed the Dharma-realm, he composed the *Tanxuan ji* (Record of Exploring the Profound) as an exegesis of the Jin translation.
Although there were many commentaries by ancient masters, only Master Xianshou alone captured its subtle essence; thus it is said that he "largely gained entry to its gate."
▲ Regarding the "Divine Chapters Translated in the Tang" (*Tángfān língpiān*): subsequent sages have not yet fathomed their profundity.

The section "Translated in the Tang" (repeated) refers to the second part, which first clarifies that the new scriptures were not transmitted [during the initial period], and subsequently establishes the correct doctrine to dispel delusions; this is the first [sub-section].

As for the "Divine Chapters Translated in the Tang," at the time of the formal translation, it coincided with Empress Wu’s establishment of the "Correct" era, when she changed the dynastic name from "Tang" to...
During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong of the Zhou dynasty, the title was restored to its former name, "Da Tang. The term "Tang" used here refers to this restoration of the title.

As for the term "lingpian" (spiritual chapters), it refers to these wondrous and sublime compositions which abound with spiritual inspiration; hence they are called "lingpian. Regarding the phrase "later sages...
established the definitive school": "zhe" (sage) means wisdom, referring specifically to Master Jingfayuan who composed and carved [this work].
The *Dingji* (Decisive Record) in twenty fascicles was composed to explain the Chinese translations of the scriptures. For those who have not yet "gazed" upon them, it provides a gaze;

for those who have not yet seen them, it provides sight. Because the established commentaries on the meanings frequently lose the essential purport of the scriptures, one has not been able to perceive the profound mysteries within them.
As the *Lunyu* says: "Shusun Wushu spoke to the great officers in the court, saying, 'Zigong is more worthy than [the Master].'"
Zhongni (Confucius) and Zifu Jingbo informed Zigong of this. Zigong said, "It is like the walls of a palace: my wall, O Ceng, reaches only to one's shoulders;
looking over it, one can see the beauty of the rooms and the family within. But the Master’s wall is several *ren* high;
unless one finds the gate and enters, one will not see the beauty of the rooms or the abundance of his myriad officials. Those who find the gate are few indeed."
Now, borrowing his text as an analogy for the Huayan hall—profound and abstruse yet not yet definitively resolved—it is said that its "mysterious depths have not been glimpsed.
Thus, Qingliang sighed: "How great! This new scripture lacks a commentary that captures its true intent;
how can it serve as a guide? This was the intention behind his undertaking this composition.
▲ Without presuming upon my own shallow understanding, I shall briefly elucidate the profound mysteries.

"Without presuming upon my own shallow understanding" refers to the three subsequent memoranda below; they are broadcasted in two parts: first, the expression of humility in the preface to the latter memoranda, and second, the remote circulation [of the teachings].
Now, first is the expression of humility in the preface. "Kui" (揆) means to measure; "fu" (膚) means skin; thus, it refers to the reception at the level of the skin.

Therefore, it is said that [the learning] is superficial (*fū*). The *Lunyu* states: "There are complaints of a superficial nature. Ma Rong commented: "Superficial" refers to external words; what is received is not internal reality. The *Dongjing fu* says:
"Those of superficial learning receive [knowledge] superficially, valuing what they hear while disparaging what they see. Ji [Zizhen] explained: "What is received is thin and shallow;
one values the ears and disparages the eyes. The intended meaning is: "I do not presume myself to be anything more than superficial."
As for this study, one should immediately provide an explanation; this is to take charge of the scripture oneself.

"Suddenly overflowing throughout the nine provinces and flying afar across the four seas"—the phrase "suddenly overflowing throughout the nine provinces" refers to the distant and widespread circulation. "Suddenly" (*ou*) means meeting without prior expectation; "overflowing" (*yi*) means filling to capacity.
Regarding the meaning of the "Nine Provinces" (*jiuzhou*), the *Tongdian* states: "Yong, Jing, Qing, Yu, Ji, You, Yuan, Yang, and Xu constitute the Nine Provinces.

Regarding "far-flying" (*xiawei*): "far" (*xia*) means distant; "flying" (*fei*) means soaring. Regarding the "Four Seas" (*saihǎi*): the Eastern Yi, Western Rong, Southern Man, and Northern Di constitute the Four Seas.
The Sub-commentary (*shu*) author, speaking with humility, says: "The commentary I have composed is sufficient for my own private record."
I did not dare hope that my instructions for the ignorant would spread far and wide, yet suddenly they have overflowed throughout the Nine Provinces and resounded far and wide within the Four Seas.
Observing his dream of the devouring image and the auspicious sign of the flying dragon,
it is truly because he was in profound accord with the Buddha-mind that this came to pass.

▲ Over a hundred lecturers all prostrated themselves before me, saying: "The essence of the Great Teaching is profound and the commentary is far-reaching; having personally received your instructions, we have gained a semblance of its core principles.

After the lectures conclude, we request that you compile the *Jiyao* (Essential Extracts). First, so that the novice disciples may seek instruction; second, in the hope that this may be further propagated for those at a distance."

Third, the Dharma Masters who received [the transmission]; fourth, the format of their compositions. Regarding the first of these four sections: first, identifying the assembly; second, stating the words;

third, establishing the determination; and fourth, expressing humility and acceptance. First, regarding the identification of the assembly: "Lecturer" (*jiangzhe*) means one who explains or discusses.
One who explains the meaning of the text and debates the correctness or error of doctrines while instructing disciples is called a lecturer; alternatively, it refers to an eminent figure of the age.

"Or perhaps, when those who have studied and practiced [this] number a hundred and simultaneously submit their request—'Xian' (賢) means 'worthy'; 'or' (或) indicates an alternative; 'then' (則) introduces the consequence; 'those who have studied and practiced' (聽習之者) refers to the students;

'filling a hundred' (盈滿百人) denotes the number; 'simultaneously' (同時) means at one time; 'submit a request' (伸請) means to petition. 'Xian' (咸) means 'all'; 'kou' (叩) means 'to strike'; 'yu' (余) means 'I'.
The meaning is that the hundred lecturers all come to my place to strike and urge me on, requesting that I compose this commentary. [Section three begins with "The Great Teaching" (大教).]
Examining this, it is established that this is not an ordinary scripture, but rather the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majestic virtue;

thus it is called a "Great Teaching" (*mahāśāsana*). "Principle" (*qù*) refers to its purport and its profundity. Since the sūtra being explained is vast and deep, the commentary (*śāstra*) that explains it is likewise profound and far-reaching.
"Personally received" and the following four phrases are expressions of humility regarding the transmission he received while listening and studying at that time.
Those who transmit this orally and impart it through the mind awaken to the True Principle (*zhēnzōng*). "Fǎngfèi" (resembling) carries the meaning of being similar;
the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*) states: "Although it is a semblance and but dregs, it has not yet fully exhausted the profound and mysterious meaning.

This implies that we do not dare claim to have thoroughly clarified the subtle nuances, but rather that we have personally received instructions regarding a semblance that approximates the fundamental principle.
▲ To serve as an exemplar for a thousand ages, I fear my delusions may hinder lofty awakening; I pray you will grant me a profound analysis so that I may behold its radiance.
Regarding the two points below "to serve as an exemplar": first, the hope for distant and repeated proclamation; second, the initial expression of compassion for future generations.

As for the first, "exemplar" (*chui fan*) means to spread; "exemplar" (*fan*) refers to a model or standard. That which is transmitted through a thousand mouths is called "antiquity" (*qian gu*). "A thousand ages" (*qian gu*) refers to...
This is indeed the provision for the ferrying of ten thousand generations. "Liu" (慮) refers to deliberation; "huo" (惑) refers to doubt.
It is feared that future generations might harbor doubts regarding the realization of these lofty and distant principles. [The author] hopes you will deign to grant a second formal request:

he entreats you to compose a further commentary (*chao*) to dissect the meanings of the *shu* (sub-commentary), so that they may be rendered brilliantly clear. Thus it is said, "May I behold its radiance."

▲ Following this refined intention, I have once again annotated and corrected this work, titling it *Sui shu yan yi* (Explication of the Meaning According to the Commentary). An ancient said, "When a person is present, it is easy;

when a person has passed away, it is difficult. I have now composed this exposition in the hope that those in distant lands throughout eternity may all feel as though they are meeting [the Master] face-to-face.
Following these three lower [categories], the Dharma Masters receive and uphold them. First, the intention for composing the *Śāstra* (Commentary) is clarified;

next, ancient exegeses are cited to establish it; finally, the specific intent of composing the *Śāstra* is presented. Regarding the first point, clarifying the intent for composing the *Śāstra*: "Ya" means correct. "Huai" refers to the inner disposition.
Following this correct disposition, one again gives rise to the thought of benefiting sentient beings. This is further said so that the principles and meanings may be systematically organized.
The inexhaustible Dharma-gate is as if before one's eyes. The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states: "It is like a net on its main rope; there are its strands, and they are not disordered.

The commentary notes: "It is like a net on its main rope; there are its strands, and they are not in chaos. Therefore, it is named *Suishu Yanyi Chao* (Commentary on the Meaning Evolved According to the Sub-commentary).

Regarding the phrase "Ancient Persons" (*Xiren*) below, this cites ancient exegeses to establish the *Zuanyuan* (Compendium of Mysteries) and other works, describing Yangzi’s book as being like the construction of a ship.
Regarding this matter, as I have not yet seen the original text, I do not dare to rely upon it. Now, following the *Fayan Wenzhen* (Questions on the Difficulties of the Classics) by Yangzi, it says:

may all who behold these notes feel as though they are facing me in person— this is what is meant by the Sub-commentary Master’s Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body.

▲ Yet, if the text is too elaborate, one grows weary of its chapters and sentences; if it is too concise, one remains ignorant of its sources and lineages. Considering this difficulty of talent, I feel some shame regarding my attempt at a balanced synthesis;
may future students find that my words are free from needless proliferation.

However, as for the elaborateness, the following four points describe the structure of the composition: first, the formal exposition; second, the expression of humility; and third, the presentation of the underlying principle. Regarding the first, the formal exposition:
to avoid the two faults of prolixity and brevity, the *Sūtra* commentary states, "If even literary elegance obscures the principle, how much more so will verbose language disturb the mind?
Thus, one knows that what has been composed is not easily [understood]. ▲ Next, the expression of humility.
From the "Tàibó" chapter of the *Lúnyǔ*, where Confucius says: "Is it not indeed so that talent is difficult to find?
During the era of the dynasties of Táng and Yú, there was a flourishing abundance; yet among them, there were only nine men, including one woman. The commentary notes: "Talent is difficult to obtain.
Even during the golden age of the Táng and Yú dynasties, among those who could fill ten positions, there was only one woman—thus there were only nine men. This is why...
Because a talent capable of making such a synthesis is difficult to find, the Master of the Commentary (Suzhu) humbly stated:
"I lack the talent for synthesis; to have ventured to compose this commentary is truly a source of shame.

His underlying intention was that, by departing from the two faults of being either overly prolix or too concise, he hoped that students would find his words free from unnecessary verbiage. The preface to the *Shu-chao* concludes.

▲ That which is without limit in its coming and going, whose movement and stillness share a single source, which contains all wonders with abundance, and which transcends words and thought to stand apart—can this be anything other than the Dharma-realm?
The section beginning with "Coming and going" is divided into ten sub-sections to accord with its inexhaustibility; the first [sub-section] sets forth the essence and substance of the school.

1. A specific praise of the expressive words; 2. The inconceivability of the Master who teaches; 3. The universality of the method of exposition; 4. How the words encompass both the fundamental and the derivative;
5. The profound and subtle nature of the ultimate intent; 6. The immense benefit that transcends the gradual; 7. A concluding praise of its vastness and distance; 8. The joy of encountering it; 9.
A brief explanation of the title. Now, for the first [section]: "The coming and going are boundless... is it not simply the Dharma-realm?"
The text consists of five phrases, whose meaning is manifold; for brevity, it may be summarized into four intentions: first, an explanation based on the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*);
second, an explanation based on the fundamental and the derivative; third, clarifying the categories of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); and fourth, generally manifesting the underlying intent.

Regarding the first, the explanation based on the three greatnesses, the intention is to clarify that the dharma-realm is endowed with the three greatnesses. The first phrase clarifies function (*vṛtti*), the second phrase clarifies essence (*svabhāva*), and the next...
The first phrase clarifies the characteristics; the second phrase harmonizes and sweeps away the secondary; the final phrase concludes by assigning it to the present.

Regarding the first [phrase], "using the Great" refers to going and returning without limit. "Going" means departing, arising, and moving. "Returning" means coming, ceasing, and being still. There are two aspects to "without limit":
first, in terms of vastness and multiplicity, there are no boundaries or limits—this pertains to phenomenal function; second, in terms of transcendence... [text ends].
Regarding the "extreme limit" (*koṭi*), based on the fact that phenomena themselves are identical to the Truth, there are briefly three meanings for their coming and going:
first, explaining by way of both delusion and awakening; second, explaining solely by way of the delusory; and third, explaining the returning to the root and source. Now, for the first:
delusion regarding the *dharmadhātu* is "going," which means departing or moving toward the six destinies; awakening to the *dharmadhātu* is "returning," which means coming back to the one mind.
Quiescence is entirely the functioning of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). When deluded, the false arises; when awakened, the false ceases. However, there are two meanings of "true" (*satya*):
first, regarding its conformity with conditions—when deluded, the true follows along with the false, such that the true ceases and the false arises;

when awakened, the false ceases and returns to the true, such that the true arises and the false ceases. Second, regarding its unchanging nature—delusion and awakening, arising and ceasing, coming and going, are all in a state of flux.
However, the true realm is as tranquil as empty space, its essence being without birth or extinction. This meaning is explained below within the section on "essence.
Regarding the term "limitless" (*ananta*): because delusion has no beginning, there is no initial limit; because awakening transcends beginning and end, the limit is itself limitless.

These two points are both spoken of solely in relation to the false. Furthermore, there are two further meanings: first, discussing them vertically in terms of past and future, the past is beginningless and so forth.
Regarding "coming without end and no beginning," there are two aspects explained horizontally: first, deluded thoughts and their攀緣 (pān-yuán, objectifications) are vast and boundless;

second, both of these are explained as being immeasurable and limitless. If one considers them in terms of the ultimate limit—where delusion is non-existent and has no source—there is no temporal beginning vertically.
Since there is no commencement, how could there be an end? Thus, it transcends the limits of beginning and end. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Great Sage..."
That which is taught is that the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) cannot be found; birth and death have neither beginning nor end.
If there is neither beginning nor end, how could there be a middle? Therefore, within this, there is neither priority, posteriority, nor simultaneity.
Seeking it crosswise, the deluded mind is found neither within nor without; thus, there is no limit. For this reason, Master Huiyuan spoke of the "original root" (*mūlāgra*).

In the end, from where do arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence, and the limits of the infinitesimal arise? A single hair’s breadth of involvement with the realm of movement creates this mountainous momentum of delusive appearances, which further perpetuate one another.

When touching upon the principle, obstructions arise spontaneously; although causes and conditions are without birth, the opening of the path is not of a single lifetime—this is precisely its meaning.
Third, explaining by way of returning to the root and source, this corresponds to the first meaning; the first meaning is the general overview.
The second point concerns delusion as going only and not coming back; here, it is because one returns once more to the original source that this constitutes the meaning of "stillness.
Thus, the hexagram *Fù* (Return) says: "In its return, do we not see the heart of Heaven and Earth? Since that which has gone must necessarily return, the hexagram *Tài* (Prosperity) says:
"There is no going without a return; this is the juncture of Heaven and Earth. Yet, within this single principle, there is inherently both going and returning.
Furthermore, in the *Acintyabuddhaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* spoken by Mañjuśrī, the Subhavyūha Devaputra asks Mañjuśrī:
"What is called the cultivation of the bodhisattva path? Mañjuśrī first speaks of the practice of the two-fold path (*ubhayacara*), and next says:
"Furthermore, Devaputra, that which has going and returning is called the cultivation of the bodhisattva path. What is this called?
To go forth and return is to observe the inclinations and desires of sentient beings—this is called "going";
to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate for them—this is called "returning.
To enter samādhi oneself is called "going," and to cause all sentient beings to attain samādhi is called "returning. To practice the noble path oneself is called "going."
To be able to teach and transform all ordinary beings is called "returning"; to have personally attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) is called "going";
to cause all sentient beings to attain this patience is called "returning";
to personally emerge from birth and death through skillful means is called "going"; and to cause sentient beings to likewise achieve liberation is called "returning."
Delighting the mind in tranquility is called "going"; constantly remaining within birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings is called "returning.
Diligently observing the practice of going and returning is called "going"; preaching such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings is called "returning.
Cultivating the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is called "going."
Causing sentient beings to sever the three types of discursive thought and mental examination, he preaches the Dharma for them;
this is called "re-establishing. Making vows and proceeding in accordance with those vows to rescue and deliver sentient beings is called "further generating the bodhicitta vow.
Taking one's seat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is called "proceeding to fully cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva."
This practice is named "returning" (*pratigamana*); this is called the Bodhisattva’s path of going and returning. The commentary states:

Of the ten pairs mentioned above, in every case the first phrase refers to "going," because one goes toward *nirvāṇa* for the sake of self-benefit; the second phrase refers to "returning," because one returns to *saṃsāra* to transform sentient beings for the sake of benefiting others.
Although there is going and returning, it is collectively termed "returning to the root and source" and "restoring the original nature."
Regarding "The mind is thus: herein there is no limit," there are two meanings: first, the ocean of the Bodhisattva’s practice is vast and limitless;
second, each [practice] accords with reality and is profoundly limitless. However, these three aforementioned meanings are all the functioning of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Second, "Movement and stillness share a single source" refers to the essence of the Dharma-realm. In contrast to the three aforementioned meanings, this is discussed from the perspective of delusion and enlightenment as movement.
"Going" is movement; "returning" is stillness. Although there are two gates—stillness and movement, delusion and awakening—the true nature that is deluded is a single source, not two.
This non-dual source is precisely the one essence. As for the duality of opposites being merely delusion:
movement involves going and returning, with coming and going; stillness is the essence of emptiness, tranquil in its mutual dependence. Thus, stillness does not exclude movement.
To seek stillness, one must necessarily seek it within all movement; because one seeks stillness within all movement, although there is movement, there is constant stillness.
Thus, while the names "movement" and "stillness" differ, their source is not two. This non-dual source is the single essence.

Regarding the three pairs, returning to the root and restoring the source refers to stillness for self-benefit and movement for the benefit of others; these two benefits guide one another in transformation.
Yet, because there is no transformation, one does not lose the single source, which constitutes the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

If contrasted with the two preceding types, "limitless" refers to the vast and manifold, while "limitless" also refers to movement; "limit" (*ji*) is the limitlessness of stillness. The non-obstruction of movement and stillness constitutes the single source.
Both "limit" and "limitlessness" are quiescent in their very substance. ▲ Third, "containing all wonders yet having a surplus":
The characteristic of the Dharma-realm is "greatness," meaning that within the profound and mysterious, all manner of wondrous qualities exist.
The pure Dharma-realm, in its vast and profound mystery, acts as the container; the subtle and wondrous characteristic of greatness acts as the contained.

This characteristic depends upon the nature (*dhātu*); since the nature encompasses everything without exception, it is called "containing. While the substance of the nature has no exterior, the characteristics and virtues do exist.
Because the enumeration of "existence" cannot encompass the substance that lies beyond existence, it is said to be "surplus";
thus, it is vast and expansive, like ground with room to spare. As stated in the following *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*:
"Within a single minute pore, unspeakably many lands enter in succession; the pore can contain all those lands, yet those lands cannot encompass [the pore]."
The "pore" (*romakūpa*) signifies this very meaning. This is because the "hair" refers to the nature (*dharmatā*) and the "land" (*kṣetra*) refers to the indestructible aspect;

thus, the expansive aspect cannot pervade the small nature. Furthermore, these aspects generally possess two meanings: first, regarding the non-empty, infinite qualities of nature, which corresponds to the intent of the *Tongjiao* (Teaching of the Same);
second, regarding the phenomena of the ten mysteries of the mutual non-obstruction of things and things (*shishi wuai*), which are inherently [present].

"Being fully endowed" (*ju-tsuk*) is precisely the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*bie-chiao*). Furthermore, the two characters "multitude" (*chung*) and "subtlety" (*miao*) also reflect the intent of Laozi;
as his *Daodejing* says: "The Way that can be spoken of is not the eternal Way; the name that can be named is not the eternal name.

Namelessness is the beginning of heaven and earth; having names is the mother of the myriad things. One should constantly be without desire in order to contemplate its subtlety, and constantly have desire in order to... [contemplate its manifestation].
"Observing their boundaries—these two emerge from the same source but have different names; they are both called the Mysterious (xuan).
The Mystery upon Mystery is the gate of all subtleties. The commentary states: Thus, his intention is to take "Non-being" (xu) and "Spontaneity" (ziran) as the Mysterious and Subtle;
yet, he further brushes away even those traces, hence saying "Mystery upon Mystery. This is the state of having no desire for non-desire, from which all things arise.
Therefore, it is said that [the Dharma-gate] is "the gate of all wonders. Here, we borrow these words but do not adopt their original meaning;

rather, we take the single true Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*) as the wondrous and subtle essence, and its manifestations as the "all wonders. ▲ Fourth, "transcending speech and thought and emerging far beyond" means to harmonize and sublate the preceding three.
"Harmonizing" means that the three and the one mutually encompass one another; "sublating" means that the three and the one...
How do the two forms of quiescence transcend [the mundane]? It is because when principle is perfect, words are partial; when words express principle, the principle is lost.
Since phenomena have no marks, conceptualization and thought give rise to disorder. Therefore, one transcends them all, which is why it is said to be "far removed.

Master Zhao said: "When the mouth wishes to debate, words fail; when the mind intends to engage with objects, deliberation ceases. Thus, it is far removed from the realm of words and images. Why is this so?
If one wishes to speak of its characteristics and functions, they are identical to its essence and quiescence; yet if one calls it quiescent, its characteristics and functions are in full disarray.
Thus, it is one while the three characteristics are not the same, and it is the three bodies while being one essence—neither two nor three.

Being unimpeded, mutually negating, and doubly absent, existence and extinction are both unrestrained; how could words or images ever reach it? Therefore, it is said to be "transcendent," and by borrowing this term "absence" (亡), [it is described].
The ultimate is used to dispel verbal thought because there is no "non-utterance" that can serve as a place of refuge; thus, the subsequent scripture states:

"Although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to non-discourse. How much more so when the characteristics of speech are fundamentally quiescent and extinguished, and even this extinction itself is extinguished?
Since both speech and the absence of speech are mutually dependent and thus quiescent, it is for this reason that the term "far-reaching transcendence" is employed.
This sweeps away the traces of words. "The fifth is surely the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu)? concludes that the locus of these dharmas belongs to the Dharma-realm;
it means that the aforementioned virtues are fully present, existing uniquely within the Dharma-realm. Second, the explanation by way of the fundamental and the derivative:
of these five preceding phrases, the first phrase shows how the derivative arises from the fundamental—that is, establishing [phenomena] without moving from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

Regarding the clarification of the categories of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there are briefly three points of intent: First, the convergence of the three Dharma-realms: the first phrase is the Dharma-realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*);
the second phrase is the Dharma-realm of principle (*li-dharmadhātu*); the third phrase is the unobstructed Dharma-realm (*wu-ai-zhang fa-jie*);
the fourth phrase integrates and sweeps away the preceding three; and the fifth phrase concludes by attributing [the result] to the aforementioned three Dharma-realms.
Second, it is the matter of the four dharma-realms meeting in an infinite cycle of coming and going. ▲ Motion and stillness share a single source, possessing three meanings:
motion is phenomena, while stillness is principle; the single source of principle and phenomena is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.
▲ Containing all wonders with abundance is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. ▲ Transcending...
When speech and thought transcend and dissolve away from the four dharma-realms, is it not solely the Dharma-realm? Yet this too is subsumed within the four dharma-realms.
Third, the convergence of the five dharma-realms—whether in their coming and going or their movement—is entirely conditioned.

▲ Stillness is non-action. ▲ If the single source has two aspects such that they mutually negate one another and both vanish, then as a single source it is neither a dharma of action nor a dharma of non-action;
this is the Dharma-realm. ▲ If they mutually integrate and are both illuminated simultaneously as a single source, then it is both a dharma of action and a dharma of non-action;
this is the Dharma-realm. ▲ Containing all wonders with abundance, it is the unobstructed Dharma.
The Realm (Dhātu). ▲ Transcending speech and thought, it stands far beyond and universally fuses the five dharma-realms.
▲ Is it not solely the Dharma-realm? This concludes the attribution to the five dharma-realms. ▲ Fourth, regarding the general clarification of the intended meaning:

as for why the Dharma-realm is described first, there should be a question: "In the commentaries and treatises of various schools, many first describe the Tathāgata manifesting birth for the sake of sentient beings."
First the small and later the great; first the non-manifest and later the manifest; first the wordless and later the verbal indication.
Why, at the very beginning, does it describe the *dharmadhātu*? The answer is: because this is the primary tenet of this sutra;

because it is the universal essence of all sutras; because it is the universal basis of all phenomena; and because it is the fundamental ground for the delusion and enlightenment of all sentient beings.
Because it exhaustively encompasses what all Buddhas have realized, because the practices of all Bodhisattvas arise from this,
and because its initial establishment is taught instantaneously— unlike other sūtras which proceed gradually— the final intention alone provides the direct answer to the initial question,
while the preceding intentions collectively establish that final intention.
▲ Only the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, which dissects the profound mysteries to illuminate the mind and its objects, exhausts principle and fulfills nature,
penetrates the fruit while encompassing the cause, and is vast, harmonious, and all-encompassing, is truly such a scripture.

The second section, "Analyzed Exposition of the Profound and Subtle," specifically praises the expressive power [of the teaching] to clarify that this sutra explicates the *dharmadhātu*, and thus it is difficult to conceive.
The text contains seven phrases, which are divided into four parts; the first two phrases provide a general explanation of the expressive words.
"Profound and subtle" (*xuánwēi*) refers to the many meanings of the aforementioned *dharmadhātu* as the profound, mysterious, and exquisite principle; "analyzed" (*pōu*) refers to...
The judgment regarding this schism lies in this sutra, which refers to the division of the unobstructed *dharmadhātu* into the two gates of mind and objects;

hence the subsequent line says, "Luminously expansive mind and objects. How can they be partitioned? It means that the single true *dharmadhātu* originally has no internal or external, nor does it belong to the categories of one or many.
It is the Buddha’s own self-realized, exhaustive knowledge [of this], yet he wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to it.
Regarding the analysis of meaning, the mind and its objects are distinguished such that the object is that which is realized and the mind is that which realizes.
Therefore, the following citation from Master Yu states: "The mind is realized by all Buddhas as the Dharma-body; the object is realized by all Buddhas as the Pure Land.
Thus, both are what is realized, while wisdom is that which realizes. The object that is realized is precisely the Mahāvaipulya (Great Extensiveness), which is the wisdom that realizes.
The mind itself is the Buddha Flower Adornment Sūtra (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*). Because it is explained extensively within the text, it is said to "cleave open.
As for the phrase "the clarity and vastness of mind and object": mind and object refer to what was opened above; "clarity and vastness" refers to this very sūtra.

"Clarity" (*zhāo*) means luminosity and illumination; "vastness" (*kuò*) means emptiness and the expansion of the small into the great. How does it clarify mind and object? It is said that this sūtra...
The center is luminous, manifest, and distinct; whether ordinary or sagely, cause or fruit, the observing mind and the observed object are fully present therein.
Thus, as stated in the "Chapter on Manifestation": "To speak of the Buddha’s realm is itself the Buddha’s realm;
to speak of the Tathāgata’s mind is itself the Buddha’s mind. All instances of subject and object should be understood according to this principle. Why is this so?
Does this illuminate both mind and objects? This scripture teaches people to observe either the mind or objects, as it says:
"If you wish to know the mind of the Buddhas, you should contemplate the wisdom of the Buddhas. Buddha-wisdom has no place of dependence; like space, it has nothing upon which to rely.
This instructs one to contemplate the Buddha-mind. Furthermore, it says: "If there are those who wish to know the realm of the Buddhas, they should purify their own minds."
Like empty space, this teaching observes the realm of the Buddha. One should understand by analogy that the mental objects and states of both bodhisattvas and ordinary beings are likewise observed.
How is the mental state of empty vastness? As it is said: "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally empty and quiescent;

there is neither grasping nor seeing. That the nature of phenomena is empty is itself the Buddha; it cannot be apprehended through thought or deliberation. This is the mental state of emptiness, which is without grasping.

That which is without object is without seeing, and that which is without seeing is without mind. It is further said: "If one wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, one should purify the mind so that it is like empty space;
by remaining far removed from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and all forms of grasping (*upādāna*), the mind will be unimpeded in whatever direction it turns.
This also implies the emptying of both mind and its objects. Furthermore, it is said: "If one wishes to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, one should abandon all delusions."

To discern existence and non-existence and penetrate their universal equality, thereby swiftly becoming a Great Teacher of humans and devas, is precisely the meaning of the "emptiness of both mind and objects.
Why then do you attempt to enlarge the small? This means that if you expand the mind, there are no objects external to the mind;
if you expand the objects, there is no mind external to the objects. Whichever one you take up, it encompasses all phenomena without omission, such that they are truly boundless.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "There is no suchness outside of wisdom that could be entered by wisdom, nor is there wisdom outside of suchness that could realize suchness.
In the preceding phrase, "mind" is emphasized; in the subsequent phrase, "object" (境) is emphasized. True mind and true object are fundamentally boundless;
when delusion is seen as identical to truth, the small is expanded to become great. The scripture says: "The profound realm of the Tathāgata."
Its measure is equal to empty space; the Buddha-realm is great. It is also said that the Buddha’s wisdom is as vast and equal as empty space; the true mind is great.
Knowing that delusion is fundamentally true, one sees the Buddha, which is the pure mind. Buddha and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
All are the manifestation of the deluded mind, which is itself boundless. Cause and effect, the myriad dharmas, the mind, and objects are all universally pervasive.

Each and every matter can be expanded and elucidated accordingly. The phrase "exhausting principle and exhausting nature, penetrating the fruit and encompassing the cause" consists of two pairs of phrases that separately manifest its profundity and vastness.
"Principle" (li) refers to the fundamental trend and the way of things; this signifies vastness. "Nature" (xing) refers to the dharma-nature and the mind-nature; this signifies profundity.
If one reaches the ultimate limit of the fundamental trend, then one exhausts the essential nature. Now, regarding this sutra:
The essential nature of the underlying intent is thoroughly investigated here. This borrows from the words in the "Explanation of the Diagrams" (*Shuogua*) of the *Zhouyi*:
"Exhausting principle and exhausting nature, one reaches destiny. The ancient sages, in creating the *Yi*, intended thereby to accord with the principle of nature and destiny.
The commentary states: "Destiny is the ultimate limit of life; to exhaust principle is to fully realize one's capacity, which is precisely [the means to reach destiny]."

The character "néng" (capable) explains the nature (*xing*); "nature" here refers to capability. Each [being] fulfills its own capacity; if one exhausts its principles and fully realizes its capacity, it accords with the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*).
Therefore, it is followed by the statement, "to accord with the principle of nature and destiny. In the current discourse, the term is used in this sense, though its intended meaning differs.
To say that it "penetrates the fruit and encompasses the cause" means it includes both the profound and the vast, thoroughly investigating the five [aggregates].
The fruits of the *Avataṃsaka* encompass the causes of the six stages; thus, its breadth is vast. Therefore, no exposition of the causes and fruits of the spiritual stages exceeds this sutra.
If one says that "the causes encompass the ocean of fruits" and "the fruits penetrate to the source of the causes," with the two mutually interpenetrating, this reveals its profundity.
At the very moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening—this is the cause encompassing the fruit. Although one has attained the Buddha-way...
"Not abandoning the gate of the cause" means that the fruit penetrates the cause. Above, this was explained according to the broad meaning:

"penetrating the fruit" refers to the fruit, and "encompassing the cause" refers to the cause; thus it clarifies that the teaching which expresses [the truth] encompasses and penetrates those causes and fruits.

Now, explaining according to the profound meaning: "penetrating the fruit" belongs to the cause, because the cause penetrates that fruit; "encompassing the cause" belongs to the fruit, because the fruit penetrates that cause. Thus...
The self-characteristics of cause and effect are mutually pervasive and belong exclusively to that which is expressed (*vācya*), yet the expressive words (*vācaka*) fully clarify this meaning.
The statement by the ancients, "The cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches the source of the cause," intends to convey a profound and vast significance;

thus, it is said here that "the fruit is pervasive and the cause is encompassed. That which is "vast, surging, harmonious, and all-encompassing" refers to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*).

These two lines conclude by praising its profundity and vastness. The first line clarifies the characteristics of profundity and vastness; the second line reveals the reason for its profundity and vastness.
*Wang-wang* describes the aspect of depth; *yang-yang* describes the aspect of breadth. *Chong* (沖) also signifies depth, and it is also said to mean "the center" (*zhong*).

Furthermore, it is called "harmonious centrality" (*chonghe*); thus, the *Laozi* says: "The Dao is centered (*chong*) yet is employed, appearing as if it were never full. It is pervasive and harmonious.
This "integration" (*yōng-tōng*) signifies both depth and vastness. Thus, Master Zhaolong said: "How vast! How expansive! Is there anything that does not proceed from this?
In the *Aṣṭācārya-sūtra*, the Brahmin Śatruṃjaya says: "I have heard that the Buddha-way is of profound and deep meaning, vast and boundless;
there is nothing it does not accomplish, and no living being it does not deliver. This is precisely the meaning of depth and vastness. It is also like... [text ends]
The harmonious and vital energy (*chonghe* qi) generates all things without becoming full or overflowing, and it penetrates all laws so that there are no obstructions.

To say that "all is vast and complete" refers to the reason for its profound breadth; because nothing is not complete, this statement also derives from the *Xici* (Appended Statements) of the *Zhouyi*.
It says: "As for the Book of Changes, it is vast and complete. Therein it is said: "The Changes, as a book, is vast and complete..."
There is the Way of Heaven, there is the Way of Humanity, and there is the Way of Earth. By combining these three powers (*sancái*) and doubling them, there are six;
these six are none other than the ways of the three powers. Now, if one takes the underlying meaning and applies it to the Sūtra, it may be illustrated as follows:
the Way of Heaven is *jñāna-saṃbodhi* (the Perfect Enlightenment of Wisdom); the Way of Humanity refers to sentient beings; and the Way of Earth refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

Furthermore, because this sutra extensively explains the three worlds, it may also be understood as the profound principle of the celestial realm (*deva-loka*), the phenomenal characteristics of the earthly realm (*pṛthivī-loka*), and the practitioners—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—of the human realm (*manuṣya-loka*). This forced correlation is intended merely to demonstrate its all-encompassing nature;
for within this fundamental wheel of Dharma, there is no teaching that is not contained. There has never been [any such thing].

Each phenomenon possesses its own principle, yet without exhausting the single cause or the single fruit; the five cycles of cause and effect are fully present, so that the fifty-two stages are clearly manifest.
The profound texts of the nine assemblies reveal this inconceivable ocean of teachings, making it visible to all.
When explaining the true and the false, the ordinary and the sagely are seen to interpenetrate with clarity; when speaking of the Dharma-realm, phenomena and principle appear distinctly and vividly.
The mutual inclusion of the Buddhas’ knowledge and vision is revealed without omission in a single verse;
the entire essence and function of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is exhausted within one chapter; the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā* do not transcend the verses of the three heavens;
and the entire treasury of the *Sūtras* is subsumed within seven characters. This is called emptying the ocean of the Buddhas' wisdom and exhausting the nature.
Because it is the vast source of all characteristics, it is said that "all is extensively and fully contained therein.

The phrase "None other than this *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*" constitutes the fourth section, which concludes by identifying the specific teaching to which these matters belong; the aforementioned sublime events belong exclusively to our *Avataṃsaka*.

▲ Therefore, our World-Honored One, having first perfected the ten bodies and attained true enlightenment, began to fulfill his vows and practices to encompass the vast emptiness as his essential nature;
he is replete with myriad virtues and utterly free from even the slightest speck of defilement.
Third, regarding the passage "Therefore, I, the World-Honored One," which concerns the inconceivable nature of the Teacher, there are six phrases whose meaning is divided into four parts:
first, two phrases that mark the perfection of the fruit; second, one phrase that clarifies the profundity of the cause of speech; third, one phrase that reveals the mystery of the essence;

and fourth, two phrases that manifest the completeness of the virtues. The initial statement, "I am therefore the World-Honored One, with the ten bodies fully perfected," generally marks the ten [bodies].

The body encompasses the two subsequent sections which correctly clarify the inconceivable; because this is the teaching of the Buddha of the ten bodies in unimpeded union, rather than that of the three bodies, it is said "I.

As for the reason for saying "I": because the aforementioned meanings and the means of expression are profound, vast, mysterious, and sublime, serving as the foundation for all teachings, our World-Honored One, immediately upon attaining perfect enlightenment, suddenly proclaimed this sutra. Regarding the term "ten bodies," [the following section] proceeds next...
Below, I shall set forth the explanation of "initial fulfillment": because at the time of attaining perfect enlightenment, the body first becomes fully complete. Therefore, the sutra below states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One, seated upon this throne, attained the most perfect enlightenment regarding all dharmas;
his wisdom entered into the equality of the three periods of time, and his body filled all worlds; his voice universally accorded with the ten directions."

The "land and so forth" refers to the initial fulfillment. Regarding the phrase "the Perfect Enlightenment is first accomplished," this is a specific description of the body of Bodhi, as it serves as the totality;

thus, the Initial Awakening is identical to the Original [Awakening], and there is no further distinction between beginning and origin. This is termed "first accomplished," which shall be explained in detail below.
The two phrases "riding upon vows and practices to encompass all" indicate that the causes are profound; herein, there are two types of causes. First:
The *Chengyuan yin jing* (Sutra on the Causes of Riding upon Vows) states: "The vow-power of Vairocana Buddha pervades the Dharma-realm.
The verse by the Mountain Deity, the Master of the Causes of the Practice of the Two Vehicles, says: "The sublime practices cultivated in the past were boundless," and so forth.

Because the causes of former vows encompass the functions of the fruition, this is called the "Vow-body" (*praṇidhāna-kāya*). The term "encompassing" (*mílún*) carries the meaning of pervading and including all; it also appears in the *Book of Zhou*.
The *Yìzhōu Yíshì* states: "The *Yì* accords with Heaven and Earth; therefore it can encompass and interweave the Way of Heaven and Earth. The commentary explains:
Since the *Yì* was created in accordance with Heaven and Earth, what is expounded within it is identical in principle to the principles of Heaven and Earth;
thus it can encompass and interweave the Way of Heaven and Earth. This serves as an analogy for the Tathāgata’s original resolve and practice, his desire to universally benefit [all beings].
Because all things now attain the fulfillment of their vows through practice, they pervade the entire Dharma-realm; this is called "encompassing" (*mílún*).
Regarding the statement that "the void is blended as its essential nature," there are three parts, the first of which clarifies the mystery of the essence. This contains two meanings:
first, concerning the Buddha’s own person, he inherently possesses the ten bodies, which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); that is, taking the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*) as the Dharma-body.

Therefore, the subsequent scripture states that "the emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha, which cannot be conceived or measured," and further states that "the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, pure as empty space.
In these two instances, the external empty space is used to harmonize with the three worlds to constitute the Buddha-body;
thus, external empty space is the *ākāśakāya* (space-body), and it is said that "empty space is blended to form the essence."

Because their nature is harmoniously fused and unimpeded. ▲ "Richly endowed with myriad virtues, vast and free from even a speck of dust" consists of two phrases that manifest the perfection of qualities.
The first phrase indicates that there is no virtue not perfected; the second phrase indicates that there is no obstruction not pacified.

"Myriad" (*wan*) is a large, general number, signifying that they truly possess inexhaustible virtues; thus, the subsequent scripture says: "The mind [is as numerous as] the motes of dust in a world-system."
One might be able to count the drops of water in the great ocean, drink it all dry, measure the void, or bind the wind; yet no one can exhaustively describe the Buddha’s merit.

His inexhaustible virtue is collectively termed the "Ten Thousand Virtues" (*sahasra-guṇa*). Because he is free from the dust-like ignorance (*avidyā*) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with all residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is said that he is "swept clean of even the finest speck of dust.
This refers in general to the two obstacles (*dvividha-āvaraṇa*). There are three types of these two obstacles: first, the manifest...

Regarding the two types of seeds and the three kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): since these habitual tendencies are subtle, how much more so are they like a speck of dust—the most minute among the minute.

If even these do not exist, what need is there to mention other forms of subtlety within the coarse? If these are collectively assigned to the three virtues, the ten thousand virtues are contained within wisdom and compassion;

the latter phrase refers to the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa*). Furthermore, taking the integration with emptiness as its essence constitutes the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while the ten thousand virtues constitute [the remaining two virtues].
The phrase "the virtue of prajñā is free from dust" refers to the virtue of liberation; it serves as the general heading for all the subsequent phrases, which are its specific virtues.
Of these, the first two phrases together constitute the body of merit (puṇya-kāya); thus four of the ten bodies are already complete, while the remaining six are found in the following section.
The clear waves of the ocean of profound wisdom serenely contain the myriad phenomena; the ten thousand moons of the luminous, empty nature suddenly descend upon the hundred rivers.

Without stirring, the King of Trees (the Bodhi tree) pervades the seven locations throughout the Dharma-realm without contradiction; the nine assemblies are fully realized within the initial enlightenment.
This vast and profound essence encompasses all, reaching the inconceivable ocean-like gathering, its perfect resonance resounding clearly across the ten lands.
Suddenly, the primary and secondary elements pervade everywhere, resonating in unison throughout the ten directions.

Fourth, the clear ripples of the profound ocean of wisdom contain all phenomena within their voidness; the following section on the "Universal Ritual" contains seven pairs, which constitute seven meanings:
first, clarifying the meditative concentration upon which it relies; second, clarifying the body that can preach it; third, the preaching of the sutra.
First, regarding the initial section on the samādhi upon which the preaching of the sutra relies:
as it is said, when preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he relied on the *Anantārthaviniścaya-samādhi*;
when preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he relied on the *Samādhirāja-samādhi*; and when preaching the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, he relied on the *Acalā-samādhi*. Therefore...
While other sutras are mostly based upon various samādhis, this present sutra is based upon which samādhi? It is the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
"Ocean Seal" is a metaphor; it receives its name from that metaphor. This shall be explained in detail in the commentary on the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*);

here, its characteristics are briefly indicated: it is like a fragrant ocean that is clear, still, and perfectly motionless, wherein the forms and bodies of all beings within the four continents appear.
All these images possess seal-marks within them, just as a seal leaves its impression upon an object. It is like a vast expanse of ten thousand li of clear waves where the sky is cloudless;
the constellations, stars, and moon appear together with brilliant clarity. There is no coming and no going; they are neither existent nor non-existent, neither one nor different.
In the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the waves of consciousness do not arise; it is still, pure, and supremely luminous.
In ultimate stillness, the mindless state suddenly manifests all sentient beings' mental activities, faculties, and desires;

these mental activities, faculties, and desires are all contained within wisdom, just as the ocean contains reflections. Therefore, the subsequent scripture says: "Like the ocean, it universally manifests the bodies of sentient beings.
For this reason, it is called the Great Ocean. Bodhi universally responds to all mental activities; therefore, Perfect Enlightenment is called "Non-existence" (Wu).
The means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not merely wisdom; the mind also relies upon this wisdom to instantaneously manifest myriad forms, universally responding to all classes of beings.

As the *Bhadramukha-parivarta* states: "Whether manifesting in the form of a boy or a girl, a deva, nāga, or asura, even up to a mahoraga, they cause all to see according to their inclinations; the physical forms of sentient beings each appear distinctly."
The sounds of all concurrent activities are likewise immeasurable; all such things can be manifested through the majestic spiritual power of the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*.
In this passage, the text contains both the dharma and its metaphor: "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the dharma, while "the ocean" is the metaphor.

Since the waves of consciousness have already subsided, the ocean of wisdom is tranquil; because it manifests instantaneously without thought, it is said to "vaguely contain" that which is capable of responding to objects.
"Should all become the myriad forms. "The full moon of the nature of emptiness suddenly descends into the hundred rivers"—this second pair clarifies the body that is capable of responding.
Of these two lines, only the character *xing* (nature) is the *dharma* (the reality); the rest are metaphors.
By using "nature" (*xing*) to encompass them, both the *dharma* and the metaphors are included. This means: if the autumn sky’s bright moon is radiant, pure, and without blemish, the myriad...
The myriad rivers flow undivided into the vessel; the emptiness of nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) is the supporting *dharmatā*;

the full moon is the perfection of the wisdom of true recompense (*vipāka-jñāna*); and the myriad rivers are a metaphor for the capacities of sentient beings. When reflections fall [into the water], they become transformations;

thus, the moon of the Buddha’s wisdom fully relies upon the emptiness of nature. With delusions exhausted and virtues perfected, it responds spontaneously and instantaneously without thought. Therefore, the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) says: "For example..."
