speaking of the present as the future; speaking of the future as the past; speaking of the future as the present; [speaking of the future as] the future; and [speaking of the future as] the past.
To speak of the inexhaustible three periods of time within a single thought-moment: the first nine [periods] are the particulars, while the single thought-moment is the totality;

thus it is said that the ten periods of time exist because the three periods are mutually dependent and mutually inclusive. Since a single thought-moment contains all ten, the ten are cited to manifest their inexhaustibility.
Thus, a single thought-moment is immeasurable kalpas, and immeasurable kalpas are a single thought-moment. (From the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra")
It is said that immeasurable and incalculable eons, when understood, are but a single thought-moment; yet one knows that even this thought-moment is devoid of thought.
To see the world in this way is like seeing it as a dream lasting a single night. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In a dream, what is called 'passing years' is but a brief moment upon awakening.
Thus, although time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa. This is from the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*).
It is said that it is like a person who, while dreaming in sleep, performs various deeds; though many billions of years may pass, they do not reach the end of even a single night.
Therefore, Zhuangzi’s "In a Dream I Became a Butterfly" (with the commentary noting:

"In the world there are those who dream for a hundred years while merely dozing") illustrates this, as such examples are numerous. Regarding the phrase "the dharma-gates are layered and repeated," this is the ninth reliance.
Regarding the statement that the "gates of phenomena arising from events" are "redundant," the intention is to show that many [phenomena] do not obstruct one another;

thus, according to each single event, they are called "many dharma-gates. Because each single event is itself the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and because the Dharma-realm is inexhaustible, the dharmas are also inexhaustible.
As the following sutra says: "These flower-canopies and so forth arise from the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

The phrase "that which arises" and so forth clarifies that all causes produce a single effect, and since this single effect inherently possesses all [causes], it is not the case that something else is indicated by relying upon this.
Regarding the phrase "the myriad practices in full bloom," this refers to the tenth gate, the Gate of the Pure and Mixed Endowments of All Treasuries (*sarva-kośa*).
This gate is found among Fazang’s Ten Mysterious Gates (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*), though there are variations.
For two reasons, Xianshou revised this into the "Gate of the Unimpeded Freedom between the Broad and the Narrow":

first, if one considers that which accords with principle to be "pure" and the myriad practices to be "mixed," then this would constitute the unimpededness of phenomena and principle (*shili wuai*), rather than the unimpededness of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

For example, if a Bodhisattva’s great compassion were "pure" such that it extended to the limits of the future, yet they saw only the practice of compassion while all other practices were as if non-existent; [this would not be true *shishi wuai*].

If emptiness is discussed according to the gate of intermingling (*miśra-mukha*), then all myriad practices are cultivated together; thus, the distinction between these two gates [of purity and intermingling] is not established.

Regarding the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena (*shishi wuai*): for example, in the single gate of giving (*dāna*), all myriad dharmas are entirely termed "giving," and for this reason it is called "pure.
Yet, because this gate of giving itself encompasses the practices of all the perfections (*pāramitā*), it is called "intermingled. Such is the nature of purity.
Because they coexist without mutual obstruction, they are called "possessing virtue" (*guṇavat*); thus, the principle of the non-obstruction of phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*) is established.

Furthermore, since all perfections (*pāramitā*) are contained within a single one, this resembles the gate of mutual inclusion (*xiāngjí mén*). Conversely, if one is identical to all perfections, it again resembles the gate of mutual identity (*xiāngjí mén*).
Therefore, rather than maintaining [the former], it is revised to "broad and narrow" (*guǎngxiá*), as this now refers exclusively to the practice (*xing*).
This section differs slightly from the preceding one in that it lacks the primary and attendant elements; therefore, it is presented again to complete the ten meanings.
The phrase "comparable to flowers blooming upon brocade" intends to convey that while the five colors complement one another and their hues differ, every single thread passes through them all.
This serves as a metaphor for the "pure" (purely identical) and the "mixed" (identical-and-different), and thus they are named "constant identity" and "constant difference."

Because they are unimpeded, they differ from mere embroidery or painting; they are distinct yet not mutually exclusive. The ten mysteries (*daśa-avyāhata*) have been briefly set forth here as a general framework;
their detailed analysis is found below in the section on "Delineation of Limits" (*vibhāga*).
As for that which is so lofty it cannot be looked up to, the Bodhisattvas who have accumulated practices expose their gills and scales at the Dragon Gate; and as for that which is so deep...
If one may peer [into this], those of superior virtue and the śrāvakas will close their sight and hearing at this sublime assembly.
As for the seventh section, "The Benefits Arise Sudden and Complete," there are ten meanings in the text.

The first two meanings generally manifest its loftiness and profundity, clarifying that the provisional and the small vehicles cannot fathom it; the latter eight correctly clarify the benefits of completion, which are universal, sudden, and perfect. Furthermore, regarding the preceding...
Second, the "High and Deep" (Gāoshēn) section reveals the benefits through contrast, clarifying that the provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle are unfathomable;

because there was no prior cause [for such realization], it conversely exhorts sentient beings to have faith and understanding. Subsequently, the "Later Entry" (Hòrù) section reveals the benefits through conformity, meaning it can be both sudden and perfect, ensuring that they must receive them.
Regarding the first of these, it clarifies the height and distance: it is like Mount Tai leaning against the heavens and Mount Min'e brushing the Milky Way, difficult to fathom.
Because one looks up to its summit, the *Lunyu* (Analects) says: "The higher one looks up to it, the higher it seems; the harder one drills into it, the harder it proves.

As for the Bodhisattva who accumulates practice, the *Chuxianpin* (Chapter on the Appearance [of the Tathāgata]) states: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated and gathered all manner of factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), yet had not heard this Tathāgata..."
If one hears this inconceivable dharma-gate of great majesty at some time, yet does not believe it, does not understand it,
does not accord with it, does not enter into it, and does not attain it, such a person cannot be called a true bodhisattva, because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata.
However, if one hears this dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom...
One who has already attained faith, understanding, compliance, and realization should be known as one born into the family of the Tathāgata.
This is like a fish ascending the Dragon Gate: if it succeeds in ascending, it is immediately transformed into a dragon; such is the capacity of those who enter the *Avataṃsaka*.
If it fails to ascend, its gills are exposed beneath the Dragon Gate; such are those "provisional-name bodhisattvas" of the expedient teachings.
Regarding "cultivating in successive order": ▲ "Profound and unfathomable" marks the second section, which demonstrates its deep and wondrous nature.

Specifically, at the beginning of the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta*, Śāriputra and the five hundred śrāvakas praise his virtues, saying: "He has fully awakened to the true reality (*satyadharma*) and realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);

he has deeply entered the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and forever transcended the ocean of existence; relying on the Buddha’s merits, he is liberated from the bonds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*)."
Dwelling in the state of non-obstruction, his mind is as tranquil as space; he has forever severed doubt regarding all Buddhas and enters with deep faith into the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom.
*Explanation:* This refers to the aforementioned virtues. In the Jeta Grove, during the Tathāgata’s sublime assembly, he neither sees nor hears [the teachings];
this is called "obstructing sight and hearing" (*du shi ting*). "Obstructing" means to block. Regarding the term "sight" (*shi*), it refers to the faculty of vision.
To have ears but not hear is to be like one who is deaf or blind, even while sitting beneath the assembly; therefore, it is said that [the senses] are "blocked and stifled. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"At that time, the foremost great Śrāvakas—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Revata, Subhūti, Aniruddha, Nanda, Kapphiṇa, and Kātyāyana..."
Rāhula and the other great śrāvakas in the Jeta Grove were all unable to perceive the Tathāgata’s supernatural power,
the Tathāgata’s majestic adornment, the Tathāgata’s realm, the Tathāgata’s play, the Tathāgata’s miraculous transformations, the Tathāgata’s supreme excellence,
the Tathāgata’s wondrous conduct, the Tathāgata’s majestic virtue, the Tathāgata’s sustaining presence, nor even the Tathāgata’s pure buddha-field.
They did not see the inconceivable realm of the bodhisattvas, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, the bodhisattvas who universally enter,
the bodhisattvas who universally arrive, the bodhisattvas who universally approach, the miraculous transformations of the bodhisattvas, the playful displays of the bodhisattvas,

the retinues of the bodhisattvas, the locations of the bodhisattvas, the adornments of the lion thrones of the bodhisattvas, the palaces of the bodhisattvas, or the dwelling places of the bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattvas who have entered samādhi-sovereignty, the Bodhisattvas of contemplation, the Bodhisattvas of yawn-like stretching,
the Bodhisattvas of valor, the Bodhisattvas of making offerings, the Bodhisattvas receiving predictions, the Bodhisattvas bringing others to maturity,
the Bodhisattvas of courageous strength, the Bodhisattvas whose Dharma-body is pure, the Bodhisattvas whose Wisdom-body is perfected, and the Bodhisattvas manifesting their Vow-bodies.

One does not see at all such things as the Bodhisattvas who have perfected their bodies, those endowed with all the marks, those adorned with the pure constant radiance of Bodhisattvas, those who emit great nets of light, those who raise clouds of transformations, those whose bodies pervade the ten directions, or those whose various practices are complete. Why is this? It is because of their roots of goodness.
Because they are different, they have not from the beginning cultivated and accumulated the roots of goodness for the mastery of seeing the Buddhas;
because they have not from the beginning praised and proclaimed the pure merits of all Buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions;

because they have not from the beginning extolled the various supernatural transformations of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; because they have not from the beginning resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* amidst the cycle of birth and death...

Because they have not originally caused others to abide in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and because they have not originally been able to ensure that the lineage of the Tathāgatas is not severed, and so forth—the preceding section first enumerates the persons, namely those of superior virtue among the *śrāvakas*.
Next, the explanation of "not seeing" and so forth indicates the closing off of sight and hearing. As for the phrase "Why is this? and below, it explains why [they do not see].
To see those of inferior causes yet not yet perceive them is not yet profound; it is only when one who lacks superior virtue suddenly comes to know the mysterious and subtle that it is so.

To take seeing and hearing as the seeds, to transcend the eight difficulties and the stages of the ten grounds, and to have understanding and practice manifest within oneself, is to realize in a single lifetime the fruit of vast kalpas.
Like the lion’s vigorous leap, the multitude of oceans is suddenly realized within the forest; like the elephant king’s turning, the six offspring are present.
The Way is perfected beneath a single word; the illumination of Dongmiao Temple is no different from the initial aspiration.

Abiding in the position of Nanqu, the fulfillment of the cause does not exceed a single pore. To unfold the sutra scrolls within a speck of dust is for the fruit to be realized in every thought-moment;
to exhaust the gates of the vows of all sentient beings is for practice to be perfected in every particle of dust.
Seeing and hearing constitute the seed; the following eight sections correctly reveal the characteristics of the perfect and pervasive fulfillment of benefits.
This first section clarifies the benefit of seeing and hearing, which is also termed the "benefit of the seed.

That is to say, in the *Anuvyañjana-parivarta*, the three levels of sudden perfection for the sons of gods in hell, as well as the statement regarding the first bhūmi—that even while dwelling amidst the waters of the ocean or within the kalpa-ending conflagration, one is capable of receiving this Dharma.
Those who, upon hearing this, harbor doubts and do not believe will never again hear such a teaching; conversely, it is revealed that through faith and hearing, one attains benefit.
The waters of the ocean are comprised within the realm of animals; the kalpa-ending fire is the fire of the world-system;
and those born in the first dhyāna are reborn in the second dhyāna, such as the Ābhāsvara Heaven. For those long-lived devas, these are difficult to encounter.
Those who have obtained this hearing include the gods of the upper realms and those from the hells; thus, three of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) have already been resolved.

Furthermore, since spirits and ghosts have obtained hearing at the Buddha’s assembly, the three miserable paths (*tridurgati*) are likewise accounted for. Even during the time of the fire calamity, as well as before and after the Buddha’s appearance, humans, devas, and followers of heterodox paths have all been included.

Moreover, although the wise and discerning are mentioned, this does not exclude the deaf of Uttarakuru; for it is said that the blind see and the deaf hear. Thus, the eight difficulties are fully encompassed.
All these are included within the meaning of "seeing and hearing as seeds," which transcends the stages of the ten bhūmis.
This is precisely because the Heavenly Son of the Avīci Hell was able to attain sudden perfection; being one who has received human form, how could I not preserve what I have encountered?
Thus, in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Minor Marks and Radiance," the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, saying: "O Son of the Buddha..."
On the soles of the Bodhisattva’s feet are wheels with a thousand spokes named King of Universal Radiance;
these possess a secondary mark named King of Perfection, which constantly emits forty kinds of light rays.
Among them is one ray named Pure Merit, capable of illuminating worlds as numerous as the atoms within billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields, according to the various karmas of sentient beings.

All those who indulge in various sensual pleasures were brought to maturity; those sentient beings suffering the extreme torments of the Avīci Hell who encountered this light all passed away and were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Once reborn in heaven, the celestial drum extensively preached the Dharma for them, even saying:
"At that time, the sons of the gods, having heard the exposition of the vast and great dedication of Samantabhadra, attained the ten..."
Because he had attained the Samādhi Adorned with All Powers and because he had purified his three karmas to the extent of the number of sentient beings,
thereby repenting and eliminating all heavy obstructions, he immediately beheld as many seven-jeweled lotuses as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-fields;
upon each flower sat a Bodhisattva in the full lotus posture, emitting light.

From the great radiance up to the scattering of flowers upon the Buddha, it is further said that from those clouds of incense, a rain falls universally upon worlds as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable Buddha-fields.
If there are sentient beings whose bodies are touched by this fragrance, their bodies become peaceful and blissful;
furthermore, they come to fully understand that even the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) are entirely illusory.
"Thus it is known that one has already accomplished the pure roots of goodness of the Sovereign Radiance of Fragrant Banner Clouds. Commentary:
This refers to the first stage of attaining the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Next, it says:

"If there are sentient beings who see its canopy, they plant the pure roots of goodness of a Wheel-Turning King of the Pure Golden Net, as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River. Commentary: This refers to the second stage.
Following the attainment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the text further states:
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the position of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) with a pure golden net, emits the pure radiance from his maṇi-crest.
If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they all attain the tenth stage of a Bodhisattva and achieve immeasurable wisdom-light, obtaining ten kinds [of qualities]."
"Endowed with the ten kinds of pure eyes up to the ten kinds of pure minds and immeasurable, profound samādhis. The commentary states:

"This refers to the third stage of attaining the ten bhūmis. Regarding the phrase "the practice of understanding resides within one's person," etc., this refers to the second stage, the benefit of the practice of understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).
In the *Seventy-eight Sūtras*, Maitreya praises Sudhana, saying: "Other bodhisattvas, having passed through..."
It takes immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas to fulfill the vows and practices of a bodhisattva and to draw near to the enlightenment of all Buddhas;
yet this son of a householder is able, within a single lifetime, to purify Buddha-fields,
to transform sentient beings, to penetrate the dharma-realm with wisdom, and to achieve accomplishment.
The various *pāramitās* can increase and broaden all practices; they can fulfill all great vows;
they can transcend all demonic activities; they can serve all spiritual friends; they can purify the paths of all bodhisattvas;
and they can bring to completion the practices and majestic radiance of Samantabhadra, as well as those of Prince Tejaprabha.
This also means that in a single lifetime one perfects the fruits of many kalpas; both of these points clarify the rapidity of realization.

Furthermore, the primary tenet of this sutra clarifies the perfection of three lifetimes: first, the lifetime of hearing and seeing; second, the lifetime of understanding and practice—these correspond to the aforementioned two lines [of verse];

and third, the lifetime of realization and entry—this corresponds to the latter two lines. Regarding "the lion’s vigorous leap" and so forth, this refers to the third benefit: instantaneous realization.
That is to say, at the beginning of the sixtieth sutra, at that time the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, took great compassion as his body,
great compassion as his gate, and great compassion as his head; employing the dharma of great compassion as his skillful means,
he pervaded all of space and entered the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the Lion’s Stretch Samādhi)— which the older translation calls the "Fenxun" (Vigorous Prowess) Samādhi.
Because the meaning was explained by the Lion [Mañjuśrī] for the sake of convenience, it proceeded until the sixty-first chapter, where after Samantabhadra had revealed it,
light was emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, illuminating everything; at that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas in the Jeta Grove all saw,
within every single atom of all Buddha-fields throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the space-realm, each containing—
In as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in all Buddha-lands— possessing various names, various colors, various purities, various dwellings, and various forms— in all such lands,
there are great Bodhisattvas seated upon thrones at sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) on lion-thrones, attaining equal and perfect awakening (samyak-saṃbodhi), O Great Bodhisattva.
The assembly surrounded the Lord of the World from front and back, making offerings and so forth, up until it was said:

"Therefore, they all enter the Tathāgata’s inconceivable and profound samādhi; throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space, they possess great supernormal powers, whether entering the Dharma-body, the form-body, or that which was accomplished in the past."
Whether it be entering the perfection of all *pāramitās*, or entering the wheel of adornment and pure conduct, or entering the various stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva,
or entering the power of attaining perfect enlightenment, or entering the great supernormal transformations of the non-differentiated samādhis in which Buddhas abide,
or entering the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and wisdom, or entering the Buddha’s unimpeded eloquence.

The "Ocean of Talent" (*caihai*) is precisely the "Forest of Sudden Realization" (*dunzheng lin*). It is explained extensively that one enters this "object of entry" (*suoruo*) by means of the ten "capacities for entry" (*nengru*).
Regarding the phrase "the elephant king’s circumambulation" (*xiangwang huixuan*) and so forth: this is the fourth [section], the "Transcendent Expedient Benefit.
It refers to the beginning of the assembly at the end of the sixty-first sutra, where the six thousand bhikṣus were led by Śāriputra to contemplate the ten virtues of Mañjuśrī. Six.

When the Thousand Invited [Bhikṣus] went to pay their respects to Mañjuśrī and Śāriputra were made to see him, at that time the Youthful Mañjuśrī was surrounded by immeasurable and sovereign Bodhisattvas along with his great assembly.
As he turned to look back at the Bhikṣus like an elephant king, it is said he performed the "elephant-king’s turn.
Regarding the phrase "six thousand attained the Way upon hearing these words," it refers to the Bhikṣus who arose.
When Mañjuśrī caused them to give rise to ten kinds of tireless minds, the bhikṣus, having heard this Dharma,
attained a samādhi called "Unobstructed Eye that Beholds the Realm of All Buddhas. Because they had attained this samādhi,
they all beheld the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, and their respective [realms] in all the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions.
There was an assembly at the site of enlightenment who also all saw all sentient beings in every realm of existence throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
they also all saw the various distinctions among all those worlds;
they also all saw every single atom within all those worlds; and they also all saw all the sentient beings within those worlds.

The palaces in which they dwell are adorned with various kinds of jewels; furthermore, they hear the diverse voices of those Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as they expound all dharmas, and they fully comprehend their phrasing and explanations.
They are also able to observe the faculties, minds, and desires of all sentient beings within those worlds, and they are able to recollect them.
One is also able to recollect ten successive births before and after all sentient beings in the world;
one is also able to recollect the events of ten past kalpas and ten future kalpas within that world;

and one is also able to recollect the ten Jātaka tales of those Tathāgatas, their ten attainments of perfect enlightenment, their ten turnings of the wheel of Dharma, their ten kinds of supernormal powers, and their ten kinds of Dharma teachings.
He was instructed in ten kinds of eloquence; furthermore, he accomplished ten thousand bodhicittas, ten thousand samādhis, and ten thousand pāramitās, all of which were completely purified.
He attained great wisdom and perfect radiance, acquired the ten supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, and dwelt in the bodhisattva-mind—supple, subtle, firm, and immovable. At that time, Mañjuśrī...
The Bodhisattva Suśīla exhorted the bhikṣus to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra. Having abided in the conduct of Samantabhadra, they entered the ocean of great vows.
Having entered the ocean of great vows, they accomplished the ocean of great vows. Because they had accomplished the ocean of great vows, their minds became pure;
because their minds were pure, their bodies became pure; because their bodies were pure, their bodies became light and agile.

Because of his lightness and agility, he attains great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) from which there is no regression. Having attained these supernormal powers, he never leaves the presence of Mañjuśrī;
he manifests his body before all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and fully accomplishes all Buddha-dharmas.
The commentary states: this is the attainment of the Way. Within a single samādhi, there are ten [qualities].
The universal [benefit] is entirely complete and beneficial. Regarding the phrase "Enlightening the Eastern Temple" (*Qīmíng Dōngmiào*) and so forth:
this refers to the fifth [section], the accomplishment of the benefit of wisdom. As for "Enlightening the Eastern Temple," it is as stated in the sixty-second sutra:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, having exhorted the bhikṣus to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, gradually proceeded southward..."

He proceeded until he reached the eastern part of Puṇyavatī city and stayed in the Śāla grove known as Vyūhadhvaja, at the site of a great stūpa where Buddhas of the past had taught and transformed sentient beings. The commentary states: This refers to the Eastern Temple;
at that time, the people of Puṇyavatī heard that the youth Mañjuśrī was in the great stūpa within the Vyūhadhvaja Śāla grove, [accompanied by] immeasurable...
The multitude emerged from that city and went to where he was;
there, arranged separately in the midst of the assembly, were five hundred upāsakas and upāsikās, five hundred young men, and five hundred young women.
Mañjuśrī, having observed Sudhana individually, comforted and instructed him, and expounded for him all the teachings of the Buddhas.

Having taught the Dharma up to this point, he earnestly exhorted and encouraged them to increase their spiritual power, causing them to rejoice and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, he caused them to recollect their past roots of goodness.
Having performed these deeds, he then once again preached the Dharma to sentient beings at that very spot according to their needs, and thereafter...
At that time, the youth Sudhana, having heard from Mañjuśrī such various merits of the Buddha, single-mindedly and diligently sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Following Mañjuśrī, he spoke in verse, which is precisely the "Illumination of Wisdom" (*Jñānaprabhāsa*). It states that the fulfillment of wisdom is no different from the initial resolve.
This refers to the eightieth sutra, the *Jñānāloka-advaya-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*, which states:
"At that time, Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar across one hundred thousand yojanas, placed it upon the crown of Sudhana’s head, and spoke these words:
'Excellent, excellent, son of good family! If you are separated from the root of faith, your mind will be weak, filled with regret and anxiety, and your meritorious practice will not succeed.'"
They possess the decline of diligence; their minds dwell with attachment upon a single root of virtue; they consider a mere trifling merit to be sufficient;
they are unable to skillfully initiate practices and vows; they are not sustained by spiritual friends; they are not remembered by the Tathāgatas;
and they are unable to understand such a nature of phenomena (dharmatā) or such a principle.
Regarding such a dharma-gate, such a practice, such a dwelling, and such a sphere—
whether it be thorough knowledge, manifold knowledge, exhaustive knowledge of the source, comprehension, entry, exposition,
discrimination, realization, or attainment— all these cannot [be fully described]; this is explained as "thoroughly knowing the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*).

The "lower" refers to the fulfillment of wisdom; if one is separated from the mind of faith, it cannot be attained. This conversely reveals that by means of the mind of faith, [attainment] is secured.

If one does not depart from the initial mind, then faith and wisdom are non-dual. If one takes the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) as the beginning, then the two wisdoms—prior and subsequent—are likewise non-dual.
Regarding the phrase "entrusting to the stages, seeking in the south," etc., this refers to the sixth [section], the benefit of establishing the stages.

When Sudhana first beheld Mañjuśrī, he was entrusted with the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*); from Meghashiri to Gopā, he was entrusted with the stages of the three sages and ten saints (*tri-saikṣa-daśāśaikṣa*);

from Māyādevī onwards, he was further entrusted with the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti-bodhi*). Upon seeing Samantabhadra, he attained the perfection of the cause, without exceeding a single pore.
As the text says: "At that time, the youth Sudhana again saw himself within the body of Samantabhadra."
He teaches and transforms sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

Furthermore, it is said that from the time the youth Sudhana first resolved his mind toward enlightenment until he beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, all the oceans of Buddha-lands he entered during that interval are now contained within a single pore of Samantabhadra in a single thought-moment. All these Buddhas are present therein.
The oceans of lands exceed by unspeakably unspeakable times the number of atoms in a Buddha-land;

as it is with one pore, so it is with all pores. Furthermore, it is said that the youth Sudhana, within the lands of the pores of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, may pass through a single eon in a single land, and thus proceeds until—

Or there may be sutras such that, even if one were to practice for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, one would not pass away from this field to appear in another field;

yet in every single thought-moment, one would universally pervade the boundless oceans of fields to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to incline toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, [the merit] was excellent...
Then the youth Sudhana successively attained the ocean of all practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva— becoming equal to Samantabhadra, equal to all Buddhas,
with a single body filling all world-systems, equal in conduct, equal in perfect enlightenment, equal in supernormal powers,
equal in the wheel of Dharma, equal in eloquence, equal in speech, equal in voice, and equal in powers and fearlessnesses.
"The Buddha’s abodes, great compassion, and so forth, as well as his inconceivable liberation and mastery, are all entirely equal.

The commentary states: "This refers to the perfection of causes within a single pore. Regarding the phrase "unfolding the sutra scrolls within a minute atom," this is the seventh [point], which reveals the benefit of the fruition of causes;
it corresponds to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, specifically the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*), which contains the parable of the hidden atom. As the scripture says:
Suppose there were a great sutra scroll, equal in size to the triple-thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust—and so it is with every mote of dust.
A person of wisdom, with pure and clear vision, perceives this all; he breaks open the mote and brings forth the scroll to universally benefit sentient beings.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: it pervades the minds of all sentient beings, yet they do not realize it because it is shrouded by their false conceptualizations.

Furthermore, they do not know that it is through the great compassion of the Buddhas that their deluded thoughts are eliminated, and that it is for this purpose that [the Buddhas] appear to benefit all bodhisattvas.
Moreover, a sutra states: "A bodhisattva should know that within every thought-moment of his own mind, a Buddha is always attaining perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain perfect enlightenment without departing from this very mind. Therefore, one should maintain mindfulness.

When one is in accord with mindfulness, then every thought-moment is perfected. Regarding the phrase "the gate of fulfilling the vows of all sentient beings" and so forth: this is the eighth [section], the accomplishment of the benefit of practice and vows.
It means that when a Bodhisattva resolves their mind to transform and exhaust the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), only when that realm is exhausted would their great vow finally end.
Since the realm of sentient beings is infinite, the great vow is inexhaustible. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "If sentient beings..."

When the realms of existence are exhausted, my vows shall be exhausted; yet, because the realm of sentient beings can never be exhausted, these roots of goodness from my great vows are likewise without end.

Although the realms of existence today are inexhaustible, because there are equally infinite scriptural volumes, I shall universally expound their essentials to bring all inexhaustible sentient beings to fulfillment—this is my Great Vow. Thus it is said: "In every atom, the practices are perfected."
Because the great compassion of these Bodhisattvas is inexhaustible, the measure of their mind is inconceivable;

for the sake of even a single sentient being, they practice the myriad deeds within a single atom for immeasurable eons without their minds ever wearying, and this is true for every atom and throughout every birth.
Only then is it revealed that their vows and practices are truly infinite. Thus, Mañjuśrī praised Sudhana, saying:

▲ Thus, while Bodhisattvas searched for the secrets in the Dragon Palace and great sages propagated them throughout the Eastern Lands, we reflect that even during the era of the True Dharma, its pure radiance remained concealed.
How fortunate it is that in this age of the Semblance Dharma, we have encountered this profound transformation!
Moreover, having met with a sagely sovereign and being present at the Mount Lingyan assembly, we exhaust our thoughts upon the profound source; how could we not feel joy and exultation?

The ninth [section] concerns how the Bodhisattva, through his downward-reaching compassion, joyfully encountered [this teaching]. This section has two parts: first, the broad exposition of the origins;

second, the formal clarification of the encounter. Regarding the first: after five hundred years had passed, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna entered the Dragon Palace and sought out this profound scripture.
The details are as recorded in the *Biographies* (*Biezhuan*) and the *Zuānlíngjì*. It is said that the Great Sage [Nāgārjuna] propagated it.

Those who propagate [this teaching] in the Eastern Xia (China) are specifically those who have awakened the worthy, as well as others of great virtue, such as Jñānagupta, Dharmakṣema, Sūryavarman, and Śikṣānanda, who have expounded these scriptures.
"In the Eastern Xia" refers to the region east of the Pamir Mountains, spanning several thousand *li*, known as the Divine Continent (Shenzhou) or Great Xia;
this is what is meant by the phrase "therefore" (*yi shi*) due to the aforementioned profound [intent].

Because it is sublime, it was sought out and elucidated; thus, Nāgārjuna entered the Dragon Palace and extensively beheld countless [sūtras], yet he recited this sūtra in particular because of its profound mystery.
For this reason, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* designates it as the "Great Sūtra of the Inconceivable.
All the great virtuous ones have observed that even if one were to exhaust the ink of the oceans, one could never finish recording a single word or phrase of this sūtra, nor a single verse or line.
Because this light shatters the intense sufferings of hell, I have devoted my entire life to its widespread propagation.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Reflecting upon the era of the True Dharma," there are two parts that clearly explain the encounter with this fortune; within these, there are again two sections: first, rejoicing in comparison to the past, and second, rejoicing in comparison to the present.
The present section is the first of these, meaning that five hundred years ago was precisely the era of the True Dharma when this sutra was pure.
When the radiance was hidden within the Dragon Palace, people of the time heard nothing of it;
how fortunate that in this final age of the Semblance Dharma, I have encountered this profound and subtle transformation! Born during the end of the Semblance Dharma, one ought to feel sorrow;

yet, looking back at the past when I did not hear these scriptures, I do not feel shame for having lived in an era of the True Dharma, and thus I rejoice in myself. This is based on the *One Thousand-Year Non-Diminution of the True Dharma*.
Because it is now the age of the semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), and because one thousand eight hundred and sixty years have passed since the Great Master’s parinirvāṇa;
furthermore, according to the first chapter of the *Mahāsannipāta-ratnaketu-muṇḍarāja-sūtra*, the "Moon-Treasury" section: in the first five hundred years, liberation is firm;
in the second five hundred years, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is firm; in the third five hundred years, learning (*bahuśruta*) is firm; and in the fourth...
The fifth five-hundred-year period is when stūpas and monasteries are firmly established; the fifth [subsequent] five-hundred-year period is when strife and contention are firmly established.

Now, dwelling at the end of the era of stūpas and monasteries and approaching the time of strife and contention, I have instead heard this inconceivable sūtra; even if I were to shatter my body, it could not repay the merit of this occasion.
How much more so now that I have encountered a sagely sovereign! [This constitutes] the second pair. Now, I personally rejoice in this joy, for there are three aspects to this joy.
First, the celebration of the time; second, the celebration of the place; third, the celebration of cultivation. Regarding the first, this refers to encountering a sagely sovereign.
It is said that a bright era is difficult to meet, yet now we have encountered a sagely and enlightened Son of Heaven who widely disseminates the five teachings and loftily expounds the One Vehicle.

Monasteries stand in rows and the sounds of bells and sutras intermingle, enabling those who dwell in leisure to study at the academy and investigate the profound gate. This is the first blessing. Second... [text fragment ends].
To be present on Mount Ling is a place of celebration. This Cool and Spiritually Resonant Mountain is the foremost among the three thousand [worlds].
Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage and Teacher of all Buddhas, though his golden body resides in the East, his dwelling place is itself the abode of the Golden Great Sage.

Although he pervades the entire Dharma-realm to gather sentient beings according to their capacities, he remains eternally upon this mountain. His responsive manifestations are universally pervasive, like the reflections of a hundred rivers falling into a pool.
Pure coolness abides eternally like the bright moon; its light illuminates the void, and ten thousand sages have offered their profound praise upon the Five Peaks.

For a hundred *kalpas*, blessings have been transmitted through the ages. How much more so for this Great Faith (Dafu) Lingjiu Temple, which bears the name of a sacred monastery, where I, a humble monk of no merit, am numbered among the residents.
Such is my fortune and joy, yet I feel shame for my many past lives—this is my second blessing. (3)
For those who exhaust their thoughts upon the profound essence, this is the joy of their cultivation.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Flower Ornament Scripture of the Great Vaipulya, is the deep treasury of Vairocana and the heart-mind of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; it is that which all Buddhas have realized and all Bodhisattvas uphold.
It encompasses both nature and characteristics without omission, and uniquely transcends through the perfection of principle and wisdom.

That it shall not fall into the hands of others—how fortunate that I may receive and uphold it! That even a Bodhisattva who has accumulated merit for eons might still be lost in confusion—how fortunate that I may explore its profound depths!
That I may sacrifice my life to find its final resting place and exhaust my thoughts to find where it truly belongs—this is my third source of fortune.
How could there not be cause for celebration? This concludes the three preceding points. It is like one drowning in a vast ocean who encounters a fragrant vessel.
Descending from the vast void upon a divine crane, my joy knows no bounds; to what degree could I express it through hand-clapping?
Thus, my gratitude and celebration can only be understood by the sages and worthies who truly know me.
The title *Da fangguang fo huayan jing* (The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra) is the collective name for the inexhaustible sūtras.
The first chapter, "The Exquisite Adornment of the World Lord," is a specific heading for the various categories of meaning within the collection of sections.
Regarding the title of the tenth [section], the *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, the following provides a brief explanation of the title;

since the ninth gate provides an extensive explanation, this is termed "brief. Within this, there are three parts: first, the dual presentation of the sūtra and the chapter; second, the dual... [text continues].
Explanation of the Two Categories and Three Pairs of Headings. First, regarding the headings of the sūtra:

from the brief to the extensive, the unfolding of this inconceivable ocean of teaching is inexhaustible, for it never departs from these seven characters; thus, they are called the general name for the "Inexhaustible Sūtras. Following this, "Chapter One:
The Sublime Array of the World Ruler" is the specific heading that distinguishes the thematic categories among the various sections. This is the heading.
The "items" (*pǐnmù*) are numerous; the chapters consist of thirty-nine items. An "item" refers to a category where the meanings differ;
as this is now one of them, it is called a "distinct item.

"Great" (*dà*) signifies vastness that encompasses the boundless; "square" (*fāng*) signifies maintaining oneself through the True Dharma (*saddharma*). "Broad" (*guǎng*) means to accord with the essence and pervade the Buddha.
This means that awakening to this profound and wondrous [teaching], adorned with the flowers of merit and the myriad practices, serves as the ornament for the person who embodies the Dharma;

the sutra is thus a gushing spring of inexhaustible [wisdom], penetrating the profound and concentrated sublime meanings, encompassing the boundless ocean-like assemblies, and establishing an eternal standard for all time.

"Great" (Mahā) signifies vastness and inclusiveness. Below, two pairs are explained to clarify the two aspects. First, the general title is explained; second, the specific chapter titles are explained. Regarding the first:

there are ten gates for explaining these seven characters, each character having ten meanings. Here, we shall briefly cite the explanation for each character as it occurs. However, these seven characters can be summarized into six pairs:
first, the character "Sūtra" (經) refers to the teaching, while the six characters above refer to the meaning.

1) "Teaching" (*jiao*) and "meaning" (*yi*) form one pair; 2) the two characters "adornment" (*yan*) are the general [term], while the preceding five are the specific [terms], forming the pair of general and specific;
3) "Flowers" (*hua*) are the adorners, while the preceding four are all that which is adorned, forming the pair of the adorer and the adorned;
4) "Buddha" is that which is adorned as the person, while the preceding three are the dharmas that adorn, forming the pair of person and dharma; 5) "Extensive" (*guang*) refers to this.

Using the first two characters, "body" (*ti*) and "function" (*yong*), constitutes the pair of essence and function; using the six directions, it constitutes the pair of characteristics (*xiang*) and nature (*xing*).

Thus, these seven characters represent the seven greatnesses: "greatness of nature" (*xing da*), "greatness of essence" (*ti da*), "greatness of characteristics" (*xiang da*), "greatness of function" (*yong da*), "greatness of fruition" (*guo da*) represented by "Buddha," "greatness of cause" (*yin da*) represented by "flower," and "greatness of wisdom" (*zhi da*) represented by "adornment. This is the *Sūtra*.
Regarding this teaching, "Great" (*mahat*) refers to all seven characters being great, as all seven characters are equal.
Now, each shall be explained according to two meanings. As for "Great" being expansive and inclusive without limit: "expansive and inclusive" clarifies its capacity for containment;

it is explained as "vast" and "pervasive" to signify "Great. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "That which is called 'Great' has a nature that is vast and extensive, like empty space. The subsequent scripture states:
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) pervades all places, all sentient beings, and all lands;

throughout the three periods of time, it exists without exception, yet it has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended. Regarding the "two boundaries," if discussed in terms of the vertical dimension, it is called Great Nirvāṇa because it is eternal.
As for what is termed "Great," it is designated as "eternal. The subsequent scripture states: "The Dharma..."
The nature is without action and without change, just as empty space is fundamentally pure; the realm of all Buddhas is likewise.

Its essence is neither a substantial entity nor a non-entity, being free from existence and non-existence. Yet, because its profound treasury cannot be fathomed, it is designated by means of the "Great";
in reality, however, it transcends both speech and thought. As the subsequent scripture says: "The Dharma-nature does not reside in..."
Speech is without speaking; free from speech, it is eternally quiescent. This is the realm of all Buddhas, immeasurable;
yet for the sake of awakening sentient beings, I have now explained it briefly. Regarding that which upholds itself by means of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), there are also two meanings:

first, "direction" (*diś*) signifies correctness; second, "direction" signifies the Dharma. To simultaneously uphold these two natures (*svabhāva*) and penetrate both meanings refers to the nature [of the Buddha] as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

Virtue is itself the magnitude of the marks (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*), and because it is entirely without partiality or falsehood, it is called "correct" (*samyak*). Since all things can serve as a standard and support, they are designated as "Dharma.

As the subsequent scripture states: "Ordinary beings lack awakening and understanding; the Buddha causes them to abide in the True Dharma (*saddharma*). All dharmas have no place of abiding; to awaken to this is to see one's own body.
When this is expanded, it is said to be pervasive throughout the essence. This is precisely the magnitude of function (*vṛtti-mahat*); its functioning is like [the following].
Because its essence is such, there is nothing it does not pervade; yet this involves two meanings, as the essence itself possesses two aspects:
first, the capacity to encompass, and second, the capacity to pervade. This is like empty space, which encompasses the myriad phenomena and pervades all places, whether material or immaterial.
Now, when we speak of the essence, we speak of its oneness; when we speak of the essence’s encompassing, then even a single speck of dust contains the non-existence of the entire world.
Regarding the two "limits" (borders), their pervasiveness as the essence itself means that in each moment they encompass the entire *dharmadhātu* without end;
the three characters above—essence, characteristic, and function—are without obstruction and constitute the *dharmadhātu* that is realized.

As for the Buddha, who is one who awakens (*buddha*) to this profound mystery, there are also two meanings: first, he is the "awakened one" (*buddha*), a Sanskrit term which here is translated as "awakening."

Therefore, these two aspects of what is awakened to are precisely the Mahāvaipulya; as this constitutes the profound and wondrous realm, it is said that "to awaken to this profundity and wonder" refers to this very thing—namely, the aforementioned Mahāvaipulya. To explain them separately:

"awakening to the function" refers to awakening to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); "awakening to the essence" refers to awakening to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); and "awakening to the characteristics" refers to...
Awakening is the Middle Way. The mutual fusion of the three truths and the unimpeded nature of the three types of awakening constitute "wondrous awakening" (*miao-jue*).

The metaphor of the flower represents the myriad practices; this also carries two meanings: first, the flower as the fruition of the result, because the myriad practices bring about the fruit of Buddhahood—either coexisting with that fruit or not yet coexisting with it.
When they coexist, it is like a lotus flower, which symbolizes the mutual penetration of cause and effect.
They do not coexist [simultaneously], like the blossoms of the peach and plum trees, because the prior cause and the subsequent fruit are not destroyed [at the same time].

Thus, the metaphor of the two adornments of the body as flowers refers to the merits of the various stages, which must coexist with the fruits of cultivation. As the sutra below states: "Dharmas such as supernormal powers are like flowers in full bloom;
the various marks are like flowers possessing the thirty-two [major characteristics]. This means that those who adorn the person through the Dharma have two kinds of adornment.
The first meaning is that the ten thousand practices adorn the fundamental essence, which is the sublime Mahāvaipulya, like polishing a bright mirror;

though the mirror is inherently pure, it is not clear unless polished. The second meaning is that through the merit of the ten thousand practices, one becomes a person who attains the fruit of Buddhahood, like carving an image from jade or casting an image from gold; thus, one completes the person through practice.

The *Qiaozhang Chengxiang Jing* (Sutra on the Skillful Artisan Forming Images) provides a commentary on the "gushing spring of inexhaustibility" (*wujie zhi yongquan*). Although the sutra below mentions only four meanings, these can be reduced to two:

namely, "pervasion" (*guan*) and "inclusion" (*she*). The "gushing spring" refers to the meaning of that which is included; "eternal flavor" (*changwei*) applies generally to the three preceding [meanings].

The first commentary, "the gushing spring of inexhaustibility," still applies generally to all teachings. The second, "pervading the profound and coagulating" (*guanyu xuanning*), applies specifically to the ultimate teaching.

The subtle meaning of this [text] generally accords with the specific, as it penetrates the profound and wondrous meaning of the *Avataṃsaka*. "Ning" (congealed) refers to a state of profound stillness and solemn order.

Third, "encompassing the boundless oceanic assemblies" means that the term "oceanic assemblies" is restricted here to the congregations of this specific sutra, thereby distinguishing them from other assemblies. Fourth, "establishing the eternal norm for all time" means...

Regarding the meaning of "constant" (*nitya*), other commentaries explain that it refers to the "pathway of the hundred kings. Here, however, it is explained through the general in relation to the particular:
because the Dharma-eye within this sutra is eternally complete and without deficiency, the teaching of its constancy is not merely provisional;
since it has never deviated from antiquity, it may be called "constant. This concludes the explanation of the general title.

▲The Buddhas and the various kings are both titled "World Lords" (*Lokendra*), and their Dharma and its physical manifestations (*dharmadhātu* and *rūpakāya*) are collectively termed "Sublime Adornment" (*Suṣṭhu-vyūha*).
By categorizing these meanings and titles, the name of this chapter is established; it stands at the head of all sections and is designated as the foremost.
The Buddha and all the kings are equally called "World Lords" (*Lokendra*). This explains the title "World Lord. "World" (*loka*) refers to the world, namely the threefold world:
the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*), and the world of the perfectly awakened ones (*vidyā-sambuddha-loka*).
"Lord" (*indra*) refers to a sovereign, namely the various kings and Buddhas. Furthermore, it refers to the lords of the earth spirits, water spirits, forest spirits, mountain spirits, and so forth.
The World-Rulers of the Receptacle World—such as the Heavenly Kings, Dragon Kings, and Yakṣa Kings—are the rulers of the sentient world;

the Tathāgata is the ruler of the world of wisdom and perfect enlightenment. Since he universally transforms the former two and universally presides over the latter three, they are all collectively termed "World-Rulers.
Regarding the statement that both the primary and secondary [environments] are called "wondrous adornments," these adornments are also explained in three ways.

The Dharma-gate of Adorning the World is that which is able to adorn; it is restricted solely to the "ruler" (the primary subject). That which is adorned—the "retinue and the supported" (the secondary objects)—pervades the three worlds.

I have cited the sūtras and śāstras to provide a detailed explanation [of the preceding stages], while in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*), I have presented them only in brief.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Transcending the World" fully encompasses all the stages; within each individual stage, the meanings are subsumed without omission.

Although some names may differ while the meaning remains the same, or there may be variations in length between earlier and later sections, there is no discrepancy whatsoever in the sequence of the forty-two stages, all of which are now fully contained herein.

I have cited and explained the textual passages from the six assemblies of the sūtra in parallel, so that they may be clearly seen. Thus, every sentence of this seven-fascicle sūtra is provided with its source.

When one examines past interpretations, it is evident that arbitrary explanations are particularly numerous. Furthermore, regarding the two schools of Nature (Dharmatā) and Characteristics (Dharma-lakṣaṇa), there are both similarities and differences in their presentation of dharmic characteristics;
for instance, such categories as the five eyes and ten eyes, or the six supernormal powers and ten supernormal powers, are each demonstrated individually to ensure there is no confusion.

Regarding the remaining afflictions, explaining them through the ten bodies as in the first fascicle’s "Praise of Virtues" constitutes the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) of the *dharmatā* school.
Regarding the explanation of the entry of wisdom into the three periods of time, the extensive citation of the four wisdoms constitutes the *dharmalakṣaṇa* of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* school.
Regarding the explanation of the name "ocean of multitudes" by means of the gates of liberation of the ocean of multitudes, this constitutes the *dharmalakṣaṇa* of the *dharmatā* school.
The nine gates and six perfections explain the ten perfections, which are the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) of the Dharmalakṣaṇa school.

Thus, the ten penetrations (*daśābhijñā*) and ten patiences (*daśakṣānti*) subsume the six penetrations and five patiences; the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) and ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) integrate the three bodies (*trikāya*) and three knowledges (*trijñāna*);
and the ten gates of *nirvāṇa* harmonize the four types of *nirvāṇa*. Through the ten kinds of Buddha-wisdom, a single wisdom is integrated.
The four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*) are the Dharma-characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) that are without contradiction between the two schools of Nature (*svabhāva*) and Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Their applications are manifold; furthermore, the Dharma-characteristics elucidated in various sutra commentaries are mostly incidental. For instance, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* merely states:
"The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge and vision, his fearlessnesses, his dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, which penetrate deeply into the boundless"—this is a general praise.

The Buddha’s wisdom is profound and far-reaching: encountering the character "One Power" (eka-bala), he establishes the Chapter on the Ten Powers; encountering the character "Fearlessness," he establishes the Chapter on the Four Fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*);

regarding dhyāna, he establishes the four dhyānas; regarding samādhi, he establishes the eight concentrations; and for the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and samādhis, each is established as a chapter heading.

If one were to continue in this manner, establishing thousands and tens of thousands of chapters to explain a single fascicle of a sutra, one would still not reach the end. How much more so if it were to be fully accomplished?

The realm of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) must be further studied through extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). If one takes the profound mystery of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it merely demonstrates that there is equality in knowledge and vision;
what was previously brought forth and internalized is what this son knows, yet the ten chapters and five sections cannot exhaust its subtlety.
If the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* differs from this—as in the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), and so forth—the single scripture contains dozens [of such categories].

Since we are situated in the light, it is necessary to synthesize a chapter to suddenly illuminate its essential meaning: within the "Ten Stages" (Daśabhūmika) section, if one does not take the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as the gate of contemplation, how can one understand the name "Stainless" (*Vimalā*) without comprehending the three aggregates? Without understanding the eight dhyānas, how can one know the practice of "Luminous" (*Prabhākārī*)?
On the fourth stage, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) accomplish the light of the wisdom of non-arising; on the fifth stage, the various truths [are realized].

Exhausting the ultimate and the conventional to transform sentient beings, the *Prajñāpāramitā* of the sixth stage involves contemplating dependent origination through ten gates arranged like a constellation;
when the moon of the three contemplations is full, one investigates and exhausts both nature and characteristics until *prajñā* manifests before one—this is not a distant pointing toward the past.

Within the three vehicles, the seventh stage exhausts all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), where provisional and ultimate truths are practiced in tandem; at the eighth stage, there are seven exhortations.
Only when one perceives the Way of Non-action can one occupy the rank of Dharma Master on the Ninth Ground;
only by knowing the appropriate medicine for each ailment can one extensively transform sentient beings through the forty kinds of eloquence.

It is only upon attaining the Tenth Ground that the profound mystery of the All-Knowing Wisdom (sarvajñā) is fully realized and the forty-two stages are clearly manifested; these are collectively termed the nine assemblies and five cycles of contemplative practice.

Because the causes and effects of the Buddha-way are both square and round, whether in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or nature (*svabhāva*), or cause or effect, there is nothing that does not constitute contemplation and nothing that does not accord with the Truth.

To practice in reliance upon the sūtras is entirely the intention of the Sages. If one does not understand the characteristics of dharmas, not only will one fail to know the Sage’s intent, but one will also not be a person capable of propagating and elucidating [the teaching]. One should know this for oneself by examining the text. [End of] Section Eight, "Extensive Explanation."

Regarding the exposition of profound words (*xuan yan*): it is said that this scripture contains many profound statements and subtle principles (*miao zhi*) which were not extensively elucidated in the past.

Some were indicated as being in separate chapters, while others were presented only briefly and incompletely. Those that should now be fully detailed are entirely contained within the commentary (*shu wen*). The phrasing is easy to follow while the meaning is deep;

by broadly unfolding its structural form, it is as if the Buddha has just attained perfect enlightenment, so that those of wisdom may harmonize it with the initial establishment of the various schools.
The three periods of time are explained by means of two, three, or four types of knowledge;
this is fully exhausted through the citation of the "Chapter on the Hare" within the analogy of an illusion. The analogy of a shadow is distinguished by dividing it into three shadows.

In the seventh dedication, various phrases such as "the lands are equal" are set forth to differentiate [the stages]. In the eighth dedication, vows are generated across objects of experience in a horizontal manner.
Establishing the successive stages to manifest them, the three heavens are eulogized through verses on the dedication that transcends all marks;

this is further harmonized with the profound and wondrous principles of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other deep sutras, as well as the *Śata-śāstra*. Throughout the nine assemblies and five cycles, both nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are extensively expounded.
The Samādhi of Samantabhadra exhausts the most subtle within the subtle, while the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) brings to completion the most profound within the profound.

The profound contemplation of the Flower Treasury of the Dharma-realm (Dharmadhātu-kusuma-garbha) as far as its ultimate aim, the subtle chapters on the vital channels of the essential gateways, and the obscure subtleties of all key points—these exhaustively investigate the boundaries of principles and meanings.
Just as the three mysteries (sanxuan) of the "Inner and Outer" (Guanzhong xibiao) contain elegant maxims, one must know that this scripture necessarily exhausts their profundity.
Furthermore, those who point to specific chapters [as being exhaustive] do not understand the primary essence. One should know this.

This does not contradict the ignorant, but merely serves to widely propagate [the truth]. Ninth, regarding the eradication of right and wrong: In the past, people were high-spirited in their pursuit of victory and defeat, and their sentiments toward right and wrong were deep.
While the wondrous meanings of antiquity were put into practice, they were not spoken of; yet the minor flaws of former sages were extensively refuted and rejected.
For instance, when it was said that the form of the Sahā world is like empty space, it was immediately remarked, "This is simply because the translators were not proficient [in the language]."
The scriptures and treatises were erroneously introduced to the translation assemblies, causing errors that have tainted the holy teachings all at once.
When our former masters worked within these translations, their chisels and axes struck far too deeply; it is like having a speck of dust inside a pearl—what need is there to strike and shatter it?

Furthermore, in the commentary on the "Ten Practices" chapter regarding non-abiding in the middle stream, various divergent interpretations were extensively set forth; because the Jin translation lost its essential meaning, the ancient commentaries resulted in mere verbal branches.

The present text is already clear; why must one recount the past? Instances of this kind are numerous, and to spend all day in disputes over right and wrong is surely not in accord with the Great Way.
As for those who refute established meanings: they are like a venomous snake that has bitten the hand—one must cut it off;

or like a poisonous tree growing in the courtyard—it must be felled. If there are erroneous interpretations that confuse the tracks of the truth, the matter must be resolved as easily as turning over one's palm.
Knowing that certain matters are not concise, they are not described; if something appears to be correct yet is not, it is resolved so that it may be made clear.

Just as one who wishes to recognize true gold must know brass, so too—driven by necessity and having set aside personal biases regarding right and wrong—one must, even when offering refutations, maintain propriety and ritual.
One must not exalt one’s own virtues while looking down upon the sages of old; one must recognize that these were the pioneers.

Regarding those who find it difficult to cultivate [the path] yet easily indulge in criticism: even if they raise objections, this merely reveals their own lack of discernment between right and wrong, as they are simply self-aggrandizing and self-promoting.

Consequently, in the present commentary (*śāstra*), instances of such partisan judgment are extremely rare. Tenth, regarding the harmonious integration of the beginning and the end: Generally speaking, the overall structure of this commentary places primary emphasis on the initial stages and treats the later stages with relative brevity.

However, if one were to further expand the scope of its thematic divisions, the exegesis of the text would become sparse; thus, it has been composed in this manner for the purpose of widely propagating and elucidating the Holy Teachings.
Zhidun now [explains] that because this Great Sūtra’s nine assemblies, from beginning to end, are profoundly profound, whenever a meaning is encountered, it is immediately clarified;
there is no selection between the beginning and the end, for what has already been explained at the outset need not be clarified again later.

Thus, the topical outlines and chapter headings are distributed like scattered stars, allowing the "goodness in the beginning, middle, and end" to be observed from start to finish. Briefly stated, there are these ten intentions for composing this commentary. Therefore:

Forgetting my own body in this sacred realm, I reverently expound these profound teachings; my original intention is solely for all sentient beings to attain equality with Samantabhadra and all Buddhas.
▲ Regarding the third section of two lines, "dedicating this supreme merit," which refers to the dedication to sentient beings:
the preceding two lines define the purpose for which this commentary is composed—namely, for the sake of sentient beings. This present section universally dedicates the benefits of taking refuge.

As for the merit of composing this commentary, if even a single phrase should accord with the Sage’s mind, may it all serve sentient beings to attain the great awakening, perfect luminosity, and the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

Fourth, because one has understood that the meaning of "perfect" (yuan) is all-encompassing, vast, profound, and deep, yet does not yet know what kind of faculties and capacities this profundity is intended for, it is followed by the section on "The Teachings and Their Intended Capacities.
