pervading the atoms within the aforementioned six types of lands, each of which contains both similar and dissimilar lands; 8.

pervading the entirety of the realm of empty space, such that within every single tip of a hair there exist boundless oceans of lands; 9. like a net of Indra (*Indrajāla*); 10. shared by other Buddhas.
Regarding these two [texts], while their ten names and general purports are largely the same, there are slight differences. The *Zhigui* (The Return to the Source) states:
first, this Jambudvīpa; second, the hundreds of billions of worlds; third, throughout the ten directions; fourth, pervading the paths of all atoms; fifth, penetrating other realms;

sixth, encompassing the atoms of all lands; seventh, returning to the Flower Treasury World; eighth, the re-inclusion of lands; ninth, like the net of Indra; tenth, the shared presence of all Buddhas. Now [the present text] follows this.
The reason why this commentary differs from that [previous one] is that returning to the Flower Treasury (*Huazang*) is identical to the aforementioned non-obstruction of the defiled and the pure;
therefore, it is not established as a separate category. Thus, the *Zhigui* (Text on the Ultimate Aim) states: "When phenomena are exhausted, principle manifests;

because the marks of defilement are exhausted, both the lands contained within the atoms and those pervading the atoms are equally atoms. Furthermore, among the seven categories, the eighth—encompassing the lands—is also included therein.
In the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*, it is explained that within each atom of the Flower Treasury World (*padma-garbha-loka-dhātu*), every single atom encompasses an ocean of other lands;

yet, because these are no different from the atoms of the first land, they are all omitted [from explicit enumeration]. Instead, the numbers four, five, and six are added to form ten meanings. Those three [numbers] correspond to these eight, and those five correspond to these three.
This is the intended meaning found in the "Chapter on the Radiance of Enlightenment" (*prabhāsa-bodhi-paṭala*) within the *Xian-shou lüeshu* (Brief Commentary by Xianshou).
And it is used [in this way]. Regarding the statement that it is "like ascending Mount Sumeru," this text serves as proof.

As for the phrase "pervading the dharma-realm in seven locations," the text says: "At that time, the World-Honored One, without leaving beneath any of the bodhi trees, ascended Mount Sumeru and proceeded to the palace of Śakra-devendra, saying: 'The worlds of the ten directions are all likewise. This is the dharma.
The *Prajñā-gāthā* states: "All those in Jambudvīpa say the Buddha is among them; we now see the Buddha dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru;
so it is in all ten directions. By the Tathāgata’s power of mastery, he pervades the entire Dharma-realm. This passage describes how it is likewise in all seven locations.
Although the text mentions only the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Worthies) and the three heavens, it expresses the meaning of being omnipresent without arising.

As stated in the commentary regarding the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance": this proves that throughout the ten billion-fold dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there are similar types within each realm.
"Similar type" means that each possesses ten billion Mount Sumerus, great oceans, Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), four continents, and twenty-eight heavens;
because they all possess these in equal measure, they are called "similar. Thus, that sutra says: "In this way..."
Innumerable, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, and unspeakable—
all worlds throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, as well as those in the south, west, north,
the four intermediate directions, and above and below, are likewise so. Within each and every one of those worlds, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas.
Extending upward even to the hundred billion Akaniṣṭha heavens, everything therein was clearly manifest.
Within each of those Jambudvīpas, the Tathāgata was seen seated upon a Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne, surrounded by bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields.
Because it specifies "only Jambudvīpa," the term "hundred billion" is used to distinguish them from other realms.
Because they differ from those below, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). Regarding the phrase "one realm," it refers to the three [realms] that pervade.
As for the "lands with the shapes of trees and so forth," the first two are both brief explanations, while the latter eight merely list their names.
The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes rivers, whirlpools, and other such shapes. The Sūtra lists twenty such shapes, concluding that there are unspeakably many unspeakable Buddhas.
The various distinct categories, as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, each pervade the space of the ten directions and the dharma-realm;

like the previously mentioned Sumeru-world-systems, they do not obstruct one another, and within each of them, this wheel of Dharma is turned. Regarding the phrase "pervading the four types of world-systems":
previously, when clarifying the distinct categories, only those among the ten billion [worlds] were cited; it is now that these are fully explained.
Regarding the phrase "the variety of world-systems" (*kṣetra-vyūha*), although the term is common to the Flower Treasury World (*puṣpa-garbha-loka-dhātu*), its general meaning here is specific.

When it says "pervading the world-systems," it refers specifically to the world-system called "Blazing Jewel Radiance Shining Universally in the Ten Directions," located within the Fragrant Water Ocean of Boundless Sublime Flower Light at the very center;
therein are contained twenty tiers of Buddha-lands, as numerous as the atoms of dust. These constitute the existence [of this world-system].
World-systems as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields are arrayed therein, and now Vairocana likewise pervades them all.

Regarding the "fivefold pervasion of the Flower Treasury" (Huazang), it means that throughout a single Flower Treasury realm, there are the aforementioned ten kinds of world-systems as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
since these are all purified and adorned by the causal practices of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he constantly dwells within it and expounds the Dharma; six times over, he pervades the oceans of lands in other realms.

As for the various types of lands and world-systems, these refer to the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions beyond the Flower Treasury World, extending limitlessly to the furthest reaches of the Dharma-realm, just as in the case of the Flower Treasury itself.
As stated in the sixth fascicle, the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs," to the east of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean, there is a world...
The ocean of realms in the south is named Pure Light Lotus Adornment;
in the west, Jewel Moon Radiance Universal Adornment Treasury; in the north, Lapis Lazuli Lotus Light Perfect Treasury;
in the northeast, Jāmbūnada Gold and Crystal-Colored Banner; and in the southeast, Golden Ornamentation.
In the southwest, it is named "Lapis Lazuli Light Universally Shining"; in the northwest, "Jewel Light Illuminating Everywhere";
in the nadir, "Lotus Fragrance Wondrous Virtue Treasury"; and in the zenith, "Maṇi Jewel Radiance Adornment.

It is stated that these are equal in number to the atoms within ten billion Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra*). Regarding the "seven pervasions," the first six categories refer to the atoms of the Buddha-fields.
The preceding six sections each constitute a distinct category. All these lands above are composed of atoms;
within every single atom there are Buddha-lands, and Tathāgatas preach the sutras within those lands inside the atoms. Therefore, the *Flower Treasury* chapter says:
"Within every single atom of all the atoms of the Flower Treasury World, one sees the Dharma-realm. Since even the Dharma-realm...
How much more so for an entire realm? Furthermore, it is said that within each and every atom, inconceivable realms abide individually according to the minds of sentient beings.
It is also said: "Just as one sees the Buddha’s seat in this assembly, so it is in all atoms. These passages are not merely words;
they exhaustively describe how even within a single hair-tip, there are infinite [realms] contained throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space.

Regarding "the oceans of lands at the boundaries," this does not refer to the atoms that constitute the lands, but rather takes the space capable of containing those atoms as extending throughout all of emptiness.
Just as the empty space between two world-systems, though devoid of material objects, is also a place capable of containing atoms,
here we take all that is capable of containing atoms— whether there be lands or no lands, whether there be atoms or no atoms— throughout the entire dharma-realm and the realm of empty space.
In every location—whether of the same or different kinds, including all infinite lands—the Tathāgata constantly turns the wheel of Dharma.
As stated in the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*: "The number of lands existing upon a single hair-tip is immeasurable and cannot be fully described;
even if one were to take as many hair-tips as there are in the measure of empty space, the lands upon each and every one of those hair-tips would be exactly like this. Thus it is of that hair-tip.
Abiding in all lands, there are immeasurable varieties of distinct dwellings; there are unspeakably many dissimilar buddha-fields and unspeakably many similar buddha-fields.
At every point the size of a hair-tip, there are pure fields that cannot be described, with unspeakably various adornments and unspeakably various wonders—such are the words that cannot be spoken.
Since these realizations are not singular, regarding the teaching of the Dharma therein, the subsequent verse states:
"In each and every tip of a hair, one proclaims the names of unspeakable numbers of Buddhas; one emits unspeakable sublime sounds;
one turns the wheel of the True Dharma unspeakably many times; and within each and every turning of that wheel of Dharma, one expounds unspeakable numbers of sūtras."
Within each of those sūtras, the differentiation of dharma-gates is unspeakable;
within each of those dharma-gates, the teaching of all dharmas is again unspeakable; within each of those dharmas, the taming of sentient beings is unspeakable—and so forth.
The phrase "like a net of Indra" means that since each and every atom already encompasses [all others], [the same applies to these teachings].
The ocean of boundless lands is equal to this very land; furthermore, within each atom there are oceans of lands.
Thus, atom by atom, the lands are inexhaustible, and land by land, they are infinite.
Like the net of Indra’s palace, layer upon layer, beyond description as to its dimensions, so too is the Vairocana Buddha infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
The statement that "he constantly expounds the Dharma inexhaustibly" refers to more than ten Buddhas, as explained below in the text itself.
Nevertheless, although each of the ten aforementioned categories individually pervades the entire dharma-realm, the first nine are precisely the locations where Vairocana expounds the Dharma.
Now, regarding the phrase "the ten categories above" and so forth, this is the third section, a summary.

Because the first two of the ten preceding sections contain the expression "pervading the dharma-realm," while from the third to the tenth these words are abbreviated, the present summary concludes that all [categories] pervade [the dharma-realm].

▲ However, although it is taught that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth each individually pervade the entire dharma-realm—even down to a single mote of dust or a hair—their respective gateways are distinct and yet remain without confusion.
Regarding this, the fourth section of the commentary on the "Ten Stages" addresses a potential objection: Suppose someone were to ask, "If the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven speaks of the ten [stages]..."
Since the Dharma-abiding already pervades empty space and extends to the path of a hair-pore, it is not yet known whether the Yāma Heaven and others also teach the Ten Abidings.
If one says they do not, what fault is there? Both positions have defects. If they do not teach them, then the locus of teaching is not all-pervasive;
if they also teach them, then there would be confusion. Why, then, does the Sūtra state only that the Ten Abidings are taught in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?

In the *Dharmāyatana-sūtra*, it is taught that there are ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and so forth; therefore, this provides a comprehensive explanation. Within this, there are three parts: first, a general response to the previous question;
second, a further clarification regarding a repeated objection; and third, a point-by-point reconciliation of the lower stages by using one case as an example for the rest.

Regarding the first part, there is the "Gate of Concealment and Manifestation": when one gate is manifested, the other gates are concealed. For example, when the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) are taken as the gate, [the others are hidden].
To say that the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi) pervade the Ten Practices (daśacaryā) as their gateway means that it clarifies only how the Ten Abodes pervade the Ten Practices and so forth;
thus, while they function as gateways differently, there is no confusion or disorder.
If one considers the Ten Abodes and the Ten Practices in terms of the complete mutual inclusion of their respective stages, then each is entirely absent from the other, yet each pervades all.
If the *dharmadhātu* is considered in terms of the mutual support of its various stages, then these subsequent stages possess one another and equally pervade the *dharmadhātu*.

If it is argued that from the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) onward they possess one another and equally pervade the *dharmadhātu*, this constitutes a second level of generalization and a further objection;
namely, there is another question: "If they are different as gates of entry, do they not see one another? Or [is it that] they do?

If they were to see one another, it would again result in confusion; if they do not see one another, how can one know that they are all-pervasive? Now, in response to this question, it is clarified that there is both seeing and non-seeing:
if we speak in terms of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*), then they do not see one another; if we speak in terms of mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*), then we allow for mutual seeing.
It is said that if we speak in terms of the ten abodes (*shízhù*) and the ten practices (*shíxíng*) fully encompassing one another’s positions, then [they are mutually inclusive].

The statement that "they are mutually non-existent yet each individually pervades the Dharma-realm" refers to the gate of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*). This means that if the ten abodes (*shí zhù*) are subsumed within the other stages, then there are only the ten abodes;
the other stages are like empty space because, having been discarded by the [subsumption of] the other stages, they become identical to the ten abodes. The same applies to the other stages.
When the ten abodes are pervasive, it is not the case that the ten practices (*shí xíng*) and so forth are pervasive; therefore, it is said that "each individually pervades the Dharma-realm."
Regarding the term "dhātu" (realm), if one considers how the various positions mutually support one another, then each possesses the others, and they collectively pervade the entire dharma-realm;

this is the "entrance through characteristics. This is because, in terms of their functional power, they mutually support one another without destroying their respective selves and others, like two mirrors reflecting each other.
Thus, when the eastern mirror moves, the reflection within it also moves; therefore, although they pervade the dharma-realm equally, there is still a distinction between host and guest.

Because they are companions, there is no confusion; for example, when the Ten Abodes serve as the gateway, the Ten Practices and so forth are associated with them as they equally pervade the Dharma-realm.

At that time, they are simply called the "pervasion of the Ten Abodes" and not the "pervasion of the Ten Practices" and so forth. The same applies when the Ten Practices and so forth serve as the gateway.

Thus, that which possesses the power to encompass is the primary [host], while that which lacks the power to encompass and is being encompassed is the companion. This prior characteristic is itself the gateway.
When the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) are universally pervasive, this does not obstruct the other universal pervasions; it is merely a difference between the hidden and the manifest.
When the ten abodes are universally pervasive, the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) and so forth are hidden; when the ten practices are universally pervasive, the others are likewise hidden.

According to the gate of mutual identity (*sōji-mon*), they are also called "purely pervasive," because within every atom and hair-pore of the dharma-realm, there are only the ten abodes and so forth. This is the subsequent gate of entering characteristics (*sōnyū-mon*).
It is also called the "Miscellaneous Gate" because all stages mutually support one another simultaneously and universally;
thus, within the Ten Abodes there are the Ten Practices and so forth, the remaining meanings of which will be explained in detail in the section on the "Delineation of Meanings."
▲ Know that each of the assemblies should be understood according to this principle.
▲ Regarding the ten or more Buddhas who are identical: since this Buddha is thus, other Buddhas follow the same example;
therefore, at the conclusion of each assembly, it is universally stated, "We, all Buddhas, also speak in this way."

Regarding the section "The Ten or More Buddhas Are Identical," this is the fifth part, the re-explanation according to difficulties, which has two sub-sections: first, the formal manifestation of identical pervasiveness;

second, "Now, as for master and master... and so forth, which explains away potential objections. In the former, it is shown that vertically throughout the three periods of time and horizontally across the ten directions, the meritorious functions and the preaching of the Dharma of every Buddha are identical; therefore, the Sūtra says: "All Buddhas of the three periods have already taught [it]."
The statement "What has been said and what shall be said" refers to the citations from the sūtras within this commentary;
our various Buddhas also speak thus, which constitutes the horizontal discourse—that is, the words of the Dharma-Buddha. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"I do not see any Buddha-worlds where those Tathāgatas do not teach this Dharma," which refers to the words of the Dharma-preaching Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
▲ However, the principal does not see the principal, and the companions do not see the companions; yet the principal and the companions see one another.
If they did not see one another, each would pervade the entire dharma-realm; because they see one another, they equally pervade the dharma-realm without confusion and without obstruction.
However, regarding the two general responses to the following objection: suppose someone asks, "Do the abodes of other Buddhas and those of Vairocana Buddha see one another?
If you say they do not, what fault is there? Both positions entail errors. For if they see one another, it contradicts their universal pervasiveness;
if they do not see one another, it contradicts the relationship between the principal and its retinue. Therefore, this response is given: whether they see one another or not...
Both meanings are established: the meaning of mutual seeing as principal and attendant is established, and the meaning of seeing and not seeing is universally established.
The only difference is that while each is universal, they are universally so in the same manner. The text contains four propositions;
regarding "the principals do not see one another," when Vairocana is the principal, the other Buddhas of the ten directions can only serve as attendants and cannot themselves be principals.
If another Buddha acts as the principal, Vairocana also acts as his attendant and cannot be the principal; therefore it is said that "principal and principal do not see one another.
As for "attendant and attendant do not see one another," this means that when various Buddhas act as attendants to Vairocana, Vairocana in turn cannot act as their attendant;
thus it is said that "attendant and attendant do not see one another. This does not mean that those attendant Buddhas themselves do not exist.
Regarding the statement that those who do not see one another are called "principal and retinue" or "retinue and principal," those who do see one another correspond to the third and fourth phrases.

Fourth, as for the mutual seeing of the retinue and the principal: this is like Vairocana acting as the principal and seeing the other Buddha-retinues, while those Buddha-retinues likewise see Vairocana.
Fifth, as for the mutual seeing of the retinue and the principal: this is like Vairocana acting as the retinue [for] the other Buddhas...
When acting as the principal [subject], one attains mutual vision; however, the meaning of the second and third lines is no different from the first and fourth.

It is simply because they are mutually interpenetrated as principal and attendant with respect to a single person that they constitute four. As for "without confusion," it means they are established as distinct gates.
As for "without obstruction," it refers to their constant, harmonious inclusion.
▲ Furthermore, these ten locations together constitute the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination), wherein taking one includes all, because each and every location accords with the *dharmatā*.
▲ Moreover, at each preceding moment, [the teaching] pervades all these locations; likewise, at each individual location, this sutra is taught instantaneously, encompassing all preceding moments.

▲ This has been explained by way of the vessel world (*bhājana-loka*). If one were to explain it by way of the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbuddha*) and the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), then every single Buddha’s body, limb, joint, and pore encompasses infinite, layered lands; the same applies to each and every sentient being of Samantabhadra.
All of these are places where Vairocana preaches the sutras.
Furthermore, regarding the upper ten locations and the lower sixth, these ten meanings are integrated as a whole, which is divided into three parts:

first, the formal revelation of the mutual integration of the ten meanings; second, the sequential correlation of the locations with time; and third, the comprehensive revelation of their profound depth.
This means that the aforementioned ten layers refer only to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), and have not yet discussed the hairs of the Buddha or the hairs of sentient beings.
Regarding each and every matter within the "pore" (kōng), all are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
When it is said that "Samantabhadra and all sentient beings are likewise," this means that if Samantabhadra is viewed from the perspective of the Tathāgata, he is called the world of sentient beings;

yet if viewed from the perspective of sentient beings, he is called the world of the Perfectly Awakened One (Jñānasamyaksambuddha). Furthermore, to mention Samantabhadra is to encompass all Bodhisattvas.
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Second;
Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Third.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Monastery at Mount Qingliang.

▲ Third, regarding the "dependent lord": The true body (*dharmakāya*) is vast and empty, merging with the *dharmadhātu*; its essence encompasses all without exterior, and its function is equal to the myriad transformations.
At the source, there is no duality; yet when adhering to its traces, it manifests in manifold ways. Whether as one body or many bodies, the sūtras and śāstras offer differing explanations.
Third, regarding the "Dependent on the Master" (依主), the commentary is divided into five parts: first, a general presentation of the main intent;
second, from "Now I shall explain this sutra" onwards, posing questions to raise the subject; third, from "Therefore I speak this sutra" onwards, a general reconciliation of the teachings;

fourth, from "Now, first clarifying" onwards, opening the chapters for detailed explanation; fifth, from "Thus one knows that sometimes it is said" onwards, reconciling with other doctrines. Regarding the first: as it says...
The coming [of the Buddha] is solely the body of non-obstruction; it is only that the teachings differ according to the capacities of sentient beings. To speak of it:

the True Body (dharmakāya) is vast and empty, merging with the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). As for its essence: if one takes the Dharma-realm itself as the body, then the Dharma-realm is the body, and one does not speak of "merging with the essence.
Now, because non-obstructive wisdom is in profound accord with Suchness (tathatā), it is said to "merge with the essence. Thus, in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*...
It is said that when only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain, these two—suchness and wisdom—are together the True Body (*dharmakāya*).
Since wisdom is united with suchness, it causes the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the Buddha-body, and its merits to all be non-different from suchness.

To say that [this wisdom] encompasses all without exception and functions in equality with the myriad transformations means that, because its essence is united with suchness, there is nowhere it does not exist; and since suchness is omnipresent, there is nothing it does not pervade.
Because [the Buddha] encompasses all, the Buddha-body likewise has nothing that it does not encompass. The myriad transformations and so forth are the great function of the Dharma-body;
as for saying they are "equal," it is because the Tathāgata has attained a body whose measure is equal to all dharmas, and thus they are said to be "equal" by way of metaphor.

The two preceding meanings clarify that the essence and function of the Buddha are identical to the essence and function of the Dharmadhātu; therefore, the myriad transformations are integrated therein.
Thus, the true essence indeed unifies the subtle and the coarse in a perfect, non-obstructive fusion. Therefore, the subsequent commentary states: "To exhaust the source, there is no duality.
This means that if one follows the root to reach the branches, the myriad streams appear as distinct tributaries;
yet if one traces the flow back to its source, the thousand paths share no different tracks. It is like the vast expanse of the Three Rivers, all of which originate from Mount Min.
Those who cling to the traces in their manifold forms rely on the fundamental to reach the derivative, yet fail to realize that this multiplicity is merely the manifestation of traces.
As for the differing explanations in the sūtras and śāstras regarding one body and many bodies, these arise from the basis of clinging to the traces.

Because the sūtras and śāstras present divergent accounts of unity and plurality, the sūtras adapt to the capacities of beings and the treatises follow the sūtras; thus, those who understand the scriptures according to them may adhere to the teachings. If one were to recognize [this truth]...
Because its source is characterized by the non-obstruction of the one and the many, the *Jingming juepin* (Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance) states:

"A single body becomes immeasurable, and the immeasurable returns to being one; understanding all worlds, it manifests forms pervading everywhere. This body comes from nowhere and accumulates nowhere;
yet because sentient beings engage in conceptual discrimination, they perceive the Buddha’s various bodies. This is precisely the meaning [of the passage]. It says:
Regarding alternative explanations, some state that there is only one [body], as this sutra says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are together in a single dharma-realm;
their single mind, single wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses are likewise so. Others speak of two bodies, as the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains:

first, the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), and second, the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). It states that both the true reward body and the dharma-body are termed the "dharma-body," which is the true function.

Because of virtue and the Dharma, both the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are called "birth-bodies" (*janmakāya*), as they are born for the sake of sentient beings;
the intent in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is also the same. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are two Buddhas: first, the true Buddha, and second, the non-true Buddha;

the former is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and the latter refers to the reward and transformation bodies. In the subsequent sutra passages, there are also many explanations of these two, stating: "All... [text fragment].
The Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*) is fundamentally non-dual, yet it manifests forms in accordance with sentient beings, filling the world.

It is further said that the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, pure as empty space; whatever various forms appear therein cause beings to enter into this Dharma. Sometimes these are divided into three:

the Dharma-body, the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). It is also said that "Reward" is the same as "Response" (*nairmāṇika-kāya*), which is the Transformation-body. Alternatively, four types are taught.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of four types of Buddha: first, the Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Buddha); second, the Saṃbhogakāya (Merit-Body Buddha); third, the Jñānakāya (Wisdom Buddha);

and fourth, the Tathatākāya (Suchness Buddha). The first is the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the second is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and the last is the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). Furthermore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* speaks of four kinds:

first, the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is not the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya* in the sense of a response to beings), referring to forms manifested for the sake of sentient beings, such as those of dragons, ghosts, and so forth. It is not... [the Response Body].

Regarding the Buddha-body, there are two types: the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the response body (*sambhogakāya*). The two types of response bodies are not transformation bodies. This refers to the Buddha-body seen by Bodhisattvas prior to the stages of the ten bhūmis;
it appears based on meditative concentration and is not subsumed within the five destinies, thus it is called a response body and not a transformation body.

Specifically, this is the single response body within one great trichiliocosm seen by those who possess the four roots of goodness. Third, that which is both a response body and a transformation body refers to what is seen by the various Śrāvakas.

Because one perceives the Buddha’s body as having been accomplished through the cultivation of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), it is called a "response-body" (*nirmāṇakāya*); because one perceives it as being of the same kind as oneself, it is called a "transformation-body" (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The fourth is neither a response-body nor a transformation-body; this refers to the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*). The first three are all transformation-bodies, while the latter one consists of the two bodies of Dharma and Enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* also states that there are four types: first, the enjoyment-body, which is not a transformation-body, referring to the [Buddha] himself...

The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is twofold: the Transformation [Body] is not the Enjoyment [Body], referring to the Transformation Body that manifests for those of the stages prior to the ten bhūmis;
the third is both Enjoyment and Transformation, referring to the Other-Enjoyment Body that manifests for Bodhisattvas of the ten bhūmis;
the fourth is neither Enjoyment nor Transformation, which is the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). Thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* previously discussed these four based on the three bodies.

The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is opened from the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body); now, based on the theory of the three bodies, these four [bodies] are all opened, and furthermore, the *saṃbhogakāya* is opened again.

Thus, although there are four [bodies], their principles are entirely different. Some speak of five bodies as stated in the *Mahāsāṃnipāta Sūtra*, yet Master Rui’s commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* explains that what is called the "body born of the dharma-nature" (*dharmatā-janman-kāya*) is also termed the "merit body" (*puṇya-kāya*).

The Dharma-body of Virtue, the Transformation Dharma-body, the Ultimate Reality Dharma-body, and the Space-like Dharma-body—when examined and distinguished in detail, they are but a single Dharma-body.
Why is this so? If one speaks of its arising, it is because its source is the Dharma-nature; thus it is called the "Dharma-nature Arising Body.
If one traces its cause, it is that which is accomplished through merit and virtue; thus it is called the "Merit and Virtue Dharma-body. As for its manifestation...

Thus, there is no stimulus that does not elicit a manifestation; this is the transformation of the Dharma-body. When its magnitude is described, it encompasses and pervades empty space—this is what is called the "Dharma-body of empty space.
When its subtlety is discussed, it is signless and unconditioned; therefore, it is called the "Dharma-body of true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
It is because it can be so subtly signless and so vastly pervasive of empty space that it universally responds to the myriad transformations, such that there is no stimulus that it does not meet.
That which has form can be clarified through analogy and deliberation. Why is this? Because the forms within the three realms of existence transform according to karma;
thus, there are myriad differences in refinement and coarseness, as well as in size. The *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, however, is the fruit of wondrous merit.
Since merit is boundless, its fruit is also boundless; since merit is signless, its fruit is also signless; it is the fruit of the skillful means of merit.
Furthermore, because skillful means (*upāya*) are boundless, its measure is equal to empty space; because it is signless (*animitta*), its subtlety accords with the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Because it is skillful means, there is no stimulus that does not manifest form. This is the Tathāgata’s truly wondrous Dharma-body. It is not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*) or fruits; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Because this body exists as the root of all transformations, one attains therein a state where there is no stimulus and thus no response.

It is like the light of the sun entering a dark chamber through a window; though the rays of light may manifest in ten thousand different ways, their source is one—this is what is called the true *dharmakāya*.
If one points directly to the *dharmatā* of merit as the *dharmakāya*, this refers to the "body" (*kāya*) of the Dharma in its conventional sense;
it does not refer to a body of physical form or appearance. The above constitutes the meaning of the five bodies (*pañcakāya*). If...

Regarding the inclusion [of all bodies] within the three bodies: the first two are the recompense body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the next one is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and the latter two are the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).

Furthermore, according to another interpretation, there are nine bodies, as each of the three bodies has three aspects. Regarding the three aspects of the dharma body: the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) constitutes the fundamental dharma body;

because it possesses the three great qualities (*trimaṇḍala*) that are primordially present, it is considered threefold; and because these are realized through cultivation, they constitute the recompense body. They are identical in this regard.

The essence is great and its function is named; thus there are the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Because it is realized by true wisdom, it is called the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*);

because its merit of wisdom is perfected, it is the Reward Body; and because it manifests for those on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is called the Transformation Body—this constitutes the three aspects of the Reward Body.
Regarding the three aspects of the Response Body (*anurūpakāya*): since a transformation must have an essence, that essence is the Dharma Body; as the Sūtra says:

This body of mine is now the eternal body; it is the Dharma-body accomplished through the cultivation of causes such as the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, which is the Reward-body;
and it is the Manifestation-body that necessarily takes form in response to conditions. Thus, there are three types of manifestation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Alternatively, it is said there are ten. This has two meanings: first, regarding the ten bodies obtained through the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); [the second refers to the ten bodies of the Buddha].

As stated in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, there are ten [aspects of the Buddha-body]: first, the body of equality; second, the pure body; third, the inexhaustible body; fourth, the well-cultivated body;
fifth, the dharma-nature body; sixth, the body free from vitarka and vicāra; seventh, the inconceivable body; eighth, the tranquil body; ninth, the space-like body;
and tenth, the body of wondrous wisdom. Second, regarding the ten qualities inherently possessed by the Buddha-body itself:

Since the body is explained below, the commentary states: "The sūtras and śāstras offer differing explanations regarding the single body and the multiple bodies; I shall briefly indicate these divergent meanings without wearying the reader with excessive detail.
Now, it is said that in this sūtra, the Buddha is considered either true (nirmāṇakāya) or responsive (sambhogakāya), and either one or many.
Now, following this discourse on the sutra, the second section consists of a provisional inquiry that raises further issues; herein, there are two parts:

first, the raising of the question, and second, the critical examination of the response. Regarding the former, it contains two pairs of propositions that already encompass all preceding and subsequent meanings.
▲If one speaks of the "True" [Body], why is it called Śākyamuni dwelling in the Sahā world, seen alike by humans and devas?
If one speaks of the "Responsive" [Body], why say that Vairocana dwells in the Lotus Treasury World and is seen by Great Bodhisattvas as the Dharma-body of the Buddha?

Within the section on raising objections, there are two parts: first, the objection regarding the True and the Responsive; second, the objection regarding the one and the many. The first part contains three sub-sections:
first, concerning names; second, concerning locations; third, concerning capacities.
If it is said that [the Buddha] is one, why does he manifest separately in many places? If it is said that they are different, why is it further stated that...?
There is no division of the body.

If one says it is "one," the following two points raise a difficulty regarding the plurality of manifestations. As for the statement that it appears distinctly in many places, the *Guanfo sanmei hai jing* (Sutra on the Ocean-like Samadhi of Contemplating the Buddha), in the chapter on "Awakening through Radiance," states:
"In this place, one sees the Buddha, the World-Honored One, seated upon a lotus-treasury lion throne; ten Buddhas..."

Surrounded by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field, in each and every one of those worlds there are ten billion Jambudvīpas and ten billion Tathāgatas seated in the same manner as these.
Furthermore, it is said that just as one sees the Buddha’s seat in this place, so it is in all atoms; the Buddha-body neither goes nor comes.
Since all lands clearly manifest [the Buddha], why does it further say that he does not divide his body? The *Prādurbhāva-parivarta* (Chapter on Manifestation) states:
"For example, when the Brahmā King dwells in his own palace, he universally manifests himself in all the abodes of the three thousand-fold world system, and all humans and devas are able to see him;
yet he does not actually divide his body to go to those places. The manifestation of the body by these Buddhas is likewise."
Throughout all the ten directions, there is nowhere his body does not pervade; it is incalculable and beyond measure, yet he neither divides his body nor makes distinctions.
For this reason, when this sutra says "the Buddha," it is not the same as what was previously stated.
Therefore, it is said that the latter three [sections] of this sutra collectively provide a comprehensive synthesis. Within these, the first two negate what is incorrect;
the next [section] is the inexhaustible cloud-body of the Dharma-realm;

and the final [section] reveals the correct [teaching]. Within this last part, there are three sections: first, a general display of the characteristics; second, a response to objections; [and third, a summary].
After "harmonizing," one forms the inconceivable.
▲ The true and the responsive are mutually harmonized, such that the one and the many are without obstruction.
Regarding the mutual harmony of the body and its manifestations, the second pair of difficult points to be harmonized is divided into two parts; first, these two lines:
Double heading. ▲ Since Vairocana is Śākyamuni, the subsequent section beginning with "Vairocana" provides a double explanation in two parts:
first, an explanation of the True and the Responsive; second, an explanation of the One and the Many. Regarding the former:
First, these two lines specifically explain that both the True and the Responsive [Bodies] apply to what precedes, posing a challenge based on their names:

since other teachings designate Vairocana as the True [Body] and Śākyamuni as the Responsive [Body], the Sūtra states, "The Pure Dharma-body is Vairocana Buddha; the thousand, ten-thousand, and hundred-million transformation-bodies are Śākyamuni Buddha.
Now, since they are shown to be mutually identical, it is clear that this is the characteristic of the True and the Responsive being one.
The *Fahua yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), in the "Chapter on Names," states: "Some call him Vairocana, while others call him Śākyamuni;

it is merely a difference in names. Furthermore, within the "Chapter on the Array of Flowers" (*Huazang pin*), it is explained that in the thirteenth layer there is a world named Sahā, and its Buddha is none other than Vairocana.
Thus, we know that their characteristics are mutually integrated.
▲ Because that which is always in this place is simultaneously in other places, and because it eternally abides here while being far away in other directions.

Regarding the phrase "always in this place" and so forth, there are two pairs of oppositions that correctly clarify the True and the Responsive (Sambhogakāya), while incidentally manifesting the unity and multiplicity of the person and the land.
As for the initial difficulty concerning the place: first, regarding the True and the Responsive, since this is discussed from the perspective of the Responsive [body], [it is said:]...
In this context, because it is real and because it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, the Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all sentient beings;
responding to conditions as they arise, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi.

The first phrase refers to the Real (the Truth), while the remaining three are its manifestations. Regarding the fourth phrase, "ever remaining in this place," the other three [phrases] are likewise implied.
"Phrase" (*pada*) refers to "other places. To say that it simultaneously manifests both the one and the many means that in this place it is one, while in other places it is many;
for example, without arising from a single location, it pervades all places. This bodhi-seat is one, yet it universally appears before the multitude of sentient beings as many.
Regarding the inclusion of the "lands" (*kṣetra*): in this place it is the Sahā world, while elsewhere it is the pervasive lotus [land].
This is the "Treasury" (Kosa).
▲ Because the body is neither differentiated nor unitary.

Regarding "the body is neither differentiated," the following two explanations clarify the relationship between the one and the many: because it is not differentiated, it is not many; yet being many does not obstruct [its unity].
First, because it is also not one, it is free from being one; thus, the one does not obstruct the many. Above, this merely explained the one and the many.
Next, because a single body is perfectly complete and fully manifests simultaneously in different locations.

Regarding the phrase "simultaneously in different places" and so forth, there are two parts: the formal explanation and the inclusion of both the True (the *dharmakāya*) and the Responsive (the *nirmāṇakāya*).
As for "one and many": because a single body manifests in its entirety, it is neither one nor many;

yet, because a single body manifests as many, the one does not obstruct the many, and because the many manifest while remaining eternally one, the many do not obstruct the one. As has already been cited above, a single body serves as...

"Immeasurable and immeasurable again become one; knowing all worlds, manifesting forms that pervade everything," and also, "The single, firm, and dense body is seen within every atom," and from the *Samantabhadra-vyūha-parivarta*:
"The Tathāgata, within a single body of perfect enlightenment, universally manifests bodies equal in number to all sentient beings, attaining perfect enlightenment [in each]. And so forth.
Regarding the phrase "simultaneously in different places": if one were to allow for a single body to travel sequentially through different times and places, that would be possible;

however, what is clarified here is that when [the body] appears simultaneously in different places, it must necessarily be many bodies. Yet, because this single body manifests in its entirety [in each location], it is not actually many.
It is like a single moon appearing simultaneously in a hundred rivers within a single kṣaṇa—it is both one and many, and moreover, universal.
Because it manifests, it is not one; because it is the single moon, it is not many. As the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu states in verse:
"For example, the pure full moon universally appears as reflections in all waters; though these reflections are immeasurable, the original moon has never been two.

Therefore, in the *Sūtra Commentary on the Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance* (*Guangming juepin shu*), it is explained that there is seeing at different times and in different places, even when [the object] exists simultaneously and in the same location.
Seeing [the Buddha] simultaneously in different places; seeing him at different times in the same place;

and seeing him both simultaneously and at different times in the same place—when one person sees him all at once, these terms "and so forth" (*ādi*) encompass both the *dharmakāya* (True Body) and the *nirmāṇakāya* (Response Body). The single body being perfectly complete is the *dharmakāya*, because it is manifested in its entirety;
this is precisely the *nirmāṇakāya*. Furthermore, the term "manifested in its entirety" means not manifested partially. To speak of "partial manifestation" is, for example, as follows:
Within the body many heads appear, and within each head there is a Buddha; at the waist, figures such as immortals appear, which is to say they manifest separately.

What is now called "manifesting in their entirety" means that this very Buddha-body is all bodies, is the bodies of all classes, and that the entire body of a Bodhisattva is the Buddha-body, and so forth.

▲Because it is inconceivable to all bodhisattvas. This concludes the section on the difficulty of conceiving [the Buddha-body] for all bodhisattvas; furthermore, this contrasts with the previous point regarding humans, showing that if even bodhisattvas cannot conceive of it, how much less can humans and devas perceive it?
This is because it is free from the marks of mental objects (*ālambana-nimitta*). Thus ends the twenty-second [section].
Among the various merits, the eightieth scripture, "The Inconceivable Body," states:
"The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body is peerless throughout all the three realms. Because it transcends the world, its nature cannot be expressed through the path of language;
it is neither existent nor non-existent. Thus, although it has no basis, there is nowhere it does not abide; although there is nothing it does not reach, it does not go."
One should contemplate the Buddha-body in this way: it is like a painting in the sky or what is seen in a dream.
Because it is neither real nor a response, neither one nor many, one must not conceive of it as being real, a response, one, or many. Thus, the *Jñānālokālaṃkāra* states:
"The Buddha-body is unborn and transcends conceptual proliferation; because it is not a composite of aggregates or a differentiated phenomenon, it is inconceivable."
Furthermore, it says: "Without defilement, without attachment, without conceptualization, and without a basis, its essential nature is immeasurable;
all who see it offer praise, and such passages are not few. Since it further states that the inconceivable clarity of a Bodhisattva is the domain of the Buddha alone, [how can this be so?]
▲ First, the ten bodies are clarified, followed by the manifestation of unimpededness.
Now, first clarifying the ten bodies constitutes the fourth section of the opening chapter and its explanation. This section has three parts: first, the two preceding lines provide the heading;
second, the words "The ten... and following provide the explanation; third, the words "By means of this cloud of bodies... and following summarize the pervasiveness.
Regarding the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), there are two senses. First, concerning the integration of the three worlds into ten bodies:
1) the body of sentient beings; 2) the body of the land; 3) the body of karmic retribution; 4) the body of the śrāvaka;
5) the body of the pratyekabuddha; 6) the body of the bodhisattva; 7) the body of the Tathāgata; 8) the body of wisdom; 9) the body of the Dharma; 10) the body of empty space.
▲ Second, regarding the Buddha himself, there are ten bodies: first, the Bodhi-body; second, the Vow-body; third, the Transformation-body; fourth, the Sustaining-body;
fifth, the Body Adorned with Marks and Signs; sixth, the Body of Majestic Power; seventh, the Mind-born-body;
eighth, the Merit-body; ninth, the Dharma-body; and tenth, the Wisdom-body. Their characteristics are extensively revealed as in the Eighth Stage and the "Chapter on Transcending the World."
Discrimination.
Regarding the "extensive manifestation of their characteristics" and so forth: in the eighth stage, it is clarified that each of the preceding ten bodies possesses ten characteristics.
The twentieth body is precisely the ten characteristics of the seventh of those ten—the Tathāgata body—and it further clarifies the preceding...
The ten types of bodily manifestations refer to the ability to manifest according to the mental inclinations of sentient beings as their own body,
the body of the land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a Tathāgata,

the wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*), the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), and the space-body (*ākāśa-kāya*). The citations from the aforementioned scriptural records and the detailed explanations of each of these characteristics are all provided below.

Regarding the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokātīta-parivarta*), among those fifty-three [buddhas], there are ten buddhas who are identical to the twenty-first body mentioned previously, though their names differ slightly.

To explain them collectively: the ten buddhas are what are called the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambuddha-buddha*), the Buddha of Vow (*praṇidhāna-buddha*), the Buddha of Karmic Retribution (*vipāka-buddha*), the Buddha of Sustenance (*adhiṣṭhāna-buddha*), the Buddha of Nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-buddha*), the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-buddha*), the Buddha of Mind (*citta-buddha*), and the Buddha of Samādhi.

In the fifty-eighth [chapter], "The Buddha of Original Nature" and "The Buddha of Following Joy," it further clarifies ten kinds of seeing the Buddha, which correspond to the ten Buddhas mentioned previously.
The text states: "That is to say: the Buddha of Abiding in the World and Attaining Perfect Enlightenment is seen through the vision of non-attachment;

the Buddha of Arising is seen through the vision of vows; the Buddha of Karmic Retribution is seen through the vision of profound faith; the Buddha of Sustenance is seen through the vision of compliance; and the Buddha of Nirvana..."
The Buddha who deeply penetrates and perceives the Dharma-realm; the Buddha who universally reaches and perceives the mind; the Buddha who dwells in peace and perceives samādhi;
the Buddha of immeasurable non-reliance who perceives the fundamental nature; the Buddha of clear understanding who perceives according to inclination;
and the Buddha of universal reception who perceives while remaining unattached—each of these ten meanings shall be explained in detail below.
▲ Regarding the unimpededness of speech (*vāk-anāvaraṇa*), there are briefly ten meanings.

Under the heading "unimpededness of speech," the subsequent section reveals this unimpededness in two parts: first, the enumeration of the number; second, the detailed explanation. This is the first part, the enumeration.

▲ "The unimpeded application of all functions" means that within the aforementioned realms of thoughts, kalpas, lands, and atoms, the Vairocana Buddha manifests clouds of bodies throughout the Dharma-realm;
his activities and functions are boundless and universally pervasive. As the sutra states:
"Just as the Buddha’s seat is seen in this place, so it is in every atom," and such passages appear more than once.
Regarding the phrase "in all atoms," etc., this refers to the second half of the verse which says: "The Buddha-body neither goes nor comes;
all lands appear clearly therein. This is the fifth verse from the *Universal Worthy Bodhisattva* chapter of the sutra.
As for the statement that "its text is not singular," it pervades the entire sutra; as the sixth verse says: "The Buddha Vairocana... [and so forth].
The power [of the Buddha] pervades all lands throughout the Dharma-realm, constantly turning the unsurpassed wheel;
it is further said that within each and every atom, one can realize all dharmas, thus moving unimpeded throughout the lands of the ten directions.

Furthermore, it is said that when the Buddha utters a single wondrous sound, it is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions, wherein all voices are fully contained and the rain of Dharma fills them all.

The functions [of the Buddha] are as extensive as these and others, being immeasurable and boundless. That is to say, he may manifest the majestic deportment of gathering and sustaining sentient beings;
or manifest the eight phases of enlightenment; or manifest the forms of the three vehicles; or manifest the forms of the five destinies; or manifest the various distinctions of the six sense objects.

His names, titles, karmic activities, and functions are manifold and beyond reckoning. Because there is not a single atom within the *dharmadhātu* that he does not pervade, it is said that his function is all-encompassing (*yōu zhōu*).
Furthermore:
▲ Second, the mutual pervasiveness and non-obstruction of the two aspects means that within the aforementioned differentiated functions, each encompasses all karmic activities.

Regarding "the mutual pervasiveness and non-obstruction of the two aspects," it refers to what was explained above concerning the encompassing of the majestic deportments (*īryāpatha*)—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" (*Acintya-parivarta*): "The Tathāgata, having finished eating while seated upon a single seat, remains in the full lotus posture without moving, pervading all directions throughout all kalpas.
This now clarifies that within this very seat, he simultaneously possesses walking, standing, and reclining.
Furthermore, regarding the previous manifestation of the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] universally, the deity of the Lumbinī grove spoke of the Tathāgata’s birth, saying: "Excellent!"

Sons of good family, when I beheld the Buddha manifesting various miraculous transformations at his initial birth within the Lumbinī Grove in Jambudvīpa among these four continents of this trichiliocosm,
I likewise beheld the Tathāgata manifesting his initial birth within the Lumbinī Grove in Jambudvīpa among the ten billion sets of four continents across the entire trichiliocosm.
They manifest various supernatural transformations and also see immeasurable Buddha-lands within every single atom of the trichiliocosm;
they also see immeasurable Buddha-lands within every single atom of a hundred Buddha-worlds, a thousand Buddha-worlds,
and even all worlds throughout the ten directions— in all such Buddha-lands, there are [Buddhas].
The Tathāgata’s manifestation of birth and various supernatural transformations, which occur thus in every thought-moment without interruption, constitute a single layer of pervasiveness;
yet here it is clarified that within each individual characteristic all eight characteristics are fully present.
As the thirty-first sutra states: "While the Bodhisattva dwells in the mother's womb, he freely manifests the path of the entire Dharma-realm."
The assembly in that place is exceedingly subtle, and the Bodhisattva within the mother’s womb manifests all the spiritual powers of the Buddhas in an exceedingly subtle manner.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Transcending the World" states: "O Son of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of exceedingly subtle approaches for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
What are these ten? They are as follows: manifesting the initial aspiration for enlightenment while remaining in the mother’s womb..."
From the stage of taking up the mind [of awakening] up to the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), while dwelling within the mother’s womb, he manifests dwelling in Tuṣita;
while dwelling within the mother’s womb, he manifests his initial birth; while dwelling within the mother’s womb, he manifests the stage of childhood;

while dwelling within the mother’s womb, he manifests residing in the royal palace; while dwelling within the mother’s womb, he manifests the going forth (*pravrajyā*); while dwelling within the mother’s womb, he manifests [all these].
Manifesting ascetic practices while in the mother’s womb; manifesting the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment at the site of awakening while in the mother’s womb;

manifesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma while in the mother’s womb; and manifesting parinirvāṇa while in the mother’s womb—this is called the great subtlety within the womb, which encompasses all bodhisattva practices and the sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas.
Regarding the gate of the distinctions of measure: "O Son of the Buddha, these are the ten subtle modes of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva while in the mother’s womb.

Commentary: The single characteristic of the mother’s womb possesses the eight characteristics, and because it is perfectly complete with all myriad virtues, it is said that its characteristics are pervasive.
Furthermore, whereas above the three vehicles were shown, here the One Vehicle encompasses the three; whereas above the five paths were shown, here the one... [is shown].
The five examples of the ritual implements can be understood from this.
▲ Third, because the three types of quiescence and function are unimpeded and accomplished without partiality.

Regarding "the three types of quiescence and function are equal": if one were to take the meaning as it is explicitly stated, one should perform contemplation; however, here the function is used without partiality.
Because his private life was not biased and because he was also without mind toward things, it is said that he was constantly in samādhi;
because he acted to benefit beings without fixed direction, this is his function—since concentration and function are one, they are called unimpeded.
Like the *maṇi* jewel or the celestial drum, which rain down jewels and produce sounds without intention, the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" states: "All Buddhas..."

Within a single thought-moment, they are able to manifest all the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time to transform all sentient beings, yet they do not depart from the Buddhas' samādhi of quiescence; this is the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the first sutra says: "The body pervades the ten directions, yet there is no coming or going. The third sutra says:
The realm of the Tathāgata is immeasurable; it is quiescent yet capable of manifesting throughout the ten directions. The Fourth Sūtra states:

"In the vast and tranquil samādhi, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going; he adorns and purifies the buddha-lands and manifests this liberation of the tree-flower deity to sentient beings."
▲ Regarding "the fourfold reliance arises": because the power of the Sea-Seal (*sāgaramudrā*) manifests instantaneously and without obstruction despite being mindless.
As for "the fourfold reliance arises," this means that although the quiescent function is mindless, it does not hinder the fact that all rely upon the power of the Sea-Seal;

furthermore, it is precisely by relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that activity arises. As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* (Chapter on the Noble Head, *Bhadrapāla-paṭala*) states: "Or he manifests as a boy or a girl."
Whether they be *rūpakāya* devas, nāgas, asuras, or even mahoragas, he causes them all to see according to their respective inclinations;
the forms of sentient beings are each different, and their karmic actions, voices, and sounds are likewise immeasurable—
all such things he is able to manifest through the supernatural power of the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrāsamādhi*).
▲ The five aspects of the true and the responsive are non-obstructive and should be understood as identical, for they share the single flavor and equality of the Dharma.
Regarding the equality of the five aspects of the true and the responsive: Śākyamuni and Vairocana are the non-dual Buddha;
thus, this present body of mine is itself the Dharmakāya. As the fifth scripture states: "The Tathatā is the equal, signless body, the stainless radiance of the pure Dharma."
The body of wisdom is quiescent; this immeasurable body universally responds to the ten directions as it expounds the Dharma.

It is further said that the Tathāgata’s true body is fundamentally non-dual, yet it manifests forms in accordance with sentient beings to fill the world. The *Guangming juepin* (Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance) states:
"The Tathāgata does not take physical marks as his essence; rather, he is the markless, quiescent Dharmakāya, yet fully endowed with all physical characteristics and dignified deportment."
"Those in the world who follow their inclinations all obtain visions [of him], etc.
Regarding "the six parts being perfectly complete and unimpeded": each individual limb is identical to the entire body.

▲ Entering the realm of sentient beings. This has two interpretations: first, it clarifies that the Buddha enters sentient beings; second, it also encompasses the following clarification that sentient beings enter the Buddha.

Next, following the citation of analogies after the section on the *tathāgatagarbha*, the subsequent section "Manifesting" cites scriptural evidence.
This is because, although the *tathāgatagarbha* manifests as sentient beings, it does not lose its own nature.
In the analogy, the true mind of sentient beings is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. Following conditions such as ignorance, it manifests as all sentient beings transmigrating through the three realms;
yet, because the self-nature of this true mind is never lost, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states:
"Being unstained yet stained is difficult to comprehend; being stained yet unstained is difficult to comprehend. To further clarify this through another analogy:
It is like the waters of the great ocean, which, though forming waves due to the wind, do not lose their moist nature; so too is the Buddha:
according to the perceptions of sentient beings, he manifests in ten thousand different forms, yet the body of the Tathāgata does not lose its own intrinsic nature.
This is because sentient beings take their own *dharmakāya* as a metaphor for themselves; thus, the true body of the Tathāgata enters into all sentient beings.

(10) Perfect Penetration and Non-obstruction: This Buddha-body is simultaneously principle and phenomenon, simultaneously one and many, and simultaneously the basis and the supported.
It is the correct and it is the person; it is the Dharma; it is this and it is that; it is the sentient and it is the non-sentient;
it is the profound and it is the vast; it is the cause and it is the fruit; it is the three bodies and it is the ten bodies.
Regarding the "ten perfect penetrations" (*daśa-samyag-vyavasthāna*), there are two parts in the text: first, a detailed explanation, and second, a summary. Now, for the former:
because the *Vairocana* Buddha takes the great *dharmadhātu* as his body through integration, there is nothing that is not "immediate" (*jī*).

Since he does not wait for a manifested body to be called "immediate to phenomena," and because the essence of the *dharmadhātu* encompasses everything without exception, there is nothing that is not immediate; thus, the body is also [immediate].

However, if one were to distinguish them by their characteristics: the physical marks and color of the Buddha’s body are the phenomena (*śarīra*), while being entirely identical to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the principle (*tattva*).

since the true and the manifested are interfused, their characteristics are mutually identical. Second, a manifestation at this single location is simultaneously a manifestation at many locations; this is also because...
The essence is fused; furthermore, this very one must be many and must be one. Thus, the *Jñānālokālaṃkāra* states:
"A single body becomes immeasurable, and the immeasurable again becomes one. One understands that throughout all worlds, forms manifest everywhere.
This body has no origin and is not accumulated; yet, due to the conceptual discriminations of sentient beings, they perceive the Buddha's various bodies."
"Identical with the basis" (*yi*) and "identical with the correct" (*zheng*) also have two meanings: first, because the Dharma-nature body and its land are fused and non-dual;
second, because there is a land-body, it is identical with the basis, and because there is a wisdom-awakened body, it is identical with the correct.

Regarding "identical with the person," it is because one becomes a person through realizing the Dharma. Regarding "identical with the Dharma," it is because the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body. Thus, it is this very [identity].

Because that [Buddha] does not depart from the Bodhi tree while pervading all places, and because he does not depart from all places while sitting at the Bodhi tree, one may say that "that" is "this" and "this" is "that. Because it differs from the material substance of stones, it is not insentient; because it shares the same nature as form (*rūpa*), it manifests as rivers, ponds, and so forth;

and because the insentient is itself the Buddha-body, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are like empty space. That which is both profound and vast is profound because it is formless and transcends all marks (*lakṣaṇa*);

Therefore, the "Chapter on the Profundity of Inquiry" states: "The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space;

The commentary states: According to this interpretation, by means of the non-empty...

Both [the previous views] fail to capture the true meaning of this sutra.
Regarding the phrase "neither [is it] both," etc., this is the second general negation. This is because the true meaning consists in the perfect interfusion of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*).

Even if one were to distinguish thirty different aspects, these would still be explained in terms of the provisional and the real; if they were not interfused, the former meaning would also lose the central tenet of the Sūtra.
Regarding the "establishment of distinctions" and so forth, this third section clarifies potential confusions. How does it clarify them?

It is said that, according to the teachings, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are provisional while the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) are real. If one does not know that the three bodies are themselves the ten bodies, they will not be integrated;
because one would establish the real as being external to the prior provisional, one loses the essential purport of the sutra.
▲ Fourth, regarding those who rely on samādhi: Movement and stillness belong to things; how could they apply to the Sage?

To demonstrate the rules for later followers, it is clarified that when one is about to speak, one must first contemplate the preceding principles with stillness and discernment. Receiving the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas, one arises from meditative concentration and speaks;
because what is spoken is necessarily true and appropriate, the minds of those who receive it naturally become sincere and profound.

The fourth section, based on the *Samādhi-vyākhyā*, is divided into two parts: first, establishing the principle to correctly clarify the meaning; second, providing a brief explanation in accordance with the text.

Regarding the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, a detailed exposition; second, the summary conclusion. Within the first, the *Commentary on the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika-vyākhyā*) clarifies that the purpose of entering meditative absorption consists of six general meanings:
first, because this samādhi is the very essence of the Dharma—this is according to the intent of the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*. Second... [text continues]

Because one does not speak unless one has realized [the truth], if one were to speak without realization, it would be a mental activity of arising and ceasing to speak of the Dharma of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Third, because the Dharma is not an object of discursive thought, it is clarified that only by extinguishing the mind can one accord with the aforementioned meaning.

The previous section was an exposition of the reality [of phenomena], while this section is an exclusion of errors. Thus, among the three preceding meanings, each subsequent one explains the preceding ones; they are largely the same, differing only slightly.
1. Because it differs from the four [preceding] by observing the capacities of beings and examining the Dharma; for it is essential that the medicine and the ailment correspond before one may preach.

2. Because it receives the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha; while the preceding four are internal causes, this one is an external condition, and only through the harmony of these causes and conditions can one preach.

3. Because it perfects the ritual procedures (*vidhi*); that is, it is solely for the sake of generating the aforementioned five [qualities] for one's own benefit, whereas this one is for the benefit of others.

Now, this commentary contains the first two phrases [of the verse], which establish the principle through general characteristics: it is not only when entering meditative concentration that one acts for the sake of beings;
it is likewise so when emerging from concentration. Thus, those who should see [the Buddha] emerging shall see him emerge, and those who should see him entering shall see him enter.

Therefore, it is said that he manifests only as a being; because the Sage is neither fixed nor distracted, it is called "Sage. How could it be otherwise? As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Neither fixed nor distracted, he manifests."
The phrase "after the track" (*gui hou*) and "the followers below" (*tu xia*) separately clarify the intent of entering [the teaching].

This is the sixth intent, which clarifies that one who is about to explain must necessarily engage in quiet contemplation (*jing jian*) of the preceding principles. "Quiet" (*jing*) means being free from discursive thought (*siliang*). "Quiet contemplation" (*jing jian*) means realizing the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*).

"Quietly contemplating the preceding principles" means observing the capacities of beings (*ganji*) and examining the teachings. The character for "preceding" (*qian*) includes both the teachings and the capacities of beings.

The Buddha’s power makes it known that he arises from meditative concentration and speaks; this explains that he does not preach without realization, and it also generally reveals the superior functions of the preceding six [perfections].
Therefore, in many assemblies, the eight meditative concentrations (*aṣṭa-samādhi*) are frequently clarified as the conditions for preaching the sūtras.
Therefore, this serves as the summary at the conclusion of each assembly. Of the nine assemblies in which the sutra was preached, eight involve entering samādhi, while the second assembly does not;

in the third assembly, Dharmamati Bodhisattva enters the Bodhisattva-apramāṇa-upāya-samādhi.

In the seventh assembly, the Tathāgata himself abided in the limit of the instant (*kṣaṇakoṭi*).
In the eighth assembly, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the Buddha’s Flower Adornment Samādhi; in the ninth assembly, the Tathāgata himself enters the Lion’s Stretch Samādhi.
As for these two instances of "not entering," it is because they have not yet attained that stage [of realization]. Some say this is merely a textual omission.

If even when expounding worldly dharmas one must enter meditative concentration, how much more so for those at the stage of the ten faiths? This is especially true if one considers what is being symbolized.
The previous interpretation is without fault.

Regarding those who do not enter [the meditative states], their specific entries will be explained in the relevant passages; all these concentrations exhaust the source of the Dharma, and their karmic functions are inconceivable.
Regarding those who do not enter, the second pair of texts below provides a brief explanation of the meaning of "not entering," as already stated above.

As for those who do enter, the following section reveals their superiority by transcending inferiority; it demonstrates that the stages entered differ in their excellence, and because both person and dharma are superior, each and every samādhi exhausts the very source and bottom of all dharmas.
This is not like when one enters the first *dhyāna*, where one does not [yet] enter [the higher stages].

Because [the practitioners] are of the second, third, and so forth [levels], and because they have exhausted the source of the Dharma, they equally receive the empowerment of the three karmas of all Buddhas.

Fifth, regarding the manifestation of signs: although the *dharmatā* is tranquil and devoid of all characteristics, the characteristic of signlessness does not obstruct the profuse arising [of phenomena].

The fifth section, based on the *Xianxiang shu* (Commentary on the Manifestation of Signs), is divided into four parts: first, a general explanation of the essential meaning; second, the manifestation of the differences between signs;
third, a specific explanation of the emission of light; and fourth, an analytical examination of similarities and differences. Now, for the first part, there should be four propositions:
first, following signs (*suxiang*); second, signlessness (*wuxiang*); third, signlessness not obstructing signs; and fourth, the identity of signs with the dharma of signlessness.
The nature of quiescence is the second phrase; the characteristic of signlessness is explained in detail within the third and fourth phrases.
Therefore, one should not cling to signlessness in order to reject all characteristics. Thus, the subsequent scripture states:

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that the Buddha dwells in the profound,
true *dharmatā*, which is quiescent and signless like space; yet, within this primary ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
he manifests various activities and deeds that benefit sentient beings— all of which exist according to *dharmatā*, possessing both signs and signlessness.
The meaning is that by entering into the ultimate state where characteristics are without distinction, one realizes that all things are devoid of characteristics.

The methods for initiating the teaching are manifold; the characteristics are not uniform. Sometimes light is emitted and lands are shaken, or flowers rain down and fragrant clouds arise—all these serve to initiate [the teaching].
