▲ Second, the section on the conformity and divergence between ancient and modern [views] is divided into two parts: first, an account of this land (China), followed by an exposition of the Western Regions (India).
Regarding the former: although there are many commentators, I shall briefly describe several schools and condense them into five gates.

Second, regarding the agreement and disagreement between ancient and modern [views], within each master’s position, there are generally two parts: first, the presentation of the former interpretation, and second, the analysis of its conformity or divergence.

▲ First, the establishment of the doctrine of a single sound (*ekasvara*): it is held that the teaching of the Tathāgata throughout his entire career does not depart from a single sound, yet there are two [aspects].
Master Bo Fazu of the Later Wei dynasty, citing Bodhiruci, says: "The Tathāgata’s single sound simultaneously responds to the ten thousand [beings], with both the great and small presented together.
(2) Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty says: "The Buddha’s single perfect sound is equal and non-dual;

without thought, it universally responds to the capacities of those who hear, each perceiving it differently according to their own faculties. This does not mean that the fundamental sound inherently presents itself as great or small. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The Buddha, by means of..."
When the Dharma is expounded in a single voice, sentient beings each understand it according to their own capacity.

Regarding the two masters mentioned above, in the former case, the Buddha’s voice possesses diversity; in the latter, diversity arises from the various capacities of the listeners, yet each attains the meaning of the perfect voice (*ekasvara*).
This is simply intended to show that both serve as the foundation for the teaching, without distinction.

Within this single sound, the two masters mentioned above [first] clarify the points of agreement and disagreement, while below they present their respective interpretations. Regarding the statement that each attains one aspect of the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*):

this means that the words contain both affirmation and negation. If one affirms them, they accord with what is explained in the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Buddha’s Body" (*Nirmāṇakāya-parivarta*), which clarifies that the Tathāgata’s perfect sound possesses ten aspects.
Following these ten aspects, there are further six phrases of integration; here, we simply obtain [the former].

This is merely one among ten meanings. According to the first master, it follows that within a single sound of the goddess Subhāṣitā, she simultaneously accords with hundreds of thousands of kinds of music; thus, within a single voice of the Buddha, there are many sounds.
According to the latter master, it follows that just as water has a single taste that takes on different forms according to its vessel, the Tathāgata originally possesses no manifold sounds.

It is said that each has obtained one meaning. Furthermore, if these two meanings are not reconciled—since they are diametrically opposed and mutually exclusive—then both sides would equally fail and both should be refuted.

However, because we accept what each respectively adheres to, we grant them each their own meaning; yet, as this is the foundation of the teaching, it will ultimately be refuted in its entirety below.
▲ Second, regarding the establishment of two types of teaching, there are four schools of thought:

first, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Western Qin established the teachings of the "Half" and the "Full," wherein the Śrāvaka Piṭaka is the Half-character Teaching and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka is the Full-character Teaching;
the Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Sui dynasty likewise established this.
The Dharma Master Suiyuan also established this same position; as stated at the beginning of his *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"Although the holy teachings are numerous, they are briefly of two kinds: first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. This is what he meant.
▲ This textual basis in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* intends to manifest the general characteristics of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) in contrast to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna);
it does not yet manifest the existence of provisional and ultimate [teachings] within the Great [Vehicle], and thus it also encompasses both the "half" and the "full."

This, then, follows the inferior [teachings] while contradicting the prior [ones]; it clarifies that "following" refers to following the ultimate teaching. Regarding the terms "half" and "full" *nirvāṇa*, they have already been explained at length previously.

This was intended as a contrast between the small [vehicle] and the inferior; the statement regarding "contradicting the superior" merely refers to following the general characteristics [of the teachings], without yet knowing the Buddha’s profound intent.
Furthermore, the terms "half" and "full" reveal the hidden meaning (*saṃdhi*) within both the small and the great [vehicles]. Moreover, there is... [the further point].
If one takes the provisional (expedient) as "half" and the real as "full," then within the Mahāyāna there are both half and full;
it is just as with the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, who, when distinguished, form two vehicles, yet when unified, share the same essence and are collectively termed "Small.
The provisional and the real are likewise so: when distinguished, they differ, and the provisional may be called "half," but when unified within the great identity, they are both termed [the Great].

The "Complete" (Man) refers to the True Teaching (Shijiao), while the "Partial" (Ban) refers only to the Small Vehicle (Xiaojiao). As for the Mahayana of Expedient Means (Quan), it is both partial and complete.

Second, the Dharma Master Yan of the Sui dynasty established the two teachings of Gradual (Jian) and Sudden (Dun), asserting that they are distinguished according to the gradual-enlightenment capacity, wherein the Great [Vehicle] arises from the Small.

Because that which is established possesses all three vehicles, it is called "gradual" (jìan); if one refers to those of sudden capacity who proceed directly to the Great Vehicle without passing through the Small Vehicle, it is called "sudden" (dùn).
Although this [distinction] is explained in terms of the capacities of sentient beings as being gradual or sudden, the Dharma taught does not transcend the "half" (bàn) and the "full" (mǎn).

Although this passage distinguishes between compliance and opposition based on the capacities [of sentient beings], it directly expresses the underlying intent without departing from the "Half" and "Full" teachings.

This compliance and opposition within the Half and Full teachings is precisely what is meant here by "compliance and opposition. As for the statement that it does not explicitly mention the Half and Full: the Sudden teaching corresponds to the aforementioned Full, while the Gradual teaching encompasses both the Half and the Full;
for it contains the Three Vehicles and Two Vehicles (the Half) as well as the Great Vehicle (the Full). Thus, the capacities [of beings] are correlated with the teachings.
Because there are both the straight and the crooked, one distinguishes between the gradual and the sudden.
▲ Third, during the early Tang dynasty, Master Yin also established two teachings.

▲ First is the Crooked Teaching (*kuqūjiào*), which refers to the scriptures of Śākyamuni; because they follow the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings to break through attachments according to their respective calculations, they are like the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra].
The two teachings of the *pán* (Vairocana) and so forth are called the *Śākyamuni Sūtras*, because they expound the Dharma-nature with sovereign freedom, such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are briefly four differences between these two teachings: first, the difference in the principal [teacher], namely, the transformation body of Śākyamuni and Vairocana.

First, they differ in their physical forms; second, they differ in their locations—meaning that the wooden trees and grass seats of the Sahā world differ from the jewel trees and jewel seats within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu);

third, they differ in their audiences—meaning that teachings given for both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas differ from those taught exclusively for Bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage; fourth, they differ in their mode of exposition—meaning that localized expositions differ from...
Because the explanations regarding the ten directions differ, [the text] addresses this.
Third, regarding the Master Yin of the early Tang dynasty—the third master—therein, the prior exposition of ancient interpretations consists of three parts: first, a general heading;
second, "First, the winding [nature]" and so forth, which establishes the formal position; and third, "Furthermore, this... and so forth, which distinguishes it from other views.
▲ This is judged according to the *huayi* (modes of conversion).

Regarding the phrase "This is judged according to the *huayi*," the following section distinguishes between conformity and opposition, first conforming and subsequently opposing. Within the section on conformity, there are three parts:

first, a single sentence that generally sets forth the underlying intent; second, the refutation [of others] and the establishment [of one's own view]; third, the conclusion that establishes the former meaning. Now, for the first part:

The first [classification] establishes the teachings according to the "half-full" and "full" bonds; the second establishes them according to the "gradual" and "sudden" based on the capacities of sentient beings.

Now, this particular master establishes them according to the ritual of transformation, meaning that because there are those who are crooked and those who are straight among the beings the Buddha transforms through the Dharma, the rituals of the transformative Dharma are simply different.

▲ However, although the *Avataṃsaka* sūtra teaches the simultaneous and sudden unfolding of skillful means that accord with the nature of reality— taming each and every sentient being according to their individual needs—
the *Nirvāṇa* and other sūtras, while speaking of the ultimate oneness, do so either by revealing the real through provisional means or by harmonizing differences into unity.
Since all Tathāgatas may either teach or not teach [in this manner], these are described as "crooked" (or indirect) teachings.
However, in the second section of the *Huayan* [commentary], there is a refutation and establishment of the argument;

that is, the *Kanding ji* does not permit this master’s established doctrine, first refuting the general name and subsequently refuting the four differences. Now, in order to provide a comprehensive response to what was previously [refuted], we merely block those refutations.
The text is divided into two parts: first, rescuing the general name, and second, rescuing the four differences. Regarding the first, it says "therefore it is called 'crooked'" (*ququ*).
This rescues [the argument] that was refuted in the general title of that commentary; having first restated the meaning therein, it says:

"If that were so, then since the *Nirvāṇa*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Ghanavyūha*, *Śrīmālādevī*, and *Buddhapiṭaka* sūtras are all spoken by Śākyamuni, they should not clarify the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). (This refutation is circuitous because there is a direct path. [The *Avataṃsaka*...]
Since the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* was spoken by Samantabhadra, why is it that within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in chapters such as those on the Four Noble Truths and the Practices of Samantabhadra,
it is stated that "one speaks in this way according to what is necessary to discipline each sentient being"? Furthermore,

[why is it so] in various chapters such as the "Chapter on the Questions of Clear and Pure Conduct," the "Chapter on Brahma Conduct," the "Three Stages of Worthiness" (*tri-śuklāḥ karmapathāḥ*), the "Ten Stages" (*daśabhūmi*), the "Leaving the World" (*lokottara*), and the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātupraveśa*)?

One should explain that all [teachings] are the practice of the antidotes (pratipakṣa), for this refutes the "level path" (sama-mārga) on the grounds that it possesses "crookedness" (vakratva). Now, the present commentary states:
"Although there is the individual subduing of each and every sentient being"—this cites the statement regarding the "crookedness" within the refutation of the level teaching.
"All are expounded simultaneously and instantaneously in accordance with the nature (dharmatā)"—this explains and establishes the meaning of the "level path."
The skillful means that accord with the nature of reality, despite their infinite distinctions, are all the level path.

Furthermore, they are expounded all at once and simultaneously, unlike the circuitous teaching of provisional means, wherein when the provisional is taught the real is not, and when the real is taught the provisional is not.

Since the Four Truths were taught solely for the sake of the Hīnayāna and the Six Perfections solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas, the fact that all are now presented together makes the level path even more manifest.

The Master further states that "teaching in accordance with sentient beings" refers to the World-Honored One’s teachings elsewhere according to their capacities, rather than this specific sutra being a teaching according to capacity.

As for the statement that although [the Buddha] speaks of a single ultimate such as *nirvāṇa*, this is merely citing the passage on the "level path" found within the *kuṭila* (crooked/indirect) teachings;
it is explained below that this was spoken in response to those for whom the provisional reveals the real, thereby establishing it as a *kuṭila* teaching.
The statement that "the meaning is circuitous" does not mean that the *dharmatā* of *tathatā* itself is circuitous;

rather, it refers to the concealment and manifestation [of the teaching] according to the capacities of sentient beings as being circuitous. The preceding sentence clarifies this circuitous nature by means of the *Lotus Sūtra*:

it shows that what was provisional in the past is now the reality, thereby subverting the three vehicles to reveal the one vehicle. Thus, while the provisional was not yet spoken when the real was to be taught, once the real is spoken, the provisional must necessarily be set aside.

Because their provisional teachings differ from those of the *Avataṃsaka*, where the provisional and the real are revealed simultaneously and applied all at once, they are termed "crooked" (*ku-chü*).

Alternatively, because they bring diverse elements back to a single unity, they are explained as "crooked" by reference to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* reconciles the meaning of the "remaining traces" of the past, bringing them all back to the single flavor of nirvāṇa;
thus, being different first and identical later also constitutes "crookedness. This is not the case with the *Avataṃsaka*.
Whether identical or different, empty or non-empty, and so forth—these are all expounded simultaneously and instantaneously.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "all Tathāgatas may either teach or not teach," the ancient masters have collectively remarked:

for instance, when the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the morning and entered parinirvāṇa at midnight, there was no other distinct time after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in which he further taught the *Nirvāṇa*. This means:
Because the faculties of people are sharp, once they have heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there is no further need to preach the *Nirvāṇa*; thus, the *Nirvāṇa* may be preached or not preached.
In some lands, only the three vehicles are taught to their ultimate conclusion, with nothing to be refuted; in other lands, only the One Vehicle is taught, as there is no third vehicle to be refuted.
Thus one knows that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* also has instances where it is preached or not preached, differing from the lotus flower itself.
I do not see a single Buddha-land where the Tathāgata does not preach this Dharma-light, for it is the level path.
If one takes Śākyamuni as the primary subject, the ten bodies are not yet fully revealed; however, when the ten bodies are taken as the primary subject, they necessarily include Śākyamuni.
Regarding the second section, which takes Śākyamuni as the primary subject, the sub-commentary refutes the four types of differences by stating:

"Furthermore, among the four differences, the two regarding the assembly and the location both contradict the scriptural teachings, for all seven locations are within the Sahā world-system" (this refutes the difference of location). It further states:
"The *Samantabhadra-avyūha-parivarta* says that the Buddhas of the ten directions praise Samantabhadra, saying: 'He is able to expound this Dharma. Now..."

Because there are beings as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field in this assembly who have resolved their minds toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), it is stated accordingly in the "Chapter on Resolving the Mind.
Based on this, one knows that there exists a "vessel" (the foundational capacity) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). [The above refutes the various divergent views.

Therefore, the positions established by this master contradict both scripture and reason in many respects and are very difficult to rely upon. [This concludes the refutation. Now, I shall clarify the two points of divergence he refuted.

Regarding the second point, the difference from the latter one is a defense against the refutation of the established distinction; regarding the difference from the first one, it is a negation of the refutation by other masters.
"Difference" means that fearing a refutation might arise—such as: "Since the sutra below states that he is either named Śākyamuni or named Vairocana, it is clear that the two lords are not different;
why then do you say they are different?"—the present text now provides a comprehensive response.

If Śākyamuni is the principal [manifestation], he is merely the *nirmāṇakāya* among the three bodies; if Vairocana is the principal, then all ten bodies are fully revealed, for the *nirmāṇakāya* is but one of those ten bodies.
Thus it is said that [the latter] must necessarily possess [the former]. Śākyamuni represents the general and the specific as distinct;
how then can you say they are not different?
▲ Where the Sahā world has not yet merged with the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) world, the Flower Treasury world must merge with the Sahā world.

Regarding the statement that "where the Sahā world has not yet merged with the Flower Treasury world, the Flower Treasury world must merge with the Sahā world," this universally establishes and refutes the distinction between locations.
In other places, such as the royal cities of Śrāvastī, it is not yet stated that these are themselves the Flower Treasury world.
Regarding "Vārāṇasī" (婆) and "now" (今), there are two meanings for the "seven locations" (七處), which are identical to the Flower Treasury World (華藏):
first, in terms of the divergence between the root and the branches, these seven locations are within the thirteenth layer of the Flower Treasury World;

second, in terms of the pervasive inclusion of both the pure and the defiled, when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached at the time of the Vajra-ground in the land of Magadha, the Flower Treasury World [was fully present]. Six.
Regarding the preface to that *Zhendong* (Trembling), it states: "The lands encompass both the pure and the defiled; when Saha trembles, Flower Treasury (Puṣpaka-ratna-kośa) moves.
How could the locus of Flower Treasury not be integrated? Thus, one should know that to claim the destruction of their distinct loci contradicts their own assertions.

As for the reason they do not defend against the refutation of the various heterodox views, it is because their refutation within the *Kanding* (Determination of the Canon) was most improper. Among those various heterodox views...
It is merely said that while the *Śākyamuni Sūtras* apply universally to all three vehicles (*triyāna*), the *Vairocana Sūtras* apply only to bodhisattvas;

thus, there is a distinction between the universal and the restricted. Yet, to refute that [position], you cite the arousal of the mind by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Are these not indeed vessels for bodhisattvas?
Moreover, since the arousal of the mind in this sūtra is exceedingly profound, its teaching differs from that of the other [sūtras]. Furthermore, he does not refute [this point].
Therefore, it is not saved.
▲ Briefly stated, there are four differences; that the reality is manifold is truly as you have judged.
[The phrase] "Briefly stated, there are four differences" marks the third section, which concludes the former position. Regarding the statement "the reality is manifold," this is raised once again.

The first of the ten points concerns the ritual procedures of the teaching, which differ from those of the Central [Land] in several respects: namely, that they rely entirely upon the Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi) without ever entering or emerging from it;

that the teaching is expounded all at once and instantaneously rather than through a sequence of preceding and succeeding stages; that the emission of light and the gathering of the assembly differ in their universality or limitation;

that the manner of requesting and answering, as well as the visualization of forms and signs, are distinct; and that the magnificence or inferiority of the adornment of the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) varies.
First, because they are equal [in essence], it is said that the ritual procedures of the teaching gates differ. Second, the principles elucidated differ;

there are many meanings such as the Perfectly Fused (*yuanrong*) and the Sequentially Distinct (*lilüe*), with numerous variations among the ten-fold dharma-gates, as detailed in the *Yifenqi* (The Determination of Meaning). Third, the speed of attaining Buddhahood differs;
that is, it may be in a single thought-moment, or over immeasurable eons, wherein thought-moments and eons are perfectly fused, transcending distinctions of long and short.
First, because [the Buddha] is sovereign and not restricted to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* or to [limited] emanations;

second, because there are differences regarding the universality or restriction of seeing the Buddha, as it is permitted that both ordinary beings and sages see the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), without being restricted by the distinction between those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those on the stages;

third, because the periods for preaching the teachings differ, as the teaching is given immediately upon attainment, with ten layers of *kalpa* and *manvantara* being perfectly interpenetrating, rather than being restricted to [fixed durations] such as twenty-one days.
Sixth, the difference in the breadth or narrowness of the transformed realms: the hells, devas, and six thousand bhikṣus see with the physical eye;

their vision reaches far, pervading the entire Dharma-realm without being restricted to the three-thousandfold world system, which has its own limitations. Seventh, the difference in cause, fruit, practice, and stage:

they possess both complete, circular fusion and sequential arrangement, such that nature and form mutually penetrate one another. Eighth, the difference in the number of vehicles established: some speak of a single vehicle (ekayāna).
First, the vehicles are immeasurable, as they are not restricted to the fixed categories of the three or five vehicles;
second, the benefits are superior and distinct, for the nine benefits are perfected instantaneously in each stage, providing inexhaustible benefit in every atom and every land;
third, the entrustment for circulation differs, as it flows continuously until the end of the future, protected by all Buddhas, and is not of the Lesser Vehicle.
If one seeks out the faults through detailed and specific analysis, there are even more beyond these; thus it is said that "the heterodox realities are many.
This truly confirms the previous interpretation as established.
However, within the midst of these devious twists, the provisional and the real aspects of the Dharma have not yet been revealed.

However, in the second section below which distinguishes contradictions, since it does not judge the depth or shallowness of the indirect (ku-chü) teachings, it causes many dharmas to become conflated without distinction;
thus, it cannot lead people to properly discern the provisional and the real, and for this reason, it is not relied upon.

▲During the Qi dynasty, the recluse Liu Qiu of the early period also established the two teachings of Gradual and Sudden. He held that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is called the Sudden Teaching, while all others are called the Gradual Teaching;
this is because they proceed from small to great, beginning at the Deer Park and concluding at the Twin Trees.

Regarding the four points concerning "recluses and others at dawn" and so forth: within the context of the formal establishment [of the teaching], one distinguishes between gradual and sudden teachings based on the ritual of conversion (*saṃdarśana-vinaya*) and the timing.
That is to say, the sudden teaching refers to the initial accomplishment of the conversion ritual, while the gradual teaching consists of five periods, which are established according to the timing.
▲However, this sutra is like the rising sun that first illuminates the high mountains; this corresponds to the meaning of the Sudden (頓).
That the rain from the Dragon of Compassion (慈龍) serves as proof for the meaning of the Gradual (漸) is reasonable.
▲The gradual teaching will be examined below in relation to the five periods (五時).▲

However, this sutra later distinguishes between conformity and opposition, first conforming and subsequently opposing. Within the section on conformity, because it relies upon the *vyavasthāna* (method of manifestation), it conforms to principle;
it thus cites the relevant passages from this very sutra as evidence. The two analogies cited both appear in the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Nirmita-parivarta*), which was already cited previously.
Here, the gradual approach is used to distinguish opposition, as restricting the teaching by time involves various difficulties and contradictions.
The contradiction with reason will be addressed later in the refutation.
Third, regarding the establishment of the three types of teachings, there are also three schools of thought.
Within the third school’s establishment of the three teachings, the first two provide a general outline.

▲ First, the various Dharma masters of the Southern School collectively established the Three Teachings by adding the "Indeterminate Teaching" (*aniyata-yāna*) to the previously mentioned "Gradual" (*krama*) and "Sudden" (*tada*) teachings.

Regarding the latter point, the Southern School further provides a detailed explanation of three masters; the first concerns how these masters collectively established [the doctrine] within their "Account of the Past. This section is divided into two parts:

first, a general clarification, and second, a specific clarification of the meaning of the gradual teaching. Within the former, there are three sub-sections: the first is the formal establishment [of the doctrine].

▲ First, regarding the gradual [attainment], it begins small and subsequently becomes large; because the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states that [the result] is achieved within six years, this objection is raised.
To refute this difficulty, the "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) category is established.
Next, regarding the gradual [attainment], the intention behind establishing the three [categories] starting from "small at first" is as follows.
▲ It is said that there are certain individual sutras which, although not included within the [sudden] teaching, clarify that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding;
these include the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and others, which constitute the "partial and indeterminate teachings."

The phrase "later" refers to the distinct appearance of the lower and indeterminate [teachings]. Regarding the term "partial teachings" (*piānfāng*), speaking in terms of the general principle, it means that within the gradual [process], one begins with the small and later proceeds to the great;

yet this does not preclude the possibility that even when teaching the small, one may also teach the great—just as a person who propagates the Vinaya for ten years might still preach the Mahāyāna during their private meditative sessions. Therefore, it is said that "partial teachings" are indeterminate and do not specifically refer to the sūtras.

Regarding the statement "like the *Śrīmālā* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*": the beginning of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that King Prasenajit and Queen Māllikā had not long believed in the Dharma; since it says "not long," it clarifies that this was an initial teaching.

As for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, since it is neither the first, sudden teaching nor the final part of the second, gradual teaching, its clarification of eternal abiding (nitya-dharmatā) makes it clear that [this teaching] is indeed [the ultimate].
Regarding the statement that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding (*nitya*), the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* explains that there are two kinds of Tathāgata-garbha, which is precisely the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, in the praise of the Buddha’s three bodies (*trikāya*), the current Sanskrit text states: "All phenomena are eternally abiding;
therefore, I take refuge. This is the meaning of "eternally abiding. This is explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" (*Trikāya-parivarta*) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
This is because it is taught that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding.
Regarding the opening and closing within the gradual [teaching], the various masters differ.
Within the gradual [teaching], the second section specifically clarifies the meaning of the gradual; the opening of the gradual into the distinct [teachings] itself comprises four levels.
From two to five. ▲ Alternatively, it may be divided into only two, namely the "Half" and the "Full. ▲ Alternatively, it may be divided into three;
this refers to what the Dharma Master Yiqie of Mount Wuqiu claimed regarding the period before the twelve years, when he saw there were those who attained [realization].

The teaching concerning the existence of marks is called the Teaching of Marks; twelve years thereafter, reaching up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the realization of emptiness and attainment of the Way is called the Teaching of No-Marks;
finally, the simultaneous illumination of the Buddha-nature in all sentient beings—that even icchantikas can attain Buddhahood—is called the Teaching of Permanence.
Within these three divisions, there are three masters; the first master establishes the correct position.
This is largely identical to the "Teachings of the Three Periods" of the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, as will be discussed in the section on the Western Regions.

The latter two masters refer to the same person, namely the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty and the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. The first [text] mentions Wuchou, which is a mountain monastery in Suzhou.

Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha established the teaching of the three wheels—turning, illuminating, and upholding—based on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*; this is also largely the same [as the former].
This [point] is first aligned with the first master among the three masters;

however, there is a slight difference regarding the timing: it is said that he turned the wheel of Dharma by teaching the Four Truths seven years prior [to his parinirvāṇa], and seven years thereafter.

It is said that the Prajñāpāramitā possesses the two wheels of turning and illuminating, because it illuminates existence through emptiness; thirty years later, it possesses the wheel of holding while turning and illuminating, because it holds the preceding two by simultaneously illuminating both emptiness and existence.
Later, at the appropriate time, [the author] provided a separate sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the specific points, which is somewhat more concise than that [work]. It states:

"The Buddha attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the second month; on the eighth day of the fourth month, he turned the Wheel of the Four Truths for the assembly of *śrāvakas* in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī.
Subsequently, in the seventh year after his enlightenment, while staying in Śrāvastī..."
In Jeta Grove, five *li* from the banks of the Wisdom River, he preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the assembly of the two vehicles;
at this time, he possessed both [aspects], namely, turning and illuminating the wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, thirty years after his enlightenment and before his parinirvāṇa, in the Dharma Hall of the Ghost King in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, he preached for the sake of the Bodhisattva True Permanence (*Tchen-ch'ang*).
At this time, the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa* and other sutras possess the three kinds of Dharma wheels: the wheel of turning, the wheel of illuminating, and the wheel of sustaining.
Alternatively, they may be divided into four;
that is, as the Dharma Master Jie of the Song dynasty maintained, there is a period following the signless (*animitta*) and preceding the eternally abiding (*nitya*).
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is designated as the "Teaching of Common Return" because it brings together the three vehicles to return to the one, and all myriad virtues are directed toward Bodhi.
Regarding the third of the four divisions by the master Jie of the Song dynasty, commentators did not wish to produce excessive verbiage;
therefore, they merely added alternative names to those of the preceding masters, which should be listed in full as follows.
▲ Some classify [the teachings] into five, yet there are two schools of thought.

▲ One school, such as Daochang, Huiquan, and others, maintains that from the stage of "signlessness" (*animitta*) up to the stage of "convergence" (*samavasaraṇa*), the teaching that points toward purity— such as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and others—
is a teaching of "suppression and exaltation" (*yiyang jiao*).

▲ Second, this refers to the aforementioned Master Liu, who did not employ the method of alternating emphasis and deprecation, but instead took the *Tiewei jing* as the "Teaching for Humans and Devas" (*rentian jiao*) at the initial stage of his instruction.

Regarding the "Dharma Hall of Huiguan," this refers to the monk of Shangyuan Daochang Monastery; as for what he called the "Five Teachings," the first is the Teaching with Characteristics (*youxiang jiao*).

The five teachings are: first, the teaching of the two vehicles; second, the teaching of signlessness; third, the teaching of suppression and exaltation; fourth, the teaching of common return; and fifth, the teaching of eternal abiding.

Regarding the "teaching of suppression and exaltation," it refers to suppressing and disparaging the śrāvakas while praising and exalting the bodhisattvas. Master Liu’s fivefold classification consists of: first, the teaching of humans and devas;
second, the teaching with signs; third, the teaching without signs; fourth, the teaching of common return; and fifth, the teaching of eternal abiding.
▲The aforementioned masters all differentiate [the teachings] based on time within the gradual approach;

however, if the teaching of the indeterminate is not added, it will give rise to many more difficulties, as there would be a contradiction regarding the existence of the Mahāyāna from the very beginning. Even if the indeterminate is added, there remain obstacles and difficulties.
I shall briefly reveal the difficulties regarding the five periods, and the rest may be understood by analogy.

The preceding section concludes; here begins the second part, which distinguishes between what is concordant and what is contradictory. This section has three parts: first, a general clarification of the concordant and the contradictory;
second, a specific refutation of that which contradicts reason; and third, a conclusion establishing the distinction between the concordant and the contradictory. Regarding the first:

since all the aforementioned masters from the second to the fifth [theories] first present the Hīnayāna and subsequently the Mahāyāna, the "indeterminate" category is not added; thus, the first [theory] possesses the Mahāyāna.
Although these difficulties, even when applied indeterminately, still present obstacles— namely, that while applying the indeterminacy one avoids the initial difficulty regarding the Mahāyāna,
there are nonetheless difficulties within the names and meanings established [by those systems]— to briefly illustrate the obstacles regarding the five periods,
I shall refute them starting from the last; once the five periods have been refuted, the four, three, and two periods will all have been refuted as well.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
First, it clarifies that those who claim the period before the twelve years was characterized by "having marks" (sanimitta) contradict the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* itself; for the *Kośa* states:
"I shall now precisely clarify the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka, and that true meaning is emptiness."

Regarding the initial clarification of the "twelve years" and so forth: this second section provides a specific refutation of the two schools' views on the five periods, which is divided into two parts.
First, the refutation of the five periods of the *Dharmaguptaka* school is further divided into five sections. As the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"I now correctly clarify the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka; that true meaning is emptiness. This constitutes the refutation of the first period, citing its third [point].
This passage explains that the first citation from a Śrāvaka treatise—the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*—states its intent as follows:
"I now establish the true meaning (*tattvārtha*) within the Śrāvaka vehicle; therefore, it is called 'Establishing Reality' (*Tattvasiddhi*).

Since the Tripiṭaka constitutes the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the mention of "true meaning" clearly indicates that emptiness has already been taught therein. How then can one say that the path cannot be attained by seeing existence?
One does not attain the Way without perceiving the true meaning.

Furthermore, it is said in the Āgamas: "There is no such thing as aging and death" refers to the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā); "there is no one who ages and dies" refers to the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
Furthermore, it is said in the Āgamas that [the following] second citation is from a Hīnayāna sūtra. The continuous text of the sūtra states:

"There is no such thing as aging-and-death; there is no one who ages-and-dies. This clarifies the meaning of the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) within the twelve links of dependent origination.
"Aging-and-death" refers to the substantial entity (*dharmasvabhāva*) of aging-and-death, while "who" refers to the person (*pudgala*). Therefore, "there is no such thing as aging-and-death" means...
The dharma of old age and death is empty; there is no one who ages and dies, for it is empty of a master, an "I," or a person.

However, there are two reasons why many sūtras and śāstras clarify only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and do not clarify the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) within the context of the Hīnayāna:

first, they speak according to the majority rather than the minority, as the Hīnayāna predominantly clarifies only the emptiness of persons; second, [they do so] from the perspective of explicitness... [text fragment].

Although it is said that the emptiness of phenomena is not fully elucidated when explained through non-manifestation or partial explanation, it is nevertheless clarified that phenomena are empty; it is from this perspective that [the present teaching] proceeds.

▲ Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Tripiṭaka, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is explained as the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*); in the Mahāyāna, the emptiness of the ten directions is explained as the Great Emptiness.
Regarding the phrase "In the Tripiṭaka, the emptiness of phenomena is explained as the Great Emptiness," etc., this is the third citation from a Mahāyāna treatise, which provides that explanation.

The eighteen kinds of emptiness distinguish the Great Emptiness from the two [other] schools; here, we simply take the words clarifying the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) from the Tripiṭaka.
The Tripiṭaka is indeed the teaching of the Hīnayāna.
Thus, it is clearly shown that the Hīnayāna already possesses both types of emptiness.
All of these manifest the conclusion of the preceding three passages.
If it is said that the second period taught emptiness, yet the extensive precepts were only established twelve years later, how could it be that he taught only emptiness?
If it is said that there was a second period, this section below refutes that second period; herein there are three parts: first, refuting the teaching of emptiness;
second, refuting the failure to clarify permanence; and third, establishing the correct meaning as a conclusion. Within the first part, there are further two sections.

First, citing the establishment of the precepts to demonstrate that the teaching of existence occurred after twelve years: the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* states, "Well guard your speech, and purify your own will."
"Let the mind and body not commit any evil; these three paths of action, when purified, can lead to such practice as this—the path of the Great Sages.
This is the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* which the Tathāgata Śākyamuni spoke for the community of those without affairs (*anavassutaka-saṅgha*) during the twelve years [following his enlightenment].

It was only after these twelve years had passed that he began to extensively analyze and explain it in detail. Thus, one should know that the detailed formulation was established only after those twelve years.
The broad precepts are themselves the manifestation of existence.

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the night of attaining the Way until his parinirvāṇa, he constantly preached Prajñā; how could it be that he did not previously preach emptiness?"
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the initial attainment of the Way [down to the second citation from the treatise, it] provides a general explanation of Prajñā.

This clarifies that emptiness was already taught twelve years prior; it is not restricted to the Prajñā teachings of the twelve years later. Thus, it clarifies that the wisdom of the nature of emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is [present throughout]."
▲If it is said that the *prajñāpāramitā* of true reality (*tathatā*) was not revealed as eternally abiding during the second period, how could it possibly be impermanent?

If it is argued that [the teaching] during the second period did not clarify eternal abiding— this constitutes the first of four sections within the refutation of the failure to clarify eternal abiding,
wherein the opponent’s position is countered by demonstrating that true reality is indeed eternal.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also states that buddha-nature is likewise called *prajñā*.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* further explains that [the previous section] established the correct view while refuting the superior [position], which is the measure of reasoning (*yukti-pramāṇa*); this [present section] is the measure of authoritative scripture (*āpta-śabda-pramāṇa*).
Since *prajñā* is identical to buddha-nature, and buddha-nature is eternal, *prajñā* is eternal.

▲ Thus we know that *prajñāpāramitā* as the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is the direct cause of Buddhahood (*samyak-hetu-buddhatva*), while its contemplative illumination (*āloka*) is the enabling cause (*parigraha-hetu*).

This constitutes the third section on reconciling the meaning: it explains the two sutras so that the second period [teaching] is made identical to the fifth period, because their meanings are the same;
namely, that the two kinds of *prajñā* are the two types of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which differ only in name.

In meaning, there is no difference; to say that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) means that the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is named Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).

That is to say, the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*) takes emptiness as its actual meaning; the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* [presents] the gate of both existence and emptiness, while the gate of neither existence nor emptiness has not yet been seen in the treatises.

To dispel these hundredfold errors through the "horns" [of dialectical analysis] is precisely the gate of neither existence nor non-existence. If one examines the scriptures and treatises:

the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* mostly elucidates the gate of existence; the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Pal-zhin) mostly explains the gate of emptiness; the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* mostly reveals the gate of both existence and emptiness;
and the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* mostly discerns the gate of neither existence nor emptiness.

Regarding the description of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa within this [text]: it is said that after the Tathāgata had accepted alms-food from Cunda’s house—consisting of *śālī* rice and *candana*-wood mushrooms—and subsequently suffered from back pain, he entered the city of Kuśinagara.

Only these two laymen, Tiwei and Bolili, who were experts in the five elements and yin-yang, and who divined by tortoise shells and the *I Ching*, knew that the Buddha had attained enlightenment; thus they are named.
The tree deity Tiwei offered parched grain flour, and the Four Heavenly Kings presented alms bowls; having accepted them, the Tathāgata first preached the causes and effects of the world for Tiwei.
This is according to the characteristics of the Hīnayāna, yet it does not preclude its application to the Mahāyāna;

for that same sutra further states that five hundred merchants, having received the five precepts, first repented of the five heinous crimes, the ten evil deeds, the slandering of the Dharma, and so forth.

The Venerable Pāpīyas attained the realization that the four great elements are fundamentally pure, the five aggregates are fundamentally pure, the six sense objects are fundamentally pure, and the five roots are fundamentally pure.

The householder Tiwei attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Three hundred merchants attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*), and two hundred merchants attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*).
The Four Heavenly Kings attained the patience of compliance, and three hundred dragon kings attained [the same].
Upon the arising of the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), immeasurable sentient beings, including the other devas and so forth, gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* states that during the second seven-day period, five hundred merchants led by Tiwei offered the Buddha parched grain flour and honey;
the Buddha bestowed upon them the prediction: "In a future age, you shall all attain Buddhahood, and you shall all share the same name: Qicheng."

It is clearly known that this does not refer solely to humans and devas; however, since the Tishyagupta Stūpa currently exists in the country of Tukhāra, and the scriptures cited above all clarify that the Great Vehicle was already taught at the very beginning, your statement contradicts the *Guhyakapada Sūtra*, which states that the Three Vehicles were taught during the second week.
If the Three Vehicles were already taught during the second week, how can you claim [that the Mahāyāna was taught later]?

The first [period] consists solely of teachings for humans and devas; this sutra is the third fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the "Assembly of the Vajrapāṇi Malla," which is the eighth [in the sequence]. It was translated by Zhu Fahu.

However, regarding the aforementioned five periods and so forth, if one were to define them strictly according to time, there would be discrepancies; therefore, those that are indeterminate have been excluded.
There is also reason to say that this is for the most part;

however, regarding the "five periods" mentioned above, the third [section] establishes the contradiction and conformity. The phrase "above" concludes the preceding discussion on contradiction, while the term "etc.
(等) includes the four, three, and two periods. The statement "setting aside the indeterminate" means that it is also said from the perspective of what occurs for the most part.

There is a logical basis for this, as it establishes a concordance with reason through two meanings. First, by excluding the indeterminate, one avoids the fault of failing to reach a definitive conclusion;

second, because it is stated from a majority perspective, it does not contradict the *Guhyakapada-sūtra* and other scriptures, nor does it conflict with the position one has established oneself. Thus, there is a logical basis.
▲ Second, regarding Fotudeng (佛圖澄) and the Vinaya Master Guangtong of the Later Wei:

First, it is called "gradual" because it teaches in a progressive sequence, such as first explaining permanence and then emptiness, followed by non-emptiness, and so forth.

Second, it is called "sudden" because for those whose faculties are mature, it fully expounds all aspects—including permanence, impermanence, emptiness, and non-emptiness—within a single Dharma-gate, leaving no room for gradual progression.
Third, it is for those who have reached the higher stages and are on the verge of entering the realm of the Buddha.
This is because it explains the Tathāgata’s secret, sovereign dharma-gate of the ultimate fruit of merit—the perfection of unimpeded liberation;

Furthermore, three teachings are established below to clarify the formulation of its meaning. Within these, the gradual teaching is explained in terms of incompleteness, while the sudden teaching is explained in terms of completeness.
This differs from Master Yan’s view that the "great" and "small" [teachings] correspond to the sudden and gradual. As for what is called "complete exposition," it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
that which is called "emptiness" refers to saṃsāra, while that which is called "not empty" refers to Mahāparinirvāṇa, and so forth.
Furthermore, it says that whether regarding emptiness or non-emptiness, permanence or impermanence, and so on, all are extensively expounded; this is precisely the sudden teaching. (3)

This also refers merely to the sequence of the pedagogical manifestation (huayi).

Regarding this phrase "this also refers merely to the sequence of the pedagogical manifestation," it distinguishes between conformity and contrariety; because the doctrines established by this master are for the most part in accord with principle, they are not [contradicted].
In resolving these contradictions, I shall first set forth my intended position and subsequently explain away potential objections. First, regarding this initial point:

this is also explained in terms of the pedagogical method (*śāsanavidhi*). If there is a sequence [of teachings], it is because within the sudden teaching, the methods of transformation do not differ from those of the gradual;

specifically, teaching emptiness and non-emptiness at different times is called "gradual," whereas teaching emptiness and non-emptiness simultaneously is called "sudden. Thus, this refers to the pedagogical method.

The third [classification] also relies on the method of transformation to distinguish it from the previous two; since this is stated according to the majority of cases, it says, "this also relies on the ritual of transformation.

The underlying intent clarifies that those capable of receiving the sudden teaching at the present time must have previously received transformation [through gradual means]; thus it says, "the faculties are matured and have reached the highest level."
The meaning of these words encompasses both the stages prior to the Grounds (*bhūmi*) and the realm of the Buddha; thus, it is also logically applicable to the Grounds themselves.

This intention clarifies that the present passage removes the obstacles and difficulties regarding the two lower interpretations. Specifically, the Master of the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determining the Text) raised two difficulties:

first, the difficulty of combining the gradual and the sudden; second, the difficulty of distinguishing between the gradual and the perfect (*yuan*). Regarding the first difficulty concerning the Perfect [Vehicle], he said: "If the faculties of the gradual [vehicle] were to mature..."
If both gradual and sudden faculties arise and mature simultaneously, then the distinction between gradual and sudden can be maintained;

however, since it is stated that what is "unripe" is called gradual and what is "ripe" is called sudden, this implies that within a single gradual faculty, the only difference lies in its state of maturation, and there is no distinct meaning of "sudden.

Alternatively, it would follow that for that single [gradual] faculty, there must be two types—gradual and sudden—since arising necessarily leads to maturation, and maturation necessarily proceeds from arising. Therefore, [the distinction is untenable].
It should be that all are gradual faculties (*krama-indriya*), for there is none that does not proceed from birth to maturation.
The commentary states: This first objection contains three internal difficulties: first, the difficulty of the non-distinction between the gradual and the sudden;

Now, this single point resolves all three difficulties as in the first objection; having established the distinction between gradual and sudden based on the faculties [of the listener], those difficulties arise.
But since we do not now establish the distinction between gradual and sudden based on the faculties, how can these difficulties exist?
It is said that for those whose faculties are developing, one preaches the Dharma-gate gradually, which is called "gradual"; for those whose faculties are mature, one preaches the Dharma suddenly.
If you maintain that [the teaching] is sudden, how can you raise the objection that both the "unripe" and the "ripe" are sudden? Thus, your first objection is refuted.

Since we do not restrict [the teaching] to the faculties, how can you raise objections such as that the unripe must necessarily reach the ripe, or that the ripe must necessarily proceed from the unripe?

That [objection] arose because the stage of superior progress (*uttara-gati*) and the stage of approaching the Buddha-realm were combined into a single meaning; therefore, this difficulty was raised. Now, to provide the resolution:

the stage of superior progress refers to the levels prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva-bhāga*), while the stage of approaching the Buddha-realm refers to the grounds themselves (*bhūmy-uttara-bhāga*). Thus, it does not contradict the text of the *Samudgata-parivarta*.
If even this does not lose sight of the great principle, how much less so when one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta?
Is this not one who has partially entered the realm of the Buddha?

Third, during the end of the Sui and beginning of the Tang dynasties, the Dharma Master Jizang established three kinds of wheels of Dharma based on the fifth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

in contrast to the three teachings of Master Kuangtong, one is based on the modes of transformation, the second is based on the transformative Dharma, and the third is based on the faculties.

Now, this master’s establishment relies solely on the modes of transformation; as for the Dharma, there are only the Great and Small Vehicles. Below, the text correctly distinguishes between what is compliant and what is contrary.
If there were only the "great" and "small," there would be no distinction between the "half" and "full" [teachings], nor would the meaning be fully encompassed.

Nevertheless, the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) reveals the beginning and the end for a certain class of beings. This section reconciles the intent of the sūtra to resolve such difficulties;
for one might raise the objection: "If the established doctrine is based upon the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is then merely an ultimate teaching. Why do you not rely upon it?"

The present commentary states: This is because those who established the teaching did not grasp the true meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The *Lotus Sutra* was taught specifically for a certain class of people who were stuck in the Lesser Vehicle;

thus, it was said that those who cling to the three [vehicles] while doubting the one, and who cling to the Lesser while doubting the Great, are therefore led through the opening of the gate of expedient means to reveal the mark of reality. The Hīnayāna represents a provisional gateway; it is not intended to synthesize the entirety of the sacred teachings of a single lifetime.

Furthermore, the sūtra merely states, "except for those who have previously... [implying that those who had already practiced elsewhere are exempt].
Those who practice and study the Hīnayāna clearly understand the intent of the sūtras; it does not indicate that the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other such texts are merely branches or secondary.
Furthermore, while the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Wuliangyi jing) previously cited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to refute [the Hīnayāna], here we cite another sūtra to refute it.
Since it is said that "at all times there are both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna," it follows that it is not the case that the beginning is exclusively Mahāyāna and the middle is exclusively Hīnayāna.

Furthermore, these were all direct refutations without inclusion; however, within the opening of the school and the establishment of the teaching, they are included under this principle, and thus they are briefly omitted here.
Moreover, since the meaning of the sutra has already been presented, they are effectively included therein.
▲ Fourth, regarding the establishment of the four teachings, there are briefly four schools.
▲ First, Master Guangzhai of the Liang dynasty, based on the second chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, established the teaching of four vehicles:

he held that the three carts at the gate represent the provisional teaching of the three vehicles, while the equal bestowal [of jeweled carriages] at the crossroads represents the real teaching of the Mahāyāna.

The fourth section establishes the four teachings; it has four parts. First, within the Guangzhai [School], there are two sections: first, recounting the past views; second, conforming to and refuting the former.

Within the latter, there are three parts: first, the formal establishment [of the doctrine]; second, providing the reasons for it; third, concluding the argument. Regarding the first of these, "four crossroads" refers to the Four Noble Truths; the rest can be understood accordingly.

▲ This teaching elucidates the principle of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing through dependent origination.

Following the phrase "this teaching elucidates dependent origination," the following section distinguishes the principles expressed therein. The term "dependent origination" (yīnyuán) applies across all four teachings:

because of dependent origination there is arising and ceasing; because of dependent origination there is emptiness; because of dependent origination there is provisional designation; and because of dependent origination there is the Middle Way.
