In accordance with the preceding heading, because all phenomena are without differentiation, the two aspects are such that the phenomenal characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the phenomenon and the dharmatā is the non-phenomenon.

Just as in the analogy of gold, where the gold represents the dharmatā and the color represents the phenomenal characteristic, the present text employs the latter sense; thus it establishes that the phenomena of the conventional level are identical to the principle, and that the two truths are mutually identical.
▲ This also serves as a metaphor for the fact that the Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna are mutually indistinguishable.
This further illustrates the meaning of the true mind within the distinction between the true and the false in the preceding "Mind-Only" section of the second pair of assemblies:
the gold represents the Tathāgatagarbha, while the color represents birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and so forth; thus, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states, "The Tathāgata is pure."
The worldly *ālayavijñāna* is like gold and a ring; they are mutually indistinguishable because this was already established in the third section above, hence the use of the word "also" (*api*).

Furthermore, because phenomena (*dharma*) are themselves the principle (*dharmatā*), although they exist, they are not eternal; because the principle is itself phenomena, although they are empty, they are not annihilated.

Furthermore, the identity of phenomena (*dharma*) with principle (*tattva*), whereby the lower [level] does not sever continuity from permanence, is also derived from within the gateway of the two truths.
Moreover, because phenomena and principle are mutually identical, arising and ceasing are simultaneous. As the *Sumeru-gāthā* says:
"The conduct of all ordinary beings inevitably and swiftly returns to exhaustion; yet their nature is like space, and thus it is said that there is no exhaustion. The wise say there is none."

Even at the point of exhaustion, there is nothing that can be said, because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is inexhaustible; thus, inconceivable exhaustion and so forth are possible. Consequently, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) exist simultaneously, without depending on subsequent non-existence (*anupalabdhi*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "due to the mutual identity of fact and principle," it means that within the distinctions of the four characteristics—whether sequential or simultaneous—the momentary [nature] is identical [to the whole].
The meaning of these matters is entirely consistent; therefore, when the phenomena cease, they do so because phenomena are empty and devoid of substantiality.
Thus, the cited verse refers to the Bodhisattva Śubhamati.
This also causes one to ultimately sever and realize the transcendence of subject and object, as stated in the "Ten Stages" chapter: "Neither beginning, nor middle, nor end."

It is beyond the reach of words; as the *Parivarta on Dedication* states: "There is no suchness outside of wisdom that could be entered by wisdom, nor is there wisdom outside of suchness that could realize suchness.
This also brings to ultimate completion the subject and object of abandonment and realization within the very midst of their non-separation, according to the meaning of the tenth [chapter].

In the scriptural passage on the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*) in the *Bhūmi*, only the first phrase describes the characteristic of abandoning afflictions, because it states that abandonment occurs only when there is no abandonment during the three times.
The subsequent phrase describes the characteristic of *prajñā*. Now, since *prajñā* is also that which performs the abandonment, this [scripture] is cited incidentally.
Therefore, the treatise explains this phrase as being the characteristic of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), namely, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The essence is beyond names and words, and true wisdom arises internally; this differs from the śrāvakas, who awaken by relying on sound.

Since it is true wisdom, it can sever delusions. As the *Parivarta on Dedication* states, "There is no suchness outside of wisdom," this also proves the meaning that subject and object are non-dual in the severing of delusions, as previously explained. All the scriptures cited above will be reached in the main text below.
You shall understand this for yourself.
▲ Ninth, the Gate of Truth Being Non-Phenomenal: The truth that is identical with the delusion is distinct from delusion, just as moisture is not motion.
Regarding the ninth, the Gate of Truth Being Non-Phenomenal: it means that the principle inherent in phenomena is not itself a phenomenon, because truth and delusion [are distinct].
Because they are distinct, [emptiness] is real and not false; because it is the basis and not that which depends upon it, it is like water that is not identical to its waves.
Since it is neither the wave nor the moisture, nor movement, it is thus not different from existence—the true emptiness within which emptiness abides.
▲ Regarding the ten matters of the irrational gate: the delusion that is not separate from reality is distinct from reality itself, just as motion is not identical to moisture.
As the *Gāthā on the Forest of Shame and Remorse* says: "Just as form and non-form, these two do not constitute one. It further states:
"Just as the characterized and the uncharacterized, as well as saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, their distinctions are each different."

Regarding the "gate of phenomena that are entirely irrational": this refers to phenomena that, while being entirely rational in their essence (*dharmatā*), are constantly irrational in their phenomenal aspect (*lakṣaṇa*).

This is because their nature and characteristics are distinct, and because the dependent is not the basis upon which it depends. Therefore, while the entire substance is entirely rational, the phenomenal characteristics remain manifestly distinct.
It is like waves in water: although they are entirely water in substance, the waves are constantly non-water, because movement is not wetness. Thus, they are not different from emptiness.
Within these illusory phenomena, all things exist.

Because the first seven and eighth sections clarify that phenomena and principle are not different, and the ninth through twelfth sections clarify that phenomena and principle are not one, the fourth dedication states: "In the realm of the conditioned, it demonstrates the unconditioned."

While abiding in the Dharma, one does not destroy the characteristics of the conditioned within the unconditioned realm; one demonstrates conditioned phenomena without discriminating the nature of the unconditioned.
The two gates above (the seventh and eighth) and the four gates below serve to reconcile the previous distinctions between the unconditioned and conditioned aspects of the Buddha-body.
This is the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within [the middle way]. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also states:

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, "If this dharma is equal and without high or low, is it conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or is it unconditioned? The Buddha replied, "It is neither a conditioned dharma nor an unconditioned dharma.
Why? Because apart from conditioned dharmas, unconditioned dharmas cannot be found; and apart from unconditioned..."
Subhūti, because neither dharmas nor conditioned dharmas can be apprehended, the non-conjunction and non-separation of the conditioned and the unconditioned are all its meanings.
Since the ten matters above share a single dependent origination, they are said to be unimpeded.

▲When one views phenomena from the perspective of principle, there is formation and destruction, union and separation; when one views principle from the perspective of phenomena, there is manifestation and concealment, identity and difference.
These arise simultaneously and instantaneously, with freedom in both contrariety and conformity, unobstructed and unhindered.

Contemplate this deeply so that the contemplation may manifest clearly, thereby achieving the perfect fusion and non-obstruction of principle and phenomena. This is the contemplation of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena (*lishi yuanrong wuai guan*).
Regarding the ten matters above, the third section is the general conclusion, which summarizes and explains the ten gates. This section has two parts: first, the summary and reference;
second, the specific grouping of the ten gates into eight characters by correlating principle with phenomena. Regarding the correlation of principle with phenomena, there are four meanings:
first, "existence," which refers to the third gate, the Gate of Principle Establishing Phenomena; second, "destruction" (or negation).
The phrase "is" refers to the fifth gate, "substituting principle for phenomenon," wherein since the phenomenon is sublated, the phenomenon is destroyed.

The phrase "the three existences are identical" refers to the seventh gate, "principle is identical to phenomenon. The phrase "there is separation" refers to the ninth gate, "principle is not phenomenon.
Regarding the statement that phenomena, in relation to principle, have both manifestation and concealment, as well as unity and difference—these also exist.
Regarding the four gates: first, that which is manifest refers to the fourth matter, the gate of the ability to manifest principle;

second, that which is hidden refers to the sixth matter, the gate of the ability to hide principle; third, that which is identical refers to the eighth matter, the gate where phenomena are identical to principle;
fourth, that which is different refers to the tenth matter, the gate where phenomena are not principle. As for the aforementioned mention of "formation and destruction" and so forth:

Speaking in terms of function, it is logical that what is established through principle (*li*) is not necessarily established as a fact (*shi*), whereas what is established by itself is so in each gate;

thus, there is the non-obstruction of fact and principle. Therefore, it is said that "in terms of principle looking toward fact" and "in terms of fact looking toward principle," and the rest may be inferred from this.

Because the preceding [sections] have been mutually integrated, there are four pairs of eight meanings; now, regarding the first pair, the characteristic of pervasion (*xiang-bian*) involves two gates.

Those who do not understand [this] fail to perceive it because the meaning of mutual pervasion (*xiāngbiàn*) implies that all phenomena are similar in nature, rather than being such that one is formed while another perishes, and so forth.
Furthermore, this mutual pervasion is precisely the raison d'être for the latter eight gates; it is only through mutual pervasion that there can be formation, destruction, and the like.
If one wishes to subsume these points, they are contained within the two meanings of the mutual identity of phenomena and principle (*shìlǐ xiāngjí*).
The "subsequent non-identity" and the "non-immediate identity" of the two gates do not destroy the relationship between the subject and object;

only when there is mutual pervasion of characteristics can one discuss non-identity. Regarding the terms "contrary," "accordant," "sovereignty," and so forth, within each of the four meanings of the mutual relation between phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*), there are two meanings that are contrary and two meanings that are accordant.
That is to say, the establishment of phenomena based on principle and the identity of true principle with phenomena are accordant.

Furthermore, when principle supersedes phenomena, the true principle is not contrary to phenomena; when phenomena can manifest principle, the dharma of phenomena is identical to principle and thus harmonious.
When phenomena can conceal principle, the dharma of phenomena is not identical to principle and is thus contrary.

Because it is established at will and destroyed at will, it is said that establishment does not obstruct destruction and destruction does not obstruct establishment; manifestation does not obstruct concealment and concealment does not obstruct manifestation.
Because they manifest through obstruction, they are called "unobstructed. Since the very moment of formation is itself destruction and so forth, they can exist simultaneously;

as all four pairs lack anteriority or posteriority, they are said to "arise instantaneously. Furthermore, regarding the first four pairs, why is it that when referring to principle (li) in relation to phenomena (shi), one speaks only of "formation" and so forth rather than "manifestation" and so forth;
yet when referring to phenomena in relation to principle, one speaks only of "manifestation" and so forth rather than "formation"?

There is a profound reason for this equality. What is it? Since phenomena arise from principle, it may be granted that they are established; yet principle is not something newly existent, so one can only say it is manifested.
Because phenomena must perish when established, one may speak of their "destruction"; yet because true principle is eternally abiding, one speaks only of its "concealment.

Whether one considers them identical or distinct, or whether one considers them separate or different, the general principle remains the same, though the detailed explanation differs regarding the nature of principle.
It has no form or appearance, yet it can only be understood through phenomena; since phenomena possess ten thousand differences, one may speak of their "mystical identity" with principle (*li*).
Since principle is devoid of all appearances, it is said to be "separate from phenomena. Because phenomena have disparities, they are said to be "different" [from principle].

Regarding these distinctions in meaning, there are these various differences. If one were to synthesize them, they would constitute five pairs of meanings of non-obstruction: first, the pair of "phenomena" (*xiang*).

The "pervasive correspondence" (biàn duì) establishes two aspects; the "correspondence of completion" (chéng duì) establishes three aspects; the "correspondence of harm" (hài duì) establishes four aspects;

and the "correspondence of identity" (jí duì) and "correspondence of non-identity" (bù jí duì) each establish five aspects. Among these five, the first four clarify that phenomena and principle are not separate, while the last one clarifies that phenomena and principle are not identical.

Furthermore, within these five correspondences, there are three meanings that establish and manifest them: the meaning of phenomena and principle acting upon one another, the meaning of negating the hidden, and the meaning of non-identity.
That is to say, the pair of "identity" (ekatva) and "pervasion" (vyāpti) refers to the meaning of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle;
furthermore, because the second characteristic functions as such, there is the fourth characteristic. Because of this identity, there is pervasion;
because of the third characteristic of "contradiction," there is the fifth characteristic of "non-identity. Moreover, if there were no [fifth characteristic of] non-identity...
Since there is nothing that can be characterized as pervasive, it is said that "True Emptiness" (zhēnkōng) and "Wondrous Existence" (miàoyǒu) each have four meanings.

First, regarding principle (*lǐ*) in relation to phenomena (*shì*), there are the four meanings of True Emptiness: 1. The meaning of abandoning oneself to become another: this is the gate of phenomena being established based on principle (*yī lǐ chéng shì mén*).

2. The meaning of submerging the other to manifest oneself: this is the gate of true principle eclipsing phenomena (*zhēn lǐ duó shì mén*). 3. The meaning of both self and other coexisting: this is the gate of true... [text truncated]
The principle is not the phenomena gate (*li-fei-shi-men*): the meaning of the mutual sublation of self and other; the principle is the phenomena gate (*ji-li-ji-shi-men*):

because they are identical, they mutually sublate one another. Furthermore, the first and third [gates] are the principle-pervading-phenomena gate (*ji-li-bian-yu-shi-men*): because it exists as itself, its entire substance becomes the other, and thus it pervades the other. Next, regarding phenomena in relation to principle, there are four meanings of the "wondrous existence" (*miaoyou*). First: [...text omitted... ...the principle is the phenomena gate: because they are identical, they mutually sublate one another. Furthermore, the first and third are the principle-pervading-phenomena gate: because it exists as itself, its entire substance becomes the other, and thus it pervades the other. Next, regarding phenomena in relation to principle, there are four meanings of the "wondrous existence. First:

1. The gate of manifesting the principle through the phenomenon by means of the meaning of manifesting the other while exhausting the self; 2. The gate of concealing the principle through the phenomenon by means of the meaning of manifesting the self while concealing the other;
3. The gate of neither principle nor phenomenon through the phenomenon by means of the meaning of the co-existence of both self and other; 4.

The gate of the identity of phenomenon and principle through the phenomenon by means of the meaning of the simultaneous vanishing of both self and other. Furthermore, the first and third are gates of the pervasion of the phenomenon throughout the principle.

Because it exists for its own sake and is able to manifest others, and because it pervades all others, it is said that illusion possesses unimpeded existence and non-existence, and true emptiness possesses sovereign concealment and manifestation.

Fourth is "Universal Containment," which refers to the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena; this shall now be explained according to the ten mysterious gates as revealed by the ancient masters.
Regarding the Chinese text, there are two parts: first, the formal exposition of the "Mysterious Gate" (xuánmén); second, the clarification of its underlying rationale.

Regarding the fourth section, "Universal Inclusion," this refers to the contemplation of universal inclusion (*zhōubiàn hánróng guān*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the headings to open the chapters;

second, the detailed explanation according to those chapters. Now, for the first part: the name of this contemplation is that which [is found] within the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*).

The name [of the principle] corresponds to the phenomena, for phenomena are unimpeded; because the principle possesses the two meanings of universality and vast capacity, it is fused with all phenomena, enabling them to pervade and contain one another in numerous ways. All these gateways of meaning exist by virtue of these two meanings.
However, since the ten contemplations established in the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* differ from the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhyaka*), this commentary states: "For now, we rely upon..."

The ancient masters’ exposition of the Ten Mysterious Gates was based on Master Zang; although Fazhitang already possessed this teaching, there are slight differences from the Chinese version, which can be understood by examining the opening chapter of the second part.
▲ 1. The Gate of Simultaneous Fulfillment and Correspondence; 2. The Gate of Unobstructed Sovereignty over the Broad and the Narrow;
3. The Gate of Mutual Interpenetration between the One and the Many; 4. The Gate of the Sovereign Identity of All Dharmas; 5.
The Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of the Secret and the Manifest; 6. The Gate of the Subtle Interpenetration and Stable Establishment; 7. The Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net; 8. [...]
The Gate of Manifesting the Dharma by Entrusting It to Phenomena (90); the Gate of Accomplishing the Diversity of Dharmas Despite the Separation of Ages (91);

and the Gate of the Perfect Clarity and Endowment of Principal and Retinue (92)—these ten gates are a single dependent origination, unimpeded and perfectly interfused; according to any one gate, all others are fully present.
Now, first, the initial [section] explains both simultaneously; second, the subsequent sections explain them according to their chapters, which constitutes two distinct parts.

Now, in explaining the first chapter, the commentary text has three sections: first, listing the names to provide a general overview; second, pointing to specific instances to provide detailed clarification;

third, concluding with examples to establish the benefits. Regarding the first: these ten names follow Xianshou (Xuanzhuo) in their entirety; therefore, it was stated above that they "mutually rely on the ancients."

In the enumeration of the names of the virtues, this second [gate], the Gate of Sovereignty over Extent and Narrowness, shares the same meaning as the "Universal Inclusiveness and Pervasiveness" in the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), though its name differs slightly.

This gate was newly established by Xianshou to replace Fazang’s "Gate of the Ten Mysteries of Mutual Interpenetration and the Exclusive and Mixed Endowment of Virtues. It states that a single practice is "exclusive," while myriad practices are "mixed."
This "equality" (sameness) is precisely the meaning of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

If one takes the single principle as "pure" and the myriad practices as "mixed," this would constitute the non-obstruction of phenomenon and principle (*shili wuai*); fearing such confusion with that [other] category, it was revised.

The gate of "Principal and Retinue" (*zhuban*) is absent in Zhixiang [Zhiyan], whereas the gate of "The Mind Alone Revolving and Excellently Accomplishing" (*weixin huizhuan shancheng*) exists there; because it serves as the gateway to the profound mystery (*xuanyuan*), it is not [included here].

Establishing them in order, their sequence also differs from that [other text]. That [text] states: (1) the gate of simultaneous and perfect mutual correspondence; (2) the gate of the realm of Indra’s net;
(3) the gate of the secret, hidden, and manifest being simultaneously accomplished; (4) the gate of subtle mutual containment and establishment;
(5) the gate of the distinct accomplishment of phenomena separated by the ten times; (6) the gates of the various treasuries of purity and mixture.
The Seventh Gate: Endowment with Virtue; The Eighth Gate: The Mutual Compatibility and Non-identity of Many Dharmas; The Ninth Gate: The Mutual Identity and Sovereign Freedom of All Dharmas;
The Tenth Gate: The Perfect Accomplishment through the Turning of Mind-Only; The Eleventh Gate: The Manifestation of Dharmas by Relying on Phenomena to Generate Understanding.
Now, we do not follow Zhi Xiang, because the sequence established by Xianshou is systematic; thus, [this section] corresponds to the First Gate: Endowment with Common Characteristics.

Because this [gate] is comprehensive, it is placed at the beginning of the nine gates. Within the distinction between the broad and the narrow gates, this is first analyzed as the reason for establishing these individual gates.
This arises from the fact that, within the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle, phenomena and principle mutually pervade one another.

For the time being, regarding phenomena as they accord with principle, [the gate is] "broad" because phenomena universally pervade, and "narrow" because the specific characteristics of phenomena are not destroyed.
This constitutes the beginning of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*). Third, regarding the non-obstruction of the broad and the narrow:
because that which is pervaded is manifold, when one takes oneself as the standard in relation to the many, there is the mutual containment of the one and the many.

When they contain one another, both entities coexist; it is merely that their functional powers interpenetrate. Fourth, because this contains that, that is immediately this; because this pervades that, that is immediately this.

Because they are equal, there is the gate of mutual identity; because they mutually encompass one another, there is the gate of mutual concealment and manifestation, since the principle encompasses the other and the other is visible;
because they encompass the other while the other lacks substantiality, there is the gate of appearance-as-such;
and because the other exists yet is invisible when encompassed, there is the gate of concealment and manifestation. These constitute the distinctions between the gates. Thus it is said.
These three gates all exist through mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*). As for mutual entry (*anupraveśa*), it is like two mirrors reflecting one another;

as for identity (*tādātmya*), it is like waves and water mutually encompassing one another; as for concealment and manifestation (*chādyacchādaka*), it is like fragments of the moon reflecting one another.

Sixth, because these six mutually include others, all things are equally included; since their inclusion is likewise so, there is subtle mutual containment (*sūkṣma-saṃyoga*). Seventh, this is due to the layering of mutual inclusion.

9. Because it is profound, there is the inexhaustible Indra’s net; since each individual element is like Indra’s net—such that following any one [element], all are simultaneously inexhaustible—there is the manifestation of the principle through the phenomenon (*vastu*). 10.

Because the preceding eight are all the supported (*āśrita*), once the supported phenomena have been integrated, when one subsequently discerns the supporter (*āśraya*), it is likewise so; for this is due to the fact that every phenomenon is thus.

Therefore, if one is cited, it immediately serves as the primary [subject], and the dependent origination of associated phenomena (sahabhū-pratyaya) necessarily involves co-arising, as will be explained extensively below.

According to the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determining the Text), however, the virtues (*guṇa*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and functions (*kriyā*) are each divided into ten; among these, the ten sublime characteristics (*śuddha-lakṣaṇa*) are:
first, the virtue of simultaneous and complete correspondence; second, the virtue of mutual identity; third, the virtue of presence; fourth, the virtue of concealment... [and so forth].

1. The virtue of manifesting [the primary and secondary]; 2. The virtue of the companionship of the primary and secondary; 3. The virtue of being of the same substance; 4. The virtue of accomplishing [the benefit of others];
5. The virtue of being endowed with inexhaustibility; 6. The virtue of purity and mixture; 7. The virtue of subtlety; 8. The virtue of Indra’s net. Regarding the ten types of functional activity: 1.
The activity of simultaneous and complete mutual correspondence; 2. The activity of mutual identity; 3. The activity of mutual inclusion; 4. The activity of mutual penetration.
1. The function of the five aspects; 2. The function of the pure and the mixed; 3. The function of concealment and manifestation; 4. The function of principal and attendant;

5. The subtle function; 6. The Indra’s net function. Regarding these, within the gate of the marks of virtue there is no gate of karmic function; within the gate of karmic function there is no gate of the marks of virtue.
As for numbers six and seven, that master’s intention was that karmic function is a provisional establishment according to the capacity of sentient beings.

Therefore, there is mutual entry and mutual functioning; because that which originally did not enter is made to appear as entering, and because sentient beings who have been so from the beginning are made to become Buddhas where they were not, this is the functional operation of the marks of virtue.

Were it otherwise, there would be no mutual entry through the non-existence of marks, for its marks of virtue are primordially complete. Thus, there is the identity of essence with all phenomena, and the virtues are fully possessed.

Because the functions of the ultimate virtues do not operate in that manner, these two [categories] do not exist there. Since these four [categories] appear interchangeably, each possesses ten aspects;

when enumerated exhaustively across all gates, they become twelve. Now, although the functions of the virtues differ, they do not hinder their being one and the same; thus, the ten mysteries are universally encompassing.
Furthermore, because the characteristics of the virtues also constantly involve the operation of mutual entry, those characteristics, in their very presence, constitute mutual entry.

Furthermore, that which is called "mutual production" (xiàngzuò) is precisely "identity" (ji). While the names differ, the meaning is the same; it causes one to see the entry and exit [of phenomena], which is the gate of functional activity (yèyòng mén).
They constantly interpenetrate one another, like mirrors reflecting each other, which is the gate of the marks of virtue (dēxiàng mén).

Taking sentient beings as Buddhas means that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas; taking Buddhas as sentient beings means that Buddhas are themselves sentient beings. Therefore, know that mutual production is itself identity.
Regarding the identity of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), if one speaks of them in relation to the capacities of sentient beings, they constitute the "Gate of Functional Activity" (*karmakārya-mukha*);

yet, from the very beginning, they are the "Gate of Virtuous Characteristics" (*guṇalakṣaṇa-mukha*). While these are distinguished based on this [identity], there is no slight difference; when their essence and phenomena are unified, there is no further distinction.

Thus, it should be known that although the two names "Identity of Characteristics" and "Functioning of Characteristics" differ, there are not two separate gates; they are slightly distinct in their minor particulars, yet identical from beginning to end.
Furthermore, if the marks of virtue could not enter into True Suchness (tathatā), then it would lack these virtues;
consequently, it should not possess the virtue of universally encompassing all dharmas, nor the virtue of pervading all dharmas.

Moreover, there would likewise be no virtue capable of establishing stability or sustaining the world, nor the virtue of accomplishing all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Therefore, they constantly enter into [True Suchness].
In principle, there is no contradiction, as a sutra states: "The Buddhas are like a pure, bright mirror; my body is like a mani jewel.
The Buddhas constantly enter my being, and my body pervasively enters the bodies of all Buddhas"—this refers to constant entry.
Furthermore, since True Suchness (tathatā) follows conditions to manifest as all phenomena, how could it be without activity? If one were to act according to emotional views, [it would be otherwise].

Entering [this gate], there is only the meaning of karmic function. Its "attaining perfection through the same essence" (tongti cheng) is precisely the "gate of generating understanding by relying on phenomena to reveal the Dharma" within this context;
it is merely a difference in name. Thus, its own commentary states: "Each and every one is all dharmas.
Therefore, this is identical in meaning to the subsequent explanation of "relying on phenomena. Its "endowment with inexhaustible virtues" is precisely the *Indra* (Emperor).
The "net-gate" (*jāla-mukha*) is also subsumed within the "subtle-gate" (*sūkṣma-mukha*), as will be explained below in the respective sections.

Furthermore, while those [gates] do not exist in terms of breadth or narrowness, they do exist in terms of purity and mixture, as also explained below in the respective sections. Moreover, those [gates] lack the "ten-time-gate" (*daśa-kāla-mukha*), because time serves as their substratum and essential entity (*vastu*).

Consequently, their essential entities are also of ten kinds: namely, form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), time (*kāla*), place (*deśa*), body (*kāya*), direction (*diś*), teaching (*śāsana*), and meaning (*artha*).
That the stages of practice encompass all phenomena without exception is indeed reasonable; however, since time has no separate substantial entity, it cannot serve as a basis [for the stages].
Rather, because they are established solely based upon phenomena, one enters the profound gateway. This is also as explained in the subsequent section.
▲ Now, let us take one phenomenon from among the ten preceding [categories] to illustrate how it possesses the ten subsequent gates. "Now, let us take one phenomenon from among the ten preceding...
and so forth; this second section, which specifically illustrates by citing examples, is divided into two parts, the first being the general overview.
▲ As stated in the following text, a single lotus petal or a single atom possesses the ten pairs—such as the teaching (*dharma*) and so forth—in simultaneous correspondence, complete and perfect.
Subsequently, as detailed in the following text, the ten gates are individually revealed; these constitute the ten distinctions, the first of which is "simultaneous possession."

Regarding the "Gate of Correspondence with the Bases" (*pādābhisambandha-mukha*): because it is proximate to the initial listing, its sequence is not explicitly marked. Within the main text, there are two parts: first, the formal elucidation;

second, the citation of scriptural evidence. Within the first part, there are further two sections: first, the elucidation of how this specific gate itself is complete; second, the elucidation of how it is complete in conjunction with the other nine gates. The commentary states:
"Thus, the ten pairs such as 'teaching' (*śāsana*) and so forth are simultaneously corresponding, complete, and perfect. This refers first to the completeness within this specific gate itself.

In this context, the primary intent is to clarify that [the Tathāgata] is "complete" (*ju*) with respect to the ten pairs of dharmas—namely, teaching and meaning, principle and phenomenon, object and wisdom, practice and stage, cause and fruit—and so forth.
These ten preceding pairs of dharmas encompass all phenomena without exception; thus, to be "suddenly complete" (*dun ju*) means there is nothing that is not complete.
As for why they are complete, there are broadly ten reasons, which, to speak briefly, consist in the fusion of the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, the ancient masters established these ten meanings based on a single flower. The *Tanyuan ji* states: "This lotus flower represents the teaching that brings about understanding;

It further states: "This flower has as its retinue flowers numbering as many as the atoms in ten worlds;

This is an interpretation of the scriptural text according to directions to clarify the relationship of principal and attendant; that is to say, when the Dharma-wisdom (*dharmaprajñā*) expounds the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), the Bodhisattvas of other directions [are likewise included].
All the Buddhas come to bear witness, saying: "In our Buddha-fields as well, we have taught this Dharma; its words and phrases, its principles and meanings, are no different from these.
This refers to the meaning of the principal and the retinue.

Therefore, the principals do not see one another, nor do the retinues see one another; yet, as principal and retinue, and retinue and principal, they are perfectly luminous and endowed with all virtues.
Therefore, the primary [principle] governs the three levels below it as an illustrative explanation: when this method-wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*) acts as the primary, it cannot act as a companion;
when the ten-directional wisdom (*daśadik-prajñā*) acts as the companion, it cannot act as the primary. Thus, when this acts as the primary, it cannot encounter that acting as the primary;
and when that acts as the primary, this must act as the companion; for this reason, they likewise do not [meet].
Because one attains the vision of these as the "leaders," they are called leaders; because the leaders and their attendants do not see one another, they are called attendants.

Regarding the phrase "the leaders and attendants, both leaders and attendants, are perfectly luminous and endowed with virtue": when this direction serves as the leader, it sees the other direction as the attendant;

when this direction serves as the attendant, it sees the other direction as the leader. If the principle of leader and attendant is thus established, they are perfectly luminous and fully endowed [with virtue].
The remaining virtues are as explained in the *Jiaoziji chao*.

Furthermore, subject and object are simultaneously complete, broad and narrow, and mutually inclusive.

the seven aspects of essence and function, the eight aspects of persons and dharmas, and the nine aspects of the inverse and the direct, each with their respective simultaneity, these are added to make one hundred.
Because there are ten gates, it is said that when this "matter" (事) and so forth are each endowed with the other nine gates such as "teaching" (教), they constitute one hundred gates.

Since the matter and phenomena are thus, and the same applies to the other gates such as "teaching" and "meaning" (義) being each endowed with the hundred [sub-gates], they likewise constitute one thousand gates.
Since the phenomena of facts (*vastu-dharma*) are thus, the second section below uses the example of the basis of facts to illustrate other bases.

That is to say, since there are one hundred gates for the phenomena of facts, there are one hundred gates for the two teachings and meanings; there are one hundred gates for the three aspects of object and wisdom;

Because there are distinctions such as the breadth and narrowness of the teachings, there are one hundred gates: the second gate of breadth and narrowness possesses one hundred examples;

the third gate of simultaneous entry possesses one hundred; the fourth gate of mutual identity possesses one hundred; and so on until the tenth gate of primary and secondary, which also possesses one hundred.
Thus, they total one thousand gates. However, these latter thousand do not differ from the former thousand; they merely alternate by taking one as the primary heading.

It merely results in a difference [in presentation]. Furthermore, while the preceding section on the general and specific aspects possesses all nine gates within the "simultaneous" category, the subsequent nine gates do not possess them within the "simultaneous" category.
Now, because they are inseparable, we apply the model of the nine gates to the "simultaneous" category as well, such that it too possesses all nine gates.
▲If one takes them up layer by layer, they will likewise reach infinity.

If one descends layer by layer, the four [preceding] points form the statement of infinity. "Taking them up layer by layer" means, for example, that within the first gate there are already a thousand;
from among these ten, one is taken, yet this one must also possess ten, possess a hundred, and possess a thousand, because...
Because they are mutually distinct, if it is thus for one, it is likewise for each of the ten gates among the thousand; thus, they possess ten thousand.

Within these ten thousand, whichever single one is selected also possesses ten thousand. Just as when one thousand coins together function as a causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), if one coin is taken as the primary, it possesses one thousand, and the others are likewise so—thus there are one thousand sets of one thousand. Within these one thousand sets of one thousand...
Whichever one of these is taken up, it likewise possesses a thousandfold thousandfold aspects, thus reaching inexhaustibility. Furthermore, regarding the "layered" nature:
within a single phenomenon there are many phenomena; within a single object there are also many objects; and within a single wisdom there are again many wisdoms, and so forth.
These mutually interpenetrate one another, also without end.
▲ When these ten gates are perfectly clear and manifest, one will constantly enter the realm of the multilayered Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding these ten gates, the second section concludes with an exhortation regarding the benefits of practice: because this is an inexhaustible Dharma-gate endowed with such virtues, it is a realm accessible only to the universal eye (*samantacakṣus*) and can be entered only by superior wisdom;
therefore, one should diligently cultivate it, for it will certainly bring about great benefit.
▲ Second, the explanation of the source of the virtuous functions.
This section on the causes of the second virtue’s functions is divided into three parts: first, a general clarification through question and answer;

second, a detailed explanation according to the gates, beginning with "First, it is only mind"; and third, a summary of their respective categories, beginning with "Due to the ten causes above. Within the first part, there are four sections. One...
This section sets forth the topical headings.
▲ Question: What causes and conditions allow these various dharmas to be thus interpenetrating and unimpeded? Second question: Regarding "What causes and conditions...
and below, this is a provisional inquiry introduced to give rise to the discourse.

▲ Answer: Because the causes are too extensive to describe in detail, ten categories are briefly presented: first, because all things are manifestations of mind alone; second, because phenomena have no fixed nature;
third, because the characteristics of dependent origination are mutually conditioned; fourth, because the dharma-nature is interpenetrating; fifth, because they are like illusions and dreams;

sixth, because they are like reflections; seventh, because causes are infinite; eighth, because the Buddhas have realized them to their ultimate limit; ninth, because of the power of profound meditative concentration; tenth, [and so forth].
Because of the liberation through supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vimokṣa*).
Third, in response to the difficulty of explaining the causes in detail, the following enumeration provides a general answer.
Among these ten, any single one is capable of causing all those phenomena to blend harmoniously and interpenetrate without obstruction.

Regarding the four [categories] within the forty, one follows the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) to provide a comprehensive synthesis. Within this, there are three parts: first, a general indication of the functional capacity.
Among the ten [aspects], the first six generally pertain to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as virtuous characteristics; because the Dharma is naturally so, they are such by their very nature.

The latter two concern the meaning of karmic function, which encompasses both cause and effect. The seventh pertains to the meaning of initiating cultivation, encompassing both virtuous characteristics and karmic function. The eighth pertains to the fruit.
Because virtue is exclusively the characteristic of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the first ten [mysteries] among the subsequent ten, the first six distinguish the differences in their lower scope:

whereas the aforementioned ten profound gates (*gūḍha-dvāra*) pertain universally to both the characteristics of virtue and their functional activities (*karma-vyāpāra*), those now presented have both universal and restricted applications.
▲The preceding ten gates encompass both the characteristics of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and its functional activity (*kriyā-vṛtti*).

▲From the perspective of the Buddha, activity is also a characteristic of virtue, because it functions within virtue; from the perspective of sentient beings (*sattva*), even the characteristics are termed "activity," because they cause [beings] to know those characteristics.
Third, based on the ten gates mentioned previously, this section harmonizes the aspects of virtue (*guṇa*) and function (*vṛtti*) to refute divergent interpretations.

Specifically, it refers to the *Kuan-ting-chi* (Record of Determination), which establishes two types of "ten mysteries" (*daśa-guhya*)—namely, the mystery of the marks and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the mystery of activity and function (*karmavṛtti*). Here, we harmonize these by clarifying that there is only a single layer [of mystery] which inherently contains both virtue and function;
thus, there is no need to divide them into two. Within this, there are two parts: first, a detailed explanation, and second, a concluding summary of what precedes.

The middle section also has two parts: first, an explanation through mutual interpenetration to show they are not distinct; second, a general discussion of the defiled and pure to demonstrate the dual fusion.
Regarding the first, there are initially two sentences that state the thesis. Following this, from "Next, regarding the Buddha... onwards is the explanation.

This means that the function upon the essence of the Buddha is itself the aspect of his qualities (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*). For example, the functions of voice, sound, and eloquence are themselves the aspects of the qualities. If one were to cause sentient beings...
Because arising and seeing enter directly into non-existence without obstruction, the characteristic is called function.
Thus, the characteristic of that very function is the dual fusion of defilement and purity; the function of that very characteristic is the capacity to defile and the capacity to purify.
Regarding the second section on the characteristics of their application, which harmonizes the defiled and the pure and demonstrates the mutual fusion of the two pairs:

the *Kanding ji* (Record of Determination) establishes two distinct categories, stating that while the "attributes" (*de xiang*) are purely pure, the "functional activity" (*ye yong*) permeates the defiled because it causes sentient beings to manifest as Buddha-bodies and so forth;

thus, it is said to permeate the defiled. Here, however, we clarify that while the attributes of the Buddha are such that both defilement and purity have been exhausted, he nevertheless manifests within the defiled.

Because it employs both the act of lifting up and the principle of sameness of essence, within the lion throne there is the instantaneous manifestation of the dwellings and houses where sentient beings reside.
How could its virtuous marks not manifest even among defiled sentient beings? If these marks were not manifested, how could there be the subtle gate?
This subtle gate instantaneously manifests all that is defiled and pure; yet it manifests while remaining eternally empty, like an image in a mirror. Therefore, it is so called.
The two are fused such that they mutually act as each other’s cause and enter into one another; this quality is absent from the characteristics of those [other] dharmas.

Now it is clarified that, by the nature of things (*dharmatā*), they constantly enter and constantly act as causes for one another, just as in the analogy of the shadows of the sun upon the mountains and between the mountains in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter:

although they can mutually reflect one another, it is sometimes said that the sun's shadow emerges between the seven mountains, and sometimes it is said that the sun's shadow enters into the seven mountains. It is just like this.
When entering and exiting, it is profoundly still and unmoving, yet it is constantly entering and exiting; how could it be that entry occurs only in response to conditions?
That "characteristics act" is precisely the meaning of "characteristics are identical," the significance of which is as understood previously.
▲The "original aspect" (*xing*) and its "function" (*yong*) are not divided into two distinct entities.

Thus, from "the original aspect and its function" onwards, this is the second section, which establishes the conclusion. It is not that the two meanings of essence (*de*) and function (*yong*) are undifferentiated;
rather, they are not established as two separate categories. The single mystery (*yi xuan*) and the ten mysteries (*shi xuan*) both encompass both essence and function.
▲ First, regarding "all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone": all dharmas are manifested by the true mind, just as the entirety of the water of a great ocean becomes waves.
Since all phenomena are none other than the one mind, their various characteristics—great and small alike—revolve according to the mind, thereby entering into non-obstruction.
Just as when the waters of the great ocean rise up, their entire substance becomes waves, so too the mind can transform objects such that the objects must resemble the mind.

Since the mind is itself unobstructed, objects are likewise unobstructed; how much more so for those manifested by the true mind, which is distinguished from the deluded mind because the true dharma possesses all virtues.
Thus it is able to enter into layers of mutual non-obstruction. To say "the entire substance" means that the whole of the true is manifested as the deluded.
▲ Regarding the fact that these two dharmas lack a fixed nature: since they are manifestations of mind alone, arising from conditions, they possess no fixed nature;

thus, both their substance and characteristics are transcended. Because the small is not fixedly small, it can contain the vast void with room to spare, for it is identical to the great in its lack of exterior.
Because the great is not fixedly great, it can enter into a minute particle without interval, for it is identical to the small in its lack of interior.
Therefore, since this is equal to the subtle atom of the great void containing a vast land as extensive as that atom, what difficulty could there be?

Regarding the second point, "equality in the lack of fixed nature," the text has three parts: first, the formal explanation based on the large and the small; second, the citation of scriptural evidence;
and third, the illustrative explanation of other dharmas. This is the first part. As for the phrase "what difficulty could there be," it means that because the small atom contains the large...
Just as within the vast realms of the great void there are smaller ones—just as small particles form larger dust motes that contain those smaller realms—there is no difficulty [in this].
The "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" in the old translation states: "The countless mountains of the Diamond Enclosure can all be placed within a single hair."
If one wishes to know how that which is supremely great can possess small characteristics, the Bodhisattva does so by means of this initial generation of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
The citation from the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika*) in the old translation serves as a second scriptural proof. The reason for citing the old translation is that its phrasing is explicit;
the current sutra states: "As if wishing to cause immeasurable and innumerable Cakravāḍa mountains to all enter into a single pore."
One can know both their smallness and their greatness; thus, when a bodhisattva first resolves their mind [on enlightenment], there is no fixed nature [to that resolve].
This principle is not as evident as the case where something truly great possesses the characteristic of smallness.
▲ Because "one" is not fixed as one, it can be all; because "many" is not fixed as many, it can be one. Because "extremes" are not fixed as extremes, they can be the middle;
because the "middle" is not fixed as the middle, it can be the extremes. This applies to each instance, such as length and brevity, stillness and agitation, and so forth.
First, "non-fixed" [refers to] the first of the three examples used to explain other dharmas. Regarding the terms "extremes" (*anta*) and "middle" (*madhya*), there are two meanings:

one is the periphery versus the central land; this refers to the non-obstruction of phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*), as in the *Nāmanirdeśa-parivarta*, where it is said that at the very edge of the Cakravāḍa mountains there are four continents, and yet there are also the ten directions—thus, the "extreme" is not an extreme, because they mutually encircle one another. Therefore, the "middle" is also...
This "extreme" (*anta*) clarifies that this is the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

If one speaks of the "Middle Way," although the two modes of practice differ, the identity of the extremes and the middle is likewise the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena, and it also extends to the non-obstruction of phenomena with principle (*shili wuai*). Regarding "prolongation and contraction":

a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is contraction, while long eons (*kalpa*) are prolongation; this is the fusion of thought-moments and eons. Regarding "stillness and agitation": entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and emerging from it...
Because the two modes of meditative concentration (samādhi) are distinct, even in the absence of fixed characteristics, they can be mutually identical;

this is especially evident in such cases as entering right concentration in the east and arising from concentration in the west, which are quintessential examples of the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena (shishi wuai).

▲ Regarding the third [section], the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination (*trividha-pratītyasamutpāda-lakṣaṇa-anyonya-viniścaya*): this refers to the infinite gateways of meaning within the ocean of dharmas of dependent origination within the Great Dharma-realm (*mahā-dharmadhātu*).

Within the commentary on this third section on the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination, there are three parts: first, the general; second, the specific; and third, the conclusion.

Now, for the first [part], there are again three sections. First, the general presentation of the manifold gateways: "dependent origination within the Great Dharma-realm" is stated to distinguish it from the internal and external [realms] as well as the defiled [dharmas].

The purification of a single object is an origination by conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), just as a sprout arises when external factors such as soil, water, human effort, and the seasons serve as conditions;
likewise, within, consciousness and so forth arise with ignorance, formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and so on as conditions.

However, this is not the case here, for the entire *dharmadhātu* is subsumed as a single origination by conditions; therefore, it is called "Great. Furthermore, this very single origination by conditions possesses many aspects of meaning in its entirety.

The single Dharma-realm is precisely the Great Dependent Origination; it is not the same as the Three Vehicles, which merely clarify that dharmas produced by causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature.
