Regarding the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), the following two sections set forth the headings:
▲ This means that the dharmas of dependent origination must possess these ten meanings for conditions to arise; if any are lacking, they will not be established.
This refers to the reasons why the ten [aspects] are manifested in the lower three [sections] of the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination).

▲ First, the meaning of the distinctness of each condition: within the great *pratītyasamutpāda*, the various conditions, when compared with one another, must necessarily have distinct essences and functions;
only when they do not become confused or intermingled can they constitute dependent origination.
▲If they were disordered, the fundamental conditions would be lost and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) would not be established.
▲In this regard, each condition maintains its own singular position.
▲The text states: "Within the many there is no single nature, and within the one there is no multiplicity."
First, regarding the meaning that the various conditions are distinct: this is the second section, the detailed explanation.
Among the ten gates, the first three are the fundamental, while the latter seven are derived from them—specifically, gates four, five, and six arise from the first gate;

gates seven, eight, and nine arise from the second gate; and the tenth gate arises from the third gate. This is because the third gate merely combines the preceding two gates; therefore, it is [treated as such].

Regarding the generation of the single gate, we first establish three gates: the first is the gate of distinct entities, the second is the gate of identical entities, and the third is the gate that clarifies both identity and difference together.
The reason there are these entities of identity and difference is that within the various gates of dependent origination there are two meanings:
first, the meaning of non-dependence, which means that things possess their own inherent qualities; for example, as in the case of a cause, it does not depend on conditions [to exist].

These two aspects correspond to the meanings of "depending on conditions" and so forth; the former is the gate of identical substance (*tongti*), while the latter is the gate of different substance (*yiti*).

If this is so, why does it state in the first [gate of] different substance that "the various conditions are distinct and do not intermingle," whereas in the second [gate of] identical substance it states that "they must mutually pervade one another to constitute dependent origination"? The commentary explains: [It is because...]
It is necessary that each distinct direction depend upon conditions, and it is only through universal correspondence that one’s own qualities become fully manifest.
Thus, for the reason that there are three aspects arising within each of the first two gates: first, because they mutually support one another, whether possessing power or lacking power;

second, because they mutually negate one another, whether possessing substance or lacking substance; and third, because substance and function are both fused, being without before or after. This concludes [the explanation].
Understanding the general meaning, we now proceed to the formal explanation of the text. The first section is the "Section on Different Entities" (*bhinnasvabhāva-mukha*), which contains four parts:
first, the formal explanation; second, the counter-demonstration beginning with "If there were confusion"; third, the summary and indication beginning with "This, then, is the various conditions";
and fourth, the citation of evidence beginning with "The text says," which refers to the *Prabhāsvara-bodhi* chapter, specifically the latter half of which states: "Thus, both are abandoned."

The first half of the verse, "Universally entering the Buddha's merits," establishes the meaning of mutual formation and co-existence; the second half, "Form and substance are both eliminated," establishes the meaning of mutual sublation and mutual disappearance.
Since the present context does not concern the meaning of the second half, it is not cited here. Nevertheless, it is precisely through mutual formation that each possesses its own substantiality.
▲ Second, the meaning of mutual interdependence through universal pervasion: these various conditions must universally correspond with one another for dependent origination to be established.
Just as one condition universally corresponds with many, each individual condition acts as a single whole for those many;
thus, this one [condition] possesses many "ones."
▲If this single condition were not complete, then the many would lack their support and the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) would fail to be universal.
▲Thus, each and every one possesses all things.
▲As the subsequent text states: "Know that through the one there is the many, and through the many there is the one."
Regarding the second point, the meaning of mutual pervasion and mutual support, this is also fourfold within the text of the "Gate of Identical Substance. First, the formal explanation states:
"This one is identical with many ones. This means that, for example, when ten coins serve as conditions, the substance of a single coin is inherently one;
yet when it functions as two, the original one is designated as "one-as-two," and when it functions as three, it is designated as "one-as-three."
...up to the point that because ten must become eleven, there are many "ones.
● If this single "one" does not serve as the second condition below, it cannot correspond to the other nine. ● This is the third example for each subsequent "one";
just as there is one, so too do the twelves, thirteens, fourteens, and so forth, each have their own [corresponding sets].
For this reason, it is said that each and every one is individually endowed [with all others], using ten coins as a metaphor;

for within the inexhaustible phenomena of the differentiation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), each manifests universally and accordingly, such that each individual phenomenon is itself endowed with the differentiated phenomena of the entire Dharma-realm.
● Regarding the passage below, the fourth citation of evidence is from the "Verse Praise" chapter of the *Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace*, concerning True Wisdom (*bhūtamatī*).
The second half of the Bodhisattva’s verse states: "All phenomena have no basis; they arise solely from conjunction.
Since this serves as proof for the meaning of the third section, I shall now cite only the first half.
▲The meaning of the unimpeded coexistence of the three is as follows: any single condition must possess the preceding two [aspects] to constitute dependent origination;
for it must abide in its own nature in order to be able to universally respond, and it is only by universally responding to multiple conditions that it constitutes a single [condition].

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the unimpeded coexistence of the three," this refers to the simultaneous integration of identity and difference. Within the text, there are also four [sections], the first of which is the formal explanation:
"Therefore, the single and the many are sovereign and unimpeded, melting into one another; herein there are six propositions."

Second, for this reason, the subsequent lines provide a detailed analysis and selection [of categories]. Within this, it first provides a general clarification: because there are many desires and many constants, or one desire and one constant, it is called "sovereign" (*svatantra*).
▲ First, either the entire substance remains entirely localized—this is "one"; or the entire substance responds universally—this is "many-ones."
Whether they coexist, whether both are extinguished, whether they are combined as a whole, or whether they are entirely separate—all these can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the first two lines of the second section, they may be understood individually. Second, "coexistence" means that [the self] coexists with both the particular and the universal;
it also means that [the self] coexists with both the one and the many. Fourth, "mutual extinction" refers to—

The fourth phrase arises because when both exist, they mutually negate one another; thus, that which abides as one must not abide as one if it is to be all-pervasive, and that which is all-pervasive must not be all-pervasive if it is to abide as one.
Fifth, "total synthesis" refers to combining the preceding four phrases to form the object of understanding (*jñeya-viṣaya*).
Sixth, "total exclusion" refers to being entirely free from the preceding five to constitute the object of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*).
▲ The text states: "All phenomena have no basis; they arise solely from conjunction.
The three passages below cite evidence as previously cited, intending to take the meaning that [phenomena] arise from conjunction.
▲ The above three sections complete the general elucidation of the fundamental dharma of dependent origination.
4. This section below summarizes the essential purport of the three sections.

▲ Fourth, the meaning of mutual inclusion through distinct entities (*bhinna-svabhāva*) refers to how the functional powers of the various gates mutually support one another and reciprocally negate each other.
The principle of dependent origination is established only when there is the sense of both being fully functional and being entirely non-functional.
Regarding the "four meanings, such as the mutual interpenetration of distinct entities," the commentary contains five sections:

(1) a general explanation, (2) citation of scriptural evidence, (3) establishment through reductio ad absurdum, (4) the conclusion establishing the correct meaning, and (5) a specific demonstration of their characteristics. Now, for the first [section], regarding "mutual support through reciprocal dependence":
Because of this dependent origination, unity, multiplicity, and so forth are not determinate natures of unity, multiplicity, and so forth.
As the treatise says: "The cause does not produce because it arises from conditions; the condition does not produce because it arises from its own cause."

Regarding the phrase "as stated in the treatise," etc., this is the second citation of scriptural authority. However, the treatise contains two intended meanings: first, to reveal the meaning of non-arising;

thus, the preceding line uses conditions (*pratyaya*) to refute intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The intrinsic nature of phenomena does not exist within conditions.
If there were an intrinsic nature, it would not depend upon the gathering of various conditions; since it does depend upon the gathering of various conditions, it is [without intrinsic nature].
Intrinsic nature should exist within conditions; however, since intrinsic nature cannot be found when sought within conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature.

The subsequent phrase [“conditions do not produce themselves”] refutes conditions by means of [the absence of] self-nature. This is because [production] arises from its own cause. That is to say, if production were from another, then conditions alone would suffice to produce [an effect];
it would not be logical to depend upon its own cause. Now, by depending upon a cause, it is demonstrated that [production from another] is not [the case].
The other birth is merely a manifestation above of the meaning of non-arising. Second, it manifests the meaning of dependent origination:

"because the cause does not arise" means the cause is entirely powerless; "because it arises from conditions" means the conditions are entirely powerful. The subsequent phrase is to be understood by analogy.
Now, we employ this very intent to corroborate the aforementioned principle.
▲If each [cause] possessed only efficacy and lacked non-efficacy, there would be the fault of multiple fruits, because each one would produce [the fruit] individually.

If each [cause] possessed only non-efficacy and lacked efficacy, there would be the fault of no fruit at all, because they would equally fail to be conditions and thus not produce [the fruit] together.
If each [cause] individually produces only the lower three [results], yet accomplishes the higher meaning, this also serves as a resolution to an objection. Suppose someone were to ask:

"If causes and conditions do not produce [the result] individually, but rather produce it through the power of their combined harmony, what fault is there in that? This establishes the doctrine of co-arising (*sahotpāda*). To this, the initial response was:
"If that were so, there would be the fault of multiple results. The explanation states: "Because each one produces [the result] individually."

Just as the grain seed is the cause and the water, soil, human effort, and season are the conditions for the production of five fruits—namely, the sprout of the grain, the sprout of the water, the sprout of the soil, and so forth—it is said that there are many fruits. Next, a question is raised:

"If that is so, and all [factors] individually lack power but can produce [the fruit] when combined, what fault is there? This also establishes the principle of 'co-arising' (sahabhū-hetu). To this, it is further replied:

The fault of non-existence of the fruit means that just as fire, gold, stone, and so forth lack the power to produce a sprout and thus cannot produce it, so too earth, water, grain, and so forth lack the power to produce a sprout;
how then could they produce it? Therefore, like fire and the others, they are not conditions and cannot produce a fruit—this is the fault of non-existence of the fruit.

▲Therefore, in dependent origination, factors must mutually rely upon one another; possessing power or lacking power is like the case where, if even one condition is missing, the whole is not established—the same applies to the others.
Thus, the following four points conclude the correct principle: namely, since conditions are either entirely powerful or entirely powerless...
For an origination to be established, it must consist of one factor that is efficacious and another that is non-efficacious; only then does the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) come to be.

This is illustrated by the example of being deficient in even a single condition, as explained below. Just as if one is absent, then two, three, and so forth are likewise absent, so too, if a pillar is absent, then the beam, the rafters, and so forth are absent.
Because all other factors fail to constitute the conditions for a house or the like when even one thing is missing, it is said that "the rest" are also [absent].
In this way, if there is no two, there is also no one, nor three, and so forth; if there is no three, there is also no two, nor one, and so forth, up to:
if there is no ten, there is also no nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or one.

Just as if there is no beam, there is no pillar, and so forth—whichever single phenomenon is cited, it cannot be established if its conditions are lacking—so too within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), if even a single thing is missing, the entire dharma-realm is incomplete.
This would fail to constitute dependent origination.
Therefore, one can sustain many; one possesses the power to sustain the many, while the many depend upon the one and lack the power to enter within the one.
Therefore, one can support many; this is the fifth section, which specifically demonstrates their characteristics. Within it, there are three parts: first, clarifying that one looks toward many;
second, applying the same principle to many looking toward one; third, concluding with the enumeration of the categories. In the first part, there are two sections:

first, clarifying the meaning of one supporting many bases, and second, applying the same principle to many supporting one base. Now, for the first [of these], there are again two sections: first, clarifying the sense of "basis" and "support."
▲ Because that which possesses singular power necessarily does not coexist with that which possesses manifold power, there is no single entity that does not subsume the manifold.
Because that which possesses manifold lack of power necessarily does not coexist with that which possesses singular lack of power, there is no manifold entity that does not enter into the single.
Subsequently, the following passage from the commentary establishes this by forceful reasoning to also address potential objections. One might raise the objection:
"Since both the 'one' and the 'many' possess the two qualities of being both powerful and powerless, how can the one be able to encompass the many? To resolve this, it is said:
"Because the two states of being powerful and the two states of being powerless cannot coexist; for that which acts as the condition (*pratyaya*) is itself [the one]."
One should reflect that what is powerful is necessarily dependent on that which has arisen, whereas that which is weak is not.
Just as it is when one [powerful] thing depends on many [weak] bases, so too is it when many [weak] things depend on one [powerful] base; one should reflect by reversing the above.
Just as in one case many [factors] depend on a single basis, so too in the following two examples a single [factor] depends on many bases.
This is because the many are that which arise and serve as conditions, while the one is that which is arisen and is what is established by the many.

▲ For example, when one looks out, there are many things that rely upon and are supported by it; the powerful and the powerless, the manifest and the latent, the many within oneself and oneself within the many, all exist simultaneously without obstruction.
Just as one [entity] relates to many, there is that which has a basis and that which is supported; this is the second example, wherein many relate to one. Within this, there are two parts:

first, the summary of the preceding, which is the presentation of the analogy (the "many" relating to the "one"); second, the subsequent generation of the explanation, which is the formal interpretation.
Regarding the former section, it was previously clarified that one supports many bases; now, following that, the meaning of many supporting one base is established.
Question: How can that which is already complete and perfect further possess such manifold expectations toward the one? Answer: This contains a profound meaning.

It means that among the preceding "one looking toward the many," the one that serves as the basis for maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) is the "one as the limit of maintenance" (*dhāraṇa-paryanta*), while the one that is capable of encompassing the many is the "one as the limit of entry" (*praveśa-paryanta*).
Although there is maintenance upon the many, because we take the one as the agent of entry, both belong to the single instance of "the one looking toward the many."
Therefore, in the commentary (*śāstra*), wishing to explain many things in relation to one, it first concludes the preceding section by stating:

"Just as when one is related to many, there is that which is relied upon (*āśraya*) and that which is supported (*upastambha*), etc. Here, "that which is relied upon" refers to the aforementioned many supports; thus, the one becomes the basis (*āśraya*).
"That which is supported" refers to the aforementioned single power acting as the support for the many; thus, it is said that the "full power" establishes the aforementioned single support.

Those who lack power achieve the former [state], which is called "always containing the many within oneself. This is because one who possesses power acts as a support, being able to encompass the many;
thus it is said that they "concealedly enter the many within themselves. Those who lack power rely on the latter [state], thereby entering into the many;
thus these two phrases both pertain to the first [category]: looking from the one toward the many.
▲ "When many are compared to one, it should be known that it is likewise.
Regarding the phrase "when many are compared to one," the first part is a preliminary explanation, while the second part is the formal exposition.

If one were to provide a general explanation, one would simply change the preceding word "one" (*eka*) to "many" (*bahu*), and change "many" to "one"; thus, the meaning would manifest of itself. Fearing that [the reader] might not understand, [I shall explain further].
To explain this fully, it should be said: "The many are capable of supporting the one" means that the many possess the power to support each individual one.
"The one is incapable of supporting the many" means that the single entity lacks the power to enter into the midst of the many.

Since that which possesses the power of multiplicity must necessarily not coexist with that which possesses the power of singularity, there can be no case where the many do not subsume the one. Furthermore, since that which possesses the power of singularity must necessarily not coexist with... [the many].
Because many [bases] lack power collectively, there is not a single [base] that does not enter into the many.
Just as it is when many hold one support, so too is it when one holds many supports; reflect on this by reversing the above.

Thus, that which is able to contain is also many, and that which is able to enter is also many. Although many contain one, this is precisely one entering into many; yet, it is designated as "many containing. Although...
When many enter into one, it is "one encompassing many," yet it is termed "many entering.

Thus, while the first two gates of inclusion both belong to the category of "one," the latter two gates of inclusion both belong to the category of "many"; these two meanings are as distinct as heaven and earth, and are not redundant.
▲Contemplate the two phrases "both existing" and "both extinguished" as being without obstruction.
Regarding the three concluding phrases following "both existing" and "both extinguished," they are enumerated as follows: "the many being subsumed by the one" is the first phrase;
"the one being subsumed by the many" is the second phrase; and "both existing" is the third phrase, meaning that the one is subsumed and enters into the one.
At that time, because the "many-inclusive" and "many-entering" are simultaneously extinguished, this constitutes the fourth phrase.

Since the "one-inclusive" and "one-entering" are identical to the "many-inclusive" and "many-entering," then by the extinction of the "many-inclusive" and "many-entering" through the one-inclusive and one-entering—and by the extinction of the one-inclusive and one-entering through the many-inclusive and many-entering—it is said that they are "simultaneously extinguished. When contrasted with the preceding distinct explanation of the two phrases, then...

There are four propositions which may also form five or six; for when both [five and six] together illuminate the preceding four, they constitute the realm of understanding (*avabodha-viṣaya*), whereas when the sixth suddenly cuts off the preceding five, it constitutes the realm of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*).

▲ Fifth, the meaning of the mutual identity of distinct entities: this means that when various conditions are compared with one another, their total being is mutually appropriated; thus, while there is the existence of the entity, there is also its non-existence.
The meaning of the essence (*tattva*) is established through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the phrase "the five distinct essences are mutually identical," etc., here the term "identical" (*sama*) is largely consistent in its syntactic force with the preceding entry on "difference.

Of the five sections of text, this one merely lacks the citation of scriptural evidence. Within it, there are four parts: first, establishing the principle to briefly clarify [the point]; second, the refutation...
This section clarifies the preceding principles, establishing the threefold correct meaning and specifically demonstrating their characteristics.

First, that which acts as the cause of arising has a substantial body, while that which is the result of arising lacks a substantial body. As it is said: "Phenomena born from conditions are themselves empty";

this intends to take the emptiness of what is produced. Emptiness is the meaning of lacking a substantial body. Regarding the term "mutual negation" (*xingduo*), it refers to the capacity of the cause to negate [the inherent nature of] the effect.
This means that when an object arises in opposition to a form, it seizes away that which has arisen, rendering it without substance.
Furthermore, if even one condition is lacking, the others cannot arise; thus, the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya) would be destroyed.
Regarding the phrase "if one condition is lacking," etc., this is a double negation that clarifies the preceding principle to establish the meaning of having substantial existence (*savastuka*).
Just as if one condition is absent, two, three, four, and so forth will all fail to be established, one thereby knows that the single [condition] possesses substantial existence.
▲ By obtaining this single condition, all that is produced and the producer are established; thus, the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya) is finally established.
By obtaining this single condition, the three lower fetters (saṃyojana) are correctly established. Since everything arises from this one, the one possesses substantial reality (svabhāva).

▲Therefore, because a single condition is that which can initiate and can accomplish, it possesses substantiality; whereas multiple conditions, being that which is initiated and accomplished, lack substantiality.

Consequently, regarding the single condition, the following four sections separately demonstrate its characteristics; therein, the first three clarify the first [point], namely, the multiplicity of aspects.

For example, many [cases] anticipate one [conclusion] at the end to form a sentence; here, the first [section] also has two parts: first, clarifying that there is a substantial entity (*sabhāva*), and second, extending this to the case where many have a substantial entity.
Within the former, there are two sections; the first is the actual clarification, which may be understood as it stands.
▲ A single existent entity cannot coexist with multiple existent entities, and multiple non-existent entities necessarily cannot coexist with a single non-existent entity;
therefore, there is no "one" that is not "many," and there is no "many" that is not "one."
The subsequent section, beginning with "By one having an essence" (*ekasya sattvāt*), provides a detailed explanation to resolve this objection. Specifically, there is a challenge:
"Since both 'one' and 'many' possess the two meanings of having an essence and lacking an essence, why do you speak of 'one' alone as having an essence? Therefore, the present response clarifies:
because the meanings of existence and non-existence cannot coexist, that which is "one" is necessarily the side that acts as the originator, whereas the "many" must [necessarily be the other].

Because it arises [from conditions], if it were not so, the relationship between the agent and the object would not be established, and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) would also be destroyed.
Therefore, there is no "one" that is not "many," because this one is itself many; nor is there a "many" that is not "one," because this many is itself one.
Question: What fault is there in asserting that the one is not identical to the many? Answer: There are two faults.
Therefore, the fault that "one does not become many" means that since one does not become many, the rest likewise do not become many;
thus, just as one does not become twelve, three, four, and so forth, ten also does not become ten, and therefore there is no fault of "ten.
The fault that "two do not become one" means that if one does not become ten, then these ten do not exist; because ten does not exist, one [does not exist].
The meaning [of oneness] is also not established because, among the ten, there is no "one" that is distinct from them; thus, the fault arises that one is not identical to the many.

Since this is so, the fault that the many are not identical to one likewise applies. Furthermore, if they were not mutually identical, then within the gateway of dependent origination, the two meanings of emptiness and existence would fail to be established, resulting in faults such as the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or annihilationism.
▲If it is so for the one and the many, it is likewise so for the many and the one; reflect upon this by reversing the above.

Regarding the phrase "if it is so for the one and the many," etc.: by reversing the above, that which previously had an essence becomes a non-essence, and that which was a plurality of non-essences becomes a plurality of essences; there is no further distinct meaning.

▲Just as when one looks at many, because there is both existence and non-existence of substance, it is able to subsume others into itself and discard itself to accord with others, simultaneously without obstruction.
Just as when one looks at many, the following second example is that of many looking at one. Within this, there are also two parts; first, the conclusion of the preceding.

This is precisely citing the general meaning of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), which is entirely identical to the previously mentioned "entry into characteristics" (*lakṣaṇapraveśa*); it differs only in its specific application.

Regarding the statement "having an entity (*sattva*) or lacking an entity (*asattva*)," that which "has an entity" refers to the first [of the two] mentioned above, as it is the agent of arising and thus possesses an entity.
That which "lacks an entity" refers to the second [of the two] mentioned in the illustrative example, which likewise clarifies that the one is without an entity. Therefore...

One who can subsume others into oneself achieves the former "existence" (sattva) by subsuming many others; this is simply the negation of the "not-many" within the aforementioned "non-existence" (asattva).
One who discards oneself to identify with others achieves the former "non-existence" (asattva).

Thus, by discarding the singular self to identify with the many others, although there are two meanings—existence and non-existence—they both belong to the perspective of the one looking toward the many.
Therefore, it is said that "many are subsumed by many.
One should know that the case of "many" in relation to "one" is likewise; reflect on this according to the preceding [analysis].

When "many" are related to "one," the two cases—arising simultaneously and arising subsequently—are exactly analogous to the previous section, with the only difference being that "one" is changed to "many."
It is merely a matter of changing "many" into "one. If one were to formulate the synthesis accordingly, it should state: "Inclusion of others as one is the same as the abandonment of many;
the abandonment of self as one is the same as the inclusion of others. In the former case, looking from the "one" toward the "many," both inclusion and abandonment are "one";

in this [latter] case, looking from the "many" toward the "one," both inclusion and abandonment are "many"—thus, the meanings are vastly different. The rest should be contemplated according to the "Entrance to the Characteristics" (Lakṣaṇamukha).
▲ It can be seen by reflecting upon the two lines "both existing" and "both extinguished" as being without obstruction.

"Both existing and both extinguished" refers to the third sentence that establishes the categories. "Both existing" means that when the one correctly subsumes the many and makes them identical to itself, or when it discards itself to make others identical to itself, at that very moment the many are subsumed into the one and made identical to itself; this is the "one. "Both" [refers to]...
"Extinction" (mín) means that the two meanings of "the one looking toward the many" are identical to the two meanings of "the many looking toward the one";

therefore, when the one looks toward the many, the two meanings are extinguished. Since the two meanings of "the many looking toward the one" are identical to the two meanings of "the one looking toward the many," when the many look toward the one, the two meanings are extinguished.
Because this principle does not differ from what was stated previously, it is so made.
Reflect upon this.

▲ The meaning of the "simultaneous fusion of essence and function" (tǐyòng shuāngróng) refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*pratyaya-dharma*) must involve the interaction of their essential power and function, merging as a single whole,
before they can constitute dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the meaning of "the six aspects where essence and function are mutually fused," there are three parts in the text; first, the establishment of the principle and a brief explanation.

Therefore, perfect penetration also has six propositions: 1. Because there is no aspect of essence that is not function, when the entire essence is raised as function, there is only the principle of mutual inclusion (*xiāng rù*) and not the principle of mutual identity (*xiāng jí*). 2. Because there is no aspect of function that is not essence, when the entire function is raised as essence...
Thus, there is only the identity of form and the entry into formlessness. The substance and function of the Three Refuges do not obstruct one another;
the substance is fully present within function, and function does not lose its substance. This is the unimpeded coexistence where both "entering" and "identifying" manifest with sovereign freedom.

Fifth, when the substance of total function dissolves, the substance as a whole vanishes; when the function of the total substance ceases, function itself perishes. It is neither identical nor entering, but a perfectly interfused single flavor.

Combining these with the preceding four phrases, they share a single dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) where all six exist without obstruction and the five are extinguished; the subsequent five phrases are absolute, beyond words, and darkly identical to the ocean of the same nature (*dharmadhātu*).

Next, from "Therefore, Perfect Penetration" (*ataḥ pariniṣpanna*) below, the chapters are opened for a specific explanation, forming six phrases; thus, the first [phrase] takes the essence (*tattva*) as its basis.
1) Using the function to accord with the essence; 2) the essence and function both existing; 3) the essence and function both being extinguished;
because the essence and function penetrate one another and both forms and their negations vanish, they enter the single source, thus forming the fifth stage of the perfectly interfused single flavor.
The sixth stage, the realm of practice, is likewise clearly manifest. These may be understood as they appear together.
▲ These three preceding sections have completed the exposition of the principles within the first section on "Distinct Entities.
The phrase "these three preceding sections" and so forth serves as a concluding summary of their respective categories.

▲ Seventh, the meaning of the mutual interpenetration of identical entities: this refers to the fact that all the many [aspects] belonging to a single condition share the same substance as that single condition.
Because there is no distinction, it is called "identical substance" (*samāna-svabhāva*).

Regarding the seventh point, the meaning of the mutual inclusion of identical substances (*samāna-svabhāva-praveśa*), there are three parts in the explanation: first, a separate explanation of the meaning of identical substance;

second, a dual explanation of the reason for simultaneous inclusion; and third, the actual interpretation of this section. Now, for the first: it says, "The preceding one, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and so forth."
This refers back to the second gate mentioned previously, because that second gate is the "gate of identical essence" (*tongti*).
For example, one original source is itself "one" as the primary; it corresponds to two as "two," and it corresponds to three as "three," and so forth.
Yet, these are ultimately just a single "one. It is like a single person who is called a "son" in relation to his father, and called a "father" in relation to his son.
To regard the elder brother as the younger brother and the younger brother as the elder brother is like having many names for a single body;
the current state is like one person having many names.
▲Furthermore, because this single condition should correspond to multiple conditions, this "one" which corresponds to the "many" and these "many" conditions are mutually inclusive;
thus, this "one" which corresponds to the "many" is also characterized by mutual inclusion.
Furthermore, by means of this single condition, the two pairs below are explained as entering into one another;

that is to say, because the same substance (samāna-bhāva) enters through the different substance (bhinnabhāva), it causes the same substance to enter [the different substance]; and because the different substance enters through the same substance, it causes the same substance to be identical [with the different substance].
This has two meanings: first, if explained directly, it is like the two cases of different substances.
That is to say, the first [aspect] is the fundamental unity; how could the second, which is identical in substance (*sābhāva*), not be that same fundamental unity?
As for the third, which is different in substance, if it is the fundamental unity, then the three aspects of identical substance are also the fundamental unity—this is precisely our current point.

The reason these two [aspects] are fundamentally one is simply that they mutually arise as conditions with the "many ones," just as the examples of identical and different substances depend upon one another; this is fully detailed in the subsequent commentary.
▲ First, clarify mutual inclusion: a single condition possesses the power to sustain many, whereas the many individually lack the power;
because they rely upon that single condition, the one can encompass the many, and the many consequently enter into the one.
▲ One entering and many encompassing; the reverse of the above should be understood.
First, clarifying "mutual entry" (xiāng rù) is the third correct explanation of this gate. This also has two parts: first, clarifying one looking toward many;
second, the subsequent meaning, which serves as an analogy for many looking toward one. Within the former, there are also two parts: first, clarifying that the one exists.

When the many possess power while the one lacks it, the one can encompass the many, and the many enter into the one; thus, the "many" refers to the other nine, and the "one" refers to the original one.
One should understand that the reverse of this—where the one enters the many and encompasses them—is the case where the many and the one possess power while the original one lacks it.
This is because, when the "many" are designated as such from a single perspective, the original one is then termed the "original one."
Therefore, when "many ones" possess power, they subsume the "one original one," and the "one original one" enters into the "many ones.
As for the remaining meanings and remaining phrases, they should be considered according to the preceding examples.
Regarding the two subsequent examples where "many" are compared to "one," these are entirely identical to the preceding case concerning the characteristics of distinct entities (*bhinnasvabhāva*).
Regarding the "other meanings" mentioned within the introduction: this refers to what was clarified above concerning the primary [one] looking toward the many.

Because there is that which possesses power and that which depends on it—namely, the state of having full power or lacking power—the primary [one] can always contain the many within itself, while the one within the many merges imperceptibly into the primary one without any obstruction.
Now, when the many look back toward the primary one, there is likewise the presence of both full power and a lack of power.
Therefore, it is able to constantly contain the original unity within multiplicity, and the entry of multiplicity-unity into the original unity is likewise without obstruction;
thus, it is called "the remaining meanings. As for the "remaining phrases," these refer to the four and six propositions of simultaneous existence and mutual negation;
as they follow the same pattern as the preceding discussion on distinct entities, they are not explained in detail here.

▲The meaning of the mutual identity of the eight as being of the same substance (*ekasvabhāva*) means that because the "many-ones" possessed by the preceding "one-condition" also possess the sense of having both substance and no-substance, they likewise mutually identify.
▲Because the many-ones lack substance, they arise from the fundamental one to become many, and thus identify with the one; because the fundamental one possesses substance, it [is able to...]
Regarding the statement, "Making the many one and causing the one to encompass the many;

the eight meanings such as 'identical substance' and 'mutual inclusion,'" the commentary (*śāstra*) also has two parts: first, it clarifies [the relationship] by viewing the one in relation to the many;

subsequently, under the heading "other meanings," it provides an analogy for viewing the many in relation to the one. Within the former section, there are also two parts: first, it clarifies that the original one possesses substantial reality; subsequently, it provides an analogy.
Regarding the first of the two [sections] concerning the existence of a substantial entity (*sattva*) within the many:

first, as for the statement that there is also the meaning of both "having a substantial entity" and "lacking a substantial entity," this generally sets forth the reason why [the gate of] identity and difference can establish a substantial entity and what is established as lacking a substantial entity.

● Below, the section beginning with "Furthermore, because the many have no substance" provides the formal explanation of the original point that "the one has substance," which can be understood from the text;
reflect upon this.
▲ Just as it is thus that the one has many emptinesses, so too is it the case that the many have one emptiness.
Just as when there is "one" there are many instances of "one," and when there are many instances of "one" there is the substance of "one":
because there are many instances of "one," the original "one" is designated as the "original one"; thus, while the many instances of "one" possess substance, the original "one" lacks substance.
Because the many instances of "one" possess substance, they are able to subsume the original "one," and the original "one," lacking substance, is submerged within the many instances of "one."
▲ Regarding the remaining meanings and phrases, reflect upon them in accordance with what precedes.

Under "remaining meanings," the second example consists of two parts: first, looking back at the source; second, [the explanation]. This means that because the preceding source-text contains both existence and non-existence of essence (*svabhāva*), it is able to subsume many instances as one.
By unifying itself with its own source and unifying with others, it is simultaneously unimpeded. Now...
Generally speaking, when one observes that "one" may possess both substantiality and non-substantiality, it can subsume "one" as identical to itself while discarding "one" as identical to others;
since this is simultaneously unimpeded, it follows entirely the previous examples within the section on "different substances," and is thus referred to as "the remaining meanings.
As for the "remaining phrases," these likewise consist of the four and six propositions of simultaneous existence and simultaneous negation.

▲ Regarding the meaning of the mutual fusion and non-obstruction of the nine [aspects]: this is also identical to the previous case where the entire substance and function are mutually fused, resulting in sovereign entry;
here too there are six phrases, which should be understood according to the preceding model.
As for the phrase "the mutual fusion and non-obstruction of the nine," the commentary (*shu-wen*) also has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the main section; second, the following...

The following concludes the preceding three gates. The phrase "as before" used in the middle [of the previous section] is the same as the "same as before" in the "Gate of Different Substances," which is the aforementioned sixth gate.
Although the meaning of the sixth gate was already clear, it merely distinguished between "identical substance" (*ekadravya*) and the "different" [substance].

Fearing that those who do not understand may be confused, I shall now explain it in full. That is to say, within the dharma of dependent origination of identical substance (*ekadravya-pratītyasamutpāda*):
Only when power and function interpenetrate and the whole is fused does dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) truly arise. Therefore, this perfect interfusion also consists of six propositions:

first, because there is no aspect of the essence that is not function, when the entire essence is raised as function, there is only the mutual inclusion of the same substance (*samatā-kāya*), but not the meaning of mutual identity;
second, because there is no aspect of function that is not essence, when the entire function is raised as essence, there is only the same... [text fragment].

The essence and its characteristics are non-characteristic; this is the meaning of "entering. The function of the essence of the Three Refuges does not obstruct the essence, and the essence of the complete function does not lose its essence.
Thus, they coexist without obstruction; both "entering" and "being identical" manifest with sovereign freedom. When the essence of the complete function is exhausted, the essence vanishes;
when the function of the total essence is extinguished, the function ceases. Being neither identical nor entering, they are perfectly interfused in a single flavor.

The fifth [point] combines the previous four phrases into one, wherein the dependent origination of the same essence (tongti yuanyi) exists without obstruction and the six [categories] are extinguished;
the fifth phrase is transcended, being beyond words and merging into the ocean of the same nature. Therefore, it is said that "it should be understood according to what precedes."
▲ The preceding three gates have completed the exposition of their principles within the second gate, the Gate of Identical Substance (tongti).
▲ Regarding the tenth [gate], the Meaning of the Perfection of Identity and Difference:
as for the phrase "the perfection of identity and difference" and so forth, the commentary text consists of three parts; this first sentence indicates the title of the section. Next...
Previously, the individual explanations were given; following this, the tenth section concludes by attributing [the teaching] and citing evidence. Regarding the first point:

the four gates concerning distinct entities and the four gates concerning identical entities discussed thus far, as well as the third gate where identity and difference coexist—none of these fail to bring together both identity and difference in a single locus without favoring one gate over another; therefore, it is called "perfect" (*paripūrṇa*).
▲ This refers to the synthesis of the preceding nine gates into one great dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), whereby numerous doctrinal perspectives are simultaneously and fully realized.
● Because it abides in a single [principle] while responding universally, there is the gate of sovereign mastery over breadth and narrowness.

● Because it accords with both essence and function, there is the gate of mutual identity and mutual inclusion. ● Because distinct essences mutually accommodate one another, there is the gate of the subtle and the minute. ●

The gate of mutual inclusion through the identity of distinct entities (*bhinna-svabhāva*) possesses the aspects of manifestation and concealment. Furthermore, when the mutual entry of functional aspects (*kāritra-lakṣaṇa*) is made manifest, the identity of essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) is made concealed;

likewise, when the entry into concealment is made manifest, it is also so. Furthermore, by means of different gates, when the entry into identity is made manifest, the entry into identity within the same substance (*eka-svabhāva*) is made concealed;
likewise, when the same is manifest and the different is concealed, it is also so. Furthermore, by means of different substances, the mutual entry carries with it the same substance.
There is the gate of the mutual entry of bodies and marks like a net of Indra, because this great dependent origination is itself the unimpeded dharma-realm;

there is the gate of manifesting the Dharma by relying on phenomena, because it is manifested within time; and there is the gate of principal and satellites, because they are mutually related and encompass one another.
In the second section, the detailed explanation, the ten mysteries are fully present; this is the first part, from the preceding nine gates up to their full completion.

This refers to the "Gate of Simultaneous Mutual Fulfillment. Regarding the various categories of meaning, there are the fundamental and the derivative, the identical and the distinct, the inclusive and the identical, as well as the fourfold and sixfold propositions; these, combined with the preceding nine gates, constitute the gate of simultaneous fulfillment.

Because these [factors] are comprehensive, and because dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) cannot be established if even one of its meanings is missing, each of the nine subsequent sections first explains the meaning and subsequently concludes by assigning it [to its category].
Regarding the "Gate of Sovereignty over Extensiveness and Restriction through Abiding in One and Pervasive Response":
this is the second section of the preceding Fundamental Gate. Because it abides in one, it is restricted; because it pervasively responds, it is extensive.
Regarding the statement "in terms of essence and function": because they are identical in essence, they are mutually identical; because they function differently, they are mutually inclusive.

Both apply to cases where the entities are the same as well as where they are different. ● As for "different entities being mutually inclusive," this specifically takes up half of the meaning from the previous fourth section on the mutual inclusion of different entities;
however, while "inclusion" (*praveśa*) applies generally to both the includer and the included, it is mostly explained in terms of the includer.
There is also the capacity to contain and that which is contained; this can likewise be explained from the perspective of the "entering.

Here, that which enters is precisely that which contains, and that which is contained is precisely that which enters. Now, in the "Subtle Door," only the sense of containing is taken, not the sense of entering; therefore, it is called "one half.

Regarding the statement, "The door of mutual identity between distinct entities possesses the aspects of concealment and manifestation," there are three sections in the commentary (*shu*) explaining this concealment and manifestation.
This is precisely the first [of the ten mysteries]. If that is so, then since their characteristics are identical, should they not likewise share the same concealment and manifestation? Answer:
The nine gates discussed above contain only four principles—identity, inclusion, sameness, and difference—and it is by means of these four principles that the Ten Mysteries are established.
Consequently, within a single principle there may be multiple meanings. Herein, because this is identical to that, this is concealed while that is manifested; because that is identical to...

For this reason, that is concealed and this is manifested; because they are mutually identical (*paraspara-ekībhāva*), the meaning of concealment and manifestation is established. The section on the "Gate of Establishing Concealment and Manifestation" is concluded. However, their meanings differ:
while mutual identity requires that this and that be unified as one, concealment and manifestation require that both this and that remain present.

For example, when one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the east, the body of absorption remains in the east; when one arises from absorption in the west, the body of arising remains in the west. Therefore, these two are not the same.

The merging [of these meanings] is even more extraordinary than possessing the latter two meanings, as they are mutually identical. Furthermore, regarding the second explanation below concerning function, it clarifies the hidden and the manifest:

this means that when one correctly discusses the entry into the gate, the meaning is like empty space. This is because if one were to further maintain "identity" (*ji*), then the meaning of "entry" (*ru*) would not be established;
for while identity implies merging into one, entry implies that the two meanings are not destroyed. Thus, it is correct.

The absence of mutual inclusion can be understood by analogy with what precedes. Furthermore, regarding the third explanation of the meaning of concealment and manifestation from a different perspective:

because the meanings of "sameness" and "difference" are mutually contradictory, these two aspects cannot be established simultaneously; thus, it must be understood that one aspect is concealed while the other is manifested.
Furthermore, regarding the mutual inclusion of distinct entities that carries within it the mutual inclusion of identical entities, which possesses the gate of the Indra’s Net:

Regarding the principle of mutual inclusion within the same substance (*samatā-svabhāva*), since that which is already one contains many, it further enters into other substances; thus, there is the meaning of "layer upon layer" (*chong-chong*).
Mutual inclusion within the same substance is like a mirror that already contains many reflections yet further enters into other substances;
this is like the mirror containing reflections further entering into another mirror, thereby establishing the meaning of inexhaustible layers. Other gates may be understood accordingly.
▲ This tenth section on the "Perfection of the Single Gate" elucidates the underlying principles based on the third gate mentioned previously.
Regarding this tenth section, the three subsequent summaries belong to the citations of evidence, while the preceding summary belongs to the introduction of the evidence. Now, for the first part:
because the third primary gate integrated both the identical and the different, this [tenth gate] now closely integrates the six preceding gates which were of distinct entities.

The three middle gates and the three gates of identical substance (samatā) are mutually established as being non-different; for without identical substance, there is no establishment of identity, and without identity, there is no establishment of difference.
Thus, these six gates are mutually established. The subsequent seven gates arise from the preceding three;
because the preceding three are fused, the subsequent seven must necessarily be fused. Therefore, the ten gates are of one principle. This follows the pattern of the third gate, "Fusion" (yūga).
There are also six propositions: first, the entire substance may be entirely different, such that both inclusion and identity are simultaneous;

second, the entire substance may be entirely identical, such that both inclusion and identity are simultaneous; third, both identity and difference may manifest together, because there is no duality of substance;
fourth, it may be neither identical nor different, because both are exhausted through mutual negation—meaning that since identity is itself difference, it is neither identical nor different.

Because they are identical, they are not different; the five [aspects] or the four [aspects] together serve as the objects of understanding. The sixth [aspect], transcending the preceding five, constitutes the object of practice.

Thus, while various gateways manifest the principle through wisdom, when one sets aside wisdom and forgets the trap, nothing can be described. Whether there is description or no description, it is unimpeded and inconceivable.
Submerged in the identical ocean of fruition, where only words are extinguished, may one perhaps attain a glimpse of illumination through the elimination of all conceptualization.
This is merely the profound meaning.

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the dharma of dependent origination; within a single dharma, he understands many dharmas, and within many dharmas, he understands one.
It further says: "Within the one, he understands the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, he understands the one," thereby comprehending them.
The mutual arising [of these qualities] and the attainment of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) and so forth are all its meanings.
Therefore, the subsequent text says—citing two passages as proof: first, from the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (*Daśakṣānti-parivarta*);

second, it further says—from the "Chapter on the Radiance of Awakening" (*Prabhābodhi-parivarta*). However, the cited texts represent the general meaning, as the significance of the tenth gate is [contained therein].
In summary. ▲ The commentary concludes the section on the gate of mutual conditioning through dependent origination.
This concludes the third part: the general summary of dependent origination.

▲ Regarding the fourth, the gate of the interpenetration of the dharma-nature: if one considers only phenomena (*dharma*), they obstruct one another and cannot be immediately interfused;
if one considers only principle (*li*), it is of a single flavor and there is nothing that can be interfused.

The fourth is the Gate of the Interfusion of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). This means that since True Suchness (*tathatā*) possesses virtues exceeding the sands of the Ganges, the phenomena (*vastu*) arising from it likewise possess inexhaustible virtues; because the true Dharma-nature interpenetrates all phenomena, there is no obstruction.

In the text, there are two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific. Within the general section, there are also two: first, the exclusion of what is not [the case], which refers to the notion that principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) proceed in opposition.

Because one cannot achieve non-obstruction in every particular matter, it is known that while there are words [to describe it], Mount Sumeru is fundamentally non-existent and the mustard seed has been empty from the beginning;
thus, one merely takes emptiness to contain emptiness. To say, "What thing is there that would not be accommodated? is simply not appropriate.
▲ Now, principle and phenomena are interfused, possessing this non-obstruction.
Regarding "Now, principle and phenomena," the second section clarifies the correct [view]; herein there are also two parts, the first of which is the formal presentation.
▲ That is to say, when a single phenomenon that is not distinct from principle fully encompasses the nature of principle, it causes those many phenomena that are not distinct from principle...
Regarding the principle that phenomena manifest within the one according to their respective bases:
the latter refers to the specific demonstration of the characteristics of a single phenomenon that is not distinct from the principle.

Within this, the first of four points clarifies in accordance with the truth that all dharmas rely upon the principle and none depart from it; thus, this single phenomenon now fully encompasses [the whole].
From the perspective of principle (*li*), all phenomena are subsumed within a single phenomenon.
If the principle were not fully subsumed within one, there would be the error of the true reality having limitations;
if the principle were fully subsumed within one yet many phenomena did not manifest in accordance with that principle, there would be the error of phenomena existing outside of principle.

Second, if one were to establish the opposite by means of the middle and lower [positions], it would mean that if the principle were not fully encompassed, there would be the fallacy of being able to divide ultimate truth into one principle, two principles, or even many principles. However, since ultimate truth is profound and still (*zhanran*), it cannot be divided;

and because it is of a single flavor and equal, there are no two principles. If one were to avoid this fault by claiming that the principle is fully encompassed, yet [the consequence] remains manifold...

If a phenomenon does not enter into a single phenomenon, then it is a phenomenon that does not enter; if a phenomenon exists outside of principle, it causes principle to be separated from the phenomenon, yet [that principle] enters into the midst of a single phenomenon. If a phenomenon is separated from principle, it does not come within a single phenomenon;

however, to claim that there is a phenomenon apart from principle—which would give phenomena a fixed nature—or that there is principle apart from phenomena—which would render principle a mere abstraction—is an even greater error.
Profound indeed!
▲ Now, since within a single phenomenon the principle is fully encompassed and exhausted, how could it not manifest within the one? III.
Now, having concluded by establishing the correct meaning: since it is free from the fault of divisibility, the principle is fully encompassed and exhausted.
Furthermore, there is no fault of phenomena and principle being separated; therefore, phenomena manifest instantaneously within a single phenomenon in accordance with principle.
As the *Avataṃsaka-saṃgraha-parivarta* states: "Within every single atom of all the worlds of the Flower Treasury, one perceives the Dharma-realm;
this Dharma-realm is precisely the phenomenal Dharma-realm."
The fourth [section], "Citing Evidence from the Flower Treasury," can be understood through its introduction.
▲ This constitutes the general meaning; specifically, it also possesses the ten gates of the Mysterious Portal.

Regarding the phrase "This constitutes," etc., this is the second part, which provides a detailed explanation. Within this, there are two sections: first, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows.
▲ First, since the ultimate truth is universally associated with and encompasses all phenomena without contradiction in principle,
all gateways and all phenomena are simultaneously and fully present.
Second, following the phrase "since the ultimate truth," the text correctly reveals that the meanings of the ten distinct gateways are all based upon the particular aspects of *tathatā* (suchness).
Having established the virtues, we now set forth the eighth dedication, which elucidates the true suchness (*tathatā*) as possessing the virtues of the hundred gates.
Herein, fourteen kinds of virtues are briefly cited to constitute the ten mysterious gates (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*).

First, for example, true suchness is both in mutual correspondence with all phenomena and inseparable from them. This virtue constitutes the first [gate]: the gate of simultaneous and complete mutual correspondence.

▲ Since these two matters accord with principle in being able to encompass all, and likewise accord with principle in being universally pervasive without destroying their narrow characteristics, there is the gate of the unimpeded interpenetration of the broad and the narrow, and the pure and the mixed.
Furthermore, because their nature is eternally equal, they are "pure," and because they universally encompass all phenomena, they are "mixed."

Second, there is the "Gate of the Extensive and the Narrow" established by two virtues: first, the analogy of the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) being eternally equal, and second, the analogy of *tathatā* universally encompassing all phenomena.
Third, since principle (*li*) already pervades all manifold things, it causes a single thing to follow that principle and pervade within all things.

Since the entire universal principle is fully present within a single phenomenon, and because all things follow that principle within a single phenomenon, there is the "Gate of the Mutual Compatibility of One and Many.
Third is the "Gate of the Entry into Characteristics through the Accomplishment of Qualities Being Everywhere Present."
Since the Four Truths are not separate from all phenomena, a single phenomenon is itself the Truth, and the Truth is itself all phenomena.
Therefore, this one is identical to all phenomena, and all are identical to this one; the reverse may be understood accordingly.
Thus, there is the Gate of Mutual Identity and Sovereignty (*xiāngjí zìzài mén*).

Fourth, the gate of mutual identity (*soku-mon*) is established through two virtues: that [the phenomenon] is not separate from all phenomena, and that it shares the same essential nature (*dharmatā*) as all phenomena.

Fifth, because the absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is fully present within each particular phenomenon and does not exist apart from them, when one is focused precisely on this [particular], the other is said to be hidden.
At that time, because this very [nature] is concealed, there is the gate of concealment and manifestation (*tirobhāva-udbhāva-mukha*).
Through the two qualities of being without limitation and constantly maintaining its own nature, the gate of concealment and manifestation is established.
▲ The sixth truth, because it universally encompasses all phenomena and brings the entities that depend upon them instantaneously into a single [reality], possesses the subtle gate.
The sixth universally encompasses all phenomena; its quality constitutes the subtle gate.

▲ Seventh, because this [reality] completely encompasses all principles, it can manifest everything; and since that [reality] which completely encompasses all is identical to this, it manifests instantaneously.

When this manifests that, both the manifesting subject and the manifested object appear therein; and when that manifests within this, both the manifesting subject and the manifested object likewise appear therein.
Because such layers upon layers are inexhaustible, there is the "Imperial Net" (Indra-jāla) gate, as True Suchness is ultimately complete.
Because it is ultimately inexhaustible,
there is the seventh gate, the Imperial Net of the Virtue of Ultimate Inexhaustibility.
Because phenomena and principle are identical, and because any single phenomenon that is raised is itself a true Dharma-gate, there is the eighth gate, the Gate of Relying on Phenomena.
8. The Gate of Accomplishing Virtue by Entrusting to Phenomena through Sharing the Same Essential Nature with All Dharmas.

9. The Gate of the Differentiation and Accomplishment of the Ten Times, because True Suchness is omnipresent—since it is fully present throughout days and nights, days and months, years and kalpas—and thus its presence during a single day is no different from its presence throughout a kalpa; for time exists because of dharmas, and dharmas are fused with time.
Is it not integrated?
The ninth [gate] is the gate of the ten worlds (*daśa-loka-dvāra*) established by the two virtues of pervading day and night and pervading years and eons (*kalpa*).

(A) This reality is the principle (*tattva*); time does not obstruct it, and it is eternally associated with all other things, characterized by cessation and possessing both principal and attendant factors.
Section on the Ten Natures Always Following and Being Constantly Conjoined with All Dharmas to Form the Principal and Retinue (Shubun).

In this section, the *Sūtra* and the *Commentary* are correlated with one another without the slightest discrepancy; even if certain passages are not fully present [in the commentary], they are implicitly applied through the subtle usage of the text.
The meaning of the sūtra text is likewise present here. Within the text, ten gates are first explained individually;
thus, because the single principle is pervasive, all ten gates are complete.
The subsequent section, beginning with "Therefore, the single principle," serves as the conclusion; the text is clear throughout.

first, the illusion, and second, the dream. In the former [the illusion], there is first the metaphor and then the application; in the middle [the dream], it is likewise.
