The Great Ultimate is a name for that which has no name, something that cannot be designated; it is so called because it represents the ultimate limit of existence, and is thus metaphorically termed 'Great Ultimate.
Kong [Yingda] says: 'The Great Ultimate refers to the state before heaven and earth were yet divided, when they were in a state of chaotic unity.'"
That which constitutes the One is precisely the *Tai-chu* (Great Beginning) or *Tai-yi* (Great Unity). As Laozi says, "The Dao gives birth to the One," this refers to the *Taiji* (Great Ultimate).

Once the primordial chaos (*hun-yuan*) has divided, heaven and earth come into being; therefore it is said that "the Great Ultimate gives birth to the Two Forms" (*liang-yi*), which corresponds to Laozi’s statement that "the One gives birth to the Two.
The reason he does not explicitly mention "heaven and earth" here is to refer to their essential substance (*wu-ti*), which subsequently correlates with the Four Images (*si-xiang*).
Regarding this, it is said that "the two polarities" (*liangyi*) refers to the two bodies and their outward manifestations. The commentary states:
"If we follow the *Liezi*, there are Taiyi (Great Ease), Taichu (Great Beginning), Taishi (Great Commencement), and Taisu (Great Purity). 'Taiyi' is when qi has not yet appeared.
'Taichu' is the beginning of qi. 'Taishi' is the beginning of form. 'Taisu' is the beginning of substance. The sub-commentary on that passage says:

This is the essential nature. Furthermore, the interpretation of "Taiyi" (the Great Ease) as referring to the "Taiji" (Great Ultimate) of the *Zhouyi* implies that if Taiyu were not Taiyi, it would constitute the Taiji at the very beginning.

If one follows the *Yi houming jue*, which explains that there are five movements (*yun*)—where the first four are identical to those in the *Liezi* and the fifth is named Taiji—then Taiji is not the primordial beginning. This interpretation is largely consistent with the *Liezi*.

It is said that the movement of the numbers signifies change; when the primal qi (*yuanqi*) first disperses, it is called the Great Beginning (*taichu*); when the qi takes on the formative aspect, it is called the Great Commencement (*taishi*);

when the form undergoes transformation and possesses substance, it is called the Great Substance (*taizhi*); and when the substance and form are fully established, it is called the Great Ultimate (*taiji*).

Although these differ slightly from one another, they all represent the primal qi giving rise to heaven and earth. It is further said that the Two Polarities (*liangyi*) give rise to the Four Images (*sixiang*).
Regarding the term "etcetera" (等), Kong [Qingjiu] says it refers to wood, metal, water, and fire, which exist by receiving the influence of Heaven and Earth;

thus it is said that the Two Polarities give rise to the Four Images (*sìxiàng*). As for earth, it presides over the four seasons and is distinct from the other elements; therefore, there are only the Four Images.

Regarding the statement that "the Four Images give rise to the Eight Trigrams" (*bāguā*): this means that Zhen (wood), Li (fire), Dui (metal), and Kan (water) each preside over one season, while Xun shares in these same principles.
Zhen (Thunder) and Mu (Wood), Qian (Heaven) and Dong (Lake) as Metal, with the addition of Kun (Earth) and Gen (Mountain) as Earth, constitute the Eight Trigrams.

As for "the Eight Trigrams determining good fortune and misfortune": once the Eight Trigrams are established, the lines and images are inferred against one another, resulting in good fortune and misfortune;

therefore, "good fortune and misfortune give rise to great undertakings," for all matters possess their respective fortunes and misfortunes, which are vast and fully contained therein, enabling them to produce the great affairs of the world.
This is a matter of practice.

▲ To take the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) as the cause is to posit a false cause; if one claims that "one yin and one yang" constitute the Dao, or calculates that the transformation of yin and yang can give rise to the myriad things, this too is a false cause;
if one calculates that the One is non-being (xūwú) and spontaneous (zìrán), [this likewise constitutes a false cause].
Thus, there is also no cause.

To say that the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) serves as the cause and so forth refers to the meaning of the two types of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). That is to say, if one employs the Great Ultimate as a cause, this is the reckoning of non-existence as existence;
it is also a false cause. If one claims that [the cause] extends downward through a single aggregate (*skandha*), this reveals a false cause or the absence of a cause.
The *Yì* says: "One yin and one yang—this is called the Way (*dào*); the unfathomability of yin and yang—this is called the Spirit (*shén*).

Regarding "one yin and one yang—this is called the Way," the commentary states: "What is the Way? It is a designation for Non-being (*wú*). There is nothing it does not penetrate; there is nothing it does not give rise to. Describing it metaphorically, we call it the Way.
It is quiescent and without substance, such that it cannot be represented by an image; yet it is through its necessary functioning that it manifests."

When one reaches the ultimate limit of non-action, its function becomes manifest; thus, one arrives at the Spirit that has no fixed location and the Change that has no form, whereby the Dao can be perceived.

Therefore, by exhausting transformations, one exhausts the Spirit; by relying on the Spirit, one clarifies the Dao. Although Yin and Yang differ, there is not a single moment for which they do not await [the Dao]:
when in Yin, it is the "non-Yin" by which Yin comes into being; when in Yang, it is the "non-Yang" by which Yang [comes into being].
Because this [Great Ultimate] is the completion [of all things], it is said that "one yin and one yang constitute the Way.
The *Kongshu* (Commentary on the Analects) states: "One" refers to non-being (*wu*). When there is neither yin nor yang, it is called the Way. That which attains "non-name" is non-being;

this non-being is void and empty, beyond differentiation, and is simply the One alone. Therefore, "One" is taken as non-being. If there were an objective realm, then there would be "that" [the other].
These manifestations take two or three forms and cannot be considered as one;
thus, when they exist as yin, their function as yin is not perceived, and when they exist as yang, their power as yang is not perceived.
They exist spontaneously as yin and yang, and naturally there is nothing contrived. This is what is called the Way (Dao); therefore it is said, "This is called the Way."
In terms of number, it is called "One"; in terms of essence, it is called "Non-being. Because it can penetrate and pervade all things, it is called the "Way" (Dharma);
because it is subtle and unfathomable, it is called the "Divine" (Shen); because it responds to conditions through transformation, it is called "Change" (Yi).
Taken as a whole, these are all designations for the Void (Vimala). The Sage names them according to their functions, following their respective meanings.
Regarding the establishment of the designation based on principle, the commentary states: "If one holds that the transformative changes of yin and yang can produce [phenomena], this is a false cause.
Furthermore, both the *Zhu* (Commentary) and the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) state: "The 'one' is non-existence; therefore, it is a causeless [cause]. Thus, it is said:

"If one calculates that the 'one' is void, non-existent, and spontaneous (*svabhāva*), then it is likewise causeless. This is because even "void non-existence" is categorized as a false cause, which is why [this point] is brought forward.
It is also said:

"Furthermore, [to claim] that there is no cause or that there is a false cause leads to a great error; namely, that things such as nature (svabhāva) and space (ākāśa) arise spontaneously, which would imply they must arise eternally."

However, regarding the third pair concerning false causes, the refutation of the faults is stated as follows: [if there were no cause,] things would arise spontaneously and thus should arise constantly;
people would arise naturally and thus should arise constantly without depending on parents and so forth;

and the bodhi of sentient beings would also arise naturally, such that all karmic fruits and retributions would not be obtained through cultivation. This precisely reveals the fault of having no cause. If one uses [emptiness]...

To take emptiness as a cause is likewise a fault of false causality; these various calculations differ from one another, so I shall not elaborate on them here. Thus ends the extensive refutation of divergent views above.
Furthermore, because they do not know that the three realms arise from my own mind, they wander endlessly through delusion and craving, losing their way from the truth.
Because of these causes and conditions, divergent views arise in confusion.
Since [people] do not know that the three realms depend upon one's own mind—this is the third section, which sets forth the correct view and refutes the heterodox; herein there are three parts:

first, a general clarification of the causes and conditions of delusion; second, an illustration of the profound intent by way of contrast; and third, the elimination of confusion to reveal the heterodox. Regarding the first of these:

The three realms arise from my own mind; this is precisely what is taught in the lower ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna. Treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* all cite this to establish it:
mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) continue in a self-similar succession from moment to moment. Since beginningless time, these realms have flowed on in succession, neither interrupted nor eternal.

They rely upon conditions and counterparts; they are neither vital breath (*qi*) nor physical endowment. They are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and mind-only (*cittamātra*). How could this not be so?

When the vital energy (*qi*) of Confucianism and Daoism transforms into spirit (*shen*), the spirit follows the energy; the energy does not follow the spirit. This arises from spontaneity (*ziran*), and through spontaneity its nature (*xing*) is formed.

Is this not a natural transformation rather than something produced by cultivation? How much more so when it comes to claiming that there is a distinct, hidden nature or subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) apart from the mind?
Furthermore, how could Brahmā and the like be the creators? To say they exist "due to ignorance and craving" [is to acknowledge their conditioned origin].
The phrase "endless transmigration" (*saṃsāra*) refers to the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna and possesses two senses:
first, ignorance (*avidyā*) initiates karma, while craving (*tṛṣṇā*) moistens that karma; second, there is past ignorance and present craving and grasping (*upādāna*).

In the Hīnayāna, only the latter sense exists; although all three poisons (*triviṣa*) are involved, these two [craving and grasping] are predominant. For this reason, even the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* speaks of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Fundamentally, there are two kinds of origins: first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, craving for existence (*bhavarāga*). Between these two lies birth, old age, sickness, and death;
this is not a minor matter. Regarding the establishment of the three poisons as the root of birth and death in the Hīnayāna, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, in the chapter on Defilement and Purity, states:
"The Sūtras say that greed, hatred, and delusion are the roots of the world."
The *Ben* (Root) chapter states that the three poisons arise through the conditions of the three karmas, and the three karmas arise through the conditions of the three realms;

therefore, all phenomena exist. The "Twelve Links of Dependent Origination" chapter states: "Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and subsequently give rise to the three types of formative action (*saṃskāra*).
Because these actions exist, consciousness receives a body within the six destinies; all of this is due to the three poisons."

The fundamental meaning is as follows: although the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) posit the three qualities (*triguṇa*), they do not know that these belong to the mind; furthermore, they calculate that activity arises from primordial darkness (*ālaya*).

Therefore, this constitutes a false view. Regarding the statement "deluded regarding the true causes and conditions," etc.: the mind alone, characterized by ignorance and craving (*avidyā-tṛṣṇā*), is precisely the true cause and condition.
If the Mahāyāna explains that the mind alone is the cause and ignorance and craving are the conditions—this refers to that very same principle.
The Hīnayāna likewise takes delusion and craving as causes and karma and so forth as conditions; the Mahāyāna likewise takes karmic seeds as conditions.
How, then, can one know that the nature of causes and conditions is emptiness, while True Suchness (Tathatā) is wondrous existence?
Regarding the phrase "How could one know... and so forth, this is the second section, which brings forth the profound intent by means of a further illustration:

if even the shallow meaning of the causal characteristics of dependent origination is still obscure, how can one fathom the limits of the true principle of the emptiness of nature? This emptiness of nature is common to the Initial, Sudden, and Final Teachings;
True Suchness as wondrous existence is the Real Teaching; and when it penetrates both emptiness and existence such that they mutually permeate and possess all virtues, it is the Perfect Teaching.

Regarding those who claim that [certain teachings] are indistinguishable from the Buddhist doctrine, these are all merely remnants of the Buddha-dharma that resemble *nirvāṇa*. This is like the analogy of stealing a cow:
although the color of the milk is the same, one cannot properly extract the *sarpis* (clarified butter); how much less can one produce *ghṛta* (butter) by churning donkey’s milk?

The statement [regarding "stillness"] risks being confused with the three [lower states] below; thus, this selection eliminates confusion and reveals what is heterodox. It refers to the *Book of Changes*, which says:
"Tranquil and unmoving, yet responding and thereby penetrating the causes of all under heaven"; and the *Book of Rites*, which says: "Human life is born quiescent—this is the nature of Heaven;
moved by external things, it acts—this is the desire of nature"; and Laozi, who said: "Profound and dark, yet within it there is an essence; that essence is exceedingly..."
In the *Zhen Zhuangzi*, it says, "The True Lord exists therein," and so forth. Later Confucian scholars all observed that such passages shared minor similarities in terminology;
however, failing to examine the fundamental principles established throughout the preceding and following sections, they sought to syncretize the Three Teachings.
Now, in the present day, Master Cheng Ying has composed commentaries on the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, extensively citing Buddhist teachings to supplement those classics. One merely observes...
To say there is a "small similarity" while failing to realize that the meanings differ greatly is a point that later scholars of shallow understanding have become even more confused about.
Regarding the analogy of the "stolen ox" used in relation to Nirvana, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in its third response to the questions of Kāśyapa, states:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Dharma of the world-transcending [path] and the world..."
What is the distinction between dharmas such that the Buddha has said: "The Buddha is a permanent dharma, an unchanging dharma"?
The world also says that Brahmā is permanent, Maheśvara is permanent and unchanging, the Self (ātman) is permanent, and the nature of the self and the atoms (paramāṇu) are also permanent.
If it is said that the Tathāgata is a permanent dharma, for what reason does the Tathāgata not appear constantly?

If it does not manifest constantly, what is the distinction? Why is this so? Because from the Brahma-heaven down to a single mote of dust, the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) likewise does not manifest.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "It is like a householder who has many cows of various colors, all belonging to the same herd.
He entrusts them to a cowherd to graze where there is water and grass, seeking only the *maṇḍa* (the finest cream)."
After the cowherds had milked the curdled milk, they consumed it themselves. When the elder passed away, all his cattle were plundered by a band of thieves.
Having seized the cattle, the thieves found no women there; they themselves milked them and, having obtained the milk, ate it.
At that time, the band of thieves each said to one another: "That great elder raised these [cattle]..."
"The ox does not expect milk or curd, but rather the *sarpis* (clarified butter). How shall we now devise a means to obtain it?
For *sarpis* is called the foremost and supreme flavor in the world. We have no vessel;
even if we were to obtain the milk, we would have no place to set it down. Then they said to one another, "Only a leather bag can contain it."
"Even though there is an abundance [of milk], if one does not know how to churn it, the whey will still be difficult to obtain;
how much more so the fresh butter! At that time, because of the ghee, the thieves added water to it; because of the excess water, the milk, curd, and ghee were all lost.
Ordinary people are also like this: although they possess wholesome dharmas, these are all merely the remnants of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma."

For this reason, after the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa, those who steal the remaining wholesome dharmas of the Tathāgata—such as morality, concentration, and wisdom—are like those thieves who plunder a herd of cattle.
Although ordinary persons may obtain these precepts, concentrations, and wisdom, they lack the skillful means and are unable to explain them; for this reason, they cannot attain [liberation].
They attain constant morality, constant concentration, constant wisdom, and constant liberation; yet, like those bandits who,
not knowing the proper method, lose the clarified butter (sarpis), or like those bandits who add water to the clarified butter for its sake,
so too do ordinary people, for the sake of liberation, speak of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, a person, Brahmā, Īśvara, atoms, and the world.

The precepts of nature, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—are themselves *nirvāṇa*, yet in reality one does not attain liberation or *nirvāṇa*.
It is like those bandits who could not obtain the clarified butter (*sarpis*).

These ordinary people, possessing a small measure of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and making offerings to their parents, by reason of these causes and conditions, are born in the heavens and receive a small [measure of] [bliss].

Their "peace and happiness" is like the milk that bandits add water to; yet these ordinary beings truly do not know the cause by which one is born in the heavens through practicing even a small amount of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and making offerings to one's parents.

Furthermore, they do not know the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, nor do they take refuge in the Triple Gem. Because of this ignorance, they speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; yet though they speak thus, it is not in reality so.
Because they did not know this, after the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he preached for them the permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
It was like when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world; by the power of his merit, the bandits disperse and the cattle suffer no loss of life.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King entrusts the cattle to a cowherd who possesses many skillful means, and this person then...
He immediately obtained the *amṛta* (the supreme essence), and because of this *amṛta*, all sentient beings were free from affliction and suffering.

When the Wheel-Turning Sage King appeared in the world, those ordinary persons who were unable to expound upon morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) would immediately retreat and disperse, just as thieves scatter.
At that time, the Tathāgata skillfully taught both worldly and world-transcending dharmas.
For the sake of sentient beings, they cause all bodhisattvas to expound accordingly.

Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have attained the *amṛta* (the supreme essence), they further enable immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to obtain the flavor of the unsurpassed *amṛta*-Dharma, namely:
the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity. For this reason, son of good family, the Tathāgata is eternal.
The nature of conditioned transformation is not like that which worldly, ordinary, and foolish people claim regarding Brahmā and others—that they are eternal dharmas.
This essential quality of being eternal refers to the Tathāgata and no other dharma; Kāśyapa, you should know it thus.
*Commentary:* By correlating the dharma with the analogy, the textual meaning becomes clear. Thus, one knows that the terminology of Confucianism and Daoism is the same [in this regard].

All are produced from the Buddha-dharma, let alone the churning of donkey’s milk. This refers to the meaning of the third passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: the Buddhist teaching is like cow’s milk;
practicing it to attain liberation is like churning milk to obtain curds, fresh butter, and the like. If one does not understand or practice [the Dharma], one will not even obtain pleasure;
how much more so for the teachings of non-Buddhists, which are like that donkey’s milk? The Buddha is compared to the cow, while non-Buddhists are like [donkeys].
Donkey's milk is fundamentally not a substance from which curd can be produced; likewise, the teachings of the non-Buddhists lack the flavor of liberation.

Therefore, churning donkey's milk results only in excrement and urine. Similarly, practicing according to the teachings of external paths brings about only bitter fruits and yields no benefit whatsoever.

The endowment of physical substance, spirit, and consciousness continues in succession, arising and ceasing according to conditions as they flow through the three periods of time.
Confucianism and Daoism regard the gathering of vital energy (*qi*) as birth and the dispersal of vital energy as death; once dead, one returns to Heaven and Earth.

Since there is no continuity and nothing remains, how can one who rests within a single body know of the three periods? [Section Four: Distinguishing the Habitual from the Non-habitual, explaining that good and evil arise from karma.]

Folly and wisdom arise from habituation; through cultivation over accumulated kalpas, the numinous consciousness becomes profound and subtle. Confucianism and Daoism maintain that good and evil are distinguished by their origins, and that folly and wisdom are naturally endowed by Heaven.
Those who receive a pure and harmonious nature become supreme sages and spirits, while those who receive a turbid nature become foolish and dark.

5. Regarding the distinct explanations of "receiving conditions" (*yinyuan*) and "receiving vital energy" (*qiqi*): [the Buddhist view] holds that the myriad phenomena of the universe all arise from conditions;

[the Confucian and Daoist views] hold that wealth, honor, fortune, and misfortune all derive from vital energy and destiny. That which is received as vital energy cannot be altered, whereas that which is received as conditions can be augmented through cultivation.

6. Regarding the distinct explanation of "internal" versus "non-internal": [the Buddhist view] holds that the myriad things of heaven and earth arise from the transformations of internal consciousness.
Confucianism and Daoism hold that all things—whether crawling insects or flying creatures—are transformations produced by Heaven and Earth.

While one may transform and purify what lies within oneself, the transformations occurring in Heaven are left to their own high and low courses. [Section on] Distinguishing the Seven Conditions from Non-conditions:

The shifting, floating, and empty nature of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), as well as their transformation and extinction, are all due to the power of conditions and not caused by the sun and moon; yet Confucianism and Daoism attribute them to the sun.
The transformation of months and the shifting of destinies are due to the power of the new and the renewal of the old; they arise spontaneously and are not brought about by my own mind. ● Eighth:

The distinction between Heaven and Non-Heaven (Asuras), and the bifurcation of Confucianism and Daoism regarding calamity and fortune, auspiciousness and misfortune, flows into two streams: first, Heaven; second, Earth.
Since that which is done on Earth can be blocked and severed, one may deliberate before a portent has manifested; however, Heaven's workings are subtle and fragile.
Because it is unavoidable, one accepts it and rejoices in it, forgetting it and returning to it;

thus, those who find peace in Heaven abandon the human realm and sever ties with the sages to follow the Way. This is the purport of Laozi. When explained through the principles of retribution and causes and conditions, there are two fundamental sources:
first, suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*); second, cessation and the path (*nirodha* and *mārga*). As for cessation and the path, they are not...
Abiding in non-defilement, free from both annihilation and permanence, one stands high upon the peak where emptiness and existence meet, far transcending the realm of birth and death.

Those who experience suffering and its accumulation do so because the mind revolves, following the heights and depths of karma as it comes and goes among the six destinies and lingers within the three realms of existence.
Therefore, those who weary of suffering sever the cause of accumulation; those who realize cessation cultivate the path.
This explains the tenet of the Śākyas. The principles of these two schools are as clear as the palm of one’s hand;
yet their gates lead to a thousand different destinations and follow divergent threads—how could they be reconciled when compared as a single whole? The nine defilements are not truly defiling;

Laozi distinguished them through benevolence (*ren*), while the Daoist path rejects such benevolence. When benevolence is severed, the Dao naturally halts; it does not reside in deliberate action, nor does it seek to harm.
The nature departs from desire and the nature spontaneously attains itself; this does not depend on cultivation. Benefit burdens life; by setting aside benefit, life spontaneously fulfills itself;
this does not depend on augmentation. Rites arise from disorder; by discarding rites, disorder spontaneously disappears;
this does not depend on creation. Principle is rooted in the Way; when the Way exists, principle spontaneously arrives; this does not depend on sageship.
Attainment occurs through the timely arrival of conditions such that the position is established of itself; it does not depend on deliberate action.
Therefore, it is obtained without seeking and accomplished without striving; those who strive will surely fail, and those who seek will surely lose—this is the teaching of the Old Lord (Laojun).
The Buddha explains that goodness is the root of fortune in the Way; by cultivating goodness, one receives fortune.
Heaven is not the root of evil paths; it is by accumulating unwholesome deeds that one sinks into the three evil realms.
Compassion is the path of non-harming, while desire is the source of birth and death. To sever desire, one must necessarily eliminate birth and death;

by cultivating compassion, one’s lifespan becomes long and far-reaching. Therefore, those who do good will surely attain [the fruits], while those who do not do good will surely lose them; thus, one should distance oneself from desire.
Those who [follow this path] will surely transcend, while those who do not leave desire behind will surely fall; such is the teaching of Śākyamuni.

Once the distinction between these teachings has been clarified, they are as manifest as the contrast between cold and warmth, for their principles cannot be combined. [The *Daśanirdeśa-sūtra*] distinguishes the ten returns from the separate returns by explaining them through the suffering of birth and death.
[This suffering] takes form through deluded thoughts as the defilement of craving, and arises because of ignorance.
Arising from ignorance, it can be cut and removed; born of delusive thought, it can be blocked and uprooted. Blocking and uprooting depend upon its conditions (*pratyaya*);
removing and cutting depend upon its substance (*svabhāva*). One who knows the substance of delusion stills that delusion and realizes *nirvāṇa*;

one who penetrates the conditions of the provisional abandons the provisional and returns to quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). Thereupon, one controls and masters the One Vehicle and floats [beyond the world].
Sailing upon the six *pāramitās*, one emerges from the bitter sea of birth and death and transcends the cage of the burning house;
one ascends loftily to the terrace of *prajñā* and enters wondrously the garden of *nirvāṇa*. Serenely abiding in eternal bliss, one coexists with empty space;
majestically perfect and luminous, one merges environment and wisdom into a dual stillness. This is the ultimate destination of the Śākya teachings. As for Laozi, he [concerns] life and—
Death is destiny; all these are the workings of the Dao. The sage and the unworthy are matters of innate nature, which is simply what Heaven has bestowed.
What Heaven bestows cannot be escaped, and what the Dao effects cannot be resisted.

One who knows that the Way of Heaven cannot be escaped or resisted is able to abide peacefully within birth and death while preserving the integrity of their nature and emotions. When nature and emotion are complete, Heaven is not destroyed.
Though one passes through the realms of birth and death, the Way remains undiminished; because the Way is undiminished, the thoughts of pleasure and aversion vanish.
Because Heaven does not destroy, the mind of joy and anger is extinguished. Thus, one departs from the realm of clamor and dust to roam the district of the Way and its Virtue.
One’s principles are solitary and noble amidst the multitude, while the spirit alone is concentrated beyond the mundane world. Serene and profoundly still, one is untainted by afflictions and harms.
The capable and diligent person dwells in non-action (*wuwei*), such that no malevolent influences can assail them; they may thus attain longevity and fulfill their natural lifespan.

This is the ultimate goal of the teachings of Laozi. Since these goals differ, their starting points likewise diverge; the distance between them is as vast as a thousand li, yet it is not far in terms of spiritual cultivation.
Regarding the ten points of difference above, I hope you will reflect upon them deeply and with great care. Most of my sincere intentions are contained herein.
The Mahāyāna principle of dependent origination surpasses the profound subtleties of external schools; how much more so its wondrous reality of true emptiness!
Here, phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused, defilement and purity encompass all, and unity and multiplicity are without obstruction, reflecting one another in ever-deepening layers.
Every thought-moment is perfectly interfused—how could one seek the petty fame of a single moment or conflate the ultimate consistency of the Three Teachings by practicing the poison of false views?
This seed is a profound cause for the hells; it opens the source of ignorance and obstructs the path to omniscience (sarvajñā).

The school of the Three Dharmas Without Past or Future— namely the Mahāsāṃghika and others— asserts that only the present and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena exist,
while past and future dharmas lack both substantial essence (svabhāva) and functional activity (kāritra).

Regarding the school that maintains the doctrine that "the three dharmas have no past or future," such as the Mahāsāṃghika and others: first, the thesis is stated by asserting the existence of the present;

below, this is explained, and the term "and others" (等) includes six schools in their entirety and one school in part—that is, seven schools in their entirety and one in part—sharing this same tenet: 1. Mahāsāṃghika, 2. Kaukkuṭika, 3. Caityaśaila, 4. [Mahīśāsaka].
The Western Mountain Dwellers (Aparaśaila) are the fifth; the Northern Mountain Dwellers (Uttaraśaila) are the sixth; the Dharmaguptaka are the seventh; and the Kāśyapīya are the eighth.
The *Śāsanodbhāvana* (*Prakaraṇābhidharma-śāstra*) states that the Western and Northern Mountain Dwellers share many other points in common with the Mahāsāṃghika.

Regarding the phrase "a small portion of one," this refers to the fundamental Mahīśāsaka school, which asserts that the past and future do not exist, while the present and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena do exist.

Master Su of Beiping stated that for this reason, the doctrine of the Dharmaguptaka school (the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*) and the doctrines of the Mahāsāṃghika school (the four Āgamas and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*) both belong to the third category: the non-existence of the past.
This is the school’s tenet.

▲ Fourth, the tenet concerning the provisional and real nature of the manifest [dharmas]: This refers to the Saṃvṛti-nirdeśa school (the School of Designation), which maintains that among the aforementioned present dharmas, those existing as aggregates (*skandha*) are real, while those existing as elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) are provisional. As for the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it was originally composed by a disciple of the Sāṃkhya school, who held that the effect is the same as the cause; later, he renounced his home and entered the monastic life.

Since the Dharma of the Buddha is subsumed within the Sautrāntika school, the Tripiṭaka states that while the Sautrāntikas hold the subtle to be real and the coarse to be provisional, this principle of "subtle reality and coarse provisionality" is identical [to our own].
Thus, the present [system] encompasses both the provisional and the real. This teaching differs from the Ekavyāvahārika and Lokottaravāda schools;

it maintains that both conventional and ultimate truths contain both the provisional and the real. Regarding the definition of "aggregate" (*skandha*) as "accumulation" (*caya*) in the section on the aggregates: "real" refers to that which is an accumulation.
Therefore, since the meaning elucidated through the gates of *dhātu* and *āyatana* is provisional (*prajñapti*), its substance is a provisional accumulation;
thus, the present commentary states that the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* is a partial offshoot of the Sautrāntika school.

▲ Regarding the teaching (śāsana), a single scripture may contain multiple teachings; regarding the school (nikāya), a single school may encompass multiple scriptures.
Since this school is present within any given scripture, to restrictively judge a single scripture as constituting a single teaching is to suppress the various Mahāyāna sūtras.

Now, regarding the second section, the "Explanation Resolving Objections," which follows the ten schools and five teachings: there is an objection that asks, "How do the ten schools differ from the five teachings, such that they are distinguished again?
Therefore, this resolution is provided. There are two points: first, the difference between the universal and the specific; second, the difference in their essential forms.
First, the initial part provides a dual heading, followed by a dual explanation beginning with "As for the teachings... and so forth.
To clarify that while the teachings are universal, the resulting doctrines are specific:

although a single scripture may contain multiple teachings—such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which encompasses all five teachings, or the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, which likewise possess all five—the resulting doctrines are restricted.

this clarifies the "penetration of the tenet" (*zongtong*), as a single principle of phenomena and noumenon (*shili wuai*) includes within its tenet such works as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Consequently, the limitation of the teaching (*jiaoju*) is implicitly revealed, for within a single sutra there may be five levels of teaching that do not interpenetrate one another.

Furthermore, in establishing the teachings, one must necessarily distinguish the various stages of realization (*prahāṇa*) and attainment (*adhigama*); however, in defining the schools (*nikāya*), one merely clarifies their differences in what they hold as supreme.

Other points are as previously explained in the section on "Establishing the Teachings."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "the establishment of the teaching," etc., this clarifies that there is a difference in their essential forms (*tǐshì*). It also serves to resolve further objections. An objection is raised:
"If each has its own scope of application (*tōngjù*), why can one not take the *zōng* (tenet) as the *jiào* (teaching), or the *jiào* as the *zōng*? To resolve this:

yet, since their realization and verification are equal and they belong only to the Hīnayāna teachings, there is no contradiction regarding the doctrinal principles.

▲ Second, to reveal the specific tenet (*viśeṣa-siddhānta*): while all sūtras each have their own tenets, this section specifically clarifies the tenet and purpose (*abhiprāya*) of this particular sūtra.

Second, the opening chapter and its detailed explanation; herein is the first part, which further divides into two sections. First, the formal establishment that each sutra possesses its own specific doctrine, and thus this section specifically clarifies the doctrine of this present sutra.

For example, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* takes the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as its doctrine, while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* takes the permanence of the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) and so forth as its own doctrine.

To distinguish [the two]:
although the *Laṅkāvatāra* states that one should not establish the thesis that "all phenomena are unarisen," this statement is intended to dispel stagnation;

● When the nine causes and effects each fully encompass the Dharma-realm, the cause and effect follow the Dharma-realm such that they mutually manifest within one another;
therefore, the Buddha exists within the Bodhisattva, and Samantabhadra exists within the Buddha.
Ninth, the principle that cause and effect each fully encompass the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as their essential tenet,

such that cause and effect exist mutually within one another. Tenth, because in both the positions of cause and effect, there is no differentiated phenomenon that is not subsumed within the dharma-realm,
every single phenomenon, every single practice, every single stage, and every single virtue individually and collectively encompasses the inexhaustible and infinite [dharma-realm].
The ocean of all dharma-gates, layered like a net, is called the inexhaustible tenet of the Avataṃsaka;
the distinctions of the twelve stages all take the inclusion of the Dharma-realm as their tenet, while the inexhaustibility of each and every practice and stage constitutes its purpose.
Regarding the first four gates above: the first is the function of the essence; the second is the essence of the function; the third is the simultaneous manifestation of both essence and function;
and the fourth is the seamless integration of essence and function.

Regarding the fourth section below the four gates above, this third part provides a general conclusion. Within it, there are four points: first, the summary by means of essence (*tī*) and function (*yòng*);
"essence" refers to the aforementioned nature (*xìng*), while "function" refers to the aforementioned characteristics (*xiàng*).
Furthermore, the first [point] concerns cause and effect as dependent origination; the second concerns the ultimate reality of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); and the third clarifies both together.
The latter one is the inconceivable.
Furthermore, the first of the two is cause and effect; below, these eleven characters from the "Principle" section are used to subsume them.
Since the fourth [gate] has already integrated the preceding ones, the four gates are of one and the same principle.
Since the third [section] below integrates the four gates as a whole,

it is thus a single perfect and luminous contemplation that both illuminates and negates, and both negates and illuminates; by simultaneously illuminating and simultaneously negating, one accords with the essential purpose of this school.

For these four reasons, one immediately illuminates the subsequent [teachings] to bring them back to the contemplation of the mind. Regarding the dharmas: to be "separate" from them is to negate their existence in the mind;

to not destroy their existence in the mind is to illuminate them. Thus, "negation" (*zhe*) refers to the first two gates, while "illumination" (*zhao*) refers to the latter two gates (the third and fourth).

Furthermore, the initial negation is the negation that is itself illumination, and the subsequent illumination is the illumination that is itself negation. The fifth gate is the simultaneous negation of both.

7. "Simultaneous Illumination" means that while correctly negating both [aspects], one illuminates them simultaneously. 8. "The Four Gates are of One Principle" means that the single, perfect observation is identical throughout. 9.
"One Observation Encompassing All" means that within each and every phrase, all four gates are fully contained; this is also the single observation that encompasses all. 10.

"The Ten Gates Simultaneously Reflected" is called "Illumination"; "being without mind regarding the ten" is called "Negation. "Simultaneous Illumination" refers to illuminating the preceding [seven] and illuminating the negation [the eighth]; "Simultaneous Negation" refers to negating both.
The preceding negation of "illumination" results in the cessation of thought, such that everything is perfectly clear and distinct;

thus, only when the ten gates are unified in a single contemplation does one accord with the purport of the ten gates and harmonize with the essence of the four gates above. This is intended to lead [the reader] to understand the significance expressed by the appended text.

This Great Inconceivable Sūtra exists in three versions; the shorter version consists of one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters.

Regarding the statement that the Mahāyāna Piṭaka was compiled by Mañjuśrī and others, the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* explains that there were three Ānandas:
first, Ānanda, translated here as "Joyful" (Qingxi), who preserved the Śrāvaka Piṭaka; second, Ānandabhadra, translated here as "Virtuous Joy" (Hixian).

Ānanda, who upholds the treasury of the Pratyekabuddhas—this name is translated as "Ocean of Joy" (Kṣemodadhi)—and who upholds the treasury of the Bodhisattvas, is in fact one and the same person whose names differ according to his specific virtues.
Because this Ānanda has heard much and retained what he heard, his accumulation of learning has perfected the three types of wisdom;

he maintains both the words and their meaning, possessing sovereign mastery over the teachings of the Three Pitakas. Regarding the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa): *Note: The term "Ānagaḷa" (阿難伽羅) is an alternative transliteration for Ānanda, here interpreted as "Ocean of Joy. In a future age, there shall be one who upholds my Dharma: a bhikṣu of great renown and virtue in the land of South India named Nāgārjuna.

He will be able to shatter the tenets of existence and non-existence and manifest my unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma within the world, attaining the first stage of joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) and being reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
This is also recorded extensively in the *Da Tang Xiyu Ji* by the Tripiṭaka Master.
Regarding the account of its history, it is said that the kingdom of Cakuka possesses its original records.
According to the *Sui Kaihuang Sanbao Lu*, more than two thousand *li* to the southeast of Khotan lies the kingdom of Cakuka.

The kings of that country have transmitted their rule through successive generations and hold the Mahāyāna in high esteem; whenever eminent monks from various countries enter its borders, they are all...
If the practitioners were of the Hīnayāna, he would have dismissed them and not allowed them to remain; however, when those of the Mahāyāna entered, he requested that they stay to receive offerings.
Within the royal palace were such scriptures as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, totaling one hundred thousand verses.
The King personally upheld them, holding the keys himself, and made offerings of incense and flowers, adorning them with various ornaments and hanging colorful banners.
Between the banners, seasonal fruits were displayed as inducements to entice the princes to enter and prostrate, thereby causing them to dedicate their merit.
Furthermore, about twenty *li* to the southeast of this country is a mountain that is extremely precipitous;
within it are enshrined the *Avataṃsaka*, *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, *Vaipulya*, *Ratnakūṭa*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Vaipulya*, and the *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī* and *Puṣpasaṃcaya-dhāraṇī*.

The twelve sections of the *Sāra-kośa*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Mahāmegha*, and other such sūtras, totaling one hundred thousand verses, were successively transmitted as national treasures according to the laws of the land and were protected with great care. Initially, during the Eastern Jin dynasty, there was the śramaṇa Zhi Falin, who was devoted to the Mahāyāna;
he sacrificed his body to seek the Dharma, carrying provisions and traveling on foot until he reached the kingdom of Kuṣāṇa, where he prayed with the utmost sincerity.

He subsequently obtained the first portion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, consisting of thirty-six thousand verses, and brought it here; this is precisely the version translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
However, while Nāgārjuna possessed the complete text, he ascended back to the heavens, leaving only half of the jewel to Fali, who then circulated it throughout the eastern lands.
Thus, the realizations of sages and ordinary beings differed, the Sanskrit and Chinese sounds were separated, the long journey was obstructed, and the wondrous intent became submerged and lost.
The fallen slips and lost compilations have been transmitted by barely half; furthermore, according to the present records, the texts submitted from Khotan exceed forty thousand *gāthās*.

The reason for this sequence is that when sages establish their teachings, there must necessarily be a gradual progression; wishing to enunciate the subtle words [of the Dharma], they first speak of the three kinds of adornments of the world.

Because this serves as the general preface for the nine assemblies and the source from which the Great Dharma arises, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Ruling Lords," which corresponds to the introductory section common to all sutras.
Once the causes and conditions have been clearly established, the formal exposition is about to be presented;

thus, the assembly in the ocean-like multitude arouses thoughts and initiates the inquiry. Before the Tathāgata provides his response, he first manifests auspicious signs, and the light from his mouth summons the Bodhisattvas from afar.

The Honored One’s arrival was marked by rays of light from his *ūrṇā-kośa* illuminating everywhere, as he manifested as the Lord of Dharma preaching the teaching; he caused the net of worlds to tremble to awaken the faculties of all beings.

Flowers appeared before the Buddha to symbolize the teaching on the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*), and a multitude emerged from his *ūrṇā-kośa* to signify that the teaching flows from the Buddha.

These constitute the preliminary signs of the preaching of the Dharma; therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs," wherein the three auspicious omens have been clearly displayed.

The Lord of Dharma was about to proclaim the teachings of the Tathāgata’s eldest son, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Having manifested the light from his ūrṇā-kośa, he suspended his own mind in liberation;

wishing to reveal the inconceivable, he first clarified the process of entering meditative absorption to internally contemplate phenomena and principles, and externally discerning the capacities of sentient beings.
Thus, through the inspiration of the Buddha above and serving as a model for beings below, he proceeded to the "Chapter on the Samādhi of Samantabhadra. Having thus entered...
Upon reaching meditative concentration, all Buddhas praise it; upon arising from concentration, they speak words that are invariably true and appropriate.

First, they present the Tathāgata’s *parivṛta-saṃbhoga* (retributive environment), providing a general exposition on the origins of the ocean of lands (*kṣetra-samudra*). Therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of Worlds" (*Lokadhātu-siddhi-paṭala*).
"Fivefold accomplishment" is the general name for the ocean of lands; next, the specific details of how our Teacher first adorned, purified, arranged, and established [his own land] are revealed.
Because its full extent of adornments is equal to the atoms of empty space and contains the entire dharma-realm, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World.
Since the excellence of the secondary environment (upabhoga) must necessarily have a cause, it is like a long stream originating from a distant source or lush fruit growing from deep roots;
therefore, it is taught that [the Buddha] was formerly a prince who attended upon inconceivable [beings], fully cultivating supreme causes to purify the ocean of lands.
Because it immediately cites persons to manifest the Dharma, it is followed by the six chapters of the first part of the "Vairocana Chapter.
These collectively clarify the cause and effect of what is to be believed, constituting the First Assembly; it is also named the "Section on Citing the Fruit to Encourage Joyful Faith.

Next, as for the six chapters of the Second Assembly: because one must first believe in that which is above [the fruit], one now cites the "dependent fruit" (niśraya-phala) with the intent to give rise to [faith].
Furthermore, because deep faith must also recognize what is correct, the *Tathāgata’s* three karmas of correct retribution are clarified first—namely, body, speech, and mind.

Since the body is the totality, it is explained first; as it manifests bodies in accordance with sentient beings and establishes names according to their needs, it is followed by the "Chapter on Names.
Then, in order to extensively expound the Dharma wheel according to the inclinations of sentient beings, the four truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*) are unfolded as the Dharma-gate.
The names pervade the entire dharma-realm, for each and every world possesses four hundred billion ten-thousand names;
therefore, this is followed by the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths. Since the nine aspects of body and speech have already been manifested, the mental karma is now about to be revealed.

As the mind is profound and unfathomable, it is further clarified through the body; thus, the wheels on the soles of the feet emit light to illuminate phenomena and awaken sentient beings, while Mañjuśrī universally expounds wisdom.

The "Radiance" illuminates both phenomena and principle, awakening and leading one to enter [enlightenment]; the two illuminations of body and wisdom are merged into a single light so that the two types of awakening may be perfected simultaneously.
Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on Radiant Awakening," the third of the ten superior [stages].

Next, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)—the fruit of the correct retribution for what has been believed—shall be correctly explained. First, there is the virtue of understanding and practice (*adhigama-caryā*).

The "Chapter on the Clarification of Understanding" (Prajñāpariccheda) exhaustively elucidates the profound ultimate reality by means of ten aspects of profundity, as the ten Bodhisattvas mutually stimulate and exhort one another;

therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Questions of the Bodhisattvas" (Bodhisattvaparipṛcchā), the eleventh. Having already established correct understanding, one must further engage in correct practice;

traversing all spheres of experience to cultivate the path, one brings together compassion and wisdom so that no obstacles remain unquiescent; therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (Caryāviśuddhi), the twelfth.
When the practice of understanding is perfected, one then achieves supreme virtue and abides in the stage of perfection;

adorning oneself with perfect merit and establishing sentient beings through perfect power and function—this is what the Honored One of Wisdom (Bhadramukha) taught, and thus it is followed by the "Chapter on the Honored One of Wisdom.
The first three chapters clarify the Dharma of the Ten Faiths. Regarding the six chapters of the third assembly, the thirteenth [chapter] is because...
The ten stages of faith having been completed, one is about to explain the stage of abiding; therefore, without moving from the Bodhi tree, one ascends to the realm of Śakra.
Its essence and function are boundless as they respond to the desires of sentient beings, much like a single moon in a clear river seen by three boats:

if one boat remains stationary while two others move north and south, the one moving south sees the moon travel a thousand *li* with it, and the one moving north likewise sees the moon travel a thousand *li*.
Those who stop their boats to the north and see that the moon does not move perceive it as such; yet this moon does not leave the center of the stream to travel to the south or north.
The Tathāgata’s manifestations should be understood as analogous to this: the function of the essence is universally pervasive.
Whether departing or abiding, the Buddha is unmoved by conditions, yet he remains motionless while responding everywhere to the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, they receive him.

Chapter Fourteen: Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru. Having arrived at that celestial realm, the assembly of Bodhisattvas gathers to extol the Buddha’s virtues and manifest the profound and mysterious nature of his abiding essence; therefore, it is followed by Chapter Fifteen: Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru.

Once the mutual resonance between teacher and disciples has been established, he formally sets forth what is to be taught, clarifying the full entry into the stages and the attainment of the mind of right concentration.
Because the profound *prajñā* abides in ultimate truth, it is followed by the Sixteenth Chapter, "The Ten Abodes.
These ten abodes represent distinct stages where practices differ; yet, if one wishes to cultivate them universally, all must be purified through conduct.

Therefore, one contemplates ten kinds of objects to enter the profound contemplation, whereby the observation of phenomena reaches its consummation. When the True Dharma flourishes, delusion and wisdom both vanish, and true wisdom alone remains.

Arising in the cultivation of the Buddha’s ten powers and the four immeasurable minds, with compassion and wisdom flowing as one, one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of the initial resolve;
therefore, this is followed by the Chapter on Holy Conduct (*Brahmacarya*). Once the seventeen stages and positions are complete, the subsequent chapter manifests superior virtues.

Regarding the virtues of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), each succeeding stage surpasses the preceding; however, only the first abode is explained here to serve as an illustration for those that follow, beginning with the initial resolve.
The virtues of abiding are already immeasurable because they are without limit, equal to the realm of empty space;
since these supreme virtues are cited to exhort beings to resolve their minds [on enlightenment], this is followed by the eighteenth chapter, "The Merit of Initial Resolve.

Having perfected the stage of self-benefit, one is about to proceed toward the ten practices; therefore, the "Chapter on the Illuminating Dharma" follows next as the gate of excellence for further advancement.
Regarding the four assemblies and four chapters: the six chapters of the first part of the nineteenth [section], beginning with the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), have already been perfected.

As one is now about to expound the practices (*caryā*), it is necessary to respond to the responsive manifestations of sentient beings; therefore, this is followed by the twentieth chapter, "Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven.

Since the Buddha has already responded to these manifestations to assist in the transformation of others and to praise and reveal the essence of the ten practices—all of which rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom—this is followed by the [twenty-first] chapter, "The Night... (Yè).

The Twenty-first Chapter: Verses of Praise in the Palace of Māyā. Since the causes and conditions have been manifested and the ten stages of the Worthy Ones (*ārya*) within the Correct Teaching have been explained, it is followed by the Twenty-second Chapter:
The Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). Having completed the stage of self-benefit, one desires to ascend to the subsequent stage;
because one accumulates all practices with the intent of dedicating them (*pariṇāmana*), it is followed by the [Twenty-third] Chapter: The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries (*daśākṣaya-kośa*).

Regarding the five assemblies and three sections: in the twenty-third chapter, "The Fourth Assembly," having completed the exposition of the virtues of practice, the text proceeds to explain the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).
Because the teaching master responds to the needs of sentient beings, it is followed by the twenty-fourth chapter, "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.

In the twenty-fifth chapter, "The Gathering from the Ten Directions," the assembly gathers to assist in the transformation and to praise the manifestation of the vows of dedication; because these all rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom, it is followed by [the next section].

Chapter Twenty-five: Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Palace. Having already manifested the causes and conditions, this section correctly explains the practices of the ten dedications of the superior sages (*udāra-ārya*).
These consist of: dedicating without obstruction toward the three spheres; dedicating to sentient beings through great compassion that universally covers all;
dedicating to Bodhi by seeking the supreme through great wisdom; and dedicating to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) because one has entered into the dual quiescence of principle.
Because the three great vows are without before or after and universally pervasive, they are followed by the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
The first three chapters above have completed the section on the "Superior Worthies" (*adhimukticaryā*), who are free from the characteristics of further progress and have no further advancement.

The single chapter of the sixth assembly is the twenty-sixth chapter, "The Ten Grounds" (*daśabhūmi*); this means that the three assemblies above have already fully provided the understanding of the three worthies.
When practice and vows are perfected and one directly realizes True Suchness, there are ten levels of supreme virtue: like the earth, which universally supports and generates all things;
like the four rivers entering the ocean, which flow toward the same destination of Buddha-wisdom; like a precious jewel with its ten virtues, which are gradually cultivated;
like the ten great mountains of the earth, which stand majestically high above the great ocean; and through these ten virtues, each virtue being all-pervasive, one becomes a Tathāgata.

Because it concerns the activity of subtle and wondrous wisdom, it is followed by the "Ten Grounds" (*Daśabhūmi*) chapter. The seventh assembly consists of eleven chapters; the twenty-seventh is the "Ten Samādhis" (*Daśasamādhi*) chapter.

This means that once the ten grounds are fulfilled and one is about to achieve perfect enlightenment, the superior progression through the ten grounds is designated by the name "Equal Enlightenment" (*Samyaksambodhi*).
The dharma-gate of Equal Enlightenment is equal in measure to the *dharmadhātu*; here, its numerical significance is briefly set forth to reveal its profundity.
Xuanxian first elucidates the Ten Concentrations (*daśa-samādhi*), which exhaustively fathom the source of all phenomena and serve as the foundation for universal wisdom;

therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations," number twenty-eight. Because the scope of these concentrations measures the entire Dharma-realm, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" (*daśābhijñā*), number twenty-nine.
Since concentration and supernatural powers are inconceivable precisely because they arise from the ultimate limit of wisdom, the section concludes with the elucidation of wisdom.
Because wisdom is profound, mysterious, vast, and expansive, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" (*daśakṣānti*). Patience is itself wisdom.
These thirty superior concentrations and supernormal powers are the functioning of wisdom; each is immeasurable. If one were to attempt to calculate them, they could not be numbered;

therefore, one must proceed through enumeration until reaching the "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*), accumulating unspeakable numbers to reach ten layers of calculation for the merit of the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Because it is difficult to know, it is used as an analogy for the virtues of the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-abhisambodhi*).
Since the *asaṃkhyeya* is the foremost among great numbers, it is followed by the "Chapter on the *Asaṃkhyeya*" (31). What is explained in the *asaṃkhyeya* is subtle and difficult to know:

the perfect fusion of thought-moments and eons (*kalpa*) is such that no limit can be reached even in a single instant; the inclusion of all lands within a single atom (*paramāṇu*), wherein existence and non-existence are both inexhaustible and universal.
The Venerable One now briefly sets forth the essential points to clarify the exhaustion of all time; therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata.
Taking kalpas as the unit of time, each subsequent one doubles the preceding; since kalpas are difficult to exhaust, the Buddha’s lifespan is likewise so—hence it is called "lifespan" (āyus-pramāṇa).
Furthermore, it clarifies that [the Buddha] pervades all places; the previous section spoke in terms of reality, wherein every single atom is [the Buddha].

The abodes where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell are now pointed out through concrete matters; this is done to lead the mind toward a specific point of focus, and for this reason, it is followed by the thirty-third chapter, "The Abodes of Bodhisattvas.
As for the chapter "The Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha," the preceding six chapters exclusively expound the dharma-gate of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);
once the meaning of Equal Enlightenment is fully established, they finally clarify the fruit of Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*).
Briefly, there are two meanings: first, that which is ineffable; second, that which may be expressed through words. Within the latter, there are again two meanings:

first, differentiated exposition; second, impartial exposition. Regarding differentiated exposition, this refers to the three subsequent sections which respond to the preceding causes by distinguishing between cause and effect.
First, the Buddha’s virtues are generally clarified as being utterly transcendent of words and thought; therefore, they are received [as such].

Following the thirty-fourth chapter, "The Inconceivable Dharmas of the Buddha," the thirty-fifth chapter, "The Ocean of the Ten Physical Marks of the Tathāgata," is presented next to distinguish the physical marks.
These marks are universally pervasive, totaling as many as the atoms within an ocean of *padma-garbha* world-systems;

since each individual mark and its function pervade the entire Dharma-realm, their profound depth and vastness are difficult to describe. Therefore, this follows [the previous section]. The major marks are as follows:

Since this is so, the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are even more numerous; within each secondary mark there are many rays of light, and each ray of light pervades the entire Dharma-realm, shattering the sufferings of the hells and causing rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven. These three layers are perfected instantaneously, and the swift fulfillment of the ten stages (bhūmi) is manifested through these functions.
Therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Merit of the Light of the Secondary Marks," the thirty-sixth, Part One.

Following the preceding section on the causes and effects of differentiation, there are two chapters that clarify the causes and effects of equality: namely, the cause that has no difference from its effect, and the effect that has no difference from its cause.
These causes and effects interpenetrate one another, being equal and non-dual; yet within this non-duality they appear as two, such that the causes and effects remain distinct and clear.
Since the cause is precisely the practice-gate of Samantabhadra, it is followed by the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra."
The thirty-seven fruits of enlightenment are the manifestation of the nature-arising (*dharmatā-utpatti*) through the ten gates in perfect fusion;

therefore, this is followed by the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta*). The first six assemblies, which collectively expound the section on "Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generating Understanding," are concluded.

The eighth assembly consists of only one chapter, namely the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), because it is based upon the aforementioned causes of differentiation and equality.

Since the generation of understanding regarding the fruit has concluded, the current section on "Subsuming Understanding to Form Practice" explains the six stages of sudden cultivation, wherein two thousand gates of practice arise simultaneously and one dwells in the world without defilement; therefore, it is followed by the ninth chapter, "Leaving the World.

This chapter consists of only one section, namely the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" (Gandavyūha), which, when viewed in proximity to the preceding text, indicates that once the great practices are fully complete, [one enters the ultimate state].

The realization of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is taken up distantly through the various assemblies, wherein the perfection of faith, understanding, and practice fundamentally resides in realization.

Because this entry into realization depends upon the person, it is explained next. When the Tathāgata himself enters the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi, he causes the great assembly to suddenly realize the Dharma-realm as the fruition;
whereas Sudhana realizes the Dharma-realm gradually through the successive stages. Thus, suddenness and gradualness are interwoven.
Because the beginning and the end are harmoniously integrated, all are realized as the Dharma-realm; therefore, it is followed by the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-realm.
Thus we know that the inexhaustible ocean of teachings culminates solely in realization, and the inexhaustible Dharma-gates are here briefly concluded.
Therefore, the final verse says: "The atoms of lands and the thoughts of the mind may be counted; the waters within the great oceans may be drunk up; space may be measured, and the winds [weighed]."
One may attempt to bind [the teachings], yet no one can exhaustively describe the Buddha’s merits; thus, the paths of speech and thought are severed.
Therefore, the thirty-nine chapters provide a systematic framework for the true exposition, making the inexhaustible Dharma-gates appear as if before one's eyes. Hence it is said:

"This present sutra has thirty-nine chapters, while that [other] sutra has only thirty-four. Below, we shall distinguish the omissions in the Jin translation and clarify its expansions and condensations.

▲ Third, the clarification of the categories of the branches (*aṅga-prabheda*).

Regarding the third section, "Clarification of the Categories of the Branches," there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. Now, for the first: the branches are themselves the branches of the flow.
"Branch" (*śākhā*) means a division; it is also like the branches of a tree that emerge from the divisions of a single trunk.

Since the *Avataṃsaka* is the root, what is spoken of here as "flowing forth" is like the various streams flowing out from a single pond. Thus, the Great Collection (*Mahāvaipulya*) is like the pond, while the individual recensions are like the streams.
"Category" (*jāti*) refers to a class of similar things; here, "flowing forth" takes up the sense of a category of similar flows.

"Meaning" (yi) refers to other distinct sūtras whose thematic force (yì-shì) is similar to that of this present sūtra because they belong to the same category; it does not mean meanings derived from the major collections.

Within this, there are two further parts: first, to reveal the branch streams, namely the *Duōshā jīng* (Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-sūtra), one fascicle, found among the separately circulating sūtra-piṭakas.
The *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-nāma-saṃghāta-sūtra* in one fascicle is the "Chapter on Names"; the *Kṣudra-daśabhūmika-sūtra* in one fascicle is the "Chapter on Pure Conduct";
the *Mahā-daśabhūmika-sūtra* in four fascicles and the *Anupūrva-sarvajñatā-guṇa-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* in four fascicles both consist of the "Chapter on the Ten Stages" and other such titles;
and the *Bodhisattvapṛcchā-samādhi-sūtra* in two fascicles consists of the "Ten Samādhis."
The *Sūtra on Immeasurable Merits* in one fascicle is the "Chapter on Lifespan"; the *Tathāgata-gotra-samudgama-guhya-kośa Sūtra* in two fascicles is the "Chapter on Manifestation";
the *Lokottara-parivarta Sūtra* in six fascicles is the "Chapter on Transcending the World";
and the *Rāmaka Sūtra* in three fascicles is the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-realm. These are all derived from the Great Text, transmitted according to the capacities of those who uphold them.

Within this, there are further two parts; the second part, the "Explanatory Section," is divided into two. First, we shall clarify the derivative branches. Regarding the *Xiǎo shí zhù jīng* (The Shorter Scripture on the Ten Abodes):

although ancient masters translated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* as either the *Shí dì* (Ten Grounds) or the *Shí zhù* (Ten Abodes), or as the *Shí zhù dì* (Ten Abodes Grounds), it is called "small" here because it refers to the ten abodes prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).
What is called "large" here refers to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*; it is not designated as such because it contains fewer fascicles.

Regarding the phrase "gradually perfecting all the virtues of omniscience" (*sarvajñatā-guṇa*): "omniscience" refers to the wisdom of the Buddha, and the "ten stages" (*daśabhūmi*) refer to the ten virtues within that Buddha-wisdom, which are like the ten qualities of the ocean. Because each subsequent stage is deeper than the preceding one through the dharmas of the ten stages, it is said that they are "gradually perfected.
Thus, within the "reflected image of the stages," the sequential manifestation of the characteristics of the ten stages is clarified.
Thus, one is able to enter into the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), which signifies the meaning of gradual fulfillment.
Furthermore, it is like the four rivers flowing from Lake Anavatapta, which continue to increase until they enter the ocean;

likewise, it is like the ten qualities of a precious gem, each subsequent one surpassing the former—all of which signify the meaning of gradual fulfillment. As for the term "Sūtra of Boundless Merit," it takes the kalpas of the preceding lands as its basis.
On subsequent days, each succeeding day is superior to the preceding one; thus, the merit of its clarity is boundless.

As for the term *Rāmaka*, it is the Sanskrit word for "entering the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-praveśa*). *Ra* has the meaning of being free from defilement; *ma* has the meaning of transformation; and *ka* has the meaning of unification.
This means that being free from defilement and undergoing transformation refers to the pure Dharma-realm, while unification refers to the sense of "entering."

▲ Second, the clarification of related categories: The *Sūtra on the Cultivation of Loving-kindness* in one fascicle, the *Vajramālā Sūtra* in one fascicle, and the *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa Sūtra* in one fascicle are all of the same category as the *Avataṃsaka*, yet they are separate recensions rather than belonging to the main body [of that scripture].

Second, concerning the "categories and types" (*liúlèi*), the commentary text has two parts: first, it correctly clarifies that these are distinct categories rather than branches of this specific collection;

second, from the phrase "Alternatively, there are other recensions... onwards, it demonstrates the existence of branch texts. The ancient masters, seeing that these are not found in the current version of the scripture, [proceeded to...]
Since the various related sections of this primary category have not yet been fully exhausted, how could these individual expositions be definitively established?
Out of a sense of humility regarding my own learning, I state that I do not yet dare to provide a detailed determination.
Fourth, regarding the commentaries on the treatise, I shall briefly cite four of them.
The fourth section, the commentary on the treatise, is divided into two parts: first, a general presentation; second, a detailed explanation. This is the initial presentation. 1.

Once Nāgārjuna had obtained the shorter version of the text, he subsequently composed the *Mahā-acintya-śāstra* (Great Treatise on the Inconceivable), also consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas, which was widely transmitted in the Western Regions.
The sixteen-fascicle *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* currently extant in this land is precisely the commentary on that treatise. Regarding the ten [stages]:
Regarding the first two stages among the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), there are four distinct commentaries; the first may be understood as follows:
*The Commentary on the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*) composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati of the Wei Dynasty.

Bodhiruci also translated one version; subsequently, Sengguang submitted a petition requesting that these two Tripiṭaka masters collaborate to synthesize them into a single work of twelve fascicles, which is what is transmitted today.

However, what is currently stated as "one year of practicing the Way" is already present in the biographical text; if one follows the preface to the treatise, it does not mention this.

It does not mention Qingliang [Mountain], as those from various regions likely wished to glorify their own locales and thus cited Taiyuan to clarify the matter for their own area. Since this is the case in the biography...

Part Eight: The Section on Translation and Miraculous Responses is divided into two: first, clarifying the dates of the translations; second, clarifying the miraculous responses of transmission.
