▲In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra (translated as Juexian) from North India translated thirty-six thousand verses of the Sanskrit original at Xiesikong Temple in Yangzhou, completing the Jin version in fifty or sixty fascicles.
The śramaṇa Fayue acted as the scribe, while Huiyan and Huiguan refined the language. Recorded by Xie.
The Sīkōng Temple is the present-day Xingyan Temple in Runzhou; it was so named because it was established by Xing Huayan.

Regarding Buddhabhadra—translated here as Juexian—and others: according to the *Zuǎnlíngjì*, his original surname was Śākya, and he was a descendant of King Amṛtodana from the kingdom of Kapilavastu. At the age of three, Xian was orphaned.
In his youth, he lost his mother and was raised by his maternal relatives. He followed Tánzhòu and Jiūmólì; hearing of his intelligence and quick wit, they ordained him as a śrāmaṇera.
While his peers required one month of study and recitation, Xuán could match them in a single day.

Upon receiving full ordination, he read widely across the various sūtras, achieving comprehensive mastery in many areas. From a young age, he gained renown for his expertise in meditation and the Vinaya, and once, while with his fellow students... [the text continues].
Kumārajīva had resided there for many years and knew that [Buddhabhadra] had already realized the fruit of *anāgāmin*. He had long wished to travel abroad to propagate the supreme teaching.
It happened that the Qin śramaṇa Zhìyán arrived at Jibin and asked the monks of that country who was fit to spread the teachings to the eastern lands;
everyone said, "Xián is suitable. Xián had originally received the practice of *dhyāna* from Fódàxiān (Buddhasvāmin).

At that time, the Immortal (Dharmakṣema) was also in the kingdom of Kaśmīra. Knowing that Guṇavarman was seeking someone to propagate the teachings in the East, he said to Varman, "There is one who can sustain and guide the monastic community and proclaim the True Dharma;
this person is indeed the worthy one. Guṇavarman then offered his sincere and earnest invitation, whereupon Dharmakṣema silently gave his consent.
Thereupon, he took leave of his teacher and set out toward the East; he traveled for three years, enduring all the hardships of both winter and summer.
Enduring hardships and perils until their exhaustion, they sometimes encountered layered cliffs closing in on all four sides, where the path for birds ascended the clouds;

at other times, they traversed a thousand li of continuous ice, where the wind blew and they lay amidst the snow. Whenever the clear light of dawn broke, they would hide away in the deep forests; when the bright moon sank into the night sky, they would face crashing waves that blocked their way.
They constructed flying ladders across the vast distances, climbing by ropes suspended in the void, seeking sustenance day after day amidst constant peril and fear.
He traveled all the way to Jiaozhi, where the terrain gradually became more level; he boarded a ship for a sea voyage, enduring many perils before finally reaching Qingzhou, Donglai Commandery.

Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an, he came there with great joy. Later, he traveled to Eastern Jin, arriving in the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An, during the time of Meng Yi, the Regional Inspector of Wu Commandery, and Chu [Fonian], the General of the Right Guard.
Shi Duhui requested that this sutra be translated and a separate pure chamber be constructed. On the tenth day of the third month of that year, Kumārajīva began the work;

holding the Sanskrit manuscript in his own hand, he collaborated with the śramaṇas Faye, Huiyan, and more than one hundred others at Daochang Temple to collate the text, harmonize it with the underlying principles, and refine the language until it reached perfection. Consequently, even today, there remain Chinese translations at Daochang Temple.
He presided over the Hall of Strictness (*Yantáng*). He passed away in the sixth year of the Yongjia era at the age of seventy-one.

He bent three fingers of his hand as a sign that he had attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*. Further details are as in his biography. Master Ye’s clan and lineage are unknown; his character was elegant and refined.
He studied under no single teacher, reading extensively across all the various teachings. He often felt, however, that he had not yet been able to fathom the subtle or illuminate the ultimate.
Feeling that his understanding was still insufficient, he later encountered Buddhabhadra and requested him to translate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

After several years of deliberating upon its principles and meanings, he attained a sudden and profound realization. Looking back at his friends, he said, "The compass for the holy teachings lies herein.
He subsequently propagated its profound purport, becoming the preeminent leader of the school, and authored the two-fascicle *Zhigui* (The Return to the Source), which remains in circulation.

In the present age, those who have seen the original texts are few; because the subtle sounds were first introduced, there was no leisure to exhaustively master them all. As time has passed for many months and years, much has been lost and neglected.

Huiyan and Huiguan were two of the "Eight Talents" of Master Kumārajīva. Their literary style was lofty and concise, while their mastery of the sūtras and śāstras was profound and vast, as recorded in the *Monastic History* (*Sengshi*).
The temple formerly belonging to the Governor Xie was the Daochang Temple, which was supported by his offerings.
Yuehu called out to Yan Guan and the monks of this temple, saying: "The present Xingyan Temple in Runzhou was called Nanfanyou during the Jin dynasty;
its territory was vast, and it has now been divided off to form Runzhou."

▲ In the first year of the Yonglong era of the second Tang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra (translated as "Sunlight" in Chinese) translated at the Taiyuan Monastery in the Western Capital two passages from within the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter that explain the text:
the first concerns the ten types of wholesome knowledge, beginning after Māyādevī and extending through the section prior to Maitreya Bodhisattva, including the Lord of Heaven Light and others.
In the passage from after Maitreya Bodhisattva until before the number of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) equal to the atoms of a trichiliocosm,
Mañjuśrī extends his hand across one hundred and ten *yojanas* to place it upon the crown of Sudhana’s head;
this fifteen-line section of the sutra was recited in concert by the Venerable Daocheng, Vinaya Master Daocheng, Dharma Master Bocen, Dharma Master Dashengji, and others.
The translation was revised by Dharma Master Fuli, who polished the text based on the sixty-fascicle edition as the definitive version.
As for Tripiṭaka Master Wuxing (Rizhao), he resided at Mahābodhi and Nālandā Monasteries;

his demeanor was mild and elegant, his spiritual faculties were refined and far-reaching, and he carried his book-bundle to study with diligence, refining himself like jade to become a vessel of wisdom. It was during his time that Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang transmitted the teachings.
Returning from the East, he divined the winds and arrived at the capital during the Yonglong era of the Sagely Dynasty.

Emperor Gaozong, who greatly promoted and manifested the Buddhist community, issued an edict to assemble ten eminent monks—such as Vinaya Master Daocheng and Dharma Master Bocen—to translate sūtras and śāstras at the Xisi Monastery in the Wei Kingdom.
At that time, there was Dharma Master Xianshou, who had previously specialized in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

He often lamented that the Great Teaching was incomplete and lacked its full perfection; thus, he went to inquire about it. [The master] replied, "The text for the eighth assembly from the Jin dynasty has arrived here.
Xianshou (Fazang) then compared it with the Tripiṭaka master, and indeed obtained the text for the ten virtuous friends, including Sudhana’s search for spiritual mentors such as Devendraprabha.
He then requested a translation to supplement the missing portions, and further translated ten sūtras, including the *Ghanavyūha*.
There was another school [of thought] totaling twenty-four fascicles. In the Chuigong era, he passed away without illness while lying on his right side.
His disciples erected a stupa at Longmen Mountain, to the right of the Yi River. Later, Prince Wu Sansi of the Later Liang petitioned for the establishment of a monastery, which was named Xiangshan;
its moon-pavilions tower above the misty waves, where the waters reflect the inverted peaks.
The jeweled banners scattered their distant shadows as they entered the soaring clouds; the work was accomplished in no time, and thus the imperial favor was turned back.
This great event in the Dharma-gate is peerless throughout all antiquity and the present.
In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda (translated as "Joyful Learning") from Khotan arrived in the East.
At the Foshouji Monastery in the capital, the existing text was retranslated and various omissions were supplemented, resulting in an increase of nine thousand stanzas;
together with the original, the total comprises forty-five thousand stanzas, compiled into eighty fascicles of the Tang edition by the Tripitaka Master Da-de Yijing,
along with Vinaya Master Hongjing, Dharma Master Yuance, Dharma Master Shenyi, Dharma Master Fabao, Dharma Master Xianshou, and others.
The same translator, Dharma Master Fuli, composed the text.
Regarding the phrase "the first year of the Zhengsheng era," it is detailed as in the ninth fascicle of the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*.

A total of thirteen monastics and five lay officials participated in the verification of the meaning and the translation of the text. Chan Master Hongjing submitted a memorial based on the scriptures.
Since the preface was originally composed by my own hand under the direct supervision of the Great Biànkōng Temple, I have inscribed "Before Your Presence" (Kai-xia) at the beginning.

Furthermore, having personally attended the Dharma seat, I have illuminated this preface with my own celestial brush, inscribing the title at its head. The seven luminaries cast their images, their beauty radiant within the Three Clarities;
the eight calligraphic styles form the text, its brilliance spreading through the Five Meanings. As the Jewel of the Dharma proceeds in its divisions, it...

The pure flowers are scattered and strung together to manifest brilliantly; the true exegesis of the nine assemblies appears entirely within the words, and the profound meaning of the hundred cities is illuminated beneath every character.
Furthermore, although several passages were added to the previous third edition, it nonetheless omitted the portion translated by Tripitaka Master Fǎzhào.
Regarding the passage on Mañjuśrī placing his hand upon Sudhana’s head: Master Xianshou compared the two versions of the sutra—the old and the new—with their Sanskrit originals.

He then supplemented the text of the "Sunlight" (Rizhao) edition at points where characters had been omitted by the scholar Anxi, thereby ensuring that the wording was continuous and the meaning coherent.
The essential points of this text will be analyzed below; the version currently transmitted is the fourth edition.
The essential meaning of this text, which will be explained in detail below, is fully clarified in the initial commentary of the first eighty fascicles. Its purport states:
at the end of the seventy-seventh [fascicle], Sudhana himself says, "Because of Mañjuśrī, I have been able to see those who are otherwise difficult to see;
may that Honored One of Great Merit quickly return so that I may behold him. At the end of the seventy-ninth [fascicle], Maitreya extensively demonstrates what follows.

A friend praised Mañjuśrī’s virtues and urged him to go and inquire. Mañjuśrī further said, "O son of good family, you should go to the presence of the spiritual friend Mañjuśrī and ask him: 'How should a bodhisattva train in the bodhisattva conduct?
How does one enter the gateway of Samantabhadra’s conduct? How is it accomplished? How is it expanded? How does one accord with it?'"
"What is conformity? What is purity? What is fulfillment? Son of good family, I shall now explain these to you in detail for you. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī, the great vows you possess are not shared by any other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas.
Having thus extensively praised him, he concluded: "Son of good family, you..."
"You should proceed to the abode of Mañjuśrī without giving rise to weariness or fatigue; do not think that Mañjuśrī’s pressing of the crown of your head is now absent.

These fifteen lines of the sutra cause Maitreya to declare that [the teaching] would otherwise be in vain. If Sudhana had not followed Maitreya’s instruction and had instead intended to go first, he would have contravened his former resolve;
furthermore, lacking the wisdom-illumination of the non-dual aspect, he would have failed to see Samantabhadra later on.

Furthermore, because it does not arise without a cause, it is free from all faults such as [the charge that] it exists now [without having existed before]; thus, it is said that this is the essential point of the text.
The preceding statement refers to the continuity of the phrasing and the connection of the meaning.
As for the third version, since it had already been circulated previously, many omissions still remain in the sutras currently available in the world. Thus:
The third original vow addresses those whose understanding and insight were deficient, continuing their lineage.
Second, regarding the manifestation of transmission and response: when the subtle words were translated during the Jin dynasty, the auspicious sign of the two youths appeared;

when the ultimate teachings were translated during the Tang, the omen of the sweet dew was presented. This divine protection is manifest and clear, having been personally inscribed by the Imperial Brush.

Second, explaining the transmission, penetration, and spiritual resonance (*saṃgati*). The commentary below is divided into three parts: first, the formal exposition of resonance; second, the explanation of the reasons for resonance;
third, the celebration of encountering [the teaching]. Within the first part, there are six sections: first, translation; second, composing treatises; third, copying;
fourth, reading and reciting; fifth, contemplative practice; sixth, lecturing and expounding. Now, for the first: the subtle words translated during the Jin dynasty by the Twin Boys.

Regarding the manifestation of auspicious omens: it is said that at the beginning, in the pond before the translation hall of the Daochang Monastery, two youths dressed in green would emerge from the pond every other day, holding fragrant flowers; this was seen by the entire assembly.
Because this sutra had long resided in the Dragon Palace and the Dragon King rejoiced at its propagation, he provided these youths as attendants, and there were also benevolent deities to protect it.
Regarding the attendants mentioned below, it is said that the "dark guardians were clearly manifest. The term "Táng" (唐) translates as "Supreme Teaching.

"The nectar of immortality (*amṛta*) presented auspicious signs" refers to Empress Wu’s dream in which nectar descended upon the entire world. Thus, the preface to the sutra states: "The nectar flowed with moisture, as foretold in the dream on the evening of Gengshen;
the drenching rain bestowed its nourishment, extending its grace through the morning of Renxu. On the fourteenth day, the Xin [day].
On the first day of the eighth month, there were spiritual responses and omens at both the beginning and the end of the translation; the protection of the unseen world was manifest.
The following two translations were completed based on the preceding one. This phrase completes the aforementioned Jin translation, as already cited above.

Furthermore, because virtuous deities protected those on all sides, it is said that the new manuscript was handled by the Imperial Scribe. Thus, the aforementioned Tang translation was completed; this matter arose specifically from the occasion of the lecture.

The Empress remarked that on the day the initial translation was completed, she had dreamed of nectar appearing as an auspicious omen; furthermore, because this was a lecture on a newly translated scripture, it was included among the records of the translation project.
According to tradition, after the new scripture was first translated, the great virtuous ones (Mahāsattvas) of Fo-shou-ji Temple requested that Master Xuanzang deliver a lecture.
By imperial decree, the lecture was to begin on the fifteenth day of the tenth month, and thus he immediately entered [upon his teaching duties].

On the evening of the twelfth day of the twelfth month, when the text reached the passage on the shaking of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātusamudra*), the lecture hall and the monastery suddenly trembled.

At that time, several thousand monastics and laypeople witnessed this together and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. The Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda and the virtuous elders of the monastery were present.
The Vinaya Master Mingquan and Dharma Master Degan have composed this account of spiritual responses and submitted it for official report.

Headed by the Metropolitan *Vaiyāvṛtyakara* Huibiao, they presented a formal petition. On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Shengli era, Empress Wu Zetian, the Great Sage Empress, personally penned an imperial decree, which stated:
"I have examined the petition, which states that all these occurrences are due to the expounding of the subtle words [of the Buddha]."
When this profound and mysterious work was first translated, a dream of sweet dew manifested as an auspicious omen;
at the moment the translation was opened, the earth trembled, marking a singular wonder. This was surely the Tathāgata manifesting his traces to accord with the texts of the nine assemblies;
how could my own meager and hollow self dare to claim such a response of the six kinds of earthquakes? Having examined the report you have sent, my joy overflows my breast. This is my formal reply.
The details are fully recorded in a separate document; hence it is said that [the Emperor] personally applied his imperial brush.
When the treatise was completed in the Western Regions, an earthquake occurred and light streamed forth; when the record reached Qingliang, there was a spiritual resonance and profound awakening.
Regarding the statement that Vasubandhu was established in the Western Regions and so forth, the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu states:
"The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu was the brother of Asaṅga. By nature he was intelligent, yet as favorable conditions had not yet matured, he took the Hīnayāna as his primary practice.
His three faculties were wondrously prominent, lofty as a peak of frost; his fourfold eloquence cut through [all difficulties] with the sharpness of a star-like sword. Asaṅga... [text fragment].

Knowing that the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna were intended to guide those of inferior capacity, to comfort weary worldly beings by establishing the "City of Transformation," and to entice the impoverished son by having him carry a vessel of filth, he thus employed skillful means. Pretending to be ill upon his bed, he had Vasubandhu summoned, intending to depart from this life.
Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu arrived before the day was out. When Asaṅga saw him, he explained the origins of his illness at length, thereby opening [the way for Vasubandhu's realization].
The Great Teaching states: "During the time before my death, read the scriptures I have studied.
Vasubandhu then read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, whereupon he beheld the Dharma-realm of Vairocana and the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices.

Like the sun’s rays illuminating all at once, and like the interpenetrating patterns of Indra’s net, he gave rise to faith and realization, exclaiming: "I must take a sharp sword and sever my own tongue-root!"
When Ming had finished praising the defects of the Hīnayāna, his elder brother stopped him, saying: "It is as if a person falls because of the ground and also rises because of the ground.
Previously you used your tongue to disparage the Mahāyāna; now you may use that same tongue to praise the Mahāyāna.
He then entered the mountains, studied the Mahāyāna scriptures, and composed the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*. On the day the treatise was completed, the great earth shook throughout its entirety.
When the earthquake occurred with brilliant light, the King came in person to inquire, saying, "Have you attained the fruits such as Arhatship? He replied, "I have attained none.
The King asked, "Since you have not yet attained the fruits of sainthood, why does the earth tremble? He replied, "In my youth, this humble monk did not believe in the Mahāyāna;
it is precisely because I have now composed a treatise on the Mahāyāna that the earth has trembled. Therefore, it is called an 'earthquake'."

Regarding the accounts of those whose aspirations were fulfilled through the penetration of light and who attained profound awakening through a resonance with the Pure Coolness (Qingliang), there are two such individuals:

first, Liu Qianzhi; second, Dharma Master Lingbian. An earlier tradition states that during the Dazhong era of the Northern Qi dynasty, the third prince sought Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva at Mount Qingliang and offered his own body as a burnt sacrifice. Beneath this prince...

The eunuch Liu Qianzhi, sighing over his own physical deformity upon witnessing the prince’s act of self-immolation, submitted a memorial requesting permission to enter the mountains to cultivate the Way.

He was subsequently granted one copy of this scripture. Day and night he applied himself with diligence, performing prostrations, repentance, and recitation, praying to the One of Wondrous Virtue for spiritual protection.
For twenty-one days he abstained from grain, subsisting only on water; although his physical strength and breath were diminished, [his resolve remained firm].
His sincere devotion grew ever more fervent; suddenly, his beard and whiskers grew back completely, restoring him to the appearance of a man.

His spiritual brilliance became enlightened, and he thoroughly understood the profound meaning. Through deep reflection and diligent cultivation, he composed a treatise on this sutra, totaling six hundred fascicles, which he then presented to the High Ancestor (Emperor Wu).
The Emperor’s reverence and faith increased manifold beyond his usual state regarding the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The teaching flourished greatly therein. Regarding the Dharma Master Lingbian, tradition says he was a śramaṇa from Puyang in Taiyuan during the Later Wei dynasty.
Having cultivated superior roots of goodness in past lives, he constantly praised the Mahāyāna; upon encountering the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he applied himself to its study with particular devotion.
He then carried this sūtra upon his head and entered the Qingliang Mountain Monastery to seek the secret protection of Mañjuśrī.

Throughout the course of one year, his feet were so worn that blood flowed, his flesh was exhausted, and his bones were pierced through; suddenly, he heard a voice from the air saying to him, "Cease this;
simply contemplate this sutra. Thereupon, he opened the scroll and attained sudden, great enlightenment.

Later, in the first month of the year Wuyin (the Great Liang) during the Xiping era, at Qingliang Temple, he respectfully composed the *Huayan lun yanyi* (Exegesis on the Meaning of the Avatamsaka Sutra).

The commentary on the text states that he exhausted the subtle and penetrated the profound; in the second year [of the reign], he moved his residence to Xuanwengshan Songyan Temple and constructed various implements as recorded in the biography.

If one follows the preface to the *Lun* (Treatise), this occurred while he was at Xuanwengshan experiencing spiritual resonance (*gantong*). However, according to the text of the biography, it was also at Qingliangshan where he experienced spiritual resonance and attained profound awakening.

As for its transcription, the sutra radiates five colors and the fragrance of mulberry paper spreads in all directions; winter chrysanthemums bloom with brilliance and auspicious birds carry its flowers.
After it was transcribed, both Yanming, Prince of Anfeng Commandery of the Later Wei, and Yuanxi, Prince of Zhongshan, [honored it].
The spiritual brilliance of the imperial clan, having attained comprehensive mastery and unified their minds in the Unsurpassed, bowed their heads in homage to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong).
He once used incense mixed with ink to transcribe one hundred copies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and one copy of the *Golden-Letter Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

These were all stored in cases made of the five fragrances and lined with the seven precious gems. On still nights and auspicious occasions, while he performed the Way in pure fasting, they would emit divine light of five colors.
The light illuminated the halls and courtyards so that all beheld it; consequently, those who resolved their minds [upon enlightenment] were beyond counting.
As for Sengde Yuan, whose family origins are unknown, he was a native of Tianshui. He constantly took the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as his primary practice;

through recitation, study, and upholding, he came to master its sublime principles and ultimate essence. He subsequently cultivated a pure garden, planting various grains, mulberry trees, and paper mulberry trees.
He planted fragrant herbs and interspersed them with fresh flowers; every time he entered the garden, he would wash himself and sprinkle his body with pure water.
Wearing clean robes and irrigating with scented water, after three years of growth, the fragrance spread in all directions. Later, he established a separate pure chamber to transcribe scriptures;
as soon as he had written a few lines, each character emitted a radiance that illuminated the entire courtyard. Furthermore, a divine being appeared, holding a halberd.
A figure of imposing presence, accompanied by a youth in blue robes who arrived unexpectedly, suddenly presented offerings of celestial flowers;
the rest is as related in the legends. As for the winter melon (*dongkui*) blooming with brilliance, this refers to Deng Yuanshuang, a native of Huayin.
During the Zhengsheng era, Yuanshuang had a relative who died suddenly and returned to life after seven days, reporting that he was about to be summoned from the underworld.

Shuangshuang was fearful of his command and transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Upon its completion, by the side of Shuang’s mother’s tomb, where he had previously planted Shu-kiel (Hibiscus), the plants had already gathered together by winter;
one morning, they burst into bloom, radiant and luxuriant. The local community marveled at this and reported it to Empress Wu Zetian, who erected a "Gate of Filial Piety" for him.
Furthermore, a miraculous bird carrying flowers appeared—this was the monk Facheng, who lived in seclusion.

Later, at Nanling, Langu constructed the Huayan Hall; having purified both the interior and exterior and completed the adornments, he commissioned artists from the Hongwen Hall and the calligrapher Zhang Jingjing to paint images of the seven locations and nine assemblies.
Cheng personally held the incense burner and made offerings with single-minded devotion. Subsequently, an auspicious bird appeared, its form and color extraordinary.

Carrying the flowers into the chamber, they circumambulated them in worship, returning again and again; after the scripture was completed, many who recited it with a focused mind received divine protection and blessings.
When reading and reciting, one feels as if treading upon the vast void, yet as clear as looking into a mirror; each time *śarīra* relics appear, one encounters a divine monk.
He surged forth from the earth, manifesting a body of golden hue, and ascended to heaven to halt the battle of the asuras.
As for recitation, there was the monk Huiewu of Jingzhao, who once dwelt in seclusion at Mount Zhongnan with another monk;

while practicing dhyāna at the Chan Meditation Hall, Huiewu attained the state of "traversing the void" (*miaoran liling kong*). He received the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* once and held the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in wood.
While the two were dwelling in seclusion among the rocks, each devoted to his own practice, a man suddenly appeared without any apparent cause.

After he had finished his greetings and inquiries, he said, "I request one Master to come to my home for the midday meal. The two men deferred to one another; the other said, "Please read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*," and the Dharma Master Wuyin followed him.
It turned out that this was a mountain deity inviting a thousand arhats, all of whom deferred to the master above them when it came to the meal.
When they had finished, they all flew off into the air. The deity summoned a youth to serve him and entered the Master’s mouth;
thus, he immediately attained the state of an immortal. He returned to retrieve his scriptures, took leave of his friend the monk, and departed into the vast distance.
As the legends relate in detail, his clarity was like looking into a mirror. This was the monk Biancai, whose origins were unknown; in his youth, he served Dharma Master Xu.

Taking the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary practice for a long time without realization, he instead maintained strict purity and fashioned a fragrant casket to enshrine the scripture, which he carried upon his head while practicing the Way.

After three years had passed, he dreamed that Samantabhadra instructed him on its profound meaning; consequently, he suddenly attained the ability to recite it from memory, as clearly as if looking into a mirror.
Whenever he held the śarīra relics, [he was moved]. Fan Xuanzhi was a native of Anding; in his youth...

While practicing the Way at the Southern Slope of the capital, he encountered Master Dushun, who instructed him to take the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary practice and exhorted him to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra according to this scripture.
Every time he recited the sūtra, śarīras frequently emerged from his mouth; over the course of time, several hundred grains were obtained.
As for the "Divine Monk" mentioned here, he was Vinaya Master Yuan, a monk of Yanxing Temple in Jingzhao.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, while traveling across the Bashi Bridge, he stayed at an inn. As the sun was about to set, he took up lodging there.
Suddenly, a strange monk arrived, his appearance and clothing coarse and tattered; he went with him to a separate room belonging to the host and stopped there.

The monk then ordered fine wine and high-quality meat, and they ate and drank to their heart's content. The Vinaya Master, being pure and fastidious, was abruptly disgusted by the filthiness of it, yet that monk proceeded to eat.
Having finished, he rinsed his mouth with ash-water, closed the door, and recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Suddenly, he completed one fascicle.

Huìyuàn then bound himself in shame and listened intently to the profound sounds; before the fifth watch had passed, he had finished sixty fascicles. Huìyuàn deeply reproached himself, and grief and weeping filled his heart.
He entered his room to perform rites of repentance and parted from him there, without being told the man's name and remaining ignorant of who he was.

Regarding his destination: The monk Huiyou of Chongfu Temple in the capital, whose physical body suddenly leaped from the ground to manifest in a golden hue, was a man of rigorous ascetic discipline who served Master Yan and specialized exclusively in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

Every dawn and on auspicious nights, he would burn incense and recite the "Manifestation" chapter (*Prakāśa-parivarta*) with single-minded devotion. Later, he suddenly beheld more than ten bodhisattvas leaping forth from the earth.

A golden-hued body appeared, emitting light from all parts and sitting upon a lotus throne; with palms joined, he listened to the recitation of this chapter of the sutra, and once it was finished, he vanished.
The one who ascended to heaven to halt the battle of the asuras was the śrāmaṇera Prajñāmaitreya of Khotan.
He possessed most excellent observance of the precepts and would regularly recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Suddenly, a person appeared...
With palms joined, he whispered, "The devas have sent me to invite you, Dharma Master. He then requested that the Master close his eyes, whereupon they arrived in the heavens.
There, the Lord of Devas knelt and entreated him, saying, "The devas are currently at war with the asuras and have been repeatedly defeated.
We now humbly request that you, Dharma Master, recite the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, hoping that the power of the Dharma may assist us. As requested, he ascended upon a celestial vehicle.

Mounting a precious chariot and holding celestial banners and streamers, one should keep the *Avataṃsaka* in mind; when the various heavenly hosts face those powerful enemies, the asuras, upon seeing them, they suddenly disperse and flee.
In a mere moment, [the practitioner] is escorted back home, their body suffused with celestial fragrance that does not fade for the rest of their life.
When he entered the realization of non-arising through contemplative practice, the verse of praise ascended into the void;
the sea deity listened and a torrential rain poured down, while Tiantong welcomed him and the great waters overflowed.
Regarding "entering the realization of non-arising through contemplative practice and the verse of praise ascending into the void," this refers to Master Jietuo, whose secular surname was Xing.
He was a native of Wutai County in Daizhou. At the age of seven, he left the household life; his aspirations were vast and far-reaching.
Initially, he sought instruction in meditative concentration from Chan Master Huichao at Baofu Rock on Mount Jie. Huichao possessed the discernment to recognize people’s potential;
seeing that [Xuan]jie was a vessel of great capacity, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The practice of Chan by this youth is profound and luminous; it is not something you can rival."
After some time, he attained great enlightenment. Later, at Foguang Temple in the southwest of Wutai, he established a vihāra and studied the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, following the scripture, he practiced the "Contemplation of Buddha-Light" (*Foguang guan*).

He frequently traveled to Huayuan to the southeast of the Central Terrace and to the ancient Dafu Temple to the north, seeking to receive the personal instructions of Mañjuśrī, who said to him: "Why must you now personally pay homage?"
I reproached myself and vowed that I would surely attain great enlightenment; subsequently, through my own seeking, I realized non-arising and simultaneously attained the joy of the Dharma.

Thereupon, I lamented this solitary excellence and contemplated universal salvation. With sincere devotion, I prayed to the Great Awakened One to bear witness to this mind, and in response, the Buddhas appeared and spoke these verses:
"The profound Dharma of the Buddhas' nirvana has been cultivated through kalpas of practice."
Now that you have attained this ability to open and clarify this Dharma-eye, all Buddhas rejoice in your liberation.
You may further inquire: how can the quiescent dharma within emptiness be explained so as to instruct others? The Buddhas then vanished, leaving behind only a voice that declared:
"The wisdom of skillful means serves as a lamp to illuminate the realm of the mind; one who seeks the truth must see it thus."

In truth, all dharmas are entirely unobservable. Furthermore, when he was formerly requested by the Provincial Governor (Dudu) to transmit the incense and confer the precepts, and his work of transformation had been completed and he was about to return eastward, the Governor and the multitude escorted him to the east of the city.
As the sun was setting, he wished to burn incense, when he heard a voice from the sky above the city walls saying: "Take your palms joined together as flowers; take your body as an offering."

With a mind of pure faith, they offer true incense and the incense of praise; its fragrance spreads throughout the realms of all Buddhas. Upon hearing this scent, the Buddhas come at once to deliver the multitudes.

Therefore, it is said that through diligent and zealous effort, one shall never again fall into doubt or error. Thus, "they ascend into the void to offer praise," as detailed extensively in the biographies.
Alternatively, this may be a manifestation of a Great Sage, though the specific details are difficult to investigate; his virtue is vast and his transformations manifold.
I have never heard of such a thing before. When the Sea God listened [to his recitation], the rains poured down in torrents;
this was Sengdaoying, surnamed Chen, a native of Puzhou. At the age of eighteen, his parents arranged a marriage for him, and they lived together for five years without ever violating their vows.
Later, while studying the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* under Dharma Master Ju at Bingzhou, he shaved his head and entered the monastic order.
While practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* at Baiti Monastery on Mount Daxing, Wengu was once attending a lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to pray for rain during a severe drought.
Two elderly men, each attended by two youths, came to listen; Wengu found them extraordinary every time.
Later, he asked them about their origins, and they replied: "We disciples are both sea deities. Because we love this sutra, we have come to listen."
Ying said, "I am now lecturing on a sutra for you, the donor; please send down a light rain. Thereupon, the deity commanded two youths, who emerged through the window lattice.
In a brief moment, the rain poured down in torrents, bringing relief to those far and near. The two elders bowed in gratitude, and the youths suddenly vanished.
Thus it is said that the Sea Deity listened and sent forth a torrential rain; his traces remain as recorded in tradition.

He spoke thus: "The 'celestial boy' who came to welcome me and the vast expanse of water were none other than the monk Linggan of the Sui court, whose secular surname was Li and who was a native of Di Commandery.
He took ordination under Master Yan at the age of eighteen and was able to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He resided at Xingshan Monastery as a śramaṇa who served as a certified interpreter for the translation of scriptures. Later, he fell ill and died; several days later, he revived and said:"
In Xingdou, he saw the two Dharma Masters Xiu and Yuan sitting together upon lotus pedestals, their radiance surpassing that of the world.
They said to Huiqian, "Inform our disciples for us; they shall all be reborn here. Huiqian was dedicated to upholding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

he constantly practiced the visualization of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*) and the visualization of Maitreya’s Tuṣita Heaven Palace based on the sūtra. When his illness became severe, his eyes rolled upward as if...
When he saw someone, the śramaṇa asked him about it, and he replied: "Just now I was led by a youth dressed in black to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace;
yet the celestial pleasures are not lasting, for one will ultimately fall back into saṃsāra. It is the Lotus Treasury World that I seek.
Having finished speaking, his breath ceased, but after a short while he revived. When the śramaṇa asked what he had seen, Duan said: "I saw a great body of water."
Flowers as vast as chariot wheels filled the space, and he sat upon them; his aspirations were fulfilled, and at the conclusion of his words, he passed away—hence these words.

When he preached, the sounds of both Chinese and Sanskrit harmonized, and both humans and devas followed his guidance. When the great flood cut off the flow of the river, divine light entered the palace.
Regarding his lectures: Later, during the Song dynasty, there was Guṇabhadra (translated into Chinese as Gōngdéxián), a native of Central India.

Initially, he studied the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) without fail in their breadth; later, he revered the Buddha-dharma, delved deeply into the Tripiṭaka, and advanced to the study of the Mahāyāna.
When his Mahāyāna teacher tested him by having him reach into a scripture chest, he immediately retrieved the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The teacher praised him highly.
He was ordered to deliver lectures. In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, the Governor of Guangzhou, Che Lang, memorialized Emperor Taizu, who dispatched an envoy to welcome him.
Nanqiao Wang Yixuan and others all took him as their teacher. He gathered a community of more than seven hundred śramaṇas at the Institute of Meaning (Yixue).
Nanqiao Wang wished to invite him to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, but as he was not yet proficient in the Chinese language, [the request was deferred].
Feeling ashamed and sighing with regret, he immediately performed prostrations and repentance morning and evening, earnestly invoking Avalokiteśvara to seek a hidden response.
Consequently, he dreamed of a person holding a sword and carrying a human head who came before him and asked, "Why do you worry? He then related his situation in detail;
[the dreamer] immediately severed Dà’s head and placed a new one upon it, saying, "Turn it around; will there not be no pain?"
The response was: "He experienced a sudden, profound awakening and immediately became fully proficient in the Chinese language. He subsequently lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* dozens of times.
As is related in tradition, he was one whom both humans and devas alike followed; his name was Ratnamati (勒那摩提), which means 'Jewel-Mind' in Chinese.
A native of Central India, he was widely learned and possessed vast erudition, having committed ten million verses of scripture to memory. He was particularly adept in the nature of dhyāna."
In the fifth year of the Zhengshi era, he first arrived in Luoyang and translated twenty-four fascicles of treatises, including the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.
His spiritual principles were lofty and his wisdom and insight peerless; he mastered the elegant sounds of the Chinese language, exhausting their subtle nuances and clarity.

The Emperor frequently ordered him to lecture on the profound meanings of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Once, while he was seated upon the high throne, there suddenly appeared a figure holding a ceremonial tablet and bearing a name.
The Great Official announced that the Emperor had sent word to invite the Dharma Master to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
While the Master alone was able to establish the presiding lecturer (*dujiang*), the incense-burner (*fensiang*) and the ritual master (*weina*) for the chanting were also required;
all the monks at the lecture seat witnessed this. With a serene and joyful countenance, he smiled and bid farewell to the assembly, then suddenly passed away upon his Dharma seat.
The *dougao* and other monks also perished at the same time; thus it is said that "humans and devas alike followed [the teaching], and the floodwaters were cut off.
This refers to the monk Fashun, whose secular surname was Du. He was a native of Duling in Jingzhao. His conduct was lofty and pure, and he had no fixed teacher;

he took the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as his primary field of study. Once, while he was living in the mountains, he was about to plant some seeds, but upon digging into the earth, he found many insects and ants. Thereupon—
While he was touring the borders to establish the demarcations, the local pests moved away to the outskirts; he exerted himself in reclamation and cultivation so that nothing was lost.
A man from San Yuan County had been deaf and mute since birth, but when Shun summoned him and spoke with him, the man’s speech was restored upon his first response.

Thereupon, Shun went to the South Mountain, where the waters of the Hengqu overflowed; he halted the flow and crossed it with a steady pace. On the day of his passing, he gathered everyone for a universal assembly.

He possessed the conditions for his passing; his voice and countenance did not change as he departed at the conclusion of his speech. He was cremated on the northern plain of the river, and his entire body now rests in a stupa at Huayan Monastery south of Chang’an.
His life story is extensive and recorded in a separate biography, which states that he was an emanation of Mañjuśrī and that his divine light entered the palace.
This Master Zang, whose religious name was Fazang and courtesy name Xianshou, was born into the Kang clan.
The people of Kangju first [heard of him] when the mother of Chūxian dreamed of a strange light and became pregnant; this was the first light.
When he was born, he admired the Buddha’s supreme age. At seventeen, he took leave of his kin to seek the Dharma at Mount Taibai.
Later, when his compassionate parents fell ill and did not recover, he returned to serve them at home, exerting himself to the utmost throughout many years. At that time, Master Yan was at Yun...
While Xianshou was lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Huasi Temple, he suddenly beheld a divine light illuminating the courtyard and halls during the middle of the night.
Xianshou sighed and said, "A person of extraordinary character shall surely emerge to propagate this vast and great teaching. When dawn broke, he encountered Master Yan;

from then on, he submitted himself to him and delved deeply into the inexhaustible [Dharma]. This was the second instance of a divine light entering the temple. Later, while at Yun... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "於雲," which likely refers to Mount Yunju or a similar location.)
During a lecture at Huasi Temple, a radiance appeared and issued from his mouth; in an instant it formed a canopy, witnessed by the entire assembly.

Furthermore, this divine light was precisely what was meant by [the phrase] "identical" [in the text]. That is the second section: "divine light entered the hall. Taking the time of the lecture, it constitutes the third section.
Since it describes the manifestation of auspicious signs while simultaneously incorporating the first section, it says: "divine light entered the hall," and so forth.
As stated in the separate tradition:
"Precisely because the subtlety of a single phrase encompasses all meanings without omission, the power of a single verse can shatter the hells;
even water used for washing one's hands can rescue living beings. Therefore, the merit of reciting, chanting, contemplating, and practicing is equal to that of the wisdom of all modes."
It is precisely because of the wondrousness of a single word that the second section clarifies the reason for response and resonance. Within this, there are four phrases;
the first phrase correctly explains the reason: because a single word or a single verse encompasses all meanings without omission, reaching the utmost perfection and subtlety.
Therefore, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva told Sudhana: "In this ocean of my Dharma, there is not a single word [that is redundant]."
There is not a single phrase that was not sought by relinquishing the position of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), nor was it sought by relinquishing all that one possesses.

The commentary states: because this "one" is the one of all things, and because it is the one that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), the function of the first verse-line is explained by the three subsequent lines; these likewise clarify its efficacy.
Regarding the matter of spiritual resonance, the first verse has the power to shatter the hells. The *Zuǎnlíng jì* (Record of Manifesting Spirits) states:
A man from Jīngzhào surnamed Wáng and named Mínggàn originally lacked precepts and had never cultivated roots of goodness.
When he died of illness, he was led by two men to hell. Before the gate of hell, he saw a monk who said, "I am Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva."
Śākyamuni then instructed him to recite a verse, saying: "If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should speak thus:
'The mind creates all Tathāgatas. After the Bodhisattva had bestowed the scripture upon him, he said to him: "By reciting this verse, you shall be able to cast off the sufferings of hell.
Once the man had finished reciting it, he entered [the presence of] the king. The king asked this man: "What do you have?"
Guṇadatta replied, "I have merely upheld a single four-line verse," as previously described. The king then released him.
At the moment he recited this verse, all those suffering in the places where the sound reached were liberated. Three days later, he finally regained consciousness;
remembering and upholding this verse, he recounted it to various monastics and laypeople. Only upon cross-referencing the text of the verse did they realize the truth.
This verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, spoken by the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha during the assembly of immeasurable bodhisattvas in the Yāma Heaven Palace, states:
"If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm:
everything is created solely by the mind. The general meaning is that this agrees with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which clarifies that the hells are created by the mind.

The mind creates the Buddha and the hells; they are empty of themselves. Since even the power of a single verse can shatter the hells, how much more so the profound mysteries of a single scroll, a single chapter, or an entire collection!
I pray you reflect upon these words and strive together to transmit and recite them.
If even the water used for washing one’s hands can rescue living beings, consider this: Saṃghamitra was originally from Siṃhala Island (Ceylon) and was the third [patriarch].

A man of realized fruition, he arrived in China at the beginning of the Linqi era. Emperor Gaozong, the Great Sovereign, treated him with the utmost respect and provided for him within the imperial palace for over a year.
At his request, he sought out sacred sites and traveled to Mount Qingliang to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
Upon arriving at the Western Taiyuan Monastery, he encountered monks reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and questioned them.

He asked, "What sutra is this? The other replied, "This is the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. At this, [the former] was struck with solemn reverence and changed his countenance, saying, "I did not know that this place also possesses such a sutra as this.
With palms joined, he rejoiced and offered praises for a long time, saying, "This *Mahāvaipulya* is of inconceivable merit.
According to tradition in the Western Regions, there were those who, when reading this sutra, would wash their hands with water, and the water would [become infused with its power]."
Even insects and ants that lose their lives [by coming into contact with this water] all attain birth in the heavens; how much more so for those who uphold, recite, observe, and contemplate it?

This is why it is said thus. While the previous section distinguished the water used for washing hands and rinsing the mouth, here we clarify that the merit of reciting, contemplating, and practicing reaches equality with that of a Buddha—that is, the liberation described in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
This is the question of Moon (Vimukticandra). Initially, Vajragarbha said:

"O Son of the Buddha, this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Door of the Bodhisattva Who Accumulates All Kinds and All Aspects of Wisdom' cannot be heard by sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness.
Liberation-Moon Bodhisattva asked: "Upon hearing this Dharma-door, how much merit is obtained? Vajragarbha Bodhisattva [replied].
It is said that the merit accumulated by one who possesses all-knowledge is equal to the merit of hearing this Dharma-gate. Why is this?
It is because it is not possible to believe, understand, accept, uphold, read, or recite this meritorious Dharma-gate without having heard it;
how much less so to apply oneself with diligence and practice according to the teaching. Therefore, one should know that it is essential to hear this collection of the merits of all-knowledge.
Only through the dharma-gates of virtue can one believe, understand, receive, uphold, and practice them, subsequently reaching the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

The commentary states: "If even hearing [the Dharma] is equal to the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), how much more so are reading, reciting, contemplating, and practicing, which are immeasurable!

Although the sutra mentions "hearing" to highlight its excellence, the underlying intent encompasses contemplation and practice as well; thus, the sub-commentary (*śu*) says: "The merit of reading, reciting, contemplating, and practicing..."
Equal to the ear of omniscience.
How fortunate was my past life to have been moved by and encountered this literature! Its traces are manifest and fully recorded in the chronicles and biographies.
"How fortunate was my past life" concludes the third section on the joy of encountering [the Dharma]; the remaining instances of spiritual resonance are detailed elsewhere.
The preceding citations from the biographies have merely been a rough enumeration of several instances;
this concludes the section on "Accounts of Miraculous Resonance in Translation. *Commentary on the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Eight.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Nine.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Qingliangshan Da Huayan Monastery.
▲ Ninth: General Explanation of the Title; herein, first the title of the sutra is interpreted, followed by the elucidation of the chapter designation.
Ninth, in the general explanation of the title of the scripture, the first section provides a general outline.
Now, for the first part: the overall title encompasses specific meanings and includes inconceivable Dharma-gates; within that which is beyond naming, we have provisionally distinguished ten sections.
Now, regarding the first part—the detailed explanation following the general title—there are two sections. First, the explanation of the general title, which has three parts:

(1) the initial presentation; (2) a general clarification of how the name is derived; (3) a comparative analysis of its expansions and contractions; (4) a full manifestation of its categories of meaning; (5) a specific explanation of how the name is derived;
(6) an infinite unfolding of its manifestations; (7) a complete synthesis of its aspects; (8) the unimpeded nature of expansion and contraction; and (9) the perfection of its meaning.
The nine are gathered and unified within the one mind; the ten are extinguished and made identical in equality.
Second, the general explanation of the names of the chapters listed below.

First, regarding the various ways in which the titles of the various sutras are derived: they are sometimes designated by way of the person [who taught them], and sometimes by way of the Dharma [they teach].

Famous masters have requested explanations regarding the various distinctions among dharmas—such as the dharma, the example, and so forth; whether they pertain to essence or function, or to fruit or cause;
and how they may be either compound or simple—their categories being numerous and extensive.
Third, regarding the first [section]: the individual explanations of the various sutras below. Within this first chapter, there are two parts:
first, a general presentation of the structural forms of the various sutras; second, a specific clarification of the present sutra.

Regarding the first, the statement that "some are titled after persons, while others are named after dharmas" is a general summary. Those titled after persons mostly explain the origins of the Dharma, whereas those named after dharmas...

The general framework of the *Saṃkṣipta-sūtra* consists of [the categories of] "requested" (*yācita*) and so forth, which differ from one another. Below is the specific explanation of these types of persons.
Among them, two categories are cited as representative examples, encompassing those who act as the requester and those who act as the speaker. Regarding "requester":

first, there are those named after the person who requests, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (as requested by the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin) and the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra*. Second, there are those named after the person who speaks, such as the *Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
Regarding the three [categories] beginning with the *Sūtra* (Sa), they depend on the persons for whom the teaching is intended, such as Sudatta, King Udayana, and others.

Regarding the four [categories] beginning with the *Vyākaraṇa* (Vya), they depend on the persons who speak the teaching, such as those in the *Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna* and other texts. As for the distinctions among the *Dharma*, *Adharma*, and *Upamā* (Metaphor), the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in the phrase "and so forth" includes many meanings within the category of *Dharma*. These many meanings of *Dharma* shall be explained below. As for the *Upamā* (Metaphor), it is as follows:

In texts such as the *Mahāmegha-sūtra* and the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*, whether it be essence (*svabhāva*), function (*karman*), fruit (*phala*), or cause (*hetu*), these are distinct meanings within the Dharma.
As for "essence," it is exemplified by the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others; "function" is exemplified by the *Ṛddhipāda-sūtra* and others; "fruit" is exemplified by the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others.
Furthermore, "cause" has many meanings; first, there is the cause as practice (*caryā-hetu*), as in the *Samyag-gaurava-sūtra*.
Regarding the two types of titles for works in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), such as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, which are sometimes compound and sometimes simple:
among the compounds, there are briefly four pairs. First, the pair of dharma and metaphor, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra).

Second, the pair of person and dharma, as in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (or *Rājasaṃghāṭa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*). Third, the pair of essence and function, as in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃgraha-sūtra*.
The four [categories] such as "equality" (*samatā*) are cited with both cause and effect together, as in the *Sarvajñatāguṇavyūharāja-sūtra*.

When terms such as "gradually" (*kramaśas*) appear alone, they apply generally to all the aforementioned meanings; that is, the terms "dharma," "simile," "entity" (*svabhāva*), "function" (*kāritra*), "cause," "effect," and "equality" are each cited individually.

As for those whose types are manifold and extensive, these have already been clarified above as being manifold and extensive. Furthermore, there are those that follow from the time of their exposition.

As for those named according to their time or non-time, such as the *Sūtra on [Teachings Given] at Appropriate or Inappropriate Times*, or those named after their place of exposition, such as the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* (The Dense Array Sūtra), these are included here to summarize the preceding and encompass the remainder;
thus it is said that "their varieties are numerous and extensive, and as they are not the primary essentials, the commentary speaks of them briefly."
▲ Furthermore, the titles received by this sutra are of many different kinds. First, names are designated based on numerical figures;

for example, as stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Liang translation), regarding the "one hundred thousand sūtras," this refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which consists of one hundred thousand verses.
Second, names are received based on metaphors; for instance, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* refer to this sutra as the *Saṃpuṣpita-sūtra* (the Flower Garland Sutra).
First, it is named from its practice, as it is the integration of the arising of myriad practices;

second, it is named from its dharma, as the *Jñānottarabodhisattvaparipṛcchā* (Wisdom Sūtra) explains in its commentary on the "Entrustment Chapter" by designating this sūtra as the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra* (Sūtra of Inconceivable Liberation);

third, it receives its name from its functional meaning, such as the ten names each found in the "Leaving the World Chapter" (*Lokānuvartanā-parivarta*) and the "Manifestation Chapter" (*Nirmāṇa-parivarta*).
Now, regarding the second section, which specifically clarifies how this present sutra received its title, there are two parts:

first, citing alternative names, and second, revealing its current designation. Within the former, there are four meanings—number, metaphor, dharma, and functional utility—which may be understood as they appear.
Regarding the "tenth chapter on the superior characteristics" in the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty, the treatise states: "That is to say, based upon the Mahāyāna..."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses ten aspects of excellence and excellence of speech: first, the excellence and excellence of speech regarding the basis of the knowable;

second, the excellence and excellence of speech regarding the characteristics of the knowable; third, the excellence and excellence of speech regarding the entry into the characteristics of the knowable;
