The meaning of the second treatise in this sequence is the same: it refers to initiating practice based on the teachings, attaining the profound principle, persevering for a long duration without stagnating in the two extremes, realizing the great and supreme fruit, and establishing the Buddha-work until the very end of saṃsāra;
therefore, it is named the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*. This is essentially the same as the *Abhidharmayoga* and largely identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Now, the body of this commentary is the *Mahā-*.

1. Among the three greatnesses of wisdom (*jñāna-mahattva*), the principle of the selflessness of the known (*jñeya-nairātmya*) is subsumed under the greatness of the object (*ālambana-mahattva*), as it is also included within the nature of the greatness of phenomena (*dharma-mahattva*), which is the objective sphere.

2. The third, the greatness of function (*kāritra-mahattva*), is the greatness of skillful means (*upāya-mahattva*); since this is the function inherent in the essence itself, it is also subsumed under the objective sphere. 3.

The fourth, the greatness of the fruit (*phala-mahattva*), is entirely identical to the fifth, the greatness of the cause (*hetu-mahattva*); thus, these five natures of greatness are mutually inclusive.
1. The initial arousal of the bodhicitta is the greatness of mind (*cittamahattva*). 2. The arising of resolve is the greatness of superior conviction (*adhimuktimahattva*). 3.
Practice, vows, and realization are all the greatness of practice (*pratipattimahattva*); this refers to the cause of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), not their fruition. 4.

Diligent and untiring effort is the greatness of pure mind and vigor (*vīryamahattva*). 5. The accomplishment of the various stages is the greatness of gathering the provisions (*sambhāramahattva*). 6. Wisdom... [is the greatness of wisdom].

1. "Great Compendium" (*Mahāsaṃgraha*) is identical [to the previous], yet its meaning differs slightly, as it comprehensively understands nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), cause and effect, and so forth.

2. "Greatness of the Teaching" (*śāsana-mahattva*) refers to the greatness of the objective phenomena (*ālambana-dharma*). 3. "Greatness of Nature" (*svabhāva-mahattva*) is identical to the preceding six [categories], but excludes the teaching. 4. "Greatness of Name" (*nāma-mahattva*) is identical to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, being the same in name but different in meaning. 5.
"Greatness of Simultaneity" (*yugapad-mahattva*) and "Skillful Means" (*upāya-kauśalya*) are identical to the sixth [category] and possess all [the aforementioned qualities].
When both treatises are included, the two names [of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Ratnagotravibhāga*] serve as the title;

because the seven characters therein encompass ten meanings, there is both expansion and contraction, as well as differences in sequence, yet there is no contradiction in their meaning. Thus it is said that the seven kinds of great nature are not separate from this.

Furthermore, regarding the single category of "greatness of characteristics," there is no fault in its being omitted in the two treatises, nor is there any deficiency. Moreover, this applies generally to the ten great doctrinal principles.
There is no harm in allowing for minor differences.

Regarding the second point, the ten meanings of "direction" (*fang*): "direction" (*fang*) here means "dharma. That is to say, the aforementioned ten "greats" are all termed dharmas—namely, the dharma of essence, the dharma of characteristics, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and the equality of phenomena (dharma-samatā)," the term "etc. includes the following eight: the application of phenomena, the fruit of phenomena, and so forth.
Because these phenomena serve as the norm (pramāṇa) and sustenance (dhāraka), and because they sustain their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), all ten are "phenomena" (dharma).

▲ Regarding the "three expanses and ten meanings," "expansive" (*guang*) means "many. Because it employs many and manifests extensively, encompassing everything without exception, the preceding ten [meanings] are all "many.
Thus, to clarify that one encompasses all is called "great" (*da*); to state that one includes all is also called "expansive" (*guang*).
This may also apply here; this is an explanation based on analytical separation (*li shi*).
Regarding the "three broad [aspects] and ten meanings," etc., the commentary text has two parts: first, the individual explanation of the character *guǎng* (broad);
second, the combined explanation of the two characters *fāng-guǎng* (vaipulya). There are also ten meanings for this: 1. The meaning of being a broad basis (*āśraya*):

because the verbal teachings are extensive and serve as the basis for sentient beings. 2. The meaning of broad exposition (*deśanā*): because it proclaims vast and profound dharmas. 3. Broad refutation... [text continues]

1. The meaning of "extensive destruction" (*vipulaprahāṇa*), because it destroys all obstacles without exception; 2. The meaning of "extensive transcendence" (*vipulātikrama*), because there are no phenomena capable of being compared to it; 3.
The meaning of "extensive remedy" (*vipulapratipakṣa*), because it fully encompasses the boundless remedial dharmas as the means of counteraction;

4. The meaning of "extensive inclusion" (*vipulasamgraha*), because it universally includes boundless dharmas of diverse categories; 5. The meaning of "extensive qualities" (*vipulaguṇa*), because it fully encompasses the two types of sublime adornment and all excellent virtues.

Thus, (8) the meaning of vast production is that it can produce an immeasurable and vast ocean of fruits; (9) the meaning of vast transcendence is that it cannot be known by the measurement of mind and consciousness;
and (10) the meaning of vast knowledge is that it is fully endowed with the wisdom of all modes, destroying the obstacles of false views without remainder.
Next, regarding the combined explanation that accords with various sūtras and śāstras, the explanation of the Vaipulya-sūtras consists of two parts. First, the formal explanation of the ten meanings.
Among these, the first four meanings correspond to the four meanings found in the eleventh chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, while the latter six correspond to the [six] entries.
In the first [chapter] of the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*, there are six meanings;

following these, there are ten meanings which conclude by indicating their source. It states that the first four are the four meanings found in the eleventh chapter of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
That treatise says: "Vipula (Extensive) refers to discourse associated with the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
It is called Vaipulya, also called Vipula-bhañjana, and also called Anupama. For what reason is it called Vaipulya?
Because it is the locus for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma.
For what reason is it called Vipula-bhañjana? Because it is able to extensively shatter all obstacles. Why?
Because it is the ultimate meaning (*artha*), it is called "incomparable" (*anupama*); for there are no phenomena (*dharma*) capable of being compared to it.
Thus, the *Vaipulya* and other [categories] are all specific names for the meaning of the Mahāyāna. The commentary explains: This treatise designates three names and establishes four meanings.
Since the *Vaipulya* contains two meanings, they are listed in sequence without deviation. It is said that the latter six [categories] constitute entry into the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the six meanings within the first section of the treatise, that treatise states: "Vaipulya" refers to the Mahāyāna.
Why is it called the Vaipulya Sūtra? It is called Vaipulya because it teaches remedial dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings;
it is called Vaipulya because there are many vehicles (yānas) within it; and it is also called Vaipulya because it is adorned with many ornaments.
The *Vaipulya* (Extensive) is so named because it can produce immeasurable great fruits and rewards;
it is so named because it cannot be known through mere calculation or measurement; and it is so named because it eradicates all false views.
The commentary states that the sequence is identical to the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), differing only in that the term *vaipulya* is inserted between them to form the structure.

Regarding these six meanings, the first—explaining the method of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*)—is similar to the third chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which extensively refutes [theories] by way of the objects to be refuted (*dūṣya*);
however, this [present text] concerns the means of refutation (*dūṣaka*), and thus they are not the same.

The fifth—being beyond measure (*atulya*)—resembles the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, "Incomparable Collection" (*Atulyasamuccaya*), which concerns phenomena that cannot be compared; however, this [present text] concerns the mind’s inability to know [such things], and thus they are likewise not the same.

Although these differ, the *Kun-don-rgya-cher-’grel-pa* (Extensive Commentary on the Meaning) states that because "counteracting" (*pratipakṣa*) and "destroying obstacles" (*āvaraṇa-vināśana*) are synonymous, the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* adds the phrase "corresponding to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka" to make five categories; this is a significant error regarding the intent of the treatise.

This is because the phrase "corresponding to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka" serves as a general exclusion of the Śrāvaka vehicle, and it is only after this general exclusion has been completed that [the specific categories] are then designated.
These three names merely establish the four meanings. If one wishes to subsume the four *saṃgraha-vastu* of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* within the six categories of this treatise:

the first corresponds to the second (*vistara-saṃgraha*), the second and third correspond to the third and fourth (*vistara-guṇa* and *vistara-janman*, both being profound dharmas), the third corresponds to the first and sixth (*pratipakṣa* and *dṛṣṭi-bheda*, both being of the nature of refutation), and the fourth corresponds to the fifth (*vistara-samatikrama*).
Since the general meaning is identical, I shall now take up the minor differences and expand them into ten points to show how the two treatises differ.

Specifically: regarding the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the first [point] concerns entry into the treatise by way of verbal teaching; the second concerns the collection by way of what is subsumed. Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the third point concerns the common analysis of profound penetration;

the fourth opens a separate category concerning the causes for the two adornments; and the fifth concerns that which is produced, referring exclusively to the result. This is the distinction between the two treatises.

Third, the combined explanation of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*. This is divided into one section on the antidote for afflictions (*kleśa*) and six sections on the destruction of cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Since the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, which resemble this treatise, have already been reconciled as previously discussed, these constitute ten topics.

However, in order to follow the sequence of the two treatises, they are not arranged according to the sequence of their titles. If one wishes to correlate them with the Sūtra, the first [section] is "Extensively Severing."
1. Great in essence, because it transcends all marks and is inconceivable; 2. Great in its universal transcendence, because this wondrous Dharma is peerless; 3.
Great in its universal inclusion, because it universally includes the boundless; 4. Great in its universal knowledge, because the Buddha is endowed with the knowledge of all modes;
5. Great in its universal destruction; 6. Great in its universal remedy; 7. Great in its universal production—these three all have the character "flower" (*hwa*) as their cause; 8. Great in virtue.
This is because it elaborates upon the two types of adornment; because it relies on the words and teachings of this sutra;
because it extensively explains this meaning by teaching the profound Dharma that is to be taught; and thus the aforementioned six characters may also apply to the seventh.
▲ Regarding the four interpretations of the ten meanings of "Buddha" (佛): "Da" (大) refers to the Dharma-realm Buddha; "Fang" (方) refers to the Original-nature Buddha;
"Guang" (廣) refers to the Nirvana Buddha and the Buddha of Accordance with Delight; "Fo" (佛) refers to the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment; "Hua" (華) refers to the Vow Buddha and the Samādhi Buddha;
"Yan" (嚴) refers to the Karma-retribution Buddha; and "Jing" (經) refers to the Sustaining Buddha. In total, these seven characters are not separate from the mind.
All these are the Buddha of Mind; the explanation of the ten meanings of the Buddha is as analyzed in the Eighth Ground and the *Lokottara-parivarta* (Chapter on Transcending the World).

Regarding the four explanations of the ten meanings of the Buddha and so forth, the text contains three interpretations. The first relies on the root sūtra, stating "as analyzed in the Eighth Ground and the *Lokottara-parivarta*";
the meaning of this was already explained extensively in the section on the conditions for the teaching above, and is now presented again in brief.

The clarification of the eight grounds and the ten bodies is found in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*) within the section on the ten Buddhas and the eight grounds, which states:

"One should know that the Tathāgata’s bodies consist of the bodhi-body, the vow-body, the transformation-body, the sustaining-power body, the body adorned with marks and signs, the body of majestic power, the mind-born body, the merit-body, the dharma-body, and the wisdom-body. This is recorded in the fifty-third fascicle of the "Chapter on Transcending the World."

Ten kinds of Buddhas are taught: namely, the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambuddha-buddha*), the Buddha of Vow (*praṇidhāna-buddha*), the Buddha of Karmic Retribution (*vipāka-buddha*), the Buddha of Sustenance (*adhiṣṭhāna-buddha*), the Buddha of Nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-buddha*), the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-buddha*), the Buddha of Mind (*citta-buddha*), the Buddha of Samādhi (*samādhi-buddha*), the Buddha of Original Nature (*prakṛti-buddha*), and the Buddha of Following Delight (*yathābhiruci-buddha*). These ten Buddhas are the ten bodies (*daśakāya*).
If one wishes to synthesize them: Perfect Enlightenment is the Bodhi-body; the Buddha of Vow is the Vow-body; and the Buddha of Karmic Retribution is the... [text fragment ends].

The Buddha of Retribution is the body adorned with the primary and secondary marks; the Buddha of Sustenance is the body sustained by power; the Buddha of Nirvana is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*);
the Buddha of the Dharma-realm is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the Buddha of Mind is the majestic body; the Buddha of Samādhi is the merit body;
the Buddha of Original Nature is the wisdom body (*jñānakāya*); and the Buddha of Accordance with Desire is the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*). Now, this commentary follows [this order].

Because of the title of the sutra, one does not follow the sequence of those two sutras. "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because "great" is the essence of the Dharma-realm.

"Square" (*caturaśra*) refers to the Buddha of Original Nature Wisdom (*prakṛti-jñāna*), because it is the fundamental nature. "Broad" (*vistīrṇa*) refers to the Buddha of Nirvāṇa, because his transformation is all-pervasive.

Furthermore, he is the Buddha who accords with desire, because there is nothing that is not produced according to the intentions of himself and others. "Buddha" is a term of the Brahmin language (*Sanskrit*).
This is precisely awakening; thus, the Flower-Buddha and the Samādhi-Buddha are both causes.

"Adornment" refers to the causal adornment of myriad practices that perfects the marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) of the physical body, and the preservation of the scriptural teachings so that the Dharma does not fall into ruin.
In sum, these do not depart from the mind; thus, the Mind-Buddha is the sovereign power by which body and mind are subdued and surpassed.

▲ Furthermore, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the Buddha also possesses ten meanings: namely, possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
being free from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); being able to awaken to all phenomena in all their modes for oneself;
and being able to awaken all sentient beings as well—like awakening from sleep or like the blooming of a lotus flower. Therefore, it is so named.
Regarding the Buddha:
furthermore, the first volume, second part, of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* cites the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* itself without providing a separate commentary;
I shall now briefly analyze these ten phrases by organizing them into five pairs: (1) the wisdom that realizes [the truth], and (2) the obstacles to be abandoned.

The reality realized consists of four aspects, and the benefits accomplished consist of five. The first four are explained through the Dharma teaching, while the last one is clarified by means of a simile.

Furthermore, these five pairs are each mutually related: (1) the realizing wisdom itself possesses both omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). (2) Regarding that which is to be abandoned, it is abandoned by means of omniscience.

Because one knows the categories of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) through the abandonment of all aspects of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), among the three principles to be realized,
"all phenomena" refers to the dharma of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), while "all aspects" refers to the dharma of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

One contemplates the nature of phenomena through the general characteristics by means of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and contemplates them through their specific characteristics by means of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are eliminated by realizing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), thereby removing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); through the penetration of these characteristics, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed.
Regarding the four benefits thus accomplished: the first is self-benefit, and the second is the benefit of others. The three aforementioned pairs both pertain to the two benefits;
however, if one takes a specific meaning, the realization of the nature of phenomena through omniscience is itself self-awakening (*svapratyātma-abhisambodhi*).

Because one awakens to the characteristics of phenomena through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one is able to awaken others; this is the fifth manifestation of the characteristic of awakening.
Among these, "like awakening from sleep" means that by awakening to the nature of phenomena through omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one suddenly shatters the sleep of ignorance and afflictions.
"Like a lotus blooming" means that through awakening to the characteristics of phenomena via the knowledge of all modes, one opens the gates of the Dharma, just as [a lotus blooms].
Because the lotus can be seen once the flower has opened, one may say that the former [stage] is awakening (*juecha*) and the latter is enlightenment (*juewu*);

alternatively, the former may be enlightenment and the latter awakening. Only when these five [aspects] are complete is it called "Perfect Awakening" (*miaojue*), for it is the state where the subject of awakening and the object of awakening are transcended and all awakening is exhausted. Although this explanation has not been seen in the sutras or treatises, by principle it must be so.
▲ Furthermore, Paramārtha cites the *Tattva-śāstra*, which also contains ten points; fearing prolixity, they are not cited here.
Moreover, regarding those points that Paramārtha does or does not cite, they are found within the *Paramārtha Tripiṭaka’s Record of the Seven Matters*. As for the ten points cited therein, they are:
1) awakening surpasses the celestial drum; 2) realization is not dependent on others; 3) the severance of the two types of ignorance; 4) having already... [text truncated]
1. It surpasses sleep and dreams; 2. It is like a lotus flower; 3. Its nature is pure and unstained; 4. It is endowed with three meanings;
5. It is endowed with three virtues; 6. It possesses the nature of the Three Jewels; 7. It is known by oneself and causes others to know it; 8.
Regarding the initial statement that it excels the celestial drum: the celestial drum possesses four qualities, all of which it now surpasses—first, it awakens the gods from their enemies.
When it comes, it says "the thief comes"; when it goes, it says "the thief goes. The Buddha is not like this;

he can cause sentient beings to awaken to the three afflictions, knowing them as they arise and knowing them as they cease. While the two celestial drums can protect the heavenly hosts and destroy the asuras, the Buddha is not like this;
he can rescue one from the three sufferings and destroy the four māras. The three celestial drums can cause... [sentence fragment]
The devas experience the pleasures of the five senses, whereas the Buddha does not; yet he is able to cause sentient beings to experience supramundane bliss.

The drums of the four heavens can cause the devas to give rise to a mind of craving and attachment, whereas the Buddha does not; yet he is able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a supramundane mind.
Because he possesses these four superiorities over the celestial drums, it is said that his awakening surpasses theirs. Second, "awakening not through another" means:
Because of his teacherless, spontaneous wisdom (*asvayaṃbhū-jñāna*), he has abandoned the three [obstructions] and possesses the two types of non-cognition (*ajñāna*):

namely, the non-cognition regarding afflictions (*kleśa-ajñāna*) and the non-cognition regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-ajñāna*). Fourth, "having transcended sleep and dreams": ordinary beings sleep but do not dream because they possess only afflictions;
those of the Two Vehicles both sleep and dream because they still possess ignorance (*avidyā*) and deluded cognition (*mithyā-jñāna*); the Buddha neither sleeps nor dreams.
5. Because there is no ignorance and one abandons deluded understanding; 6.
Like a lotus flower—just as a lotus flower blooms when touched by the light of the sun, so too does the Buddha-wisdom spontaneously arise through the practice of the ten stages; 7.

Because the nature is pure and unstained—although afflictions exist during the causal stage, they do not defile it for five reasons; 8. Because the Buddha is signless—just as smoke and mist cannot [obscure the sun].
1. Because the two—defilement and emptiness—are antidotes; for example, like molten iron, it does not allow mosquitoes or gnats to alight upon it. 2. Because it is not a place [for defilement];
for example, like a great boulder, it cannot remain suspended in the air. 3. Because it is subject to transformation; for example, like white jade, it is not blackened even when smeared with ink.
4. Because falsehood does not defile the real; for example, like a magical sword, it cannot cut stone. 5. Because it exists as a cause at the time [of its arising].

If delusions cannot even defile [the Buddha] at the time of fruition, how could there be any defilement when delusions have been exhausted? The seven [types of Buddha] that possess three meanings are the three Buddhas:
first, the Buddha of provisional designation, which refers to the six supernormal powers; second, the Buddha of tranquility, which refers to the non-arising of delusions;
and third, the Buddha of ultimate reality, which refers to suchness itself. The eight [types of Buddha] that possess three virtues refer to the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
If the Dharma-body of liberation possesses the nature of the Three Jewels in nine ways, it refers to the Three Jewels of identical essence (*sāmbhogika-ratnatraya*).

Tenth, "knowing for oneself and causing others to know" constitutes the two benefits: the power of the Buddha’s wisdom illuminating the realm of *tathatā* (suchness) is called "knowing for oneself," while the power of compassion preaching the twelvefold scriptures to cause others to know is "causing others to know. The commentary states: by means of...
Since these ten meanings are identical to those in the *Buddhabhūmi*, I fear that further elaboration would result in excessive prolixity.

Fifth, regarding the explanation of the ten meanings of "flower" (*puṣpa*): first, the meaning of "containing the fruit," which signifies that the Dharma-realm contains the inherent virtues of nature;

second, the meaning of "luminous purity," which signifies that fundamental wisdom is clearly manifest; third, the meaning of "subtlety and excellence," which signifies that each and every conditioned phenomenon is identical to the Dharma-realm.

1. The meaning of "appropriateness" (*sukha*), because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings; 2. The meaning of "inducing results" (*phalākarṣaṇa*), because conduct serves as the cause for producing right awakening;

3. The meaning of "excellence" (*prāsādikatva*), because conduct is accompanied by vows and lacks any deficiency; 4. The meaning of "being unstained" (*asaṃkliṣṭatva*), because every single door of practice is conjoined with samādhi; 5.
The meaning of "accomplishment of merit" (*guṇasiddhi*), because the virtuous deeds cultivated are skillfully perfected; 6. The meaning of "fragrance" (*saugandhya*).

Because the abiding and maintenance of manifold virtues cause their fragrance to spread far and wide, it has the meaning of "tenfold blossoming" (*daśa-vikāsa*); because the mind of mindfulness awakens as the various practices flourish, it has the meaning of "flower.

Regarding the five explanations of the ten meanings of "flower," the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) below has two parts: first, the individual explanation of the ten flowers; second, the general [explanation].

Upon careful examination, the preceding and middle sections correspond respectively to the ten Buddhas: the first, containing the meaning of "reality," represents the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-buddha*), as it contains the inherent virtues of nature;

this sequence is established both to correspond to the ten Buddhas and to align with the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) as causes, though not strictly following their order for the sake of conforming to the title.
Specifically, the first corresponds to Prajñā (Wisdom) and the second to Jñāna-pāramitā (Knowledge-perfection).
The third is skillful means; the fourth is ethical discipline (*śīla*); the fifth is patience (*kṣānti*); the sixth is aspiration (*praṇidhāna*);
the seventh is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the eighth is generosity (*dāna*); the ninth is power (*bala*); and the tenth is vigor (*vīrya*). This meaning is as follows:
because the Elder Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣu*) attained the fruit of the ten bodies through the causes of the ten perfections, that sūtra states: "In order to cause him to be endowed with..."
First, because the Buddha’s marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) are praised as the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), they constitute the adornment of the physical body.

Second, because one desires to cause them to attain the pure body of a Buddha that is able to reach all places, the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) is praised as the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya). Third, because one desires to cause them to attain the purity of a Buddha...
4. To cause them to obtain the inconceivable, pure body, he extols and praises the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), which is the body of awakening (*bodhi-kāya*).

5. To cause them to obtain the Tathāgata’s invincible body, he extols and praises the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), which is the body of majestic power (*vibhūti-kāya*). 6. To cause them to obtain a pure and peerless body, he extols... [the perfection of meditation].
Sixth, in order to cause the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya*, one extols and praises the *prajñāpāramitā*; this is the *dharmakāya*.
Seventh, in order to cause the manifestation of the Buddha-World-Honored One’s pure *rūpakāya*, one extols and praises the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*.
The perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is itself the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*);

eight, because it desires to cause all sentient beings to abide for all kalpas and to extol and praise [the Buddha], the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) is itself the vow body (*praṇidhānakāya*);
nine, because it desires to manifest a pure body that completely transcends all Buddha-fields and to extol and praise [the Buddha], the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is itself...
The tenth [power] is to maintain the body so as to manifest a pure body that brings joy to all sentient beings according to their minds;
the Prajñāpāramitā is itself the Wisdom-body. It concludes by saying:
"In order to cause them to attain the ultimately pure and wondrous body, one extols and praises it, forever departing from all that is unwholesome."
The Dharma is the perfect purity of the ten pāramitās and the eighty-four thousand gates of pāramitā, wherein the myriad virtues are instantaneously complete.
