By citing the text of the third assembly, it is shown that within each of these assemblies that pervade the Dharma-realm, there are further layers of primary and attendant members; this statement serves as an analogy for the aforementioned pervasion of the Dharma-realm.
This is the ninth assembly.
"Even pervading all dust-like lands" refers to the seventh section;
previously it was merely pervasive throughout the lands, but now it is pervasive even within the dust motes.
▲ Regarding "the realms of different categories" (*vilakṣaṇadhātu*) and so forth: "the realms of different categories" refers to the eighth and ninth sections.

While the preceding seven sections only pervade [realms] of the same category, the eighth pervades buddha-lands of different categories, such as those shaped like trees. As for the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) used in the commentary, it includes the ninth section.

Regarding the lands as numerous as the atoms of dissimilar categories— meaning that even lands of similar categories are composed of atoms, and within those atoms there are further lands where sutras are preached,
and these sutras are exceedingly numerous.
This constitutes the assembly of inexhaustible time.

The "Inexhaustible Assembly" refers to the tenth section; it means that whether they be lands or atoms, all things of the same or different categories are infinitely layered upon one another like Indra’s net, such that both the assembly and the Dharma are inexhaustible.
▲All do not transcend the pure dharma-realm of the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka.

The phrase "all do not transcend" raises the title to encompass them as a whole; "pure dharma-realm" raises the fundamental source to encompass them as a whole, clarifying that from within this single dharma-realm—which is nameless and signless—there unfolds an inexhaustible manifestation.

▲ Sixth Fascicle: Comprehending the Characteristics to their Ultimate Extent. This means that by gradually rolling back from the end, one reaches the point where there is no emergence beyond the nine assemblies (*navasaṃnipāta*).

These nine assemblies do not depart from the first assembly; the first assembly does not depart from the general title; and the general title does not emerge apart from principle and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because there is no wisdom apart from principle and no principle apart from wisdom, there is no wisdom outside of principle, and no principle outside of wisdom. Thus, principle and wisdom are non-dual. Furthermore—
Subsuming wisdom according to principle means that apart from its essence there is no function; subsuming function back into the essence means that the nature of the essence is itself detached.
Therefore, the essence is non-essence, primordially pure, and is given the provisional name "Pure Dharma-realm.
Thus, from the ultimate infinite down to a single character or no character, all are subsumed within the Nature-Ocean of the *Avataṃsaka* without exception.

Regarding "the sixth fascicle summarizes the characteristics to their ultimate limit" (*xiāng jìn*): the character *xiāng* (characteristics) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*), up to the word "none" (*wú*).
Since even the characteristics of the Dharma-realm do not exist, one simply understands this fascicle by understanding the preceding unfolding; thus it says, "successively rolling up from the latter.
As for the phrase "up to not exceeding the nine assemblies," the two characters "up to" (*nǎi zhì*) abbreviate the fact that the latter five stages do not exceed the nine assemblies.

This constitutes the fourth section. To be complete, it should be stated as follows: Volume One: The inexhaustible time and place returning to the realms of dissimilar categories (*vaimātra-dhātu*). Volume Two:

The particles of the realms of dissimilar categories returning to the realms of dissimilar categories. Volume Three: The particles of the realms of dissimilar categories not emerging from the particles of the realms of similar categories (*sabhāga-dhātu*).
Volume Four: The particles of the realms of similar categories not emerging from the realms of similar categories; the Sūtra on the Principal and Retinue. Volume Five.

The primary and secondary elements of this fascicle do not depart from the primary scripture. It encompasses the ten directions across six fascicles; it encompasses the ten directions without departing from the nine assemblies.
The seventh refers to the first assembly; the eighth refers to the general title; the ninth refers to principle and wisdom; the tenth refers to the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Neither non-principle nor non-wisdom" constitutes the tenth section. Within the phrase "the principle and wisdom of the fascicle return to the dharma-realm," there are two meanings.
First, within the unity of principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*), taking either one mentions both, as they merge into a single flavor.
Second, taking wisdom as the function and principle as the essence, one merely subsumes wisdom back into principle, rather than subsuming principle back into wisdom.
Initially, the two are gathered into one; yet even this single word "principle" is devoid of intrinsic nature, and thus even "one" does not exist. Therefore, it is so called.
Regarding the "Wordless," it should also follow the previous method of expansion, stating that the general title does not depart from essence and function, cause and effect.
Although cause and effect differ, they do not transcend a single wisdom; although essence and function differ, they do not transcend a single principle. Only then are principle and wisdom harmonized.

However, because this is not different from what preceded, it is shown only briefly. If one were to collect [the meaning] by reversing the seven characters, the teaching would be subsumed within [the principle].
In meaning, there is only the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka which encompasses all people through the Dharma;

in its function, it returns to its essence and does not depart from the "Great. As the ancients said: "A single word leaves nothing unsummarized; even diverse explanations do not differ from this fullness.
Furthermore, the great essence and nature transcend words and thought, being utterly beyond them; they can only be realized through direct correspondence.
▲ Seventh, the unimpeded nature of unfolding and rolling up: This means that at the very moment one unfolds [the scroll] in front, it is simultaneously and constantly rolled up behind;
at the very moment one rolls it up behind, it is simultaneously and constantly unfolded in front.

Because unfolding is itself rolling up, the ocean of immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates is fully expounded in a single utterance without remainder. Because rolling up is itself unfolding, the Tathāgata expounds the boundless within a single word.
The ocean of sūtras.
Seventh, "unimpeded in unfolding and rolling up" means that although there is a sequence of before and after in the teaching, they actually exist simultaneously;
it is only according to different perspectives that there are three gates. The commentary states: "The ocean of immeasurable and boundless dharma-gates" refers to the time of unfolding. First.
To speak of expounding exhaustively without remainder refers to the time of contraction; when the Tathāgata, within a single utterance, performs this contraction, it is the time of contraction.
To expound the ocean of boundless sūtras refers to the time of expansion.
▲ Eighth, regarding the comprehensive inclusion by way of meaning: Among the various preceding sections, some may be fully subsumed within seven characters, as has already been analyzed.

Regarding this eighth section on comprehensive inclusion by way of meaning, the commentary consists of two parts: first, inclusion by way of phenomena (*dharma*), and second, inclusion by way of persons (*pudgala*).
Within the preceding section, there are again two parts; first, pointing back to what was not previously stated in the general title:

either by exhausting [the subject] through teaching and meaning, or by exhausting it through principle and wisdom, or by exhausting it through person and dharma, or by exhausting it through understanding, practice, and realization.

Later, some may provide a further sub-commentary on the meaning based on the doctrine. While this commentary briefly cites the essential points, if one were to explain them in full, the number of categories should be increased for clarity.
That is to say, within a single character, one character may encompass everything—whether it be the teaching (*dharma*), the meaning (*artha*), the nature (*svabhāva*), or the mind (*citta*).
Alternatively, two characters may encompass everything; the commentary contains three sections, and furthermore, one should also mention "or the phenomena" (*dharmas*).
The character "jie" (界, *dhātu*) encompasses all three; alternatively, the three characters [of the title] encompass all.

According to one interpretation in the commentary, because it accords with the latter, it expresses the three sages (*ārya*), and thus it should also be said that they are encompassed by the "person-dharma realm. Alternatively, they are encompassed by the principle, practice, and fruit, as these are what is expressed.

Fourthly, the four characters [of the title] encompass all: namely, teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. "Teaching" refers to the word of the sutra; "principle" refers to the Great Fangguang [Prajñāpāramitā].
"Extensive practice" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, and "fruit" refers to the Buddha. Alternatively, regarding how the teaching and its meaning are fully encompassed:
first, although the text is vast and extensive, it is subsumed within the single character for "teaching," which is the character "Sūtra" (*jing*) in the title;

second, although the meanings are immeasurable, they are subsumed within the single meaning of "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which is "Great, Vast, and Broad" (*Mahāvaipulya*) in the title; third, this constitutes the completion of practice, understanding, cause, and fruit.

Although the aspects of virtue (*guṇa*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and functions (*vṛtti*) arise through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in various ways, when considered in terms of their ultimate establishment, they are entirely subsumed within the single character "one" (*eka*).

This refers precisely to the title of the scripture, the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*. Regarding the "four locations," all the infinitely layered realms of dust-like lands—whether of the same or different categories—are but a single location, the character "one. Therefore, the meaning of the entire compendium is the teaching of the single nature (*ekadhātu*).
The single letter, the single mindfulness, and the single dust-mote—this one is the "one of all," for it is the one that encompasses everything.
Alternatively, it may be understood as being fully subsumed by faith, understanding, practice, and realization; thus, the sutra has four sections:

the first assembly concerns faith, the next six clarify understanding, the eighth pertains to the accomplishment of practice, and the ninth is solely realization, as will be known from below. Or, it may be fully subsumed by the five [factors], namely:
One may add the character "teaching" (jiao), or [the character] "principle" (li). Principle is that which is believed, understood, practiced, and realized.
Alternatively, the six characters [of the title] encompass everything; specifically, the six characters excluding "sūtra" (jing) from the title are the objects of exposition.
Or, principle refers to what is believed, while understanding, practice, vow, and realization constitute the three aspects of understanding, practice, and vow.
It encompasses the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*), the realization of the *abhijñās*, the stages above the ground (*bhūmi*), and the ultimate fruit;
or it is fully subsumed by seven characters, as the single title in its entirety refers to the inexhaustible Dharma;

or it is fully subsumed by eight characters, as it represents the reality of cause and effect within the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*; or it is fully subsumed by nine characters, namely: the unobstructed dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*.

Alternatively, it is fully subsumed by ten categories, namely: essence (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), wisdom (*jñāna*), function (*kriyā*), cause (*hetu*), fruit (*phala*), teaching (*deśanā*), meaning (*artha*), object (*viṣaya*), and activity (*karman*).
Alternatively, it is subsumed solely by the three holy ones—Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and Vairocana—wherein "Mahāvaipulya" refers to...
Samantabhadra, Samantabhadra, represents the Dharma-realm that is realized; therefore, the Avataṃsaka is Mañjuśrī, for Mañjuśrī represents the means of realization.
Thus, the Buddha is Vairocana, who embodies both the means and the object of realization.
Furthermore, "Great" (*mahā*) refers to Samantabhadra, for the essence of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is all-pervasive;
"Extensive" (*vaipulya*) refers to Mañjuśrī, for Mañjuśrī represents the wisdom that manifests from the essence. "Flower" (*puṣpa*) refers to Samantabhadra, for he is the practice;

"Adornment" (*vyūha*) refers to Mañjuśrī, for Mañjuśrī initiates practice through understanding. Thus, the Buddha is the Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī of perfected understanding and practice, who realize the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.
By employing them, Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī accomplish the all-pervading illumination of Vairocana.
Alternatively, they may be considered as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī alone, which constitutes the second [category] of "persons" (pudgala) within the sub-classification; however, there are two layers:

first, the two sages are distinguished by contrasting "person" and "dharma" (dharmas); subsequently, within each of these [categories of] person and dharma, there are again the two sages. The word "Buddha" stands in the center.
The two layers that comprehensively subsume [all phenomena] should be contemplated.

▲ Ninth, the subsumption into the single mind: All the various gates mentioned above, up to the inexhaustible, do not depart from the single mind, for the single mind is itself the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As the *Awakening of Faith* says: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings."
▲The essence of mind is the Great Mind; its fundamental wisdom is the Vaipulya. When the contemplation of the mind gives rise to practice, it is the Avataṃsaka.

The nature and characteristics of awakening are themselves the Buddha; awakening does not come from without, for it is entirely identical to that which is awakened to. Thus, principle and wisdom are not distinct.
When principle and wisdom mutually negate one another and both vanish, stillness and illumination are present in every thought-moment as the ocean of the Avataṃsaka’s nature.
Regarding the ninth [section], "Inclusion within the One Mind," there are two parts. First, it refers back to what was previously stated in general terms:
since the preceding eight gates have already been shown to be the One Mind, it says that the various gates mentioned above do not depart from the One Mind.
Furthermore, because those who practice the flow of *dhyāna* all wish to discard the texts to cultivate meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), this gate is now introduced to clarify the mind itself.
The essence is precisely the Great [Vehicle]. Following this, the text correctly explains by means of contemplating the mind: "The essence of the mind is free from thought;
that which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space—is this not the Great? The fundamental wisdom of the mind is precisely the Vast and Broad (Vaipulya).
The aforementioned 'Great' is the quiescence of wisdom, and the 'Vast and Broad' is the wisdom of quiescence; therefore it is said: 'Quiescent quiescence operates without limit.'"

The illumination of this [mind] is the fusion of the mind’s essence, attributes, and functions as the object of contemplation. To contemplate the mind and give rise to practice is precisely the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra:
contemplating the essence, its illumination is itself quiescent cessation (*śamatha*); contemplating the function, its quiescence is constant illumination (*vipaśyanā*).
When the six perfections and myriad practices all arise from the single mind, and the mind’s nature and attributes are themselves the Buddha—this is the resonance of a single thought-moment.
Because this is awakening, the Sūtra says: "What else could the Buddha-mind be? It is simply perfect awakening that awakens the world.

The nature of awakening is without [subjective] awakening, which is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); the manifestation of awakening is clearly distinct, which is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

The non-duality of these two is unobstructed wisdom. Awakening does not come from without; it is entirely identical to that which is awakened to. Below, the six characters are established for clarity. Now...
Clarifying that the characteristics of phenomena are empty and subsumed within this, the above is fused into a single flavor; from here below, they mutually negate one another until both are stilled.
Thus, in such contemplative practice, there is not a single thought-moment that does not accord with the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
▲ Tenth, regarding the merging into equality: for those who have not yet realized it, one must cause them to understand that their own mind is the source.

If one knows that all objects encountered are but the mind, only then does one realize the nature of the mind. Thus, the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* states: "To know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind is to achieve the body of wisdom;
this is not attained through awakening from another. Yet nowadays, many who study the Dharma abandon the internal while seeking it externally.
Those who practice meditation often prefer to eliminate external conditions and illuminate within; both are attachments to the Buddha’s teachings and remain stuck in the two extremes.
Once mind and objects are realized as *tathatā* (suchness), they are equal and unimpeded.
The tenth [gate], "Merging into Equality," is this single section that universally synthesizes the preceding nine; the eight preceding dharmas are not the objective referents.
Knowing that the Ninth Chan Master’s preference lay in this, I now synthesize it within the middle three sections: first, the teaching by means of the Dharma;
second, the clarification through the metaphor of "I once polished two mirrors on both sides," which borrows the analogy of Indra’s net to illustrate the mutual reflection of mind and object;
third, "Seeing that mind and object reflect each other," which applies the meaning of the metaphor. This has a single core meaning, yet the text is divided into four sections.

▲ Yu Cengying arranged two mirrors facing each other with a single lamp placed between them, and a Buddha image set within; the lights reflected back and forth in infinite layers, such that every Buddha was inexhaustible.

In the first section, he took the two mirrors and the lamp and combined them: one mirror is a metaphor for the objective realm (*viṣaya*), and the other mirror is a metaphor for the mind (*citta*); the lamp represents [the luminosity of awareness].
The metaphor for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) merely takes the sense of clarity.

Observe how the mind and objects mutually illuminate one another, and fundamental wisdom enters both simultaneously; within the mind, one awakens to the inexhaustible realm, and upon that realm, one realizes the inconceivable mind.
As mind and objects unfold in successive layers, the illumination of wisdom is ever-present therein.

Regarding the statement that "fundamental wisdom enters both simultaneously," it is because the nature of wisdom and the nature of form are fundamentally non-dual, and because one knows that all phenomena are the self-nature of mind;

therefore, this nature of wisdom enters both the realm of mind and the realm of objects. Regarding the statement that "mind and objects are layered upon one another," it is like two mirrors reflecting each other;
that "wisdom shines therein" is like a single lamp entering both [mirrors] simultaneously. Thus, by means of fundamental wisdom—
Because the mind that is capable of illuminating and the objects of that illumination are both what is illuminated, fundamental wisdom causes the mind and its objects to merge with one another.

Furthermore, when the mind itself realizes the Buddha within its objects, the object is seen as being nothing but the Tathāgata’s mind; thus, the Buddhas of the mind and the Buddha of the objects are layered and manifold, yet their fundamental enlightened nature is one.
Furthermore, regarding the passage "The Buddha who is the very mind cognizing objects," the second part involves taking two mirrors and one statue and joining them to the statue;
this serves as a metaphor for the True Buddha. Thus, people nowadays only understand that "the mind is the Buddha" and that "the mind makes the Buddha.
They do not know that "objects are the Buddha" and that "objects make the Buddha. Here it is clarified that, with *tathatā* (suchness) as the Buddha, both mind and objects are [that Buddha].
As the mind is suchness, so too is the Buddha-realm suchness. It is not that there is a mind apart from the nature of mind; the mind is able to constitute the Buddha-realm.
Since the nature of mind exists, why would it not manifest as a Buddha? If one subsumes the realm within the mind, then the Buddha seen within the mind is the Buddha of the objective realm.
If one subsumes the mind within the realm, then the Buddha seen within the realm is the Tathāgata who is solely mind. Thus, the mind and the Buddha are mutually emphasized.
The "multiplicity" refers to the layered reflections of two mirrors, while the "oneness of the fundamental awakened nature" refers to the dual entry into the honored countenance.
Since neither can be grasped when sought, both mind and object vanish; since they cannot be exhausted when contemplated, wisdom and principle are fused.

The intersection and penetration [of stillness and insight]. Taking both of these together, one cannot grasp them as separate; this constitutes the third pair. By fusing the preceding two, cessation (śamatha) and contemplation (vipaśyanā) are established.
When both the mental object and the subjective mind have perished, this is cessation; when principle and wisdom intersect and penetrate, this is contemplation.
When the mind and its objects are thus, and as object meets object and mind studies mind, the myriad transformations unfold in a profusion that is nonetheless of a single consistency.
Only when realization and correspondence coincide is it called the Buddha-Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka).
The mind and its objects being thus—as stated below in the fourth section, which concludes by applying this analogy to all things—where there are many objects there are many minds;
each pair corresponds to one another, and each is mutually fused. This applies to all myriad transformations.
Thus, in summary, when one realizes the correspondence [of cause and effect], they merge into the ocean of fruition.

▲ Second, regarding the explanation of the title: in Sanskrit it is called *Sarvalokendra-vyūha-dharmaparyāya-tejo-nāma-parivarta*, which translates as "The Chapter on the Name of the Majestic Power of the Dharma Gate Adorned by the Lord of All Worlds.
In the present text, this has been abbreviated.
The second section, the commentary on the title of the chapter, consists of four parts: first, correlating the Sanskrit sounds; second, explaining the meaning and principles;
third, the reason for establishing the name; and fourth, correlating and explaining the Jin (Chinese) translation. Regarding the first, the general correspondence within the commentary:
if one were to provide a specific correspondence, *sarva* means "all"; *loka* means "world"; *indra* means "lord"; and *bhūṣaṇa* means "adornment."
*Śrī* means discipline (*vinaya*); *dharmaparyāya* means the gateway of the Dharma; *bala-prabhāva* means majestic power;
*nāman* means name; *parivarta* means chapter.
Regarding the word "World" (*loka*), it refers to time, which is to say the Lord of the World—the sovereign—referring specifically to various kings and Buddhas.

There are three worlds in the world: first, the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), which is the place of transformation; second, the sentient-being-world (*sattva-loka*), which refers to those who are to be transformed;
and third, the world of wisdom and perfect enlightenment (*jñāna-sambuddha-loka*), which refers to the master of transformation. This master is of only two kinds: various kings and Buddhas.
Because these masters preside over both the vessel-world and the sentient-being-world, the Buddha is not [merely] the world; he receives his designation from that which he governs.

"World" (*loka*) refers to time. The following second section explains the underlying meaning and principles. Within this, there are two parts; first, the explanation of the "Lord of the World" (*lokanātha*).

"Sublime" (*praṇīta*) refers to the essence and function of the Dharma-gate, which are profound, vast, and inconceivable—this is what the Lord has attained. "Adorned" (*vyūha*) means ornamentation, which carries several meanings:
first, the adornment of the *bhājana-loka* (receptacle world), referring to its ground being firm and stable, and so forth; second, the adornment of the *sattva-loka* (sentient world).
"Adornment" refers to the fact that each of the oceans of assemblies possesses the majestic power (*vibhūti*) of its respective dharma-gates;

it refers to the "adornment of the world through the perfect enlightenment of the three wisdoms," meaning that one attains supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena, such that the three karmas universally pervade and the dharma-gates are inexhaustible.
Therefore, while the prose sections describe the adornments of various kings, the verses praising his virtues all manifest the adornment of the Buddha.

The subsequent "Excellence" refers to the following explanation of the "Excellence of Adornment. Within this, there are three parts. First, the primary exposition of the adornments of the three worlds:
if sentient beings are not adorned, they will not elicit the arising of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment; if the [sentient] realm is not adorned, it cannot serve as a vessel for the Master;
and if the physical environment is not adorned, it is not a true abode for the Buddha.
Next, regarding the reason why sentient beings who lack adornment emerge from below to provide adornment:

furthermore, it is because the Buddha’s adornment is manifested through those encountered who possess virtue, and sentient beings’ adornment assists in manifesting the Buddha’s transcendent excellence;
thus, this mutual adornment also constitutes a sublime adornment.
Subsequently, the text again proceeds from the "Adornment of the Buddha" to clarify how the three types of adornment are mutually perfected.

Since other sutras do not contain such extensive descriptions of adornment, they merely designate the opening section as the "Introduction Chapter. Here, however, having already clarified the introduction, it also encompasses the main body;
therefore, it extensively praises the various adornments to serve as the prologue to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Third, this section clarifies the reason for establishing the title and distinguishes it from other schools by showing that it is not called the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta).
Regarding the old translation as the "Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World": this means that the Dharma-eye attained therein is able to purify the world; hence [it is so named]. Furthermore...
As previously stated,

the "Old" (Chinese) version refers to the fourth assembly of the *Lokadhātu-parivarta* (World Chapter), which explains the attainment of the Dharma-eye in the Jin translation; this is precisely what is now called the majestic power (*vīrya*) of the Dharma-gate.
▲ Tenth, the separate explanation of the text and its meaning. This section is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation of the preface to the sutra;

second, the separate explanation of the text and its meaning. Within the first part, there are three sections: (1) "The Great Fang... and so forth, which clarifies the title; (2) "Under the Tianche [Era]...

and so forth, which clarifies the author of the preface; and (3) "I have heard... and so forth, which directly explains the text of the preface. Now, for the first: this refers to the title of the sutra's preface.
Preface to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* of the Buddha. The explanation of the preface is as previously set forth.
▲ Composed by the Celestial Edict Golden Wheel Sage-Spirit Emperor.

Second, clarifying the phonology and meaning of the person who composed the preface: *cè* (冊) is pronounced *cè* (with the *zhěng* [entering tone] final). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A *cè* is a tally of imperial edicts."

It is also said that the sacred sages bestowed symbols of authority and divine mandates to confer the imperial throne; these characters were sometimes written with the "bamboo" radical or in ancient forms as circular shapes.
Now, I have heard that at the very beginning of the creative process, when the Way of Heaven had not yet been differentiated...
The *Yanyi* (Exegesis) states: Regarding the passage beginning with "Now I have heard," the preface of the direct commentary is divided into six sections:

first, clarifying that while the Buddha-sun had not yet arisen, the multitudes of sentient beings were submerged in suffering; second, from "And furthermore" onwards, clarifying that the meritorious functions of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world are inconceivable;

third, from "I, in the past" onwards, expressing personal joy at having encountered the times and heard these teachings and transformations; fourth, from "In all directions" onwards, specifically manifesting this [text]; fifth... [and so forth].

The essential purport is profound and subtle; contemplating it from afar across five ages, I have transmitted it down to the present. From ancient times to the present day, there has been a sense of joy at encountering this "Six-One" (the *Ṣaḍdharmaprakāśamukha*).

A brief glance at the general commentary on the meaning of the preface reveals that while he praises the principle, he remains humble regarding himself. This section is divided into three parts: first, clarifying the divergences in the methods of transformation (*dharmaparyāya*);

second, clarifying the shallowness and proximity of the transformer; third, clarifying the delusion and wandering of those being transformed. The first part also consists of two sections, the first of which is a discernment.

At the beginning of the Chunyuan era, the two luminaries [sun and moon] appeared and the three powers [Heaven, Earth, and Man] were already manifest; now, at the very commencement, we hear the phrase "as we have heard," which serves as the opening of a discourse.

Regarding "the creation and transformation" (*zaohua*), the *Commentary on the Appended Phrases* of the *I Ching* states: "The hard and the soft push against one another, thereby producing change and transformation.
It further states: "Change and transformation are the images of advancing and retreating. As for "the beginning" (*quan yu*), the *Erya* says: "It means the start, the beginning."
"Shou," "ji," "zhaozu," "yuantai," "chuluo," "quan yu," and "shi" all signify the beginning. These two [categories] both refer to the commencement;

when it is said that the Way of Heaven has not yet been differentiated, it means that the primordial qi was in a state of chaotic undifferentiation before heaven and earth were established. When it is said below that "human patterns first became manifest," this refers to the initial differentiation of the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity).
Since the Way of Heaven is here said to be "undifferentiated," this refers to the period of the Five Phases (*wuyun*). Therefore, the *Yi*...
The *Gouming jue* states: Before heaven and earth were divided, it was called the One Qi (One Pneuma).

Within this, there are five stages—Taiyi (Great Ease), Taichu (Great Beginning), Taishi (Great Origin), Taisu (Great Purity), and Taiji (Great Ultimate)—which constitute the five movements (*yun*). "Movement" refers to numerical progression; it signifies the transformation of time.

Taking the meaning of "change" (*yi*) from the beginning, when the primal pneuma first begins to disperse, it is called Taichu. When the pneuma reaches the point where form emerges, it is called Tai... [Taiji].
When the initial transformations possess substance, they are called the Great Purity (*Taisu*); when the substance and form are already complete, they are called the Great Ultimate (*Taiji*).
Because it transforms the five qi, it is termed the Five Phases (*Wuyun*); all these belong to the Way of Heaven (*Tiandao*) before it has been differentiated.

Regarding the "Way of Heaven," the *Appended Statements* of the *I Ching* say: "The Book of the Changes is vast and great, containing everything in its entirety; therein lies the Way of Heaven and the Way of Man."
There is the Way of the Earth. The *Shuogua* says: "In ancient times, when the sages created the *Yi*, they did so with the intent to accord with the principle of nature and destiny (*xingming*).
Therefore, they established the Way of Heaven as Yin and Yang; they established the Way of Earth as Softness and Hardness;
they established the Way of Humanity as Benevolence and Righteousness. By combining these three powers (*sancai*) and doubling them, the *Yi* consists of six [lines]."
"By painting [the trigrams], the hexagrams are formed. It further says: "In the heavens they form images; on the earth they take shape; thus the transformations are made manifest.
The commentary states: "Images refer to the sun, moon, and stars; shapes refer to mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees. It also says: "The *Yi* accords with Heaven and Earth;
therefore it can encompass and interweave the Way of Heaven and Earth. Looking upward, one contemplates the celestial patterns; looking downward, one examines..."
Geography: Therefore, one knows the causes of the hidden and the manifest; by tracing back the origin and reversing to the end, one knows the discourse on death and life.

The commentary states: "The hidden and the manifest refer to the forms of the corporeal and the incorporeal; death and life refer to the numerical sequence of the beginning and the end. The *Commentary on the Zhouyi* states:
"Heaven possesses dark phenomena (*xuanxiang*) which constitute celestial patterns (*tianwen*); Earth possesses mountains, rivers, plains, and marshes."
Because each possesses its own order, it is called "geography" (dili). All that has been discussed above constitutes the characteristics of the differentiated realm;
since this explains the Way of Heaven (tiandao), it is mentioned here. This [discussion] refers specifically to the period prior to differentiation.
▲ At the initial stage when the tortoise and dragon were used to tie the images, the patterns of human culture first became manifest.

Regarding the phrase "at the initial stage when the tortoise and dragon were used to tie the images," the second couplet clarifies that the manifestations of the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) have already become manifest, as briefly explained above.
The *Appended Statements* of the *I Ching* say: "Therefore, Heaven produced the divine objects, which the Sage took as his model; Heaven and Earth undergo transformations..."

The Sage transforms by emulating Heaven; as Heaven displays its phenomena to reveal good and ill fortune, the Sage takes these as his model. When the River yielded the diagrams and the Luo yielded the writings, the Sage followed them as his standard.

The *Kongshu* (Commentary on the Analects) states that according to the interpretation of Zheng Kangcheng, this relies on the *Chunqiu Weishi* (Spring and Autumn Annals with Apocryphal Explanations), which says:
"The River, in order to communicate with Qian, produces the celestial envelope; the Luo, in order to flow through Kun, emits the terrestrial tally. This refers to the dragon-diagram of the River.

The *Gui-shu* (Tortoise Script) appeared at Falo, and the *He-tu* (River Chart) was moved by its manifestation; the *He-tu* consists of nine sections, while the *Luo-shu* (Lo Book) consists of six sections.
Kong Anguo held that the *He-tu* refers to the Eight Trigrams (*ba-gua*), and the *Luo-shu* refers to the Nine Categories (*jiu-chou*). The commentary on the phonology and meaning states:
"When Yao had a divine tortoise bearing a chart emerge, and when Shun was moved by a yellow dragon bearing a chart appear, the patterns of human culture first became manifest."
The *Appended Phrases* (*Xici*) state: "In ancient times, when Fu Xi ruled over the world, he looked upward and observed the patterns in heaven;
he looked downward and observed the laws on earth; he observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the terrain. Kong Yingda’s commentary states:

"The following clarifies how the Sage modeled himself upon the principles of nature to create the hexagram images, which follow the sequence of the *Yi*. Furthermore, it says [the following] is proximate..."

"Taking from his own body and taking from external objects, he then began to create the Eight Trigrams (Bagua) to communicate the virtue of the spiritual intelligences and to categorize the essence of the myriad things.
*Commentary:* It was stated above that the diagrams produced the Eight Trigrams; now it says "he contemplated Heaven and Earth.
This may refer to the tortoise shell or to the fact that the trigrams imitate Heaven and Earth; there is no contradiction in principle. *Phonetic Gloss:* *Guān hū* (觀乎).

"Observing the celestial phenomena to examine human transformations, and observing the patterns of human culture to transform and perfect the world"—this was not the original intent [of the *Xici*], but rather how later generations have employed it.
What is termed "human culture" (*renwen*) refers to the relationships between ruler and subject, father and son, and the distinctions of honor and subordination, high and low.

When the *Xiangzhuan* mentions the dragon, it refers to the era of the Three Sovereigns, which constitutes the High Antiquity (*shanggu*). When the *Xiangzhuan* mentions the "tethered image," it refers to the time of Confucius, which constitutes the Later Antiquity (*xiagu*).

However, since King Wen composed the words for the hexagrams and lines during the Middle Antiquity, these already contained the *xiang* (images). Thus, [the text] encompasses all three periods of antiquity.

Furthermore, while the previous mention of "Heavenly Way" (*tian dao*) referred to the time when [the principles] were not yet differentiated, the current mention of "Human Pattern" (*ren wen*) refers to the time when they first became manifest.

These two terms are used in a complementary and abbreviated manner; thus, at the very moment of initial differentiation, they were likewise not yet manifest, and it was only upon the composition of the *Xiangzhuan* (Commentary on the Images) that they finally became so.
The *Jufang* says: "To 'attach' means that because there was already something prior, there was the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*), which produced the Two Polarities (*liangyi*);

the Two Polarities produced the Four Images (*sxiang*); the Four Images produced the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*); the Eight Trigrams determined good fortune and misfortune; and good fortune and misfortune gave rise to great undertakings—thus the Three Powers (*sancai*) were complete."
▲ Although eighteen thousand years have passed, all have ruled only within the bounded realm; how could the seventy-two sovereigns have known the meaning of the boundless?

Although eighteen thousand years have elapsed, the second [section] clarifies that the capacity for transformation is shallow and near; this is according to the *Record of the Sexagenary Cycle of Emperors and Kings*.

It is said that the Celestial Sovereigns (Tianhuangshi) ruled for eighteen thousand years, the Earthly Sovereigns (Dihuangshi) for nine thousand years, and the Human Sovereigns (Renhuangshi) for four thousand five hundred years;
however, there is a source stating that all Three Sovereigns ruled for eighteen thousand years each, hence the expression "eighteen thousand years.
Regarding the phrase "ruling together over the bounded realm," the commentary on the *Shijing* states that "bounded" (*jie*) refers to...
"Qi" (齊) means "to delimit" (區), referring to the four seas and the realm within them being brought into orderly submission.
This speaks of the seventy-two rulers who did not yet understand the meaning of the boundless. As the *Fengshan Shu* (Book on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices) by Sima Xiangru states:

"Those who succeeded in the lineage of Zhao and Mu and received posthumous titles and names that can be briefly enumerated number seventy-two. Thus, the *Guanzi* says: "In the past, [the Emperor] performed the Feng sacrifice..."
Regarding the seventy-two houses of practitioners on Mount Tai and Mount Liangfu— Mount Liangfu being the name of a small mountain beneath Mount Tai—

the word "jù" (詎) means "how could. It clarifies that how could the seventy-two houses of wise and enlightened rulers have been able to recognize the boundless meaning of the profound principle that accords with the nature of reality?

▲ Consequently, people are deluded regarding the four patiences (*kṣānti*) and transmigrate within the six realms of existence; bound by the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), they sink into the depths of the three miserable paths.

Regarding the phrase "Consequently, people are deluded regarding the four patiences," the third section clarifies the description of the delusions and wanderings of those to be converted. As for the word "consequently" (*yōushi*), it refers back to the preceding [context].
The enlightened teacher and the methods of transformation are both shallow and mundane; they are merely the work of a single body within this realm.

[These teachings] do not enable those being transformed to escape the sea of sinking suffering. Among them, at the superior level, they address those who are deluded regarding principle and transmigrate through the six destinies;

at the lower level, they address those entangled in delusion and submerged in the three miserable paths. As for the "four kinds of patience," these refer to what the Buddha taught in the fourth chapter, "On Dharmas," of the *Sāṃkhyātikasūtra* (思益經).
It is said that there are four dharmas by which a Bodhisattva Brahmā excels in escaping the offense of violating the prohibitions. What are these four?
First, attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), because all phenomena have no coming; second, attaining the patience of non-extinction, because all phenomena have no going;
third, attaining the patience of causes and conditions, knowing that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; and fourth, [the attainment of the patience of the non-self-nature of phenomena].
To attain the patience of non-abiding because of the continuity of a mind free from differentiation constitutes the four patiences.
It is said that those who are deluded are all deluded; however, being deluded regarding these four patiences may cause one to drift among humans and devas.

Thus, it is said that "one wanders within the six realms of rebirth," and if one is entangled by the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), one will drown in the three miserable paths. The five hindrances are: first, sensual desire; second, ill-will... [and so forth].

[The five hindrances are] 1) covetousness, 2) ill-will, 3) dullness and torpor, 4) restlessness and agitation, and 5) doubt. Regarding the "household fetters" (*kula-saṃyojana*), these refer to the fetters of each respective household.
The first three clarify that [these afflictions existed] before the Buddha appeared in the world.
Subsequently, when Vulture Peak stood to the west and the Elephant Mount moved toward the east, [the Dharma was established].
Furthermore, regarding the two Tathāgatas appearing in the world beneath Vulture Peak, their virtuous functions are inconceivable. Within this, there are four sections:

first, a general praise of the sublime and profound qualities of the Teacher who transforms others; second, clarifying the long duration and vast extent of the time and place of those who transform others;

third, specifically praising the supreme virtues of the Tathāgata; and fourth, concluding by dedicating these virtues to the Tathāgata. Regarding the first of these, the four lines are divided into two parts, with the first two lines providing a general summary.

In the introduction to the subsequent two lines concerning the rise and spread of Buddhism, the excellence [of this tradition] is revealed through contrast. First, regarding the upper line, it clarifies that the Master appeared in the Western Heaven;
thus it says, "The Vulture Peak stands westward. "Stands" (*zhi*) means to be situated. This praises the person by way of his location.

The subsequent line refers to the transformation-dharma being transmitted to the East; thus it says, "The elephant-vehicle drives eastward. Regarding the term "elephant-vehicle," there are briefly two meanings.

First, because it was only during the period of the Semblance Dharma (xiangfa), one thousand years after the True Dharma, that Buddhism was first spread; second, because it is the *Hastikakṣya-sūtra* (Elephant-Drawn Sūtra).

Although white horses were initially used for the ceremonial procession, elephants were originally employed for this purpose. To correspond with the Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), the elephant-drawn carriage was utilized.
As Song Gong stated in his poem titled "On An Guo Temple": "The Crown Prince has departed on his dragon; the Dharma King returns riding an elephant."
▲ The Dharma King of the Sun of Wisdom transcends the four great elements and gazes loftily upon the central heavens; the Tamer of Men surpasses the ten stages and dwells in supreme honor.

Regarding the second section, "The Dharma King of the Sun of Wisdom Descends," which relies on contrast to manifest superiority: the first phrase [describes] his departure from the mundane realm, while the latter phrase [describes] his transcendence of causal stages.

Now, when the first Sun of Wisdom, the Dharma King who transcends the four great elements and gazes from on high, appears within the realm, he differs from previous manifestations that remained within the realm.
Regarding this "Sun of Wisdom," taking the Buddha as the sun, there are briefly four meanings: first, destroying darkness like wisdom (*prajñā*);
second, illuminating what is present like knowledge (*jñāna*); third, the purity of the wheels like liberation (*vimukti*); and fourth, the inseparability of these three aforementioned qualities.

Just as the Dharma-realm is sovereign over all phenomena, it is called the "Dharma King. Regarding the statement that one "transcends the four greats and looks down from on high," this refers to what is said in Laozi’s *Daodejing*:
"The Way is great, Heaven is great, Earth is great, and the King is also great. Within the realm there are these four greats, and the King occupies one of them.
Man models himself after Earth; Earth models itself after Heaven; Heaven models itself after the Way; and the Way models itself after Nature (*ziran*)."
The *Ziran* (Spontaneity) commentary states: "That which is called the Way is pure, empty, and pervasive; therefore it is said that 'the Dharma of the Way is spontaneous' (*ziran*).

'Spontaneous' means that one does not know why it is so, yet it is so. Thus, regarding the initial formation of the world and the immediate affairs within its domain, people do not understand the causes of karma;
hence it is called 'spontaneous. Now, the Buddha has appeared and perfectly realized the True and Constant."
Excellently exhausting the Two Truths, the creation of heaven and earth belongs to the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—it is merely a matter of karmic causes within the mundane sphere.
The subsequent phrase transcends the discourse on causes; the Heavenly Tamer (*Śāstṛ*) surpasses the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to abide in the state of the Honored One.

When a Bodhisattva of the ten stages has passed through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, having severed the ten obstructions, realized the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), and perfected the ten supreme practices, his transformation is complete throughout the ten [directions].
Now, comparing the World-Honored One to a single clod of earth against the vastness of the great earth, how could he possibly surpass the four great elements?
He encompasses the Iron Ring Mountains and extends through the kalpas of shifting sands.

This includes the second clarification regarding time and place: the first phrase briefly cites the area within the three thousand great Iron Ring Mountains as the scope of transformation, which is by no means the same as the aforementioned limited regions;

the subsequent phrase concerns time, wherein many kalpas are condensed into a single thought-moment and a single thought-moment is extended into many kalpas, which is by no means the same as the aforementioned ten thousand [years].
Eight thousand years.
Regarding its essence, it is neither born nor extinguished.
Within the third section of the praise for the Tathāgata’s supreme virtues, this passage simultaneously clarifies both the transformer (the Lord) and the transformation (the manifested).

The Dharma is praised by way of its three greatnesses. First, it praises the greatness of its essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*). The Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body is unborn, transcending conceptual proliferation;
it is not a dharma consisting of a collection of aggregates. It further says: "The Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, pure as empty space.
And it says: "All dharmas are unborn; all dharmas are unceasing. One who can understand them in this way is [a true follower]."
Beholding the Tathāgata:
as for his marks, he neither comes nor goes.
Regarding these marks, the second section of the praise [in] the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata does not take marks as his essence; rather..."
This signless, quiescent Dharma-body is fully endowed with all physical marks and dignified deportment; it is perceived by all according to their worldly inclinations.
Since it is signless, it serves as the very mark; it is profoundly still, without coming or going, its virtue pervading the Dharma-realm, yet it neither comes nor goes.

▲The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, consisting of the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts, constitute his practice; he employs the four immeasurable states of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity to direct his mind.
The power of his skillful means is inconceivable, and the various ways in which he perfectly accords with the capacities of sentient beings are manifold.
In the third section, "Praising the Greatness of Function," following the Foundations of Mindfulness and Right Efforts, it first addresses the transformation of beings through the Dharma.

This transformation is profound and subtle, differing from that within the mundane realms. Here, action is exclusively the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), while the mind is exclusively the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*).

The various gates of skillful means respond perfectly and unfathomably, as described in the sutras. Regarding "perfect correspondence": the body turns in all directions to respond universally, like the moon descending upon a hundred [lakes].

As for the resonance of the stream, it names all things and is universally heard, like the wind blowing through ten thousand pipes; as for the meaning, it is sudden awakening in a single kṣaṇa, like the clear reflection in the Ocean Seal Samādhi.
Therefore, it is said that its strands are manifold.
It merges with the vast void as its measure—how could numerical calculation ever exhaust it? It enters the subtlest region of a tiny speck of dust, yet it is not...
This can be described through names and words.
"Mingled with the great void" and the following two phrases clarify the function based on the essence of transformation. That is to say, when expanded, there is nothing external;
when contracted, there is nothing internal. As the Sūtra says: "For example, it is like empty space, which pervades all places, whether material or non-material; it is also like empty space."
Because space contains all phenomena and is as vast as the atoms of a buddha-field, such that it cannot be known by calculation, it is said: "How could it be exhausted by counting?
The subsequent phrase, "entering subtly into the interstices," means entering the minute realm of a single speck of dust; thus the following scripture says:
"Just as one sees the Buddha seated in this assembly, so it is in every atom; within each atom there are worlds, and within those worlds there are further lands."

Furthermore, there are dust motes within dust motes and lands within lands, infinitely layered and inexhaustible; because this is not an object of mental consciousness or discursive thought, it transcends the realm of names and words.

It is difficult to describe through names and words, for the path of language is severed. Since the names and words that express the manifested realm do not know it, the movements of the mind are extinguished therein.
This also clarifies that the scope of the transformation is pervasive and subtle; the preceding phrase indicated that the transformation pervades the Dharma-realm.

The latter phrase describes subtlety: the *Anupraveśa-sūtra* states that "upon each and every tip of a hair, one can contain boundless worlds without obstruction, manifesting to tame immeasurable sentient beings."
▲ "Is there anyone who, lacking virtue, yet receives praise? It must be the Great Awakened One (the Tathāgata).
'Lacking virtue, yet receiving praise'—the following four lines conclude that these virtues are attributed to the Tathāgata, meaning that the three preceding sections all pertain to the Tathāgata;
thus, one praises him as being beyond full description. As the *Analects* says: 'Tàibó may indeed be called one of supreme virtue. (3)

When he yielded the world to the people, there was no virtue by which they could praise him; thus, the Sūtra says: "The thoughts in the minds of beings as numerous as the atoms of all lands may be counted;
the water in the great oceans may be drunk up; empty space may be measured; and the wind may be bound.
But none can fully describe the merits of the Buddha"—this is precisely what that refers to.

▲ In a former kalpa, I planted the causes for this merit and was humbly granted the Buddha’s prophecy. The Golden Immortal descended with his decree, and the verses of the *Mahāmegha* first manifested before my imperial throne;
the texts of the "Jewel Rain" subsequently reached me as auspicious signs.

I, the Emperor, formerly planted the causes for three kalpas; now, celebrating that I have encountered this auspicious time, I divide this into three parts: first, the distant reception of the Buddha’s prophecy; second, the profound gratitude for the Great Peace;

and third, the myriad nations paying court as tributaries. Regarding the first: "I, the Emperor, formerly planted the causes for three kalpas" means that because the causes were sown long ago, I was able to receive the personal prophecy of the Great Awakened One.
"Tao" (叨) signifies being unworthy or receiving by grace. From the phrase "descending from the Golden Immortal," the specific characteristics of the prophecy are clarified. First: [the prophecy].
Regarding the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, some have doubted its authenticity. Later, under the "Jade Screen" (Yù yǐ) section, the *Ratnavarṣa-sūtra* was mentioned;
Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Zhouli* states that a *fáng* refers to a screen (*píngfēng*), and that the Emperor’s screen was adorned with jade.
Furthermore, the first fascicle of the *Kāiyuán zhèngyuán* states: "At that time, there was a deva from the east..."
The son, named Candrasūryavimalaprabha, arrived at the place where the Buddha was riding upon a five-colored cloud;
he circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha addressed the devaputra: "Your radiance is truly rare.
Devaputra, in the past, at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas, you have already offered various kinds of incense, flowers, and precious jewels as adornments."
"O Devaputra, you who possess robes, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal requisites, and who have planted various roots of goodness by means of respectful offerings—
by virtue of the causes and conditions of the immeasurable roots of goodness you planted in the past, you now obtain such radiant and brilliant light.
Devaputra, for this reason, five hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, during the fourth period of five hundred years, the Dharma will be on the verge of extinction."
At that time, you shall be in this Jambudvīpa, in the land of Mahācīna in the northeast;
dwelling in the stage of *avaivartika*, you are in truth a bodhisattva who manifests in the form of a woman as a sovereign ruler.

Having passed many years, you shall transform and guide sentient beings through the True Dharma, nurturing them like an only child, and cause them to cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action within my teaching.
He extensively maintained and established stupas and monasteries, and further provided robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal supplies to support the śramaṇas;
at all times he constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya). He was named Sūryacandraprabha-vimala.

As for the remainder, it is explained according to that sūtra. The commentary states: "At this time, there was no female ruler to propagate and establish [the Dharma]; if these words are not false, then [it must be so]."

Furthermore, through the accumulated blessings of past goodness, a subtle grace has descended upon this humble person, whereby the earth is level and the heavens are perfected, the rivers are clear and the seas are tranquil.
This is because, as stated in the *Book of Changes*, "In a family that accumulates goodness, there will surely be an abundance of blessings. Thus, we now enjoy the peace of the Great Tranquility.

"In the house where non-virtue has accumulated, there will surely be lingering calamities; now, because of the accumulation of goodness, the earth is level and the heavens are perfected, the rivers are clear and the seas are tranquil—'yan' (晏) meaning 'peaceful.
Auspicious omens and extraordinary portents arrive daily and are recorded monthly; divine texts and sacred writings likewise reach us seasonally and annually."

Reaching across the seas and beyond the deserts, the rites of presenting rare treasures were fully prepared; traversing perilous heights and navigating deep waters, the words of successive translations were exhaustedly conveyed.

Extraordinary portents and supreme auspicious omens descended upon the land, as the myriad nations of the three myriads of worlds came to pay court and offer tribute through successive translations; these two initial pairs stand as the foremost markers.
That is to say, as the myriad regions look up in admiration of his virtue, extraordinary portents and rare auspicious responses arrive day after day and are recorded month after month;
these are inscribed in the historical annals. Furthermore, sacred texts upon shell-leaf tablets also arrive from time to time, providing continuous nourishment year after year.
[The first pair] refers to the auspicious signs arriving from above the sea, while the latter pair explains the subsequent construction.
Descending precipices and ascending heights, crossing over jade tablets and reaching distant harmonies—traversing the sea and navigating the deep are all journeys by water;
crossing the deserts and spanning the perils are all journeys by land.
This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Flower Ornament Scripture of the Buddha, is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and the nature of the Tathāgatas.
Those who gaze upon it cannot discern its destination; those who draw from it rarely fathom its limits.
In the fourth section of the *Mahāvaipulya*, there is a specific praise for the profound and subtle purport of this scripture. This section is divided into two parts:

first, a general praise, and second, a specific praise. Regarding the first, there are two lines that mark its depth and breadth, followed by the passage beginning with "Those who gaze upon it," which establishes [the point].

Since the first two lines constitute the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*), it is said that one cannot see it; thus it is called the Ocean of Nature (*dharmatā-samudra*). Its boundaries and shores are unfathomable.
Regarding the term "to draw" (*yi*), the *Zhuzong lun* states that it refers to measuring water with a vessel. Thus, the "Stele of the Dhūta Monastery" in the *Wenxuan* says:
"I have heard that those who draw from the pond of morning and evening have no means to fathom its depth; they look up at the azure heavens..."
Because the color [of the Buddha] is difficult to know in its distance or proximity, our current measurements are like peering at the heavens through a tube or fathoming the ocean with a clam shell.
Those with or without training who have severed the desire for mere observation, as well as those of the Two Vehicles and Three Vehicles, how could they not hope to hear and receive [this teaching]?

The second section, "Specific Praise," following the general praise for those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), consists of three parts: first, praise by way of persons; second, praise by way of dharmas;

and third, praise by way of locations. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, manifesting superiority in contrast to inferiority; second, manifesting superiority through the essential nature itself.

Regarding the first of these, the initial phrase speaks generally of the three vehicles, while the subsequent phrase speaks specifically of the three vehicles. However, as for the two vehicles [the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*] being present in the assembly...
"Deaf as if blind" means that Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles cannot fathom it despite accumulating practices over many kalpas;
"to peer" (*kuī*) is as stated in the *Zuǒzhuan*, meaning to look up while lifting one's feet; "to covet" (*yù*) is as stated in the *Zhūcóng*, meaning to harbor expectations.

The traces of the most supreme wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) being magnificently adorned are already flourishing; thus, the causes of the vow-practices of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī are fulfilled.

Regarding the phrase "the most supreme wisdom of all modes," the latter two [phrases] manifest its excellence through its essential nature, while the preceding sentence describes the fulfillment of the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*) by way of the perfection of the fruit.
"Attaining the Wisdom of All Modes" refers to the fulfillment of the causes: the practice of Samantabhadra and the vow of Mañjuśrī; both are perfected.
Thus, it is also possible for both practice and vow to apply to these two sages.
Within a single phrase, the boundlessness of the Dharma-realm is encompassed; within a single hair’s breadth, a Buddha-land is placed without being cramped.
In the first phrase, the latter two lines praise the Dharma in terms of its content, while the preceding line praises the profound and vast nature of the expressive medium.
Therefore, the meaning of a single phrase could not be exhausted even by using as much ink as there is water in the ocean;
yet the subsequent phrase summarizes the principle that all phenomena are mutually unimpeded (*shishi wuai*), such that a world-system can be placed within a single hair-tip without it being cramped.

▲In the Kingdom of Magadha, the conditions for the inaugural emergence of this wondrous assembly were met; thus, in the Hall of Universal Radiance, the principle of quiescent extinction was expounded.
[The phrase] "In the Kingdom of Magadha" is the third section, which praises and cites the location; it mentions "Magadha" because it is the locus of the nine assemblies.
Because he arose at the site of enlightenment and pervaded everywhere, the mention of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*) brings one close to the field of bodhi;
furthermore, because it is said that the gate of faith encompasses the ocean of fruition, it is stated: "Thus he unfolds the principle of quiescent extinction."
Reflecting upon these profound meanings, their translation dates back to the Jin dynasty; over six dynasties have passed and nearly four hundred years elapsed.
Yet, of this single canonical work, only some thirty thousand words have been obtained—merely opening half a pearl, without yet exhausting the entirety of its treasure.
Reflecting deeply upon the profound meaning, this is the fifth section on the successive translations throughout antiquity and the present, expressing the joy of encountering [this teaching].

Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying that previous translations were largely deficient; second, clarifying that the current translation is largely complete. Regarding the first: "Mian" (緬) means distant; "wei" (惟) means to contemplate.
The "six dynasties" refers to the Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, and Sui. This states that [in the past] one had merely opened half of a pearl, yet had not yet fully beheld it.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Noble Practice of Nirvāṇa" in the *Sarvaratna*, it is said that when the Snowy Mountain Youth heard the transformed rākṣasa say, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they are dharmas of arising and ceasing," he was startled and looked around. Seeing only the rākṣasa, he asked him:
"Great Being, where did you obtain this half-verse spoken by the one who was free from fear in the past?"
