these are also the Buddha’s assemblies, as the Buddha is the principal figure. From the section beginning with Mañjuśrī up to the point where [the Buddha] reaches the eastern side of Puṇyavatī, all subsequent sections are the secondary assemblies.
Furthermore, because these assemblies of Bodhisattvas take various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) as their presiding leaders, there are two parts:

first, within the preceding section, there are two sub-sections—the first eight assemblies clarify the practices of understanding and conduct (*adhimukti-caryā*) that are accomplished, while the final one reveals the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that is realized. Third, within the preceding [of those two], there are again two parts:

the first seven assemblies clarify the practices cultivated through successive stages (*bhūmi*), while the final one clarifies the practice of perfect interpenetration and universal pervasion. Fourth, the preceding...

Within the middle [section], there are again two parts: first, the explanation of the causes and fruits of the developmental stage (*utpattikrama*); second, from "Samantabhadra" onwards in the next two chapters, the explanation of the causes and fruits of the completion stage (*sampannakrama*).

Regarding the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the explanation of the causes for the developmental stage; second, from "The Inconceivable Dharma" (*Acintyadharmatā*) onwards in the three subsequent chapters, the explanation of the fruits of the developmental stage.

Regarding the first of these, there are again two parts: first, the explanation of the causal practices within the stages (*bhūmi*); second, from "The Ten Samādhis" (*Daśaniṣṭhā*) onwards in the six subsequent chapters, the explanation of...

Regarding the practices subsequent to the stages (*bhūmi*), there are seven; following the previous [section], there are two more: first, the practices of analogy prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva-anvaya-pratipatti*) are clarified;

subsequently, the sixth assembly clarifies the practices of realization within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi-sākṣātkāra-pratipatti*). Regarding the latter, there are also two: first, the practices of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) prior to the stages;

subsequently, from the third assembly onwards, three assemblies clarify the practices of the three types of worthies (*tri-kalyāṇaka*) who have entered the stages. Regarding the ninth, there are also two: first, the Buddha who is the object of faith is clarified.

Regarding the "Fruit Dharmas," the latter part of the "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications" consists of three sections that clarify the fruits of the Bodhisattva’s practice—the basis upon which one relies and the faith by which one believes.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the initial assembly clarifies the fruit of the Buddha’s *āśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment); second, from the section on "Names and Epithets" onwards, the three subsequent sections clarify the fruit of the Buddha’s *samyak-vipāka* (retributive body).
Regarding the fourth section, the "Reciprocal Subsumption of the Antecedent and Subsequent," although there are ten stages, they are collectively divided into two parts.

By subsuming from the end backward and excluding the subsequent stage at each step, one proceeds to divide the preceding stage into two. Thus, in the initial position, the forty-two stages clarify the meaning;

since the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) have not yet been established as formal stages, they serve merely as the causes for abiding. Therefore, the *Ratnaketu-dharani* (Renwang jing) designates the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) as the ten levels of faith.
Therefore, because it takes that which can accomplish faith as the designation for the abiding accomplished thereby.
Section Five: The Interlocking Chain of Before and After is also divided into ten parts.
Regarding "the five before and after," etc., this refers to the new interpretation; within the text, there are two sections: first, the indication of the number, and second, the formal explanation.

▲ First, the first assembly constitutes the cause and fruit of the *paratantra* (environmental) retribution: the fruit of environmental retribution was clarified previously, while the "Vairocana" chapter subsequently distinguishes its causes.
Second, taking the "Vairocana" chapter along with the first three chapters of the second assembly as the cause and fruit of the *sambhogakāya* (physical) retribution:
the cause is presented first, followed by the fruit. Third, from the "Names and Epithets" up to the "Bodhisattva Abodes," these constitute the cause and fruit of the arising of the environment.

Because they are cultivated and established based on what is originally possessed, there is the sequence of prior effect and subsequent cause; from the "Chapter on the Clarification of Questions" through the "Chapter on the Minor Marks," the distinctions between cause and effect are clarified, showing the sequence of prior cause and subsequent effect.
First, the second part of the first assembly: the formal explanation. This is divided into three sections: first, a general explanation of the preceding four [sections];

second, a specific explanation of the fifth; and third, a general explanation of the final five. Now, for the first: the text contains ten sections, namely: (1) the first five chapters at the beginning of the sutra;
(2) the three chapters on the names and titles following the Vairocana chapter; (3) the fourth, the Questions on Illumination (*Prajñāparipṛcchā*); and so forth.
The first section consists of twenty-three chapters from the "Abiding" chapter to the "Inconceivable" chapter;

the second section consists of three chapters from the "Marks and Subtle Features" chapter to the "Universal Worthy’s Practices" chapter; the third section is the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter;
the fourth section is the "Transcending the World" chapter; and the fifth section is the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter. These constitute the initial [division].
Although they are not treated as separate layers later on, there should actually be eight layers of cause and effect;
since the ninth chapter, "On Transcending the World," and the tenth chapter, "On the Dharma-realm," each constitute a distinct layer of cause and effect, they together form ten.

▲ From "The Five Appropriations are Inconceivable" down to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Practices" constitutes the section on the Perfectly Interfused Cause and Effect, wherein the effect precedes the cause.

Regarding the two distinct explanations from "The Five Appropriations are Inconceivable" downward, the fifth section is divided into four parts: first, the direct explanation; second... [text truncated]
This consists of four parts: (1) explaining the obstacles, (2) citing three proofs, (3) concluding, and (4) the actual present exposition.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the inconceivable," etc.: when contrasted with what precedes it as a fruit-of-fruits, it is distinct from the cause; when compared with what follows it as a fruit, each [aspect] is mutually inclusive and harmonized.
The two subsequent sections below resolve the objection regarding the inconceivable. This means that there may be a question:

"Since the two meanings of differentiation and perfect fusion are not one and the same, how can the previously mentioned fruit of differentiation become the fruit of perfect fusion? Therefore, the general intent is explained as follows:

although the scriptural passage beginning with "inconceivable" refers to a single principle, it is viewed from different perspectives; thus, while the fruit is distinct from the cause, it establishes differentiation within the cause.
The fruits and fruits themselves are perfectly interfused, thereby accomplishing the fruit of perfect interfusion.

"Perfectly interfused" means that each and every virtue pervades the Dharma-realm; for within each of the thirty-six gates, ten phrases are contained, and because the characteristics thus explained are difficult to fathom, the title of this chapter is designated as "Inconceivable."
▲ However, there are six points that establish this proof.

Regarding the phrase "However, there are six points," the following three citations of evidence establish that the three chapters beginning with "Inconceivable" (*acintya*) constitute the fruit of the conduct of Samantabhadra (*samantabhadracaryā-phala*),
while the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" constitutes the cause (*hetu*) for "Inconceivable" and the others.
In the section on the "Mutual Relation between Cause and Effect," causes are generally presented after effects.
Regarding this mutual relation of cause and effect, within the five cycles of cause and effect that constitute the object of faith and the point of entry, the two fruits are placed first;
furthermore, because a fruit also exists prior to the specific causes, it is said that "causes are mostly preceded by fruits. Here, too, the fruit is presented first and the cause follows.

This is the same as the previous example. As for the section on "the mutual connection of cause and effect," it refers to the third section from the preceding part, "classifying the text according to its meaning";
that is to say, because five sections are established by classifying them according to the meaning of the mutual connection between cause and effect.
Regarding the phrase "after the second, fourth, and eighth," there is no subsequent proof for the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s conduct; rather, any subsequent proof belongs to what precedes it.
As for the phrase "the second, fourth, and eighth, etc.," from the inconceivable up to the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), these belong exclusively to the fruit of differentiation.
Since the causes and effects have already concluded, there ought to be a manifested omen to certify their fulfillment; yet now there is no such certification.
Since the "Chapter on the Practice of Samantabhadra" belongs solely to the causes for manifestation, and since the fruit has not yet been described, how could there be a certification?
It is known that the conclusion of the certification belongs to what preceded it—the "Inconceivable" chapter and so forth.

Regarding the statement "At the beginning of the 'Chapter on the Universal Worthy Conduct' (Samantabhadra-caryā-pratipatti-paṭala), there is no separate introductory section, and it immediately follows upon the preceding [chapter] because it briefly indicates a small portion of the Tathāgata’s realm":
if the phrase "At the beginning of the Chapter on the Universal Worthy Conduct" and so forth did not belong to the start of this chapter, it would have had to exist separately.
Therefore, since there is no initiation for what has already arisen, it is clear that this belongs to the preceding section.
Fourth, to clarify this through its meaning: the inconceivable Dharma reveals the Buddha’s virtues as being difficult to fathom, for each and every one is perfectly interfused.
Fourth, regarding "equal in meaning" (*artha-samatā*): because the merit of the fruit is inconceivable, it cannot be regarded merely as a differentiated fruit.
Fifth, although there was a question previously, it was asked again at the beginning of the *Acintya-parivarta* (Chapter on the Inconceivable).

Although the question regarding "existence" and so forth was already asked previously, it is asked again at the beginning of the second assembly because it is intended to reveal that the "inconceivable" and "beyond thought" which follow are the starting point of the perfectly integrated cause and effect.
Sixth, because at the beginning of the second assembly there are already three types of karma as differentiated fruits.
Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of the second assembly," etc.: if there were no fruits previously, then [terms such as] "inconceivable" would have to serve as differentiated fruits;
since these inconceivable elements already exist previously, they belong entirely to the subsequent section, while the preceding segment constitutes the differentiation.
The four fruits are also sufficient.
Because of these six meanings, the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" is connected to the preceding causes.
By virtue of these six meanings, the following four sections establish the fifth [section], which is the perfect interfusion of cause and fruit.

▲ The sixth [section] takes the "Universal Good Conduct" (Samantabhadra-caryā) and the "Manifestation" (Prādurbhāva) chapters as the equality of cause and effect, with the former being the cause and the latter the effect.
From the sixth section, "Having taken up the Universal Good Conduct," the following three sections collectively explain the latter five [chapters].

The seventh chapter, "The Manifestation and Transcendence of the World," treats manifestation as cause and effect; because the prior fruit and subsequent cause, as well as the attainment of Buddhahood and nirvana, are manifested through causes, this is not said to be the ultimate realization.
Regarding the phrase "attaining Buddhahood and entering nirvāṇa," this serves to preclude external objections. For one might raise the objection:

"Since the 'Chapter on Transcending the World' possesses its own causes and effects, how can it be considered the general cause for the manifestation [of the Buddha]? Therefore, this passage provides the resolution.
It is precisely by taking detachment from the world as the cause that one is able to manifest in the world;
thus, the subsequent explanation of "detachment from the world" carries the meaning of being the cause for manifestation.
The eighth chapter, "Detachment from the World," serves to establish the causes and effects of practice by comprehensively discussing practice itself, as it encompasses both cause and effect.
Regarding the eighth [point], "Transcending the World" (*lokottara*) and so forth: it will naturally establish itself as cause and effect within this assembly.
Regarding the ninth, taking the "Chapter on Transcending the World" and the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātu*) as the cause and effect of the Dharma Realm:

because the former is the cause and the latter is the result, and because they are called the "Dharma Realm" by virtue of transcending the world, the cause does not depend on sequential stages, whereas the result is solely the realization and entry [into that realm].
Ninth, the two assemblies are combined as a single cause-and-effect;
tenth, within each stage of the ten dharma realms, there is an independent realization of cause-and-effect where the result precedes the cause.

Regarding the section beginning with Sudhana, these also constitute an inexhaustible cause-and-effect where the cause precedes the result; thus, by attending upon the [Bodhisattvas] one after another until reaching Samantabhadra, one reaches the cause of a single pore.
Furthermore, because the inexhaustible Samantabhadra speaks of the Buddha’s virtues as exceeding the void, and because the fruit is likewise inexhaustible for the sake of universal circulation,

these are not explained here. Tenth, while the entry into the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) should, in this assembly, constitute the completion of cause and effect, although the eighth assembly does not explicitly link back to the preceding [sections], [the connection is nonetheless established].
The previous "Chapter on Manifestation" already linked this tenth [chapter] as cause to the eighth assembly, while the eighth assembly already linked it to the ninth;

therefore, they are all termed "linked causes and effects. This is because Sudhana’s successive acts of service constitute the cause, and Samantabhadra’s exposition of the Buddha’s virtues constitutes the effect.
Regarding the structural outline (*pinda-vibhāga*) of the *Ṣaḍvargika-vastu* within the *Dīrgha-varga*:
the *Dīrgha-varga* consists of ten sections. As for the structural outline of the *Ṣaḍvargika-vastu*, it does not combine with the *Saṃyukta-varga*;
rather, it outlines the thirty-nine chapters directly as ten sections.
The first section, "A General Exposition on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching," has two parts.

The second part, "The Section Clarifying the Boundless Great Function of the Buddha-Fruit" (beginning from the "Manifestation of Signs" chapter), clarifies the boundless great function of the Buddha-Fruit; within this, the "Manifestation of Signs" chapter concerns the great function.
The meaning can be understood as follows: regarding the "great function" of Samantabhadra’s samādhi, it refers to the simultaneous empowerment by Samantabhadra such that he arrives without coming;
because there is no obstruction between the one and the many, or between extension and contraction; because the light from a single pore praises his virtues so that they reach everywhere;

and because the accomplishment of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha) describes how the Tathāgata pervades the pure Dharma-realm and universally responds to the ocean of lands, causing the environment and its inhabitants to interpenetrate within every atom.
The inclusion of the entire dharma-realm is the boundlessly great function.
The third chapter, "Vairocana," presents the causes for that abiding and establishes the fourth division, titled "Names.

The subsequent three chapters clarify the great function responding to capacities and pervading everywhere. From the fifth chapter, "Questions on Clarity," down to the end of the tenth chapter, "The Ten Grounds," the various stages are elucidated.
Section Seven: The Section on the Perfection of the Cause and the Fulfillment of the Result, from the end of the "Chapter on the Sixty Samādhis" down to the end of the "Chapter on the Minor Marks.
Section Eight: The Section on the Manifestation of the Result through the Accomplishment of Universal Practice, comprising the final two chapters from the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra.

Section Nine: The Section on the Transcendence of Cause and Effect beyond the World, as clarified in the "Chapter on Leaving the World. Within the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm," the preceding section clarifies [the nature of the Dharma Realm].

The Great Assembly’s Sudden Realization of the Dharma Realm, divided into ten sections; at this point, Mañjuśrī descends to clarify the section on the gradual realization through successive stages by a single individual.
Regarding the seven divisions according to their original assemblies, these are also divided into ten parts: the first assembly is titled "Holding up the Fruit to Inspire Faith."
Part Two: The Second Assembly, Clarifying the Section on Accomplishing Virtues through Faith; Part Three: The Third Assembly, the Initial Section on the Ten Abodes of the Worthy (*Śrāvaka-bhūmi*);
Part Four: The Fourth Assembly, the Middle Section on the Ten Practices of the Worthy; Part Five: The Fifth Assembly, the Upper Section on the Ten Transferences of the Worthy; Part Six:

The Sixth Assembly, the Section on the Ten Stages of the Noble (*Ārya-bhūmi*); Part Seven: The Seventh Assembly, the Section on the Perfection of Causes and the Fulfillment of the Fruit; Part Eight: The Eighth Assembly.
The Ninth Assembly of the *Samantabhadra-mahācaryā-vibhāga*, Part One: The Section on Initial Practice, Accomplished Practice, and Realization-Entry; Part Ten:
The Section on the Teaching and Realization of the Benevolent Friends by Sudhana.
Regarding these ten sections of Sudhana’s journey, according to the headings, each assembly is divided into its respective parts, thus forming [the structure].

The nine divisions are intended to manifest the perfection of ten; thus, the final one is expanded. According to reality, there should be ten assemblies to symbolize perfection, though perhaps the scripture has not yet been fully transmitted, so for now I shall explain it according to the extant text.
Regarding the eighth section, the "Great Positions of Root and Branch": the root assembly constitutes nine, while the branch assemblies number fifty-five, totaling [sixty-four].
Sixty-four sections.
Regarding the "Section on the Comprehensive Collection of the Nine Originals and Their Branches": first, the nine assemblies constitute nine sections;

the teaching of Mañjuśrī to six thousand bhikṣus constitutes the tenth section; and the journey of Sudhana through one hundred and ten spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) constitutes the total [eleventh] section.
If one divides the [text] into one hundred and twenty sections, including the assemblies of the various nāgas and the three vehicles,
as well as the passage concerning Maitreya and the subsequent section on the three bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and [Maitreya], it totals one hundred and twenty-five. Since Maitreya says,
"This son of a householder has already passed through one hundred and ten spiritual friends before coming to me," this must refer to the period prior to Maitreya.
Since there are already one hundred and ten, and the number of virtuous friends is as vast as the atoms in a trichiliocosm, their proportion is even greater;
if these were combined into a single unit, it would constitute one hundred and twenty-six parts.
If one were to open up the assemblies of the various nāgas by dividing them into one hundred and twenty sections, then all three vehicles of the nāgas would belong to the *Sudhana-parivarta*.
This is because the initial arrival at Puṇyavatī was originally for the sake of Sudhana; therefore, the assemblies of the various vehicles and so forth are not separately opened.
Now, although they have reached Puṇyavatī, within the city, the two thousand four hundred members of the assembly, including Sudhana and others, have not yet [arrived].
Upon exiting the city, he first preached the *Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm* to benefit the various dragons and those of the Three Vehicles;
thus, it is distinguished from the rest, the details of which may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the tenth section, "The Infinite Interdependence of Principal and Retinue," each assembly, each chapter, and each teaching is universally connected.
In the ten directions, as it is spoken here, so it is spoken throughout the empty space of the dharma-realm in all worlds, even within every single atom;
this constitutes the "Principal" (the main assembly). Furthermore, in each and every assembly, there are bodhisattvas from other lands, as numerous as atoms, who come to witness the Dharma;
this constitutes the "Associates. Thus, the Principal and the Associates together pervade everywhere.
The dharma-realm is layered and inexhaustible; thus, its divisions and sections are likewise inexhaustible and infinite.
*Commentary on the Explication of the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
